A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. When two keys produce the same integer, they land in the same bucket. That is a collision, and the map needs a rule for storing both.

The oldest rule is chaining. Each bucket holds a pointer to a linked list. On insert, the map appends the new key-value pair to that list. On lookup, it walks the list and compares keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The cost is linear in the number of entries sharing one bucket. If the hash function spreads keys evenly and the load factor stays below one, the average list length is one, and a lookup touches a single node. If the function clusters keys, one bucket grows long and lookups degrade toward a full scan.

Open addressing skips the linked list. Every entry lives in the array itself. On insert, the map computes the bucket index, and if that slot is occupied, it probes another slot according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the probe count. Double hashing computes a second hash to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed stride. Lookup follows the same probe sequence and stops when it finds the key or an empty slot.

Open addressing is cache-friendly because the entries sit in a contiguous array and probing touches nearby memory. It fails when the table fills: a 90-percent-full table forces long probe chains, and a full table cannot accept new entries at all. Chaining tolerates a load factor above one without breaking, because the lists grow to whatever length the collisions produce, but it pays for every list node with a separate allocation and a pointer chase on every access.

Both schemes depend on the hash function. A function that distributes keys uniformly across buckets keeps chains short and probe sequences short. A function that biases toward a narrow range of indices concentrates entries in a few buckets, and the map's performance collapses toward that of a list. Most production hash maps combine a mixing step with the table lookup to break up patterns in the input keys, so that similar keys do not cluster under the same index.

When the load factor crosses a threshold, the map resizes. It allocates a larger array, typically twice the size, and reinserts every entry by recomputing its bucket index against the new array length. This is an O(n) operation, but it amortizes to constant time per insert across a sequence of operations, because each resize is followed by enough inserts at the new load factor to pay for it. Resizing also gives clustered entries a chance to spread across the larger table, which shortens probe chains and list lengths until the next wave of inserts fills the table again.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row. The most common form is a B-tree, which keeps a sorted list of column values paired with pointers to the rows that hold them. A query against a million-row table for `users.email = 'x@y.com'` reads a few B-tree pages — perhaps four or five disk reads — instead of reading all million rows. The index trades space and write cost for read speed.

The cost is real. Every index adds storage: an index on a 40 GB table might occupy 8 GB more. Every insert, update, and delete that touches an indexed column must update the index too, so a table with five indexes takes roughly six times longer to write a row than a table with none. The database does not get this for free; it does the work at commit time.

An index hurts when the query cannot use it, or when the index serves a query that did not need help. A query like `WHERE lower(email) = 'x@y.com'` cannot use a plain index on `email`, because the function breaks the sort order — the index is dead weight for that query, and the planner falls back to a full scan. A function-based index on `lower(email)` fixes that, but only for that specific query shape.

Multi-column indexes carry an ordering constraint. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name`, or both columns, but not a query that filters on `first_name` alone, because the index is sorted by `last_name` first and `first_name` is unordered within it. Adding an index that looks comprehensive but serves no actual query pattern wastes write throughput on every insert.

The planner can also choose wrongly. A low-cardinality index on a boolean `is_active` column, where 95 percent of rows are true, returns almost the whole table. The planner recognizes this and skips the index, but the index still costs writes. A selective index — one that narrows a million rows to a hundred — earns its keep. One that narrows a million rows to 950,000 does not.

Indexes on columns that change often are the worst trade. A `updated_at` column touched by every write forces the B-tree to rebalance on every transaction, moving pages and splitting nodes. An index on a stable column like `created_at` pays its write cost once and serves reads for the life of the row.

The decision is mechanical. An index helps when it serves a query the application actually runs, when it narrows the result set sharply, and when the read frequency outweighs the write cost. It hurts when it serves no query, when it returns most of the table, or when the column changes so often that the maintenance cost exceeds the read savings. Dropping an unused index is the cheapest performance win available, because it removes write overhead and asks nothing in return.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a series of messages. The sender attaches a sequence number to every byte it transmits. That number is not a packet counter; it is an offset into the byte stream, and it tells the receiver where each byte belongs in the original order.

The receiver collects these bytes and places them in a receive buffer. Bytes may arrive out of order because IP routes packets independently, and a later packet can overtake an earlier one across different network paths. The receiver uses the sequence numbers to slot each byte into its correct position. If bytes 1 through 100 arrive, then bytes 201 through 300, the receiver holds the 200-range in the buffer and waits for 101 through 200 to fill the gap.

The receiver acknowledges received data. An ACK carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects, not the last byte it received. If the receiver has bytes 1 through 100 and 201 through 300, it sends ACK 101. That single number tells the sender everything up to 100 arrived in order, and everything from 101 onward is still missing.

The sender maintains a send window. Bytes inside the window have been sent but not yet acknowledged. When an ACK arrives, the window slides forward. If the sender transmits bytes 1 through 500 and receives ACK 101, it knows bytes 1 through 100 are safe and can discard their copies from its retransmission buffer.

A gap in the acknowledgements triggers retransmission. The sender runs a timer for every unacknowledged byte. If the timer expires before an ACK arrives, the sender retransmits the byte. TCP also uses duplicate ACKs as a faster signal: if the receiver gets byte 101 again because 201 through 300 were retransmitted out of order, it sends ACK 101 a second time, because 101 is still the next byte it expects. Three duplicate ACKs for the same sequence number tell the sender that a specific byte was lost, and it retransmits that byte without waiting for the timer.

The receiver hands data to the application only in order. Bytes 201 through 300 sitting in the buffer are useless to the application until 101 through 200 arrive. Once the gap fills, the receiver delivers the contiguous run to the application and sends a single ACK for the next expected byte after the run. The application never sees reordering, because the buffer absorbs it.

The sequence number space is finite. A 32-bit field counts roughly 4.3 billion bytes, which a high-speed link can exhaust in seconds. TCP handles this with window scaling, which extends the field, and with PAWS, a timestamp option that lets the receiver distinguish a new byte 1 from an old byte 1 still circulating in the network. Without PAWS, a delayed packet from one connection could land in a later connection carrying the same sequence number, and the receiver would place it in the wrong position.

A mutex protects one thing: the invariant a thread needs while it reads or writes shared state. Without it, two threads that touch the same memory at the same time produce a state neither intended.

Consider a counter incremented by two threads. The increment is three steps: read the current value into a register, add one, write it back. Thread A reads 5. Thread B reads 5 before A writes. A writes 6. B writes 6. Two increments produced one. The counter lost an update because the read-modify-write sequence was not atomic.

A mutex makes it atomic. A thread that needs the shared variable calls `lock` on the mutex first. The mutex is a flag with a queue: only one thread holds it at a time, and the operating system parks the others. While A holds the lock, B's call to `lock` blocks — the kernel suspends B until A calls `unlock`. The read-modify-write sequence runs to completion before the second thread enters it. The counter reaches 7.

The mutex protects against interleaving. It does not protect against anything else. It does not make a data structure thread-safe by existing; it makes it thread-safe if every thread that touches the structure locks the same mutex first. A thread that bypasses the lock and writes directly corrupts the state, because the mutex has no power over code that ignores it. The protection is a contract, not a force field.

The mutex also protects against compiler and hardware reordering. A thread that writes `data[i] = x` and then sets `ready = true` under a lock forces both writes to become visible to a second thread that locks the same mutex before reading `ready`. Without the lock, the CPU may reorder the stores, and the second thread sees `ready == true` while `data[i]` still holds garbage. The mutex inserts memory barriers that constrain the hardware to the order the code specifies.

A mutex protects against deadlock if used with discipline, but it can also cause it. Thread A locks mutex 1 then waits for mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then waits for mutex 1. Both sleep forever. The fix is an ordering rule: every thread acquires the mutexes in the same sequence, so the lock graph never forms a cycle.

The cost is contention. When three threads want the same mutex, two sleep while one works. The lock serializes the parallel section, and the program's throughput on that section drops to single-thread speed. A mutex held for a microsecond across a thousand calls per second costs a millisecond of stalled threads per second. The remedy is to hold the lock for the shortest scope that preserves the invariant — lock, touch the shared variable, unlock — and to do no I/O, no allocation, no computation that does not need the protection while holding it.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. A running program holds references to objects through variables, fields, and the call stack. An object is reachable if some chain of references connects it to a root: a local variable, a static field, a CPU register. An object is garbage if no such chain exists. The collector's job is to tell the two apart and reclaim the garbage.

The mark-and-sweep algorithm walks that chain. It starts from the roots and traces every reference it can follow, marking each object it visits. When the trace stops, every marked object is reachable, and every unmarked object is not. The collector then sweeps the heap: it walks every allocated object, frees the unmarked ones, and clears the marks on the rest. The live objects stay where they are; the dead ones become free space.

Mark-and-sweep leaves holes. Freeing objects in the middle of the heap creates fragments of free space scattered among live objects. A program that allocates a ten-megabyte array may fail even when the heap holds twenty megabytes free, because no single gap is large enough. Compacting collectors solve this by moving the live objects together, sliding them toward one end of the heap and leaving a single contiguous free region behind. The collector must update every reference it moves, because the object's address changed. That work is expensive but it defeats fragmentation.

Generational collectors exploit one observation: most objects die young. A function that builds a temporary string or a scratch list discards it the moment it returns. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. New allocations go into the young space, which the collector scans frequently. Most of those objects are already dead, so the scan reclaims them cheaply. Objects that survive several young-generation scans earn a promotion to the old generation, which the collector scans rarely.

The pause is the cost. While the collector traces and sweeps, the application threads stop. A mark-and-sweep pass over a four-gigabyte heap can freeze the program for tens of milliseconds. Concurrent collectors reduce this by tracing the heap while the application runs, but they pay for concurrency with higher CPU overhead and the risk of missing a reference that changed mid-trace. Incremental collectors break the pause into smaller slices, trading one long freeze for several short ones.

Reference counting is a different approach that reclaims memory the instant the last reference drops. Each object carries a counter incremented when a reference is copied and decremented when one is destroyed. When the counter hits zero, the object is freed. This avoids a tracing pause, but it cannot handle cycles: two objects that reference each other keep both counters above zero forever, even when nothing else reaches them. A cycle collector must run periodically to find and break those loops. Reference counting also pays a cost on every assignment, because copying a pointer means updating a counter, and that overhead lands on hot paths where a tracing collector would do nothing.

The collector does not know what the program means by an object. It knows only what the program can reach. An object that holds a ten-megabyte buffer but is never read again stays alive as long as one reference to it remains, because the collector sees the reference and marks the object. Memory leaks in garbage-collected languages are references the program forgot to clear, not allocations the program forgot to free. The collector reclaims exactly what the program cannot reach, and nothing more.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on which thread reaches a line of code first. Two threads share state. The scheduler interleaves their steps in an order the programmer did not plan for. The program computes a wrong value, and the wrong value is not random — it is the product of a specific, repeatable interleaving that the test suite happened not to trigger.

A bank account holds a balance of 100. Two threads each withdraw 60. The code reads the balance, subtracts 60, and writes the result back. Thread A reads 100. Thread B reads 100 before A writes. A writes 40. B writes 40. Two withdrawals of 60 produced a final balance of 40 on an account that should hold negative 20. The bank lost 60. The invariant — balance equals the sum of deposits minus withdrawals — broke because the read and the write were not one operation.

The bug hides. Run the code a thousand times and the scheduler interleaves the threads differently each time. Nine hundred runs produce 40. Ninety runs produce negative 20, because B read after A wrote. Ten runs produce negative 80, because A read after B wrote. The test that passes on the developer's machine fails on the build server, then passes again on rerun, because the scheduler is not deterministic and the bug depends on timing the program does not control.

The fix is a lock around the read and the write, so the second thread cannot enter the sequence until the first exits it. Thread A reads 100, subtracts 60, writes 40, and releases the lock. Thread B reads 40, subtracts 60, writes negative 20, and releases. The balance is correct. The lock turned two racing steps into two ordered steps, and the invariant held.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. Main memory, DRAM, takes roughly 100 nanoseconds to return a value. The cache, SRAM, takes one. The program runs at the speed of the cache, not the speed of DRAM, because the processor reads instructions and data from the cache on almost every cycle.

The cache works because of locality. A program that reads `array[0]` almost always reads `array[1]` next. That is spatial locality: nearby memory gets touched close in time. A program that reads the same loop counter on every iteration shows temporal locality: the same memory gets touched again and again. The cache exploits both. When the processor requests a byte from DRAM, the memory controller does not return one byte. It returns a cache line — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors — and the cache stores the whole line. The next seven reads from that line hit the cache and cost one nanosecond each instead of 100.

A cache miss is the expensive case. The processor requests a byte, the cache does not have it, and the processor stalls for the full DRAM latency while the line loads. A program that strides through memory 64 bytes at a time — reading one int from each cache line and discarding the rest — pays the full 100-nanosecond cost on every access. The cache is doing nothing useful, because each line is used once and evicted before its other bytes are read.

Caches are organized in levels. The L1 cache is 32 kilobytes on a typical core, split into 32 KB for instructions and 32 KB for data, and it answers in four cycles. The L2 cache is larger, 256 KB to 1 MB, and answers in 12 to 14 cycles. The L3 cache is shared across all cores on the die, 8 MB to 32 MB, and answers in 40 cycles. Main memory answers in 200 to 300 cycles. Each level is a filter: L1 catches most requests, L2 catches what L1 missed, L3 catches what L2 missed, and the rare request that escapes all three reaches DRAM.

The replacement policy decides what stays. A cache holds a fixed number of lines, and a new line evicts an old one. Most caches use an approximation of least-recently-used: the line that went longest without a read is the one removed. This works because of temporal locality — a line used recently will likely be used again soon, and a line untouched for a long time probably will not. A program that streams through a large array faster than the cache can hold it thrashes the cache: every new line evicts a line the program still needs, and the hit rate collapses toward zero.

The practical consequence is that data layout changes program speed more than algorithmic complexity in many real programs. A linked list of one million nodes, each allocated separately, forces a pointer chase on every step. Each chase loads a cache line from a random address, and the line probably is not in the cache. The same one million items in a contiguous array load sequentially, and seven out of every eight reads hit the cache. The array is not algorithmically faster — both are O(n) — but it runs ten times quicker because it pays for DRAM on one access in eight instead of eight in eight. The cache rewards programs that touch memory in order and punishes programs that jump.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once. The second call does not duplicate the first. It either repeats the first call's effect or recognizes that the effect already happened and does nothing.

`GET` is idempotent by construction. Two identical GETs return the same representation, and neither changes anything on the server. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces a resource wholesale. A PUT that sets `user.email = 'x@y.com'` leaves the user in that state whether it runs once or a hundred times. The fifth call overwrites the fourth, which overwrote the third, and the final state is the one the last call specified.

`POST` is not idempotent. A POST that charges a credit card 50 dollars, sent twice, charges 100. The server has no way to know the second request is a duplicate of the first rather than a second purchase. The state diverges with each call.

The distinction matters when the network lies. TCP delivers most packets, but a packet can arrive at the server while the response is still in flight, and the connection drops before the client reads it. The client does not know whether the server processed the request. It retries. If the request is a PUT, the retry is harmless. If it is a POST that debits an account, the retry debits twice.

The fix for non-idempotent operations is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token for the logical operation and sends it in a header. The server records the key with the operation's result. On a retry, the server finds the key, recognizes the operation already ran, and returns the stored result instead of executing again. One key, one effect. The second charge never happens.

A key must scope to the operation, not the resource. A key sent with a charge of 50 dollars must not also suppress a later charge of 75 dollars to the same card. The server ties the key to the request body or to a specific intent, so a different amount with the same key either fails or starts a new operation. Without that scoping, the key blocks legitimate follow-up actions.

DELETE is idempotent in the HTTP sense but carries a wrinkle. The first DELETE on `/users/42` removes the user. The second DELETE on `/users/42` finds nothing there. The server state after both calls is the same — user 42 is gone — so the operation is idempotent, but the responses differ: the first returns 200, the second returns 404. Idempotency governs state, not response codes. A client that treats a 404 on retry as a failure breaks the contract.

The practical rule: PUT and DELETE for state changes the client might retry, POST for state changes the client must not repeat without a key. The network will drop a connection at the worst moment. Idempotent methods absorb the retry. Non-idempotent methods demand a key, or they demand a reconciliation process that catches the duplicates later.

DNS turns a name into an address through a chain of lookups. A browser types `example.com` and needs its IP. The operating system hands the name to a resolver, and the resolver does the walking.

The resolver first asks a root server. There are thirteen root server addresses, labeled A through M, operated by twelve organizations. The root server does not know `example.com`. It knows only the servers for `.com`, and it returns their addresses.

The resolver asks a `.com` server. That server does not know `example.com` either. It knows the authoritative servers for `example.com`, the name servers run by the domain's owner, and it returns those.

The resolver asks the authoritative server for `example.com`. That server holds the actual record. It returns an A record with an IPv4 address like `93.184.216.34`, or an AAAA record with an IPv6 address. The resolver hands the address to the operating system, and the browser opens a TCP connection to it.

Each step caches. The browser caches the answer for the record's time-to-live, a number of seconds the authoritative server sets. The operating system caches it. The resolver caches it. A second lookup of `example.com` within the TTL returns from cache and never touches a root server. The TTL might be 300 seconds for a record that changes often, or 86400 for one that does not. A short TTL means changes propagate fast but the resolver asks more often. A long TTL means fewer lookups but stale addresses when the record changes.

The resolver does not query the root for every name. It also holds the root server addresses as a file, typically the 13 numeric addresses, loaded at startup. The first lookup after boot starts at the root. Every lookup after that starts with whatever the resolver's cache holds, and it walks down only as far as the cache allows. A lookup for `shop.example.com` that finds `example.com` cached skips the root and the `.com` server and asks the `example.com` authoritative server directly for `shop`.

The chain is short in practice. A warm resolver answers most names from its own cache in one round trip, because popular domains are looked up constantly and their records stay warm. The root sees traffic only for names no one has asked for recently, and the root servers handle roughly a thousand queries per second each, almost all for obscure or mistyped names. The system scales because the cache absorbs the load, and the authoritative servers answer only the misses.

A deadlock is two threads frozen, each holding a lock the other needs. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A waits for B forever. B waits for A forever. Neither releases what it holds until it gets what it wants, and neither gets what it wants until the other releases. The program stops.

The condition is circular wait. Four things must hold at once: threads hold the locks they already have (mutual exclusion), they wait without giving up (no preemption), they hold one lock while asking for the next (hold and wait), and the lock graph forms a cycle (circular wait). Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest break is a lock ordering rule. Every thread acquires mutexes in the same global sequence. If the rule is "lock 1 before lock 2," thread A locks 1 then 2, and thread B locks 1 then 2. B cannot hold 2 while waiting for 1, because the rule forbids acquiring 2 first. The cycle cannot close, because the wait edges all point the same direction.

The rule costs nothing at runtime. It costs discipline at design time: every code path that takes two locks must know the order, and a path that violates it reintroduces the deadlock. A thread that locks 2 then 1, against the rule, deadlocks against a thread that follows the rule. The order is a contract, enforced by review, not by the machine.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. The hash function spreads keys across the array's slots, called buckets. When two keys hash to the same bucket, a collision occurs, and the map needs a strategy to store both.

The oldest strategy is separate chaining. Each bucket holds a pointer to a linked list. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list at that bucket, and appends the new entry if the key is absent. On lookup, it walks the same list comparing keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The cost grows with the list's length. If a thousand keys land in one bucket, that bucket's lookup degrades to linear search while the rest of the array sits idle.

The second strategy is open addressing, sometimes called probing. There is no list; the entry lives in the array itself. On insert, the map hashes the key and checks that slot. If it is occupied, the map probes the next slot according to a fixed rule and keeps going until it finds an empty one. Linear probing checks slot *i+1*, then *i+2*, then *i+3*. Quadratic probing jumps by squares: *i+1*, *i+4*, *i+9*. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed stride.

Open addressing trades memory for cache locality. A linked list node in separate chaining is a pointer chase on every hop; a probing sequence stays inside the array, so consecutive slots often share a cache line. The cost shows up under deletion. Removing an entry from a probed table cannot just empty the slot, because a later key might have been pushed past it during an earlier collision. The map marks the slot with a tombstone, a value that means "occupied for probing, empty for insertion." Tombstones accumulate until the table is rehashed, and a table full of tombstones degrades probe lengths until it is rebuilt.

Both strategies break down when the table fills. The load factor is the ratio of stored entries to array slots. Separate chaining tolerates a high load factor because lists simply grow longer, but each extra element adds a comparison. Open addressing degrades faster: as slots fill, probe sequences lengthen, and a table near capacity forces long chains of checks on every insert and lookup. Most implementations pick a threshold around 0.7 for open addressing and 1.0 or higher for chaining. When the threshold is crossed, the map allocates a larger array, often twice the size, rehashes every entry into its new bucket, and frees the old array. That rehash is *O(n)*, and it happens rarely enough that the amortized cost of insert stays constant.

Real implementations mix these ideas. Java's `HashMap` uses chaining but converts a long chain into a balanced tree when it exceeds eight entries, capping the worst case at *O(log n)* instead of *O(n)*. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence derived from the hash, so a bad hash function cannot produce a simple linear walk through the array. Rust's `HashMap` uses Robin Hood probing, a variant that minimizes the gap between a key's ideal slot and its actual slot, keeping probe sequences short on average by stealing slots from richer entries to give to poorer ones.

The collision strategy is the whole game. A perfect hash function with a table sized to its keys would never collide and never probe, making every operation *O(1)*. Real hash functions are not perfect, real keys are not uniform, and real tables are not infinite, so the strategy that resolves the gap between the ideal and the actual determines whether the map stays fast or quietly becomes a linear search.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row. The table itself is an unordered pile of rows on disk. The index is a sorted list of column values, each paired with a pointer back to the row it came from. Finding a row by an indexed column becomes a binary search through the sorted list instead of a linear scan through the table.

The most common structure is the B-tree. A B-tree keeps values sorted in a balanced tree whose fan-out is tuned to disk page size, so a search touches three or four pages instead of thousands. A table of fifty million rows might fit its primary-key index in a tree four levels deep, meaning four disk reads to find any row by key. Without the index, the same query reads every page in the table until it stumbles on the match.

Indexes hurt in three ways.

First, they cost storage. Every index is a copy of part of the table, sorted and organized. A table with five indexes on different columns can spend more disk space on indexes than on the rows themselves. A wide secondary index on a large table can double the database's footprint.

Second, they slow writes. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must update every index that covers that column. A table with six indexes pays six index writes for one row insert. On a high-throughput insert workload — a log table, an event stream — those index maintenance writes dominate. The index that makes ad-hoc queries fast makes the ingest path slow.

Third, they can be useless or worse than useless. A query that selects most of the rows in a table gains nothing from an index, because the database still has to read all those rows, and following index pointers to scattered row locations causes random disk access. A sequential table scan reads pages in order, which is faster on spinning disk and on SSDs when the row count is high. Most query planners will choose a full table scan over an index scan when the predicate matches more than roughly five to ten percent of the table, because the random I/O cost of following index pointers exceeds the sequential cost of just reading the whole thing.

The specific failure mode is the low-selectivity index. An index on a boolean `is_active` column splits the table into two halves; any query on it returns half the rows, so the planner ignores the index and scans anyway. The index sits on disk, soaks up write effort on every insert and update, and never gets used. An index on a `status` column with three values — `pending`, `processing`, `done` — where ninety percent of rows are `done` has the same problem. Queries for `done` trigger a scan; queries for `pending` might use the index, but the index exists for the common case, which is the case it cannot help.

Composite indexes have their own trap. A two-column index on `(last_name, first_name)` speeds queries that filter on `last_name` or on both columns, but a query that filters only on `first_name` cannot use it, because the index is sorted by `last_name` first and `first_name` is unordered within each `last_name` group. The index exists, the query planner sees it, and the index is useless for that query. The order of columns in a composite index is a decision about which queries the index serves, and it serves only the queries whose predicates match the leftmost prefix of that order.

The rule is simple. An index earns its place when it serves queries that return a small fraction of the table — single-digit percent or less — and when the columns it covers are queried frequently enough that the read savings outweigh the write cost across the workload. An index that serves no query, serves a query that returns most of the table, or duplicates another index's prefix is pure overhead. It makes every write slower and every backup bigger, and it does nothing in return.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. Every byte gets a sequence number. The first byte's number is chosen randomly during the handshake — the Initial Sequence Number — and each byte after it increments by one. A packet carrying bytes 1001 through 1500 has sequence number 1001 in its header. The receiver knows exactly which bytes in the stream that packet fills.

The connection is full-duplex, so each direction has its own sequence number space. The sequence numbers flowing from the server to the client have no relationship to the numbers flowing from the client to the server. The two halves are independent streams with independent counters.

When a packet arrives, the receiver places its bytes into a receive buffer at the position dictated by the sequence number. If bytes 1001 through 1500 arrive, they go into buffer slots 1001 through 1500. If bytes 2001 through 2500 arrive next, they go into slots 2001 through 2500. The gap from 1501 to 2000 stays empty. The receiver does not wait for the missing bytes before accepting the later ones; it stores them out of order and tracks the gap.

The receiver acknowledges data using the Acknowledgment Number field in its own packets. The acknowledgment number is the next byte the receiver expects, not the last byte it received. If the receiver has cleanly received bytes up through 1500, it sends an acknowledgment with number 1501, meaning "I have everything through 1500; send 1501 next." If bytes 2001 through 2500 arrived but 1501 through 2000 did not, the receiver still acknowledges 1501. The acknowledgment number advances only when the bytes arriving at the receiver form a contiguous run from the last acknowledged position. This is a cumulative acknowledgment: it confirms everything before the number in one stroke, and it says nothing about whether bytes after that number have arrived.

The sender keeps every sent byte in its send buffer until it receives an acknowledgment covering that byte. When the sender sends bytes 1001 through 1500 and gets back an acknowledgment of 1501, it can discard those bytes. If it does not get an acknowledgment within a timeout — the Retransmission Timeout, calculated from measured round-trip times — it sends the unacknowledged bytes again. This is the core of TCP's reliability: the sender keeps retransmitting until the receiver acknowledges, and the receiver keeps acknowledging the next byte it needs.

The ordering problem reduces to the gap problem. The receiver's buffer is a fixed array indexed by sequence number. Bytes arrive, the receiver writes them at their sequence-number positions, and the application reads from the buffer only at the contiguous frontier — the point where there are no gaps. If bytes 1 through 1000 are in the buffer and bytes 1001 through 1500 are missing, the application gets bytes 1 through 1000 and blocks on 1001. When the retransmission of 1001 through 1500 arrives, the frontier jumps forward, and the application reads the newly contiguous block. The application never sees out-of-order data. It sees a byte stream that advances in order, because the receiver holds back everything past the first gap until the gap fills.

The sequence number space is finite: a 32-bit field, so numbers wrap from 4,294,967,295 back to 0. TCP handles this because the window — the amount of unacknowledged data in flight at once — is limited to a size where wraparound cannot cause ambiguity. The window is at most half the sequence number space in theory, and in practice the receive window advertised by the receiver is far smaller, bounded by the buffer space the receiver has available. Two packets whose sequence numbers differ by the window size cannot both be outstanding, so a wrapped number cannot be confused with an old number from the previous pass through the space.

The handshake establishes the starting point. The client picks an Initial Sequence Number, sends it in a SYN packet, and the server acknowledges it by sending back its own SYN with its own Initial Sequence Number plus an acknowledgment of the client's number plus one. When the client acknowledges the server's SYN, both sides have agreed on where the byte stream starts in each direction. From that point, every byte is numbered relative to that start, and the ordering machinery runs until one side sends a FIN at its current sequence number to mark the end of its stream.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes against shared state.

Two threads running on two cores can both touch the same memory at the same instant. Thread A reads `balance`, adds 100, writes it back. Thread B reads `balance` in the nanosecond between A's read and A's write, adds 50, writes it back. A's write overwrites B's. One hundred dollars vanished. The code is correct in isolation and wrong under concurrency, and the compiler and the CPU will not warn either party.

The mutex is a lock with one rule. Only one thread can hold it at a time. A thread that wants to touch the shared data acquires the lock first, does its work, and releases it. A thread that arrives while the lock is held blocks — the operating system parks it off the run queue — until the holder releases. The section of code between acquire and release is the critical section, and the mutex makes that section atomic with respect to other critical sections guarded by the same lock.

Atomic here does not mean fast or indivisible in hardware. It means serialized. Three threads contending for one mutex run their critical sections one after another, in some order, never overlapping. The outcome is the same as if each critical section ran to completion before the next began. Without the lock, the three threads' reads and writes interleave in whatever order the scheduler and the memory bus produce, and that order can leave the data in a state no single thread intended.

The mutex protects against lost updates, torn reads, and invariant violations. A lost update is the `balance` example: two writes, one survives. A torn read happens when one thread reads a multi-word structure while another is halfway through updating it — reading a linked list whose node has a new `next` pointer but an old `value`, or a 64-bit integer on a 32-bit machine where the write of the high word and the low word are separate instructions and the reader catches it between them. An invariant violation happens when a thread observes a data structure in a state that its operations never produce: a tree whose parent pointers do not point back at the parent, a counter that went negative, a queue whose head and tail have crossed.

What a mutex does not protect against is the data being shared in the first place. It narrows the window for corruption to zero by serializing access, but it does not make the access correct. A thread that acquires the lock, reads stale data, releases the lock, and then acts on that stale data outside the critical section has a race the mutex never covered. The lock guarantees that the read and another thread's write do not overlap; it does not guarantee that the read reflects the most recent write if the read happened before the write. The discipline is not "lock everything" but "lock the span over which the data must stay consistent, and hold it long enough to make the decision, not just long enough to peek at the value."

The cost is contention. Two threads that never touch the same data do not need a mutex between them, and a mutex shared across a hot path turns parallel work into serial work. A server with one lock around every request handler runs one request at a time regardless of how many cores the machine has. The lock that prevents corruption also prevents throughput, and the engineering question is which data needs serialization and how narrow the critical section can be — not whether to lock, but what exactly the lock is guarding and whether that span is as small as the invariant requires.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that a program can no longer reach. The question is how it knows what is unreachable, and the answer is a graph traversal.

Every object a program allocates is a node. Every reference from one object to another is an edge. The roots are the starting points: registers on the CPU, local variables on each thread's stack, and global or static fields. An object is reachable if there is a path from a root to it. An object is garbage if there is not. The collector walks the graph from the roots, marks every object it touches, and sweeps everything unmarked into the free list. That is mark-and-sweep, the foundational algorithm, and every modern collector is a refinement of it.

The traversal has to stop the world. While the collector walks the graph, the mutator — the application thread — cannot move references or create new edges, or the traversal would see an inconsistent picture and mark something live as dead. The pause is the cost. A heap with ten million objects means the collector walks ten million edges before the mutator resumes. Early collectors paused for hundreds of milliseconds on heaps that size. The engineering problem since then has been shrinking that pause.

Reference counting is the other approach. Each object carries a counter. Assign a reference, increment. Drop a reference, decrement. Hit zero, free. It finds garbage immediately and without a traversal, so there is no stop-the-world pause. It breaks on cycles. Object A points to B, B points to A, nothing else points to either. Both counters sit at one. Both are garbage. Neither drops to zero. A reference-counting collector needs a separate cycle detector — which is a tracing collector — to find those structures, or it leaks them forever. CPython uses reference counting and runs a tracing collector periodically to catch cycles. The tracing collector is the one that matters.

The tracing collectors in production today differ in how they manage the pause and the heap layout.

Mark-and-sweep leaves objects where they are and frees the dead ones. The heap fragments. Live objects scatter across pages with gaps between them, and allocating a new object means searching the free list for a gap that fits. Fragmentation wastes memory and hurts cache locality, because related objects no longer sit next to each other in memory.

A copying collector solves fragmentation by splitting the heap into two halves. It allocates in one half until it fills, then copies every live object into the other half, packing them contiguously. The old half becomes one contiguous free range. The copy step updates every reference, because each object's address changes. The pause covers the copy. The win is that the heap never fragments and allocation is pointer bumping — the allocator increments a single pointer by the object's size and returns the previous value. The loss is that half the heap is unused at any given time. Java's young generation uses copying.

A generational collector bets that most objects die young. It splits the heap into a young region and an old region. New allocations go to the young region, which is small and collected often. Objects that survive a few young collections get promoted to the old region, which is large and collected rarely. The bet pays off because the distribution is real: temporary objects — loop variables, intermediate strings, request buffers — are allocated and discarded within milliseconds. The young collection is fast because the region is small, and it reclaims most of the garbage. The old collection, which requires the long pause, runs infrequently. The HotSpot JVM, V8, and the .NET runtime all use generational collection.

The hard part is the barrier. A generational collector collects the young region without scanning the old region, but an object in the old region can hold a reference into the young region. If the collector does not know about that reference, it might mark a young object as unreachable while an old object still points to it. The collector installs a write barrier: every time the mutator writes a reference into an old object, the runtime records that the old object now points into the young region. The young collection consults that record as an additional root set. The barrier adds overhead to every pointer write, and the trade is that overhead against the shorter young-collection pause.

Concurrent collectors move work outside the pause. G1, Shenandoah, and ZGC trace the live set while the mutator runs. They use barriers to reconcile the mutator's changes against the collector's view. ZGC colors pointers — storing metadata bits in the pointer's high bits — so the mutator and the collector can cooperate on a single object without locking. The pauses on large heaps drop below ten milliseconds. The throughput cost is the barrier overhead on every reference access, which is higher than a stop-the-world collector's cost. The trade is pause time against raw speed, and the right choice depends on whether the application is latency-bound or throughput-bound.

The collector does not find unused memory by any clever inference. It draws the graph from the roots, and whatever is not on the graph is dead. The algorithms differ in how fast they draw, how long they pause to draw, and what they do with the heap afterward. The graph is the whole mechanism.

A race condition is a bug that appears only when the timing of two operations interleave in a way the programmer did not plan for. The code is correct in isolation and wrong under concurrency. The name comes from the root cause: two threads race for the same data, and the outcome depends on which one wins.

A bank account holds a balance of 500. Two threads run at the same time, one depositing 100, the other depositing 50. The deposit function reads the balance, adds the amount, and writes the result back. Three instructions: read, add, write.

Thread A reads 500. Thread B reads 500. Thread A adds 100, writes 600. Thread B adds 50, writes 550. The final balance is 550. One hundred dollars vanished. The correct answer is 650.

The failure is not in any single thread's logic. Thread A did read, add, write. Thread B did read, add, write. Both followed the code exactly. The failure is in the gap between A's read and A's write. Thread B slipped its read into that gap, saw the old value, and overwrote A's result. The lost update is the signature of a data race: two read-modify-write sequences overlapped on the same memory, and the later write clobbered the earlier one.

The bug is nondeterministic. Run the program a thousand times and the balance might come out right 999 times, because the scheduler happened to run one thread's three instructions to completion before starting the other's. The thousandth run hits the gap, the deposit disappears, and the bug report says "cannot reproduce." A race condition hides in the timing the scheduler chose, and timing is not repeatable.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write atomic. A mutex around the deposit function forces the two threads to take turns. Thread A acquires the lock, reads 500, adds 100, writes 600, releases. Thread B acquires the lock, reads 600, adds 50, writes 650, releases. The lock serialized the two operations, and the result is correct regardless of which thread runs first. The cost is that the two deposits can no longer happen at the same time. The lock that prevents the lost update also prevents the parallelism.

Not every race involves a mutex. A flag set by one thread and read by another is a race if the reader acts before the writer sets it. A lazy initialization that checks whether a singleton exists and creates it if not is a race if two threads both see "not created" and both create it. The shared element in every case is state that two threads touch without an ordering constraint between them. The fix is always the same: impose the ordering. A lock, an atomic operation, a memory barrier, a channel that serializes the messages — each one forces a sequence onto operations that were free to interleave. The race disappears when the interleaving does.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program because it is closer and faster, and because it exploits two patterns in how programs actually touch data.

Main memory is slow. A modern processor can execute dozens of instructions in the time it takes to fetch one value from DRAM. A read that goes all the way to main memory costs around 100 nanoseconds. A read that hits the cache costs one or two. The cache exists to keep that read from going to main memory.

The cache is built from static RAM, which is faster and more expensive than the dynamic RAM that makes up main memory. A typical machine has three levels. L1 is smallest and closest, 32 or 48 kilobytes, one or two nanoseconds to reach, one per core. L2 is larger, 256 kilobytes to a megabyte, around ten nanoseconds, one per core. L3 is largest, several megabytes to tens of megabytes, 30 to 50 nanoseconds, shared across all cores. Main memory sits behind all three at 100 nanoseconds or more. The hierarchy is a funnel: the smallest, fastest layer is checked first, and each miss falls through to the next larger, slower layer.

The first pattern the cache exploits is temporal locality. A program that reads a variable once is likely to read it again soon. A loop counter, a working buffer, a node in a linked list — the code touches the same memory repeatedly within a short window. The cache keeps recently accessed data. When the processor reads an address, the cache stores it. The next read of that address hits the cache instead of main memory.

The second pattern is spatial locality. A program that reads one byte is likely to read the bytes next to it. An array walked in order, the fields of a struct, the instructions of a function — memory access clusters in contiguous ranges. The cache does not store individual bytes. It stores cache lines, contiguous blocks of 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the processor reads one byte, the cache pulls the entire 64-byte line containing it from main memory. The next 63 bytes are already in the cache when the program asks for them. A loop scanning an array byte by byte pays one memory fetch for every 64 elements instead of one per element.

The cache speeds up a program when the accesses match these patterns. A loop summing an array of integers hits the cache on nearly every element, because the array is contiguous and the access is sequential. The first read of each 64-byte line misses, and the remaining 15 four-byte integers in that line hit. The miss rate is one in sixteen. The effective cost per element is one main-memory fetch plus fifteen cache hits, amortized to a few nanoseconds each instead of a hundred.

The cache slows a program when the accesses defeat both patterns. A linked list scattered across the heap defeats spatial locality, because each node's `next` pointer jumps to an arbitrary address, and each jump lands in a different cache line. Walking a linked list of a thousand nodes costs a thousand cache misses, each at 100 nanoseconds, because no two nodes share a line. Walking an array of a thousand elements costs about 63 misses, because the elements are packed into consecutive lines. Same number of elements, different memory layout, a fifteenfold difference in speed.

A hash map with open addressing has good cache behavior because the probe sequence walks consecutive array slots, and consecutive slots share cache lines. A hash map with separate chaining has poor cache behavior because each bucket is a pointer to a linked list, and following the pointer is a jump to a new line. The algorithmic complexity is the same — both are *O(1)* on average — but the constant factor differs by the cache miss rate, and the constant factor is what the cache measures.

The cache also speeds up instruction fetch. The code itself lives in memory, and the processor fetches each instruction before it executes. A tight loop fits in a few cache lines and runs entirely from L1. A large function with scattered branches misses on each branch target, and each miss stalls the pipeline until the instruction arrives. This is why small loops are fast beyond their instruction count: the instructions themselves stay in the cache.

The processor does not ask the program which data to cache. The hardware watches the addresses the program touches and keeps what it has seen recently, evicting the oldest lines when a set fills. The replacement policy is approximation, not oracle. A program that streams through a large array once, never revisiting any element, fills the cache with data it will never read again, evicting data that would have been reused. The cache is a bet on locality, and a workload with no locality loses the bet. The program runs at main-memory speed, and the cache adds nothing but overhead.

Okay — explain idempotency as it applies to HTTP APIs, in plain register with a fact per sentence.

An HTTP method is idempotent when a client can send the same request twice and leave the server's state exactly where a single request would have left it. The second request does not double the effect. It does not undo it. The server ends in the same state either way.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads. Two reads do not change a row in the database, so the second read is harmless. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces. A `PUT` to `/users/42` with a body of `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada. Sending it a hundred times sets the name to Ada a hundred times. The final state is one user named Ada, not a hundred users and not a name concatenated a hundred times. `DELETE` is idempotent because it removes. The first `DELETE /users/42` removes user 42. The second `DELETE /users/42` finds no user 42 and removes nothing. The end state is the same: user 42 is gone.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST` to `/users` with a body of `{"name": "Ada"}` creates a new user. Sending it twice creates two users named Ada, each with its own ID. The server's state after two requests differs from its state after one. That is the distinction: idempotency is about the resulting state, not the response body. The first `DELETE` returns `200 OK`; the second might return `404 Not Found`. The response differs. The state does not. The method is idempotent because the state converges.

Idempotency matters because clients fail and networks drop packets. A client sends `POST /orders` to charge a credit card. The server processes the charge, sends a response, and the response is lost in transit. The client does not know whether the server received the request. It retries. The server processes the charge again. The customer's card is charged twice for one order. The retry was correct — the client had to assume the first request never arrived — and the duplicate charge is the server's fault for exposing a non-idempotent operation without protection.

The fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique string — a UUID — and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key on first receipt, processes the request, and records the response. On the second request with the same key, the server finds the stored key and returns the recorded response without processing again. The key turns a non-idempotent `POST` into an operation that behaves idempotently across retries. Stripe's API documents this pattern: the key scopes to a resource and expires after 24 hours, and the server returns the original response body and status code verbatim on a replay.

The HTTP specification declares `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` idempotent as a contract. A server that implements `DELETE /users/42` to decrement a global counter on every call has broken that contract. The method is idempotent by definition; the implementation is not. A client that retries a `DELETE` on that server decrements the counter twice. The spec does not protect against an implementation that ignores it. Idempotency is a promise the server makes about its own behavior, and the promise is only as good as the code behind the route.

Okay — explain DNS resolution from name to address, plain register, fact per sentence.

A browser types `example.com` into a URL bar. The operating system hands that name to a resolver and expects a 32-bit IPv4 address or a 128-bit IPv6 address back. The resolver is usually a process run by the ISP or a public resolver like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8. The work is a tree walk.

The name is a hierarchy read right to left. `example.com` is two labels: `com` at the top, `example` beneath it. `www.api.example.com` is four labels: `com`, `example`, `api`, `www`. Each label is a level in the Domain Name System's tree. The root of the tree is the empty label to the right of the final dot.

The resolver does not know where `example.com` lives. It starts at the root. Thirteen root server clusters, identified by the letters A through M, sit at the top of the tree. Their addresses are published as 13 IPv4 addresses and 13 IPv6 addresses, though hundreds of physical machines answer behind those addresses using anycast routing. The resolver picks one, geographically near, and sends a query for `www.example.com`.

The root server does not know `www.example.com` either. What it knows is which servers are authoritative for the `com` top-level domain. It returns a referral: a list of name servers for `com`, plus their addresses. The referral is not the answer. It is a pointer to the next level down.

The resolver sends the same query to one of the `com` servers. The `com` server does not know `www.example.com`. It knows which servers are authoritative for `example.com`. It returns a referral to those servers — `a.iana-servers.net`, `b.iana-servers.net`, and their addresses.

The resolver sends the query to `a.iana-servers.net`. This server is authoritative for `example.com`. It holds the actual records. It finds a record for `www` and returns the address: `93.184.216.34`. The resolver hands that address to the operating system, which hands it to the browser, which opens a TCP connection to port 443 at that address.

Three round trips: root, `com`, `example.com`. Each is a UDP packet out and a UDP packet back, costing one network round trip. A resolver in New York querying a root server in Frankfurt, a `com` server in Amsterdam, and an `example.com` server in Los Angeles spends roughly 160 milliseconds in transit, dominated by the transatlantic leg to the authoritative server.

The resolver caches. When it fetches the `com` referral, it stores it for the time-to-live listed in the response — typically two days for a TLD referral. The next query for any `com` domain skips the root and goes straight to the `com` servers. A query for `example.com` an hour after the first one skips root and `com` and goes straight to the `example.com` servers, because both referrals are still in cache. A query a minute later for `www.example.com` hits the full answer in cache and returns without sending anything to the network. The cache is why DNS feels instant after the first lookup.

The record types matter. The query above assumed `www.example.com` had an A record holding an IPv4 address directly. Often it does not. `www.example.com` may have a CNAME record pointing to `example.com`, which means "I am not the answer; go ask that name instead." The resolver follows the CNAME, queries `example.com`, and gets the A record there. One name produced two lookups. A CNAME chain can stack — `www` points to `cdn.example.com`, which points to `cdn-edge.provider.net`, which points to an A record — and each hop is another query unless the intermediate answers are cached.

The resolver itself may not do the walk. A home router typically forwards DNS queries to the ISP's resolver, which does the tree walk and caches the result for all its customers. A laptop on a coffee-shop network sends its query to the router, the router sends it to the ISP, the ISP walks the tree. The laptop sees one round trip to the router. The ISP absorbs the three-round-trip walk once and serves the cached answer to the next thousand customers who ask for the same domain.

The system is recursive on the resolver side and iterative on the server side. The resolver asks, gets a pointer, asks again, gets a pointer, asks again, gets the answer. Each authoritative server it visits gives it the next pointer rather than doing the work itself. The resolver does the walking. The authoritative servers just answer the question in front of them. The root does not resolve `www.example.com`. It points at `com`. The `com` server does not resolve it either. It points at `example.com`. Only the authoritative server for `example.com` resolves it, and only because someone configured a record for `www` in that zone's file. The name becomes an address because each server in the chain knows exactly one level of the hierarchy and hands the resolver to the next.

Okay — explain deadlock with a concrete example, then one avoidance strategy, in plain register.

A deadlock is two threads stopped forever, each waiting for a lock the other holds. Neither moves. Neither times out. The program hangs.

Thread A holds lock X and wants lock Y. Thread B holds lock Y and wants lock X. A cannot proceed until it gets Y, which B holds. B cannot proceed until it gets X, which A holds. The cycle has no exit. Both threads sleep on the run queue, and the scheduler never wakes them because the event each waits for is produced by the other.

The code in each thread is correct in isolation. A acquires X, does work, acquires Y, does more work, releases both. B acquires Y, does work, acquires X, does more work, releases both. The deadlock appears only when the two run at the same time and the scheduler interleaves them at the wrong point. A grabs X. The scheduler switches to B before A grabs Y. B grabs Y. Now both are stuck.

Four conditions must hold at once for this to happen. Mutual exclusion: the locks allow one holder at a time. Hold and wait: each thread holds one lock while asking for another. No preemption: a thread cannot force another to release a lock. Circular wait: the dependency graph of threads and locks forms a cycle. Break any one and the deadlock cannot occur.

The cleanest fix is lock ordering. Pick a global order for every lock in the program. Every thread acquires locks in that order. Thread A wants X and Y, so it acquires X first, then Y. Thread B wants X and Y, so it acquires X first, then Y. B can no longer grab Y while holding something A needs, because B never holds Y without already holding X. The circular wait is impossible. The dependency graph is a straight line, and a line has no cycle.

The cost is discipline. Every developer who touches shared state must know the order and follow it. A single thread that acquires locks in the wrong order reopens the deadlock. The order must be global, documented, and enforced — by code review, by linting, or by a runtime that checks acquisition order and fails fast when a thread tries to grab a lock out of sequence. The fix is not clever. It is a rule, applied everywhere, that makes the cycle structurally impossible to form.

A hash map turns a key into an integer with a hash function, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. Two keys that hash to the same index collide. The map needs a rule for storing both.

**Chaining** keeps a list at each bucket. On insert, the map appends the new entry to that bucket's list. On lookup, it walks the list and compares keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. On delete, it finds the entry and unlinks it. The list is a linked list in the simple case; Java's `HashMap` switches each bucket to a balanced tree once it holds eight or more entries, which holds worst-case lookup at O(log n) instead of O(n) for hostile or pathological key sets.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the array itself. On insert, if the target slot is occupied, the map probes another slot by a rule: linear probing checks the next slot, quadratic probing checks slots at squared intervals, double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step. On lookup, the map probes the same sequence until it finds the key, an empty slot, or has checked the whole table. Delete is the hard case: removing an entry and leaving an empty slot breaks the probe chain for keys that passed through it, so the map marks the slot with a tombstone flag instead of clearing it. Tombstones accumulate, so the map must rehash to reclaim them.

Both methods degrade as the load factor — the ratio of entries to slots — rises. Chaining's lists grow longer; open addressing's probe sequences grow longer and collide more often. The map tracks the load factor and, at a threshold (0.75 in Java's `HashMap`, 0.75 in Go's `map`), allocates a larger array and reinserts every entry, which redistributes entries across the new, larger set of buckets.

The choice between the two trades memory for traversal cost. Chaining spends a pointer per entry on list overhead but tolerates load factors above 1.0 because the buckets themselves never fill. Open addressing spends no per-entry memory on pointers and has better cache behavior because the entries stay packed in one array, but it cannot store more entries than slots and degrades sharply as the load factor approaches 1.0.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row. The common form is a B-tree, which keeps a sorted copy of one or more columns paired with pointers back to the full rows. A query that filters on an indexed column walks the tree in O(log n) time instead of reading the table top to bottom in O(n).

The cost is storage and write work. Every index is a separate structure on disk. A table with five indexes holds six copies of its data, one per index plus the base table. Every insert, update, and delete must update the base table and every index that covers the changed column. A table that takes 2 milliseconds to insert a row with no indexes takes longer with each one added, because each insert also rebalances a tree.

Indexes hurt in three specific cases. First, on columns that change often: the read savings never repay the write cost. Second, on small tables: a full scan of 200 rows fits in a few disk pages and beats the tree walk plus the pointer chase back to the row. Third, when the query planner chooses not to use them. A query like `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4 AND status = 'shipped'` has a two-column index on `(customer_id, status)`, but if the planner's statistics say most rows match the filter, it skips the index and scans, because reading the whole table in sequence is cheaper than thousands of random reads through the tree.

A composite index also has a leftmost-prefix rule. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone, but it does not serve queries that filter on `first_name` alone, because the tree is sorted by `last_name` first and `first_name` is only ordered within each `last_name` group. A query on `first_name` alone must scan.

The practical test is whether an index earns its keep. A table read a million times a day and written twice benefits from every useful index. A table written ten thousand times a day and read by a nightly batch of fifty queries is better served by one index on the column the batch filters on, or none at all.

TCP sends each byte with a sequence number. The sender starts with a random value — the initial sequence number — and counts forward by one for every byte it transmits. A 1000-byte segment carrying sequence number 5001 covers bytes 5001 through 6000.

The receiver reads that number from the segment header. If it expects byte 5001 and the segment says 5001, the bytes are in order, and the receiver hands them to the application in that sequence. If the next segment arrives carrying 6001 but the one before it — 5001 through 6000 — was lost in transit, the receiver buffers 6001 and waits. It does not deliver 6001 to the application yet, because the application expects bytes in the order they were sent.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Its acknowledgment field carries the sequence number of the next byte it wants — the first byte after the longest unbroken run it has received. If bytes 5001 through 6000 arrived, the acknowledgment is 6001. If 5001 through 6000 arrived and 6001 through 7000 also arrived, the acknowledgment is 7001. If 5001 through 6000 was lost but 6001 through 7000 arrived, the acknowledgment stays at 5001, because that is still the first missing byte. The buffered 6001 through 7000 sits in the receiver's memory, held out of order.

The sender reads that acknowledgment. If it does not see 6001 come back within a timeout — typically a round-trip estimate that TCP adjusts as it measures the connection — it sends segment 5001 again. When the retransmitted 5001 arrives, the receiver now holds an unbroken run from 5001 through 7000. It delivers all of it to the application in sequence and acknowledges 7001.

Gaps close from the left. The receiver tracks the lowest sequence number it has not yet received, and everything above that gap waits in a buffer sized by the receive window advertised in its headers. Bytes above the gap can arrive in any order — 9001 before 7001, 8001 before 7001 — and the receiver stores each one by sequence number until the missing piece fills the hole. Once the hole fills, the receiver releases the contiguous run to the application and advances its acknowledgment past it.

The sequence number is what makes the order. TCP does not trust the network to deliver packets in sequence, because IP routes each packet independently and a later packet can beat an earlier one across the network. The sequence number lets the receiver reconstruct the original order regardless of arrival order, and the acknowledgment tells the sender which bytes it must send again.

A mutex protects a region of code so that only one thread can run it at a time. The name is short for mutual exclusion. A thread that needs the region calls `lock` on the mutex, runs the code inside, then calls `unlock`. While one thread holds the lock, every other thread that calls `lock` on the same mutex blocks — it stops running and waits until the holder calls `unlock`.

The thing it protects is shared state that would corrupt if two threads touched it at once. A bank balance stored in a single integer is the plain case. Thread A reads the balance as 100, adds 50, and writes 150. Thread B reads the balance as 100 at the same instant, subtracts 30, and writes 70. The final balance is 70 or 150, depending on which thread wrote last, and one update is lost. A mutex around the read-modify-write sequence forces the threads to take turns: A locks, reads 100, writes 150, unlocks; only then does B lock, read 150, write 120, unlock. The balance is correct at 120.

The protection covers data races, which the C++ and Java memory models define precisely: two threads access the same memory location, at least one of them writes, and no ordering constraint forces one access to happen before the other. The mutex supplies that ordering constraint. The lock call establishes a happens-before edge: every write the previous holder made before unlocking is visible to the next thread that acquires the lock. Without that edge, a thread can see a stale value from its own cache or register, even on a machine where the writes already reached main memory.

A mutex does not protect against everything. It does not protect against deadlock — two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's. It does not protect against priority inversion, where a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority thread preempts the low-priority thread so the lock never releases. It does not make a single operation atomic across multiple mutexes; locking two mutexes in sequence leaves a window between the first lock and the second where another thread can change the state the first lock was meant to guard.

The cost is contention. Every lock call is a kernel or userspace operation that takes time — tens of nanoseconds for an uncontended futex on Linux, microseconds when threads queue. A mutex held across a long computation serializes every thread that wants it, and the program runs as fast as a single thread for that section. The discipline is to hold the lock for the shortest span that covers the shared access, and to touch no shared state outside it.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches and returns it to the allocator. The core question is reachability: can any live thread still get to this object through a chain of references?

**Tracing** starts from the roots — the references a running thread can touch directly: local variables on its stack, static fields, the stack frames of JNI calls. The collector walks from those roots through every reference they hold, then through the references those objects hold, and marks each object it reaches. When the walk finishes, every unmarked object is unreachable. The collector then sweeps the heap and frees the unmarked memory. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme HotSpot and V8 use.

**Reference counting** takes the other approach. Each object carries a count of how many references point to it. A new reference increments the count; a dropped reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, no one can reach the object, and the collector frees it on the spot. This runs incrementally, with no pause to walk the heap. It fails on cycles: two objects that reference each other but nothing else both hold counts of one, and neither drops to zero. Python's CPython runtime uses reference counting and runs a separate cycle detector to catch those pairs.

Tracing collectors divide the heap by how long objects live. Most objects die young — a method's local list, a temporary string built for a log line. The collector runs a minor collection on the young generation frequently, copying survivors to the old generation and clearing the rest. The old generation holds long-lived objects — caches, singletons, configuration — and the collector scans it less often because few objects there are dead. This is generational collection, and it cuts the pause time because a minor collection scans a small fraction of the heap.

The pause is the cost. A tracing collector must stop every thread at a safepoint to get a stable view of the reference graph, because a thread mutating the graph mid-trace can miss an object or free one still in use. That stop-the-world pause is milliseconds on a tuned young collection and can reach hundreds of milliseconds on a full heap compaction. Concurrent collectors — HotSpot's G1 and ZGC, .NET's background GC — trace while the application runs to hold that pause down. ZGC colors pointers to track object moves without pausing the mutator threads, trading CPU time on the tracing side for shorter pauses.

The collector also handles fragmentation. Mark-and-sweep frees objects in place, leaving gaps between survivors. Over time the gaps fragment the heap, and a large allocation fails even when enough free bytes exist, because no contiguous span is large enough. A compacting collector moves survivors into a contiguous block and updates every reference to the new addresses. Copying collectors do this by design: they copy live objects from one region to another, leaving the source region empty and contiguous. HotSpot's young generation uses copying; G1 compacts the old generation region by region during a mixed collection.

The collector's job is to answer one question for every object on the heap: can a live thread still reach it? Tracing answers it by walking the reference graph from the roots. Reference counting answers it by tracking the edges as they appear and disappear. Both leave the program with memory it can still use and reclaim memory it cannot.

A race condition is a bug where a program's output depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not fixed.

Two threads share a counter. Thread A reads the counter at 5, adds 1, and writes 6. Thread B reads the counter at 5 at the same instant, adds 1, and writes 6. The counter should be 7 after two increments. It is 6. One increment is lost.

The race is the gap between read and write. Thread A reads the value, holds it in a register, computes the new value, and writes it back. Thread B does the same. Neither thread knows the other touched the value in between. The CPU ran the reads and writes in an order the program never chose, and the program got a wrong answer.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write indivisible. A mutex around the counter forces the threads to take turns: A locks, reads 5, writes 6, unlocks; only then does B lock, read 6, write 7, unlock. An atomic instruction like `fetch-and-add` does the same work in hardware, holding the cache line for the duration of the operation so no other core can read or write it mid-update.

The bug is not that the program crashed. The bug is that the program produced a plausible, wrong result. The counter reads 6, the account balance is off by one deposit, the ticket was sold to two buyers. The program ran to completion and returned a value that no sequential execution of the same code would have produced. That silent wrongness is what makes a race worse than a crash: the crash is visible, the race is not.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It holds copies of the bytes the processor is most likely to need next. When the processor asks for a byte, the cache answers if it can, and main memory never sees the request.
