The speed gap is the reason the cache exists. Reading from main memory takes roughly 100 cycles on a modern desktop chip. Reading from the L1 cache takes three or four. A load that hits the cache finishes before a main-memory load has left the memory controller.

The cache works because programs touch memory in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then 1, then 2, in order. When the processor reads byte 1000, the cache pulls a whole block — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM chips — into a cache line in one memory transaction. Bytes 1001 through 1063 arrive with it. The next seven reads hit the cache and cost four cycles each instead of a hundred.

The cache also exploits temporal locality. A program that writes a variable tends to read it again soon. The cache keeps recently used lines and discards old ones. When a line that was evicted is needed again, the processor pays the main-memory cost a second time.

The hierarchy has levels. The L1 cache is smallest and closest — 32 kilobytes per core on a Skylake processor, split into 32 KB for data and 32 KB for instructions, with a four-cycle latency. The L2 cache is larger and slower — 256 KB on the same chip, 12 cycles. The L3 cache is shared across all cores — several megabytes, 40 cycles. A load checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory, and stops at the first hit.

The cost of a miss is the reason cache-friendly code matters. A program that strides through an array reading one element per cache line pays 100 cycles per element. A program that packs its data so each cache line holds eight elements pays 100 cycles for the first and four for the other seven, an average of 16. Same bytes read, six times faster.

The cache is finite, so two pieces of code fight over it. A function that touches a megabyte of data evicts lines another function wanted. A loop that calls a distant function in its inner body pulls that function's code into the instruction cache and pushes out the loop's own code. The miss that follows costs a hundred cycles the loop never paid before.

The cache does not speed up a program by doing work faster. It speeds up the program by not doing work at all — by answering the processor's question from memory it already holds, and sparing main memory the trip.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once.

`PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Alice"}` is the textbook case. The first request sets the name to Alice. The second request sets the name to Alice again. The stored value is Alice. A client that lost the first response and retried gets the same result, and no second user is created.

`POST /users` with the same body is not idempotent. The first request creates user 42. The second request creates user 43. Two retries produce two rows. The state diverges with each call.

The HTTP specification names five idempotent methods: `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS`. `GET` and `HEAD` change nothing, so idempotency is trivial. `DELETE` is idempotent by a specific rule: deleting user 42 once removes it; deleting it again finds no row and removes nothing. The end state — user 42 absent — is the same after either call.

`POST` is neither idempotent nor safe. `PATCH` is absent from the specification's idempotent list because a patch's effect depends on its format. A `PATCH` that sets a field to a fixed value behaves idempotently. A `PATCH` that appends to a list or increments a counter does not.

The property that matters is the retry. Network protocols drop requests and drop responses. A client sends a payment, the server processes it, the response is lost, the client does not know whether the charge happened, and it sends the payment again. An idempotent API takes the second call and returns the result of the first. A non-idempotent API charges the customer twice.

The mechanism for turning `POST` idempotent is the idempotency key. The client generates a unique string — a UUID — and sends it in the `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with the first request's result. The second request arrives with the same key. The server finds the stored result and returns it without running the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern on its charge endpoints. The key turns a non-idempotent `POST` into an operation that behaves idempotently across retries, within a window the server defines.

Idempotency is a contract about state, not about the response. The second `PUT` returns `200 OK` with the updated resource. The second call to a key-protected `POST` returns `200 OK` with the original resource, or a cached copy of the original response. The body can differ. The server's state does not.

DNS turns a domain name into an IP address by walking a tree of name servers, each one answering with a tighter piece of the answer until the address is found.

The browser asks the resolver. The resolver is the first name server the machine talks to, usually run by the ISP or a public service like Google's 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1. The resolver does not know the address for `www.example.com`. It knows where to start.

The start is the root servers. There are thirteen root server addresses, published in a file every resolver ships with called the root hints. The resolver picks one and sends the query: where is `www.example.com`?

The root server does not know the address either. It knows who handles the top-level domains. It answers with a referral: a list of name servers for the `.com` domain. The resolver caches that referral so it does not have to ask the root again for the next `.com` lookup.

The resolver picks a `.com` server and sends the same query. The `.com` server does not know the address for `www.example.com`. It knows who handles `example.com`. It answers with a referral to the name servers for `example.com`.

The resolver picks one of those and sends the query a third time. This server holds the actual records for `example.com`. It reads the `www` record, finds the IP address — say, `93.184.216.34` — and sends it back as a final answer.

The resolver hands that address to the browser and caches the answer for as long as the record's time-to-live field says it is valid. A TTL of 300 seconds means the resolver will answer the next query for `www.example.com` from its own cache for five minutes, then ask the chain again.

Each step is a question and an answer. The root answers with the `.com` servers. The `.com` servers answer with the `example.com` servers. The `example.com` server answers with the address. The resolver assembles the path and returns the final value, and the cache spares the chain the repeat work.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither can proceed. Each waits forever for the other to release.

Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A holds 1 and waits for 2. B holds 2 and waits for 1. Neither thread releases what it holds until it gets what it wants. The program halts at that point, and the two threads sit blocked until the process is killed.

The four conditions that produce this were named by Coffman in 1971: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four must hold. Break any one and the deadlock cannot occur.

The cleanest break is a lock ordering. Every thread acquires mutexes in the same global order. If the rule is "lock 1 before 2," thread A locks 1 then 2 as before. Thread B, wanting both, also locks 1 first, then 2. Thread B blocks on mutex 1 while thread A holds it, but thread A never blocks on mutex 2 because thread B never acquired it. Thread A finishes, releases both, and thread B proceeds. The circular wait never forms.

The discipline costs one thing: every caller must know the order. A function that locks 2 without first locking 1 breaks the rule and reintroduces the deadlock. The order is a contract the whole codebase shares, enforced by review and convention, not by the compiler.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array. It computes an integer from the key, then maps that integer to an array index. Two different keys can land on the same index. That event is a collision, and every hash map has a strategy for it.

**Chaining** keeps a linked list at each array slot. When two keys hash to the same index, both entries live in that slot's list. A lookup walks the list and compares keys one by one. The list is short on average — roughly *load factor* entries long, where load factor is the count of stored entries divided by the array length. At a load factor of 0.75, the average list holds under one entry. The worst case is every key colliding into one slot, which degrades a lookup from O(1) to O(n). Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both use chaining; Java converts a bin to a red-black tree after eight entries to cap the worst case at O(log n).

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the array, no list. On collision, the map probes another slot according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. This is fast on modern CPUs because consecutive memory accesses stay in cache. Quadratic probing jumps by squares — 1, 4, 9, 16 — to avoid clustering under localized collision patterns. Double hashing computes a second hash from the key and uses it as the probe step, which spreads entries more evenly than either fixed sequence. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Rust's `std::collections::HashMap` all use open addressing. Python uses pseudorandom probing keyed on the entry's full hash so the probe sequence depends on the key, not just the index.

Open addressing needs a way to distinguish an empty slot from a deleted one. A tombstone marker — a special entry state, not a sentinel value — lets a probe sequence skip past a deleted slot without stopping short. Tombstones accumulate, so the map rehashes to clear them when the load factor crosses a threshold.

Both strategies share one cost control: when the array fills past a threshold, the map allocates a larger array — typically double the size — and reinserts every entry. Rehashing spreads entries across more slots, which shrinks the average chain or probe length. The threshold is the load factor. Chaining tolerates load factors above 1.0 because lists can grow without bound; open addressing cannot, because the array has no room past full. Most open-addressing maps resize at 0.6 to 0.75.

The choice between the two trades memory for cache locality. Chaining spends a pointer per entry on list overhead. Open addressing spends no per-entry memory but degrades faster as the array fills, because collisions pile into longer probe runs. A poor hash function makes either strategy slow — it concentrates keys into few slots, and no collision strategy fixes a function that maps most keys to the same index.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each entry paired with a pointer back to the full row. The database queries the index instead of scanning the table when a query filters on an indexed column.

Without an index, finding rows matching a condition means reading every row in the table and discarding the ones that fail. A table of ten million rows takes ten million row reads. With a B-tree index on the filtered column, the database walks a balanced tree of depth four or five, compares keys at each node, and reaches the matching leaf in four or five disk reads. That is the case where an index helps: a query narrows a large table to a small set of rows using a column the index sorts.

The index hurts in four concrete situations.

**Writes pay twice.** An `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must modify both the table and the index. A table with six indexes takes seven writes per inserted row — one to the table, one to each index. A bulk load of one million rows into a table with six indexes performs seven million writes instead of one million. Indexes trade read speed for write speed, and that trade is literal: every index on a table adds one write operation to every row modification on the indexed columns.

**Low-selectivity columns waste the index.** An index on a column with few distinct values — a boolean flag, a status field with three states — selects large fractions of the table. A query for `WHERE active = true` on a table where 90% of rows are active returns nine million of ten million rows. The database reads the index, collects nine million row pointers, then fetches nine million rows by pointer. Random row fetches by pointer are slower than a sequential scan, because sequential reads exploit disk and cache bandwidth that random access cannot. The database's query planner knows this and will skip the index, scanning the table directly — which means the index sits on disk, consuming space and slowing writes, while serving no query.

**Storage cost is real.** An index on a 40 GB table adds storage proportional to the indexed columns plus pointer overhead. A composite index on two columns of a wide table can reach 20% of the table's own size. Six indexes on a 40 GB table can add 30 GB of index storage. That is disk space, backup time, and memory pressure when the database tries to cache hot indexes in RAM.

**The planner can choose wrong.** A query planner estimates how many rows an index will return using table statistics. If those statistics are stale — the table grew or shifted distribution since the last statistics update — the planner may pick an index path that returns far more rows than estimated, triggering millions of random reads where a sequential scan would have been faster. The index is not broken; the planner's information was. Most databases expose an `EXPLAIN` command that shows which path the planner chose and why. Running `EXPLAIN` on a slow query reveals whether the planner picked an index scan that fetches more rows than it expected.

The rule is narrow. An index helps when a query filters a large table down to a small result set on a column with many distinct values. It hurts when the column selects most of the table, when writes outnumber reads, or when the storage and maintenance cost buys no query speedup. Dropping an unused index is free performance gain on every write, and most databases expose per-index read and write counts to identify which indexes earn their keep.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. The sender attaches a 32-bit sequence number to the first byte of every segment it transmits. That number is not a segment index — it is the byte offset within the connection's data stream. If the first segment carries bytes 1 through 1000, the second carries 1001 through 2000, and its sequence number is 1001.

IP, the protocol that carries TCP segments between machines, makes no delivery guarantee. Segments can arrive out of order, in duplicate, or not at all. TCP's sequence numbers are the mechanism that turns that unreliable transport into an ordered byte stream.

The receiver stores incoming segments in a receive buffer. When segment 2001 arrives before segment 1001, the receiver holds it. It cannot deliver bytes 2001 through 3000 to the application yet, because the application expects the stream in order, and byte 1001 has not arrived. The buffer holds the out-of-order segment until the gap fills.

Each segment the receiver sends back carries an acknowledgment number. That number is the byte offset of the next byte the receiver expects. If the receiver has correctly received bytes 1 through 2000, its acknowledgment says 2001. An acknowledgment of 2001 implicitly confirms receipt of every byte before 2001. This is a cumulative acknowledgment: the receiver tells the sender the lowest byte it has not yet seen, not the set of bytes it has.

When the sender transmits segment 1001 and receives no acknowledgment within a timeout, it retransmits. The timeout is adaptive — TCP measures the round-trip time to the receiver and sets the timeout as a multiple of that measurement, adjusted as network conditions change. A timeout that fires too early causes redundant retransmissions; one that fires too late stalls the connection. The adaptive estimate, called the retransmission timeout, balances both.

Once the missing segment arrives, the receiver checks its buffer. If bytes 1001 through 3000 are now all present, the receiver delivers them to the application in order and sends an acknowledgment for 3001. The application never sees the gap or the reordering. It receives a single, contiguous stream of bytes in the order the sender wrote them.

Duplicate segments are handled by the same numbers. If the network retransmits a segment that already arrived, the receiver sees a sequence number within the range it has already acknowledged. It drops the duplicate and re-sends the current acknowledgment, which tells the sender the segment already arrived.

Flow control bounds the buffer. The receiver's acknowledgment includes a window size — the number of bytes of free space remaining in its receive buffer. If the application reads slowly, the buffer fills, the window shrinks, and the sender stops transmitting until the window opens. This prevents the sender from overrunning a slow receiver, which would force dropped segments and retransmissions.

The sequence number, the cumulative acknowledgment, the buffer, and the timeout together maintain order. The numbers identify each byte. The acknowledgment tells the sender what the receiver has. The buffer holds what arrived early. The timeout recovers what never arrived. The application reads the result as a stream in the order it was written.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state across two or more threads.

A thread is a sequence of instructions that runs concurrently with others on the same memory. Two threads can read and write the same variable. The CPU executes their instructions in an order it chooses, switching between threads at any point — between instructions, and on most architectures, partway through a compound read-modify-write at the hardware level. A mutex serializes those accesses so the interleaving cannot corrupt the state.

The corruption is concrete. A counter increment reads the current value, adds one, and writes the result back. Three instructions. If thread A reads 5, and thread B reads 5 before A writes, both write 6. Two increments produced one. The counter lost an update. A mutex around the increment forces A's read and write to complete before B begins its read. The counter reaches 7.

The mutex does this with two operations. A thread locks the mutex before touching the shared state and unlocks it after. While one thread holds the lock, any other thread that calls lock blocks — it stops running and waits until the holder unlocks. The lock and unlock bracket a region called the critical section. Inside that region, only one thread executes at a time. The state is consistent because no other thread can observe or modify it mid-operation.

The protection is narrower than it looks. A mutex guards against concurrent access to the state behind it, nothing more. It does not guard against access through a second pointer that bypasses the lock. It does not guard against a thread that reads the protected value, unlocks, and then uses the stale value after another thread has changed it — the lock was released, the protection ended. It does not make a non-reentrant operation safe if the same thread locks the mutex twice and deadlocks against itself.

A mutex does not protect against deadlocks. Two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's mutex will both block forever. The mutex caused the deadlock; it did not prevent it. The fix is lock ordering — a rule that all threads acquire the same set of mutexes in the same sequence — and that fix is discipline in the code, not a property of the mutex.

What a mutex does not protect is the larger category. It does not protect against memory being freed by one thread while another holds a pointer to it — that is a lifetime problem, solved by reference counting or garbage collection. It does not protect against cache-line contention where many threads hammer the same lock and serialize the whole program — that is a performance problem, solved by finer-grained locks or lock-free structures. It does not protect against priority inversion, where a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority thread preempts the low-priority thread so the high-priority thread waits behind work that does not matter — that is a scheduling problem, addressed by priority inheritance protocols in the kernel.

The mutex is one tool with one job. It makes a region of code execute on one thread at a time. The state inside that region stays consistent because the interleaving is gone. Everything outside that job — lifetime, performance, scheduling, the discipline of acquiring locks in order — is a separate problem the mutex does not touch.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches and returns it to the allocator. The core question is reachability: can any running code still get to this object through a chain of references starting from a root?

**Tracing** walks that chain. The collector starts from a fixed set of roots — the stack frames of every running thread, the global variables, the CPU registers that hold object pointers. From each root it follows every pointer to the object it names, marks that object as live, then follows every pointer inside that object to the next, and the next. When the walk stops, every object the mark reached is reachable. Every object the mark did not reach is garbage. The collector then sweeps the heap: it walks every allocated object, frees the unmarked ones, and clears the marks on the survivors for the next cycle. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme used by the JVM and the .NET CLR.

**Reference counting** takes the other path. Every object carries a counter of how many pointers currently name it. A new pointer increments the counter; a dropped pointer decrements it. When the counter hits zero, no reference to the object exists, and the collector frees it immediately. The object frees itself the instant the last reference dies, with no pause to walk the heap. CPython uses this for most objects; Swift's ARC and C++'s `shared_ptr` apply the same mechanism at compile time through inserted increment and decrement calls.

Reference counting breaks on cycles. Object A points to B, B points to A, and both have a count of one. Neither counter reaches zero. Both are garbage — nothing outside the cycle reaches either — but the counters say live. A tracing collector catches the cycle because the mark walk never starts from a root and never reaches A or B. A reference-counting collector needs a separate cycle detector: a periodic trace that identifies groups of objects whose only references come from inside the group. CPython runs such a detector every few hundred allocations; without it, a cycle of two objects leaks forever.

Tracing pauses the program while it walks. A heap of ten million objects means the collector touches ten million objects before the program resumes. The pause grows with the heap, which is why tracing collectors partition the work. **Generational collection** rests on the observation that most objects die young — a study of Lisp systems in the 1980s measured that 80 to 98 percent of objects are unreachable by the time the first collection runs. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and one or more old generations. It collects the young generation frequently and cheaply, because it is small and most of its contents are already dead. Objects that survive several young-generation collections get promoted to an old generation, which the collector scans rarely. The JVM's G1 collector and .NET's managed heap both work this way.

**Concurrent collection** moves the trace work off the application's threads. The collector marks objects while the program runs, which means a pointer the program holds could change while the collector is following it. The collector handles this with a write barrier: every pointer write the program makes triggers a small piece of bookkeeping that tells the collector the object's references changed, so it re-examines that object before the cycle ends. The barrier costs a few instructions per write. The trade is shorter pauses at the price of steady overhead. Go's garbage collector is concurrent and uses a write barrier; the JVM's ZGC and Shenandoah do the same to keep pauses under ten milliseconds on multi-gigabyte heaps.

The two strategies answer the same question differently. Tracing asks what is reachable and frees the rest in a batch. Reference counting asks whether each object still has a holder and frees it the moment the answer is no. Tracing handles cycles and tolerates high allocation rates but pauses the program. Reference counting avoids pauses on death but leaks on cycles and spends a counter update on every pointer write. Most production runtimes pick tracing, because the allocation patterns of real programs — many short-lived objects, few long-lived ones — make the generational trace cheap on average, and the cycle problem in reference counting is harder to solve than the pause problem in tracing.

A race condition is a bug where a program's output depends on the order in which two concurrent operations execute, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads the balance, adds 50, and writes 150 back. Thread B reads the balance, subtracts 30, and writes 70 back. If A reads before B writes, the balance should be 120. If B reads before A writes, it should be 120. The arithmetic is commutative. The problem is the interleaving.

A balance update is three instructions: read the current value into a register, add or subtract, write the result back. The CPU can switch threads between any two of those instructions. Thread A reads 100. Before A writes 150, the scheduler switches to thread B. B reads 100, subtracts 30, writes 70. The scheduler switches back to A. A writes 150. The balance is 150. Thirty dollars vanished. B's write happened, then A's write overwrote it, and nothing in the program recorded that B's update existed.

The word "race" names the cause. Both threads race to read the balance before either writes it back. Whichever thread writes last wins, and the other thread's update is lost. The operating system's scheduler, not the program, decides who wins. Run the code twice and the result can differ. Run it a thousand times and the failure appears at random, which is why races are hard to reproduce and hard to debug.

The fix is to make the three instructions atomic — indivisible from the perspective of the other thread. A mutex around the read-add-write block forces thread B to wait until A has written 150. B then reads 150, subtracts 30, writes 120. Both updates survive. The balance is correct because the interleaving is gone.

The bug is not in the arithmetic. Each thread's logic is correct in isolation. The bug is in the assumption that reading the balance means the balance will not change before the write. That assumption holds when one thread runs. It breaks when two do, because "read, then write" is not one operation to the CPU. It is two, and anything can happen between them.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by holding copies of the data the processor is most likely to read next, so the processor does not wait on the slower main memory to supply it.

The speed gap is the reason the cache exists. A modern CPU can execute several instructions per nanosecond. Main memory, by contrast, takes roughly 100 nanoseconds to return a single value. A processor reading every value from main memory would spend most of its time idle, waiting on the wire. The cache closes that gap. A hit — data already in the cache — returns in one to three nanoseconds, roughly fifty times faster than the round trip to main memory.

The cache exploits a pattern called locality. Programs do not read memory at random. They read a byte, then the next byte, then the one after that. A loop walking an array touches consecutive addresses. That is spatial locality. They also read the same byte over and over. A loop variable, a function's local variables, the top of a stack frame — the processor returns to them each iteration. That is temporal locality. The cache loads data based on both. On a miss, it does not fetch one byte from main memory. It fetches a block, called a cache line, typically 64 bytes. If the program reads the next byte, it is already in the cache.

Caches sit in levels. A chip has a small L1 cache, 32 to 64 kilobytes, split into one for data and one for instructions, close enough to the core to return in a single cycle. A larger L2 cache, 256 kilobytes to one megabyte, serves a miss from L1 in roughly ten cycles. A still larger L3 cache, eight to sixty-four megabytes, shared across the cores on the die, serves a miss from L2 in roughly forty cycles. A miss from L3 drops to main memory and its hundred-nanosecond penalty. Each level is larger and slower than the one before. The hierarchy works because a program's working set — the data it touches in a short window — is usually small enough to fit in the upper levels.

The cache is finite, so it must evict. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, the controller discards an old line to make room. The policy is usually least-recently-used: throw out the line that has gone longest without a read. The assumption is that data used recently will be used again soon, and data ignored for a long time will not. The policy is a heuristic, and it fails when the working set is larger than the cache. A program scanning a 200-megabyte array through a 32-kilobyte L1 will thrash: every new line evicts a line the program has not finished with, and the hit rate collapses. The cache is not helping; it is just adding the cost of loading lines the program will not read again before they are evicted.

The program that respects the cache is faster than the one that ignores it. Storing data in contiguous arrays rather than linked lists keeps consecutive reads in the same cache line. Walking an array in order rather than by strided access keeps the prefetcher — a hardware unit that guesses which lines are coming next and loads them ahead of the request — fed with a predictable pattern. The cache does not make a slow algorithm fast. It makes a cache-friendly algorithm run at the speed of the cache instead of the speed of main memory, and that difference is a factor of fifty.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as if it received it once.

`GET` is the clear case. A `GET /users/42` returns the same user representation on the first call and the tenth. The server's state does not change, so the state after one call matches the state after ten. The HTTP specification lists `GET` as safe — it reads without writing — and idempotent.

`PUT` writes, and it is idempotent by contract. `PUT /users/42` with a body of `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada. The first call changes the name from Grace to Ada. The second call sets the name from Ada to Ada. The server's state after the second call is identical to its state after the first. The client can retry the request after a network timeout without risk of duplicating or compounding the change.

`DELETE` is idempotent by the same logic. `DELETE /users/42` removes user 42. The first call deletes the user. The second call finds no user 42 and returns 404, or returns 204 to signal the resource is gone. The server's state — user 42 absent — is the same after both calls. The response body or status code can differ between the first and second call. Idempotency governs the server's state, not the response bytes.

`POST` is the method that breaks idempotency. `POST /users` with a body of `{"name": "Ada"}` creates a new user. The first call creates user 43. The second call creates user 44. The server's state differs after the second call — two users exist where one did. A client that retries the `POST` after a timeout produces a duplicate. This is why payment APIs warn against retrying `POST /charges`, and why order systems generate duplicate orders when a client resubmits a form.

The practical fix for non-idempotent `POST` is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique string — a UUID — and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. On the second request with the same key, the server returns the stored result instead of executing the operation again. Stripe's API documents this pattern: a key is retained for 24 hours, and a retried request with a stored key returns the original response's status code and body. The key turns a non-idempotent `POST` into an idempotent operation by making the server remember the first execution and refuse to repeat it.

The distinction matters where networks are unreliable. A client sends a request. The server processes it and sends a response. The response is lost. The client does not know whether the server processed the request, so it retries. If the operation is idempotent — `PUT`, `DELETE`, a `GET` — the retry is safe. The server's state is the same whether the original succeeded or not. If the operation is a bare `POST`, the retry risks a duplicate. The HTTP specification's method safety table exists so a client can decide whether to retry without asking the server.

DNS resolves a hostname through a hierarchy of servers, each answering only the part it knows. The resolver, the client, the root, the top-level domain, and the authoritative server each hold a different piece of the answer.

A program asks the operating system's resolver for `www.example.com`. The resolver is usually a stub — a small library routine that forwards the query to a caching resolver run by the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1 or Google at 8.8.8.8. The caching resolver does the actual walk.

If the caching resolver has `www.example.com` in memory from a recent query, it returns the address immediately. That cache entry has a time-to-live, a TTL in seconds set by the domain owner. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver holds the answer for one hour, then discards it and asks again. The cache is why DNS is fast on average: most lookups never traverse the hierarchy.

On a cache miss, the caching resolver asks a root server. The root servers are thirteen named clusters, A through M, operated by ICANN, Verisign, and universities. Their addresses are compiled into every resolver. The root server does not know `www.example.com`. It knows only which servers hold the `.com` top-level domain. It returns that list.

The caching resolver picks a `.com` server and asks the same question. The `.com` registry, run by Verisign, does not know `www.example.com` either. It knows which name servers are authoritative for `example.com`. It returns those.

The caching resolver asks the authoritative server for `example.com`. This server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds the A record for `www`, which contains the IPv4 address — say, `93.184.216.34` — and returns it. The caching resolver caches that address for the record's TTL, then hands it to the stub resolver, which hands it to the program.

The full walk touches four servers: the root, the `.com` registry, the `example.com` authoritative server, and the caching resolver in between. Each step narrows the question. The root answers "who knows `.com`?" The `.com` server answers "who knows `example.com`?" The authoritative server answers "what is the address of `www`?" No single server holds the whole answer. The hierarchy distributes the knowledge so no one server must track every domain on the network.

The system handles aliases through CNAME records. If `www.example.com` is a CNAME pointing to `example.com`, the authoritative server returns the CNAME instead of an address. The caching resolver restarts the walk for `example.com`, asking the same authoritative server for its A record. One name becomes two lookups. A chain of CNAMEs becomes three or four. Most resolvers cap the chain at five or ten to stop loops.

The protocol runs over UDP port 53. A query and its response each fit in a single UDP packet, which keeps the round trip cheap. If the response exceeds 512 bytes — a domain with many records — the resolver retries over TCP. DNSSEC, an extension that signs records cryptographically, adds signature data that pushes responses past the UDP limit, so signed domains usually resolve over TCP. The signature lets the resolver verify that the answer came from the authoritative server and was not modified in transit.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads each hold a resource the other needs, and each waits for the other to release it. Neither moves. The program stalls at that point forever.

The structure is a cycle. Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y. Thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. A cannot proceed because B holds Y. B cannot proceed because A holds X. Each thread's progress depends on the other's, and neither gives ground. The operating system will not break the tie. It schedules both threads, finds each blocked on a lock the other owns, and leaves them blocked. The deadlock persists until the process is killed.

Four conditions must hold at once for this to happen. The threads hold resources exclusively — one lock, one owner. They hold while waiting — a thread does not release X before requesting Y. The resources are not preempted — the kernel will not force a lock away from its holder. And there is a circular wait — A waits on B, B waits on A, closing the loop. Break any one condition and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest condition to break is the circular wait, and the standard way to break it is lock ordering. Every thread in the program acquires locks in the same sequence. If the rule is "acquire X before Y," thread A locks X, then Y. Thread B locks X, then Y. Thread B cannot hold Y while waiting for X, because it must acquire X first, and X is held by A. B blocks at the first lock, before it owns anything. A finishes its work, releases both, and B proceeds. The cycle never closes because the ordering rule makes it impossible for two threads to hold locks in opposite order.

The discipline costs little when the lock order is local to one function. It costs more when locks are held across function boundaries, where a caller holds one lock and the callee acquires another. The callee must know the caller's lock state to place its own acquisition correctly, and that knowledge spreads through the code as an implicit contract. A violation in one function can reintroduce the cycle the rest of the program avoids. The rule is simple to state and hard to keep: pick an order, write it down, and never acquire out of order. The deadlock disappears because the structure that produced it cannot form.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. The hash function spreads keys across the array; the array stores the values. When two different keys hash to the same index, a collision occurs, and the map needs a strategy to keep both.

The two strategies in real use are separate chaining and open addressing.

**Separate chaining** stores a linked list at each bucket. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list at that index, and appends a new node if the key is absent. On lookup, it walks the same list comparing keys one by one. A bucket with eight colliding keys holds eight nodes; the map finds the right one by scanning. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` work this way. The cost is an extra pointer per entry and a list walk that grows with the chain length.

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the array, no lists. On insert, the map hashes the key and checks the slot at that index. If it is occupied, the map probes a second index computed from the first, and keeps probing until it finds an empty slot. On lookup, it follows the same probe sequence, comparing keys at each occupied slot, until it finds the key or an empty slot. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Go's built-in map use open addressing.

The probe sequence is where implementations diverge. **Linear probing** steps forward by one: index, index+1, index+2. It is cache-friendly because consecutive slots sit in the same cache line, but it creates clustering — a run of occupied slots grows longer with each collision, and every probe that lands inside the run extends it. **Quadratic probing** jumps by squares: index+1, index+4, index+9. It breaks up clusters but can miss slots if the table size and step constants share a factor. **Double hashing** computes the probe step from a second hash of the key, so different keys follow different paths through the table. It avoids clustering but costs a second hash per probe.

Robin Hood hashing, used in Rust's `HashMap`, is a variant of open addressing. On insert, the map tracks how far each entry sits from its ideal slot. When a probe encounters an entry that is closer to home than the one being inserted, it evicts that entry and continues inserting the displaced one. This keeps the maximum probe length small — the worst case improves at the cost of more work on the average insert.

Every strategy degrades when the table fills. A chained bucket with twenty keys takes twenty comparisons. An open-addressed table at 99% capacity probes dozens of slots per insert. So hash maps resize. When the load — the ratio of entries to slots — crosses a threshold, the map allocates a larger array, rehashes every entry into it, and discards the old one. Chained maps tolerate high load factors; Java's `HashMap` resizes at 0.75. Open-addressed maps need headroom; Python's `dict` keeps at least one-third of slots empty. Resizing is O(n) in entries, but it happens rarely enough that the amortized cost per operation stays O(1).

Deletion adds a wrinkle to open addressing. Removing an entry and leaving its slot empty breaks probe sequences: a lookup that passed through that slot stops early and reports the key absent. The fix is a tombstone — a marker that says "this slot was occupied; keep probing past it." Tombstones accumulate, wasting slots and lengthening probes, until the next resize clears them. Chained maps have no such problem; removing a node from a list leaves the rest intact.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast. Without one, finding rows where `last_name = 'Smith'` requires reading every row in the table and discarding the non-matches. With an index on `last_name`, the database finds the matching rows in roughly three or four page reads instead of thousands.

The structure is usually a B-tree. The B-tree keeps its keys in sorted order and balances itself on every insert, so the depth stays around three or four levels for tens of millions of rows. Each level is one disk read. The leaf nodes hold the key values and pointers to the actual table rows, or in a covering index, the values of other columns too, so the database never touches the main table at all.

An index hurts in three situations.

The first is write load. Every insert, update, or delete on an indexed column requires updating the index as well as the table. A table with five indexes takes six writes per row insert. On a system that logs a thousand events per second, those extra writes dominate disk I/O. The read speedup on the query side has to outweigh the write cost on the ingest side, or the index is a net loss.

The second is low selectivity. An index on a column with two values, like `is_active` where 99% of rows are true, helps nothing. The query planner sees that the index would return almost the entire table and skips it, scanning instead. The index still costs writes on every update to `is_active`, and it still occupies disk space, but it never gets used. The rule of thumb is that an index pays off when it narrows the result to a small fraction of the table — under 5% is the common threshold, though the real number depends on the database, the disk, and the query.

The third is storage and memory. Each index is a copy of part of the table, sorted and organized. A table with a primary key plus four secondary indexes plus a covering index can easily spend more bytes on indexes than on data. Those bytes compete for the buffer pool — the in-memory cache the database uses to avoid disk reads. An index that is never queried but sits in the cache evicts a table page that is queried constantly. The index not only wastes disk; it slows the reads it was supposed to help.

The query planner decides whether to use an index per query, based on table statistics the database collects. A planner can choose wrong if the statistics are stale — a table that grew tenfold since the last statistics update can fool the planner into using an index that now returns half the table. Most databases collect statistics automatically, but the schedule varies. PostgreSQL's autovacuum does it; MySQL's `ANALYZE TABLE` runs on a configurable cadence. Stale statistics produce slow queries on tables that have the right indexes.

A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone, because the B-tree sorts by the leftmost column first. It does not serve queries that filter on `first_name` alone, because the first names are only sorted within each last name. This leftmost-prefix rule means column order in a composite index determines which queries it helps. Ordering the columns by selectivity — most selective first — is the usual heuristic, though queries that filter on the first column alone override it.

The cost of an index is paid on every write whether the index is used or not. The benefit is paid only on the queries that hit it. An index that serves one nightly report and slows a thousand inserts per second is a net cost. Dropping it and letting the report run slower is the better trade.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. The sender attaches a sequence number to every byte; the receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order before handing it to the application.

The handshake establishes the starting point. When a connection opens, the sender transmits a SYN segment carrying an initial sequence number — a 32-bit value chosen by the sender's clock or a counter, not zero. The receiver acknowledges it with SYN-ACK, echoing that number plus one. Once the handshake completes, both sides agree on the first byte's sequence number, and every subsequent segment counts forward from there.

Each data segment carries two fields: the sequence number of the first byte in its payload, and an acknowledgment number indicating the next byte the sender of the segment expects to receive. A segment carrying sequence number 1000 and 500 bytes of payload covers bytes 1000 through 1499. The receiver, on getting it intact, sends back an ACK with acknowledgment number 1500 — "I have everything through 1499; send 1500 next."

Segments can arrive out of order. IP routes each packet independently, and a later packet can take a shorter path and overtake an earlier one. A segment for bytes 2000–2499 might land before the segment for bytes 1500–1999. The receiver holds the early one in a buffer and waits. When 1500–1999 arrives, the receiver places both in sequence, acknowledges 2500, and releases the contiguous run to the application.

The receive buffer is a sliding window. It holds out-of-order segments that arrived ahead of their predecessors, plus a pointer to the next byte the application has not yet read. The window's size, advertised in every ACK, tells the sender how much free space remains. If the buffer holds 64 KB and 40 KB is filled with bytes the application has not consumed, the receiver advertises a window of 24 KB. The sender stops transmitting once it has that many bytes in flight unacknowledged.

Gaps trigger retransmission. The receiver ACKs only the highest contiguous byte it has received, so a missing segment produces a stream of duplicate ACKs — the same acknowledgment number repeated as later segments arrive and fill the buffer beyond the gap. Three duplicate ACKs for the same number tell the sender that the segment starting at that byte was lost. The sender retransmits it without waiting for its retransmission timer to expire. This is fast retransmit, and it closes most gaps in one round-trip rather than waiting for a timeout.

The retransmission timer handles the cases fast retransmit misses. The sender starts a timer when it transmits a segment and resets it on each ACK. If the timer expires, the sender resends the oldest unacknowledged segment. The timer duration adapts to the connection's measured round-trip time, smoothed over recent samples, with a variance multiplier to absorb jitter. A connection over a 40 ms link sets a shorter timeout than one over a 200 ms link.

The sequence number space is finite — 32 bits, about 4.3 billion values — and wraps. A long-lived connection sending a gigabyte per second exhausts the space in four seconds. TCP handles this by treating the numbers as a circular space and using the window size to keep the in-flight range narrow enough that old and new segments with the same number cannot coexist. The wrap is arithmetic, not a special event; the receiver compares numbers using modular subtraction, so 4294967295 and 0 are one byte apart, not four billion.

What the application receives is a byte stream with no gaps and no reordering, regardless of what happened underneath. TCP's contract is that the bytes arrive in the order they were sent, or the connection reports an error. The sequence numbers, the buffer, the ACKs, and the retransmissions are the machinery that keeps that contract.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can touch the same variable at the same instant. Thread A reads `balance`, adds 100, writes it back. Thread B reads `balance`, subtracts 50, writes it back. If both reads happen before either write, one update vanishes. The final balance reflects one operation, not two. The CPU did exactly what it was told; the instructions just overlapped in a way that lost a result.

The mutex fixes this by making the read-modify-write sequence atomic. A thread that wants the variable locks the mutex, does its work, unlocks. A second thread that calls lock while the first holds it blocks — the operating system parks it off the run queue — until the first unlocks. Only one thread is inside the critical section at a time. The lost update cannot happen.

What a mutex does not protect against is everything else. It does not make a single read or write atomic on its own; most architectures guarantee that for aligned words, but a 64-bit write on a 32-bit machine is two bus cycles, and a mutex around it is the difference between a torn value and a clean one. It does not provide ordering between threads on separate variables — that is a memory barrier's job, and most mutex implementations fold one in, but the barrier is doing work the lock itself does not describe. It does not prevent deadlock: two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other will wait forever, and the mutex has no opinion on that.

It also does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. A standard mutex locked twice by the same thread deadlocks on the second call — the lock is already held, and the thread blocks on itself. A recursive mutex permits this by tracking ownership and a count, but recursive locks mask design problems: a function that locks because it does not know whether its caller already locked is a function with an unclear contract.

The cost is two things. Contention: when N threads want the mutex, N−1 wait, and the work goes serial. On a four-core box, four threads contending on one mutex run at the speed of one. The system call: a lock acquired without contention is a single atomic instruction in user space, tens of nanoseconds. A contended lock that parks the thread is a context switch through the kernel, one to ten microseconds. The difference is a factor of a thousand, and it is the difference between a mutex that scales and one that does not.

A mutex is a binary gate around a piece of state. It admits one thread at a time and blocks the rest. It carries no opinion on what the state means, no ordering of unrelated accesses, no protection from the threads that hold it getting stuck on each other. It is the smallest tool that makes shared mutable state safe, and its limits are exactly the places where the larger tools — condition variables, read-write locks, lock-free structures — begin.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches, then frees it. The program allocates objects on a heap; the collector walks the ones still in use and reclaims the rest.

The root set is the starting point. Roots are the pointers the program can touch right now: registers, stack frames, global variables, fields in objects the runtime treats as always live. Every object reachable from a root is live. Every object not reachable from any root is garbage.

**Tracing** starts at the roots and follows pointers outward. The collector marks each object it reaches, walks that object's fields, marks the objects they point to, and continues until it has visited every reachable object. When the trace finishes, the heap divides into two sets: marked objects the program still uses, and unmarked objects it does not. The collector then sweeps the unmarked ones back onto the free list. This is mark-and-sweep, the algorithm behind Go's runtime, the JVM's basic collectors, and V8's major heap.

**Reference counting** takes the other approach: it counts, per object, how many pointers point to it. Assign `x = obj` and the count rises. Overwrite `x` and the count falls. When the count hits zero, no one holds the object, and the collector frees it at that moment rather than waiting for a trace. CPython uses this for everything; Objective-C's ARC does the same at compile time. The cost is two: every pointer assignment does a pair of atomic increments and decrements, and cycles defeat it. Two objects pointing at each other hold counts of one forever, even if nothing else reaches them. A reference-counting collector needs a separate tracing pass to find cycles, or it leaks them.

Tracing collectors pause the program while they work. A naive mark-and-sweep walks the entire heap with the mutator stopped, and on a four-gigabyte heap that pause runs hundreds of milliseconds. Real collectors cut that down several ways.

**Generational collection** rests on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. The heap splits into a young generation and an old one. New allocations go to the young space, which the collector scans frequently. Objects that survive a few young-gen collections get promoted to the old space, which the collector scans rarely. A web request that allocates a hundred temporary strings frees all of them in the next young-gen pass without ever touching the old space. The JVM, V8, and .NET all use this.

**Concurrent collection** moves the trace work onto a separate thread that runs alongside the program. The collector marks objects while the mutator keeps allocating and mutating. The hard part is the handoff: the mutator can change a pointer the collector already passed, leaving a reachable object unmarked. Collectors handle this with write barriers — the mutator notes every pointer change during the trace, and the collector re-scans those at the end. Go's concurrent mark-and-sweep does this, and its pauses stay under a millisecond on heaps of tens of gigabytes.

**Copying collection** trades space for simplicity. The heap splits into two equal halves, from-space and to-space. The collector copies every reachable object from from-space into to-space, packing them contiguously, and leaves the old space to be overwritten wholesale. Allocation in the new space is a pointer bump — no free list, no fragmentation. The cost is that half the heap sits empty at any given time. Young generations in the JVM and V8 use copying; old generations, where objects live long and copying them repeatedly wastes work, use mark-and-sweep or mark-and-compact instead.

**Mark-and-compact** is the third old-gen strategy. It marks live objects as in mark-and-sweep, then slides them together toward one end of the heap, closing the gaps left by dead objects. It reclaims fragmentation without reserving half the heap, but it touches every live object on every collection, and the compaction pass is the slowest part.

The collector's job is to distinguish live from dead. Live means reachable from a root, directly or through a chain of pointers. Dead means unreachable. The mechanism — tracing, counting, copying, compacting — is how it draws that line fast enough that the program does not notice.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

A bank account starts at 500. Two threads each deposit 100. Thread A reads the balance, sees 500, adds 100, gets 600. Thread B reads the balance before A writes, sees 500, adds 100, gets 600. A writes 600. B writes 600. The final balance is 600. One deposit is gone. The CPU ran both reads before either write, and the later write overwrote the earlier one.

The word "race" is literal. The two threads race to read the balance before either writes it back. Whoever reads first gets a stale value. The lost update is the consequence.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write sequence atomic — a mutex around the deposit, or an atomic compare-and-swap that retries if the value changed between read and write. Either way, the second thread cannot read until the first has written. The order is controlled, and both deposits land.

Races do not require threads. A signal handler that increments a counter while the main program reads it races the same way. An interrupt that updates a flag while the main loop checks it races too. Any time two execution contexts touch the same memory and at least one writes, the order matters, and uncontrolled order is the bug.

The danger is that the program works most of the time. A and B run in one order on one run, another order on the next. The bug surfaces only when the scheduler interleaves them in the losing pattern. A test that runs a thousand times and passes has not proven the race is absent; it has proven the losing interleaving did not occur in those thousand runs. A race is a correctness bug that hides behind timing.

Okay: explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain White/Orwell register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A CPU cache is a small block of SRAM sitting between the processor core and main memory. It speeds up a program by holding copies of the memory locations the program is about to read, so the processor does not wait for DRAM.

The speed difference is the whole reason. A register read takes one cycle. A cache hit takes three or four. A DRAM read takes two hundred to three hundred. A modern processor runs at three billion cycles per second, and DRAM has not kept pace. Without the cache, the core spends most of its time idle, waiting on a wire that delivers data two hundred times slower than the core can use it.

The cache works because programs do not touch memory at random. They touch it in patterns, and the two patterns are locality of reference.

The first is temporal locality. A program that reads a variable tends to read it again soon. A loop counter is read and written on every iteration. A stack pointer moves with every function call. The cache keeps recently accessed locations on the assumption that they will be needed again. The assumption is right often enough that the cache hits on most of those re-reads.

The second is spatial locality. A program that reads one byte tends to read the bytes next to it. Walking an array, executing sequential instructions, reading the fields of a struct — all step through memory in order. The cache exploits this by loading in blocks, not single locations. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. One miss pulls all 64 bytes from DRAM into the cache. The next seven reads hit the cache, because the bytes were fetched together.

The hierarchy is several layers. The L1 cache is smallest and closest: 32 to 48 kilobytes, on the core, one or two cycle latency. The L2 is larger and one step farther: 256 kilobytes to one megabyte, ten to twelve cycles. The L3 is shared across cores: eight to thirty-two megabytes, thirty to forty cycles. DRAM is the last resort, two hundred cycles out. A read checks L1, then L2, then L3, then memory. Each miss costs more time, and the goal of the hardware is to satisfy the read at the shallowest level that holds the data.

The hit rate determines the speedup. A program with a 95% L1 hit rate, 4% L2, and 1% DRAM has an average memory latency under eight cycles. The same program with a 90% L1 hit rate — five percentage points worse — averages closer to twelve. The cache turns a two-hundred-cycle operation into a three-cycle operation most of the time, and the program runs at the speed of the cache, not the speed of the RAM.

Cache misses come in three kinds, and the distinction matters for understanding why a program is slow.

A compulsory miss is the first read of a location. The data was never in the cache, so it must be fetched. Nothing avoids the first miss except prefetching — asking the hardware to fetch the next cache line before the program reads it.

A capacity miss happens when the cache is full. The program touched more data than the cache holds, and a line was evicted to make room. A loop that scans a four-megabyte array on a 32-kilobyte L1 will evict the first elements before it loops back, so the second pass reads them from DRAM again. The cache was too small for the working set.

A conflict miss happens when the cache's mapping forces a collision. Most caches are set-associative: a given memory location can sit in one of two or eight or sixteen slots, determined by a hash of its address. Two hot variables that hash to the same set will evict each other even when the rest of the cache is empty. The cache has room; the mapping does not.

The program controls the first two by how it touches memory. Sequential access, compact data structures, and reusing data while it is still in the cache turn misses into hits. Striding through memory with a large step, touching more data than the cache holds, and re-reading the same locations after they have been evicted turn hits into misses. The cache is hardware, but the hit rate is a property of the code.

Okay: explain idempotency for an HTTP API, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

An HTTP method is idempotent when a client can issue the same request twice and the server's observable state ends up the same as if it had been issued once. The second call does not duplicate the first; it produces the same result or reports the result the first call already produced.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads. Two identical GETs return the same representation, and neither changes the server. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces. A PUT that sets resource 42's body to `{"name":"Alice"}` leaves the resource in that state; issuing it again sets the same state again. `DELETE` is idempotent because it removes. The first DELETE on `/users/42` removes the user; the second returns 404, because the user is already gone, and the server state is unchanged from after the first.

`POST` is not idempotent. A POST that creates a new resource from the request body produces a new resource each time. Two identical POSTs to `/users` create two users with two different IDs. The server state grows with each call.

The distinction matters because networks are unreliable. A client sends a PUT, the server applies it, the response is lost in transit, and the client does not know whether the request landed. Retrying the PUT is safe: the server applies the same state again, and the resource ends up correct. Retrying a POST is not safe: the client cannot tell a lost response from a lost request, and re-sending creates a second order, a second charge, a second record.

The contract is defined in RFC 9110, which states that idempotency is a property of the method, not the implementation. A server that makes GET increment a counter has broken the contract, but the method is still idempotent by specification. The property tells clients which methods are safe to retry without reading the response, and which require a separate mechanism to avoid duplication.

That separate mechanism is an idempotency key. The client attaches a unique token to a POST request, usually in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key and the response it produced. On a retry with the same key, the server returns the stored response instead of running the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern: a POST to `/v1/charges` with a given key creates one charge, and every subsequent call with that key returns the original charge object. The key turns a non-idempotent method into an idempotent operation at the application layer.

Idempotency is not the same as safety. A safe method, defined in the same RFC, changes no server state at all — GET and HEAD are safe. An idempotent method may change state, but the change is the same on repeat calls — PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe. POST is neither. The two properties answer different questions: safety asks whether the method has side effects; idempotency asks whether the side effects accumulate on retry.

Okay: explain how DNS resolves a name to an address, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

DNS is a lookup system that translates a hostname like `www.example.com` into an IP address like `93.184.216.34`. The translation happens in steps, and each step involves a different server.

The process starts in the resolver. The resolver is a DNS server run by the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at `1.1.1.1` or Google at `8.8.8.8`. When an application asks for a name, the operating system sends the query to the resolver, which then does the work of finding the answer.

The resolver first checks its cache. If it recently looked up `www.example.com` and still holds the address, it returns that address immediately. No further network traffic occurs. Cache entries expire after a time-to-live, a number of seconds set by the name's owner. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver keeps the answer for one hour, then discards it and asks again.

On a cache miss, the resolver begins an iterative walk. It starts at the root servers, thirteen IP addresses authoritative for the top of the DNS hierarchy. The resolver asks the root for `www.example.com`. The root does not know the address, but it knows which servers handle the `.com` top-level domain. It returns those servers' names and addresses.

The resolver asks a `.com` TLD server the same question. The TLD server does not know the address either, but it knows the authoritative servers for `example.com`. It returns those. The resolver then asks `example.com`'s authoritative server, which holds the actual records for the domain. That server looks up `www` in its zone file and returns the A record containing `93.184.216.34`.

The resolver receives that address, caches it for the TTL, and hands it to the operating system, which hands it to the application. The application can now open a TCP connection to that address.

One more step appears when the target is a subdomain delegated to another service. `www.example.com` might be a CNAME pointing to `example.cdn.net`. The authoritative server for `example.com` returns the CNAME instead of an address. The resolver then starts a new lookup for `example.cdn.net`, walking from the root through the `.net` TLD to the CDN's authoritative servers, until it finds the A record. The application receives the final address, never seeing the intermediate name.

The walk sounds slow — root, TLD, authoritative, plus a CNAME chain — but the cache collapses it. The root and TLD server addresses almost never change, so resolvers cache them permanently. Popular domains stay in the resolver's cache from prior lookups. A cold resolution of `www.example.com` takes four round trips. A warm one takes zero. The system is fast because it remembers.

Okay: explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, White/Orwell register, every sentence carrying a fact.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither proceeds. Each waits forever for the other to release.

Two threads, A and B, and two mutexes, M1 and M2, produce the classic case. A locks M1, then tries to lock M2. B locks M2, then tries to lock M1. A holds M1 and waits for M2; B holds M2 and waits for M1. Neither releases what it holds until it gets what it waits for. The cycle never breaks.

Four conditions must hold simultaneously for this to happen. Mutual exclusion: each mutex is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one mutex requests another. No preemption: a thread cannot force another to release a mutex. Circular wait: a cycle of threads exists, each holding a mutex the next thread in the cycle needs. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The simplest avoidance is lock ordering. Every thread acquires mutexes in the same global order. If the rule is M1 before M2, A locks M1 then M2, and B locks M1 then M2. B cannot lock M2 first, so it cannot hold M2 while waiting for M1. The circular wait has no edge to form on. A thread that needs M2 alone locks M1 first, holds it briefly, locks M2, then releases M1 — or the protocol is defined so M2 is never acquired without M1 already held.

Lock ordering breaks the circular-wait condition. It costs nothing at runtime when the order is consistent, and it turns a bug that hides until the scheduler picks the losing interleaving into a structural impossibility. The cost is discipline: every code path that touches two mutexes must follow the order, and a single violation reintroduces the deadlock.

A hash map stores values at array slots chosen by a hash function over each key. Two keys that hash to the same slot collide, and the map needs a rule for keeping both.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each slot. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list, and either updates an existing entry or appends a new node. On lookup it walks the same list. The cost grows with the list length, so the map resizes its backing array — typically doubling — when the ratio of entries to slots crosses a threshold, often 0.75. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `unordered_map` both chain.

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the array. A collision sends the probe to another slot by a fixed rule: linear probing checks the next slot, quadratic probing checks slots at squared offsets, double hashing uses a second hash function as the step. Robin Hood hashing, used in Rust's `HashMap`, is a variant that minimizes the gap between a key's ideal and actual slot by stealing slots from richer keys. Lookup follows the same probe sequence until it finds the key or an empty slot. Deletion is the hard part: removing an entry and leaving a bare hole breaks the probe chain for keys that passed through it, so the map writes a tombstone marker that probes skip on insert but follow on lookup, and clears tombstones during a resize.

Chaining tolerates high load factors and never needs tombstones, but each entry carries a pointer and a node allocation that fragment cache locality. Open addressing keeps everything in one contiguous array, which modern CPUs prefetch well, but degrades sharply past about 70% full and requires careful deletion. The choice is a trade between memory overhead and cache behavior, not a question of one being correct.

A database index is a separate structure that lets a query find rows without scanning the table. It holds a copy of one or more columns in sorted order, each entry paired with a pointer back to the full row. The database walks this structure — usually a B-tree — to find matching keys, then fetches the rows by pointer. On a table of ten million rows, an index on a `user_id` column turns a query that reads all ten million into one that reads a handful.

Indexes cost storage and they cost writes. Every insert, update, or delete on an indexed column must update the index as well as the table. A table with five indexes pays six writes per row change. The B-tree must also stay balanced, so a single insert can trigger a page split that rewrites several disk blocks. On a read-heavy table this trade is obvious. On a table that absorbs thousands of writes per second, each index is a drag on the write path.

An index hurts when the query does not use it. A query that filters on `last_name` does not benefit from an index on `first_name`; the planner either ignores it and scans, or the database carries the index's write cost for nothing. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone, but an index on `(first_name, last_name)` does not serve a query that filters on `last_name` alone, because the B-tree is sorted leftmost-column first. This is the column-order rule, and it is the most common reason an index sits unused.

An index also hurts when it returns too much of the table. A query that selects all rows where `status = 'active'` on a table where ninety percent of rows are active will likely scan the table anyway, because reading the index and then fetching scattered rows is slower than reading the table in order. The planner estimates this selectivity and switches to a scan when the index would touch more than roughly five to ten percent of rows. An index on a low-cardinality column — a boolean flag, a status with three values — rarely helps a point query and never helps a range query that returns most of the table.

The index that earns its place is the one a real query uses. The way to know is the query plan: `EXPLAIN` in Postgres and MySQL, the execution plan in SQL Server. If the plan shows an index scan or index seek, the index is doing work. If it shows a table scan, the index is dead weight on the write path. Dropping an unused index is the cheapest performance win available, because it removes write cost and storage cost and returns nothing.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. Each byte gets a sequence number from a 32-bit counter that starts at a random value chosen during the handshake. Every segment the sender puts on the wire carries the sequence number of its first byte.

The receiver collects these segments and puts them in order by that number. A segment that arrives out of order — say, bytes 2001 through 3000 before bytes 1001 through 2000 — sits in a buffer until the gap fills. The receiver hands bytes to the application only in sequence, so the application never sees data out of order.

Acknowledgments close the loop. The receiver sends back an ACK carrying the next sequence number it expects, which is the number of the highest contiguous byte received plus one. An ACK of 3001 means the receiver has every byte through 3000. If bytes 1001 through 2000 are still missing, the receiver keeps ACKing 1001, even as later segments fill the buffer beyond the gap.

That repeated ACK is the signal for retransmission. Three duplicate ACKs with the same number tell the sender a segment was lost, and it resends the missing segment without waiting for a timer. This is fast retransmit. If no ACK arrives at all, a retransmission timer fires and the sender sends the oldest unacknowledged segment again.

The sequence number is what makes the guarantee. The receiver reassembles the stream by number, the sender retransmits by number, and the application reads bytes in the order they left the sender. The network can deliver segments late, early, or in duplicate; the receiver discards duplicates and buffers the early ones until the gap closes.

A mutex protects a region of code so that only one thread can run it at a time.

The problem it solves is the data race. Two threads read and write the same variable without coordination, and the result depends on which thread ran first. A counter increment is the textbook case: the CPU loads the value, adds one, stores it back. If a second thread loads between the first thread's load and its store, one increment is lost. The counter ends up one short.

The mutex fixes this by wrapping the read-modify-write in a lock and an unlock. A thread that wants the counter calls `lock`, does its work, and calls `unlock`. A second thread that calls `lock` while the first holds it blocks — the operating system suspends it — until the first calls `unlock`. The increment becomes atomic from the outside, even though the hardware instruction sequence is not.

A mutex protects the data, not the code. Two functions that touch the same shared variable must lock the same mutex, or the protection fails. A mutex private to one function leaves the variable exposed to any other function that reaches it. The discipline is: one mutex per shared resource, locked by every code path that reads or writes that resource.

The cost is contention. Threads that would have run in parallel queue up at the lock. A mutex held for a microsecond is cheap; a mutex held across a disk read or a network call serializes every thread that wants it. Locking only the short critical section — the load, the add, the store — and doing the slow work outside it keeps the lock hot and the threads parallel.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread. A function that locks a mutex and then calls another function that locks the same mutex deadlocks itself, because the lock is not recursive by default. A recursive mutex permits this, but it costs more and masks designs that should be restructured.

The guarantee is narrow and exact. One thread in the critical section, shared data consistent, threads blocked at the lock until it frees. Everything outside that scope — deadlocks from wrong ordering, priority inversion under scheduling, corruption from a forgotten unlock — is a failure to use the mutex correctly, not a failure of the mutex.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches and returns it to the heap.

A garbage collector starts from the roots: the stack's local variables, the CPU's registers, and the global variables the program can name directly. These are the things the running code can touch right now. From each root, the collector walks every pointer it finds, marking each object it reaches. An object that the trace visits is alive. An object that the trace never visits is garbage, because no path from any root leads to it.

The mark phase builds the set of live objects. The sweep phase walks the heap and frees everything unmarked. Together these are mark-and-sweep, the algorithm behind Go's runtime collector and the JVM's basic mode.
