The heap pauses while the collector works, because moving or freeing objects while the program holds pointers to them corrupts the program. That pause is the cost.

Generational collection cuts the pause by exploiting one observed fact: most objects die young. A generational collector splits the heap into a young region and an old region. New allocations go to the young region, which the collector scans frequently and cheaply. Objects that survive several young-region scans graduate to the old region, which the collector scans rarely. A web server that allocates a request object, builds a response, and discards it never touches the old region's collector. The young region is small, so scanning it is fast, and the pause shrinks.

A moving collector goes further. During the mark phase it copies every live object from the old heap region to a new one, packing them contiguously and leaving the gaps behind. It then rewrites every pointer the program holds to point at the new location. The old region, now empty, becomes free space in one move. Copying eliminates fragmentation — the scattered holes between live objects that make allocation slow — because the surviving objects are packed tight. The .NET runtime and the JVM's young generation both copy.

The collector that does not move must live with fragmentation. Mark-and-sweep leaves dead objects where they lay, and the heap fills with holes of varying sizes. An allocation that needs a block larger than any single hole fails, even if the total free space is enough. The collector can compact — slide live objects together and patch their pointers — but compaction is a moving collection in everything but name, and it pays the same pause.

Reference counting is the other branch, and it fails differently. Each object carries a count of incoming pointers; the collector decrements the count when a pointer drops and frees the object when the count hits zero. This reclaims memory the instant it becomes unreachable, with no pause and no trace. The failure is cycles. Two objects that point at each other keep each other's count above zero forever, even if no root reaches either. Python's runtime reference-counts but runs a periodic tracing collector to break cycles. A pure reference counter without a trace leaks.

The core idea is the same across every variant. The program holds pointers; the collector follows them; what no pointer reaches is free. The differences are in when the collector runs, how long it pauses, and whether it moves the survivors.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads the balance, adds 50, and writes 150. Thread B reads the balance, adds 50, and writes 150. The correct result is 200. Both threads read 100 before either writes, so one update overwrites the other and 50 vanishes. The balance is 150, not 200.

The load and the store are separate instructions. A thread that reads the balance does not hold a claim on it. Between the read and the write, the other thread is free to read the same stale value. The CPU does not know that the load and the store belong to one logical operation. It runs them as independent steps, and any other thread can interleave its own steps between them.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write atomic. A mutex around the balance update forces the second thread to wait until the first finishes its load, add, and store. The first thread writes 150 and releases the lock. The second thread reads 150, adds 50, and writes 200. The order is now fixed: one thread completes the full operation before the next begins.

Races exist outside threads. A program checks whether a file exists, then opens it. Between the check and the open, another process deletes the file. The open fails. This is a TOCTOU race — time-of-check to time-of-use — and the file system has no lock that prevents it. The fix is to open the file and handle the error if it is missing, collapsing the check and the use into one operation.

The defining trait is uncontrolled ordering. Two operations touch the same state, the scheduler or the operating system picks their sequence, and the program assumes a sequence it never enforced. The result is correct under one order and wrong under another, and the program has no control over which one runs.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It holds copies of the bytes the program is most likely to touch next.

The problem it solves is the speed gap. A modern processor can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but fetching a byte from DRAM takes around 100 nanoseconds. A CPU running at 3 GHz completes three instructions every nanosecycle, so a single memory stall costs roughly 300 instructions of lost work. The cache closes that gap by keeping hot data on the chip itself, where a read takes one to three nanoseconds.

The cache works because of locality. A program that reads `array[0]` almost always reads `array[1]` next. This is spatial locality, and the cache exploits it by fetching data in blocks, not single bytes. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors, so one memory read pulls 64 consecutive bytes into the cache. The next 63 reads hit the cache instead of main memory. A program that reads the same variable in a loop exhibits temporal locality, and the cache exploits that too: a recently accessed line stays in the cache until something evicts it.

The cache is a hardware hash table. The processor takes the memory address, splits it into a tag, an index, and a block offset, and checks the corresponding cache set. A hit returns the data immediately. A miss fetches the line from a slower level — L1 to L2, L2 to L3, L3 to DRAM — and each level is larger and slower than the last. A typical desktop CPU has 32 KB of L1 per core, 512 KB of L2 per core, and 8 to 16 MB of L3 shared across all cores.

The cost of a miss is the reason data layout matters. A program that walks a 64-byte struct to read one field, then walks the next struct to read the same field, pays one cache miss per struct. Packing the needed fields into a separate array of 8-byte values lets the program read 8 values per cache line, an eightfold reduction in misses. This is the difference between an array of structs and a struct of arrays, and it is why high-performance code reorganizes data around the access pattern.

The cache also explains why linked lists are slow for traversal. Each node is allocated separately, so the pointer chase from one node to the next lands on a new cache line with no spatial locality. A contiguous array walks memory in order, and the hardware prefetcher detects the stride and loads the next lines before the program asks for them. The linked list defeats both the cache and the prefetcher, and the program pays a DRAM latency for every node.

An HTTP method is idempotent when a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once.

`PUT` is the clean case. A client sends `PUT /items/42` with a body of `{"name": "widget"}`. The server creates item 42 or overwrites whatever item 42 held. The client sends the same request again. The server overwrites item 42 with the same body. The stored state is identical to the state after one request. The second call did work, but it left nothing changed that the first call had not already changed.

`DELETE` is idempotent by the same logic. The first request removes item 42. The second request finds no item 42 and returns 404, or returns 204 with no content. The server's state after the second response matches the state after the first: item 42 is gone. The response body differs, but idempotency is a property of state, not of the response.

`POST` is not idempotent. A client sends `POST /orders` with `{"item": "widget"}`. The server creates order 1001. The client sends the same request again. The server creates order 1002. Each call advanced the state, and repeating the call advanced it again. A client that retries a failed `POST` because the network dropped the response gets a duplicate order, because the server processed the first request and never told the client.

This distinction drives how clients retry safely. A phone that loses its connection after sending a request does not know whether the server received it. Retrying a `PUT` or `DELETE` is safe because a duplicate leaves the state unchanged. Retrying a `POST` is dangerous because the duplicate creates a second side effect. The fix is a client-generated idempotency key: a unique token in the request header that the server stores with the first result. On a retry, the server recognizes the key and returns the stored result instead of running the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern in its `Idempotency-Key` header.

`GET` and `HEAD` are idempotent in a weaker sense. They carry no side effects, so repeating them changes nothing because they change nothing the first time. The HTTP spec calls this "safe," a stricter property: a safe method changes no state on any call, while an idempotent method may change state on the first call but not on subsequent calls. `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent but not safe. `GET` is both.

The property that matters is the invariant. Send the request once, send it ten times, crash halfway and resend: the server's state is the state after one successful call. A method that breaks this invariant under retries is a bug in the API contract, not a quirk of the network.

Okay, explain DNS resolution end to end, in the plain register already established.

A program types `www.example.com` into a socket call and expects an IP address back. The operating system hands the name to a resolver, and the resolver walks a hierarchy of servers until one of them can answer.

The resolver first checks its own cache. If it has answered this name recently, it returns the address and stops. If not, it asks the root servers. There are thirteen root server addresses, published in a file every operating system ships, and each address is anycast to hundreds of physical machines. The root server does not know `www.example.com`. It knows which servers hold the top-level domains, and it returns a list of servers for `.com`.

The resolver takes that list and asks a `.com` server the same question. The `.com` server does not know `www.example.com` either. It holds the nameservers registered for `example.com`, and it returns those. The delegation is the whole mechanism: each server either answers or points one level down.

The resolver now asks `example.com`'s authoritative server. That server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds a record for `www`, reads the address, and returns it. The resolver caches the answer for the time-to-live the record carries, then hands the address to the program. The whole walk took three round trips, and the program never saw any of them.

Caching collapses the walk in practice. A home router or an ISP resolver sits between the program and the root, and it caches every answer it sees. A name that a neighbor looked up ten seconds ago returns from the ISP's cache in one round trip. The root servers see almost no traffic from end users, because nearly every query is answered by a cache somewhere above them.

The address record is the common case, but the hierarchy carries other types. A mail server looking up `example.com` asks for an MX record, which returns the name of the mail handler rather than an address, and the resolver then resolves that name. A browser looking up `www.example.com` may ask for an AAAA record, which returns an IPv6 address instead of the IPv4 address an A record carries. The query type tells the server what to return, and the server answers from its zone file or delegates downward.

The system works because the hierarchy is strict. The root delegates to `.com`, `.com` delegates to `example.com`, and `example.com` answers. A resolver that skips a level and asks the root for `www.example.com` gets a referral, not an answer. The walk is the protocol, and the cache is the optimization that keeps the walk from happening twice.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in the plain register already established.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and both wait forever for the other to give it up.

Thread A locks mutex X, then tries to lock mutex Y. Thread B locks mutex Y, then tries to lock mutex X. A holds X and waits for Y. B holds Y and waits for X. Neither releases what it holds until it gets what it waits for. Both stall. The program hangs.

The four conditions are necessary, and all four must hold at once. Mutual exclusion: the mutex lets only one thread hold it. Hold and wait: a thread keeps its lock while asking for the next. No preemption: the operating system will not force a lock away from a thread. Circular wait: the wait graph forms a loop, A→B→A. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest fix breaks circular wait by imposing a global order on the locks. The rule: every thread acquires mutexes in the same fixed sequence. If the order is X before Y, thread A locks X then Y and succeeds. Thread B, wanting both, also locks X first. It blocks at X until A releases Y and then X. Once B holds X it takes Y. The wait graph is a line, never a loop, because no thread holding a later lock ever waits for an earlier one.

The discipline is total. A code path that locks Y then X, even once, breaks the order and reintroduces the cycle. A function that calls into code locking an unknown mutex has stepped outside the guarantee. The order must cover every mutex in the program, or the unprotected pair can still deadlock.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array. It computes a hash from the key, maps that hash to an array index, and places the entry there. Two keys can land on the same index. That is a collision, and the map has to resolve it.

The oldest method is chaining. Each array slot holds a pointer to a linked list. When a key hashes to an occupied slot, the map appends the new entry to that list. Lookup walks the list, comparing keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The list grows with collisions, and a badly behaved hash function can turn the map into a set of linked lists — lookup degrades from O(1) to O(n). Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` use this approach.

Open addressing takes the other road. There is no list; the entry lives in the array itself. When a key's slot is taken, the map probes another slot according to a fixed rule. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the index. Double hashing computes a second hash to set the probe stride, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed step. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence; Robin Hood hashing, used in Rust's `HashMap`, steals slots from rich keys to keep the probe distance short.

Open addressing pays for its cache locality. Deleting an entry is not as simple as clearing a slot, because a later probe may have skipped past that slot. The map marks the slot as a tombstone — present for probing, absent for lookup — and reclaims it on the next insert or rehash. When the array fills past a load factor, typically 0.6 to 0.75, the map allocates a larger array and reinserts every entry. That rehash is O(n) but amortized to O(1) per operation.

Chaining tolerates high load factors because the lists absorb overflow. Open addressing degrades fast past its load threshold, since every filled slot forces another probe. The trade is memory locality against worst-case behavior under a hostile set of keys.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each entry paired with a pointer back to the full row. The database queries the index instead of scanning the table when a `WHERE` clause touches an indexed column. A B-tree index keeps those entries ordered, so the engine finds a value in O(log n) comparisons rather than reading every row.

The index earns its cost on writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that changes an indexed column must also update the index tree, sometimes rebalancing it. A table with five indexes takes roughly six times the write work of a table with none. The index also consumes disk and memory; an index on a wide text column can approach the size of the table itself.

An index hurts when the query cannot use it. A predicate like `WHERE lower(name) = 'alice'` defeats a plain index on `name` in most engines, because the function transforms the value after the index would have matched it. The same applies to `WHERE col + 1 = 5`. The engine falls back to a full scan, paying the write penalty on every modification while gaining nothing on read. Multi-column indexes carry an ordering constraint: an index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` but not `WHERE first_name = 'Alice'`, because the index sorts by last name first and the first names within each last name are not globally ordered.

A low-cardinality index — one on a column with few distinct values, like a boolean flag — rarely helps a point query. The engine still matches a large fraction of the table, and the cost of reading the index plus fetching the rows exceeds a direct scan. The optimizer recognizes this and ignores the index, but the write penalty remains.

The useful case is narrow and specific: a column queried often, written rarely, with enough distinct values that the index excludes most rows. A primary key fits this. A foreign key joined in a common query fits this. An audit timestamp queried by range fits this. Everything else is storage spent for speed never recovered.

TCP assigns each byte in a stream a sequence number drawn from a 32-bit counter the sender picks at connection start. The sender writes that number into the `Sequence Number` field of every segment it transmits. The receiver reads the field, uses it to place the segment's payload at the correct offset in the receive buffer, and delivers bytes to the application in order regardless of which segment arrived first.

Segment 2 can cross the wire before segment 1. A router reorders them; a link drops one and a retransmission fills the gap two seconds later. The receiver does not care. It buffers whatever arrives, sorts by sequence number, and hands the application a contiguous run from the lowest byte it has not yet delivered. The number is the address of each byte in the stream, and the buffer is the slot where that address lands.

When the receiver sees a gap — sequence 1000 arrived, 1001 did not, 1002 did — it holds 1002 in the buffer and sends an ACK carrying 1001. That number tells the sender "I have everything below this; send this one next." The ACK is cumulative: it acknowledges all bytes prior to the field's value, not just the last segment received. A duplicate ACK for 1001 means the receiver got something past the gap but still lacks 1001. Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit: the sender resends 1001 without waiting for its retransmission timer to expire.

The sender keeps a sliding window of bytes it has sent but not yet acknowledged. The left edge of the window is the lowest unacknowledged sequence number. When an ACK advances that edge, the window slides forward and the sender transmits new bytes. If an ACK does not arrive before the retransmission timer fires, the sender resends the leftmost segment and restarts the timer. The timer's duration adjusts to measured round-trip time, tightening on fast links and stretching on slow ones.

The sequence number space is finite: 32 bits, roughly 4.3 billion values. A connection running at 10 Gbps exhausts that space in 3.4 seconds. Two segments with sequence numbers 4.2 billion apart could wrap around and collide if one lingered in the network. TCP prevents this with PAWS — Protection Against Wrapped Sequence numbers — which stamps every segment with a 32-bit timestamp from the sender's clock. The receiver discards any segment whose timestamp is older than the most recent one seen on the connection, killing duplicates that survived a long detour even when their sequence numbers look valid.

The result is a byte stream that arrives in order at the application, whether the segments crossed the network in order, backward, in pieces, or twice.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of operations on shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can read and write the same memory at the same time. Thread A reads a balance of 100, adds 10, writes 110. Thread B reads 100 in the gap between A's read and A's write, adds 20, writes 120. The final balance is 120, not 130. Ten dollars vanished. The mutex exists to close that gap.

A mutex — mutual exclusion lock — is a flag with a queue. A thread calls `lock()` before touching the shared data and `unlock()` after. While one thread holds the lock, every other thread that calls `lock()` blocks until the holder calls `unlock()`. The operating system parks the blocked thread off the CPU and wakes it when the lock frees. The critical section, the code between `lock()` and `unlock()`, runs one thread at a time.

The protection is narrower than it looks. The mutex guards against concurrent access to whatever the critical section touches. It does not guard against access from a different mutex, from an interrupt handler that ignores the lock, or from a second thread that reads the variable without calling `lock()`. The mutex is a contract among the code paths that know about it. A thread that bypasses the contract breaks the invariant.

A mutex does not compose without care. Thread A locks mutex X then mutex Y. Thread B locks Y then X. Each holds one and waits for the other. That is deadlock — both sleep forever. The fix is a lock ordering discipline: every thread acquires the mutexes in the same sequence. The rule is simple to state and hard to enforce across a large codebase.

A mutex held too long serializes the program. Ten threads contending for one lock run no faster than one. The lock is the point where parallel work collapses back into a single stream. The discipline is to hold the lock for the shortest span that preserves the invariant — read the shared value, compute the update, write it back, release. Work that does not touch shared state stays outside the lock.

The mutex protects against reordering and tearing. Without it, a compiler may reorder memory writes for optimization, and a CPU may reorder them for execution. Another thread can see a half-written struct or fields in an unexpected sequence. The lock pairs an acquire on entry with a release on exit, and those operations insert memory barriers. The barriers force prior writes to become visible before the lock releases and prevent reads inside the section from floating above the acquire. The data is consistent because the ordering is enforced, not because the lock is fast.

Okay — explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, in the plain register already established.

A program allocates memory it cannot always free by hand. It asks the runtime for an object, uses it, and at some point loses the last pointer to it. The object is still alive in memory, but nothing in the program can reach it. Garbage collection is the mechanism that finds those unreachable objects and reclaims their space.

The collector starts from a fixed set of roots: the CPU registers, the call stacks of every thread, and the global or static variables the program can name directly. These are the things the program can touch right now. From each root, the collector walks every pointer it finds, then every pointer inside those objects, and marks each one it reaches. When the walk finishes, every object that was not marked is unreachable. The collector sweeps the heap, frees the unmarked objects, and leaves the marked ones in place. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme McCarthy described in 1960 and the ancestor of most collectors in use today.

The pause is the cost. The collector cannot safely walk a heap while a thread is mutating it, because a pointer could move mid-traversal and send the collector into dead memory. The original collectors stopped every thread, ran the full trace, and resumed. A program with a large heap could freeze for hundreds of milliseconds. That pause is what later designs attack.

A copying collector does not sweep. It divides the heap into two halves and allocates only from one. When that half fills, it traces from the roots, but instead of marking, it copies every reachable object into the empty half, packing them contiguously. Every pointer the collector copies gets updated to the new address. When the trace finishes, the old half is garbage in its entirety — one free operation, no sweep. The compacted heap has no fragmentation, and allocation is pointer bumping: the next object goes at the current free address, full stop. The cost is that the program runs with half its heap, because the other half sits empty until the next collection.

Generational collection rests on an observation: most objects die young. A function allocates a temporary list, builds it, returns a result, and the list is garbage. The collector partitions the heap by age. New objects go in the young generation, which is small and collected often. Objects that survive several young-generation collections get promoted to the old generation, which is large and collected rarely. The young collection is fast because the space is small and most of it is already dead. The old collection runs less often because old objects tend to stay alive. The trade is that a pointer from an old object to a young one — a new element inserted into a long-lived list — creates a reference the young collection must trace. The runtime maintains a remembered set, a card table or similar structure that records which old objects hold pointers into the young generation, so the young collector does not have to scan the entire old heap to find them.

Concurrent collectors move the trace off the application thread. The collector runs alongside the program, reading and marking the heap while the program mutates it. The hard problem is the race: the program stores a pointer into an object the collector has already visited, the collector does not see the new reference, and the object it points to gets collected while still reachable. Concurrent collectors solve this with write barriers — a small piece of code the runtime inserts after every pointer write, recording the mutation in a log the collector reprocesses before it decides what is dead. The pause shrinks to the barriers and the final reconciliation, not the full trace. The OpenJDK G1 collector and .NET's server GC work this way.

What every collector shares is the root set. The definition of garbage is not "the program is done with it" but "no root can reach it." An object held in a forgotten list that no code ever reads is not garbage. It is live, and the collector will not touch it. The collector cannot know intent. It knows reachability, and reachability is the only test it applies.

Okay — explain a race condition with a concrete example, in the plain register already established.

A race condition is what happens when two threads act on the same data and the outcome depends on which one gets there first. The program is correct if thread A runs before thread B, and wrong if B runs before A. Nothing inside the program fixes the order. The operating system scheduler picks it, and the scheduler does not care about the program's invariants.

The standard example is a bank balance. Two threads both read the balance, both add to it, both write it back. The balance starts at 100. Thread A reads 100, computes 100 + 10, and prepares to write 110. Before A writes, thread B reads 100, computes 100 + 20, and writes 120. Then A writes 110. The final balance is 110. Twenty dollars is gone. The code in both threads is correct in isolation. The failure exists only in the interleaving.

The read-modify-write sequence is three instructions, and a context switch can land between any two of them. A thread that reads the balance into a register is not holding a lock on the account. Another thread can read the same value, and both will write as though the other never ran. The memory is shared. The operations are not atomic.

The fix is to make the sequence atomic. A mutex around the read, the modify, and the write forces the threads through one at a time. Thread A locks, reads 100, writes 110, unlocks. Thread B locks, reads 110, writes 130, unlocks. The balance is correct. The lock turned three separate instructions into one indivisible operation, and the scheduler's choice of order no longer affects the result.

The race is not a bug in any single thread. It is a property of the system: shared state plus unsynchronized access plus an ordering the program does not control. Remove any one of the three and the race disappears. The mutex removes the unsynchronized access. Making the variable thread-local removes the shared state. Running the threads sequentially removes the uncontrolled ordering. Each fix has a cost, and the cost is why races persist in real code — the fix is easy to state and hard to apply without slowing the program down.

Okay — explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in the plain register already established.

A CPU executes instructions at roughly four billion per second on a modern core. Main memory delivers a value in about 80 nanoseconds — 240 cycles of waiting. The cache is a smaller, faster memory that sits between the two and holds copies of the data the processor is most likely to ask for next.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element 0, then 1, then 2, each one byte after the last. A function that processes a struct touches its fields, which sit next to each other in memory. This is locality of reference, and it is why a cache built on the right guess about what comes next pays off.

When the CPU loads a value from memory, it does not fetch one byte. It fetches a cache line — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors — and stores the whole line in the nearest cache. The next load from that line hits the cache and returns in one cycle, not 240. The first load paid the memory latency; the next seven reads on the same line are nearly free.

The cache is not one pool. It is a hierarchy. The L1 cache is 32 to 48 kilobytes, sits on the core, and answers in four cycles. The L2 cache is 256 kilobytes to one megabyte and answers in ten to fourteen cycles. The L3 cache is shared across cores, holds 8 to 64 megabytes, and answers in 30 to 50 cycles. Main memory is the fallback at 240. Each layer is larger and slower than the one above it. A load checks L1, then L2, then L3, then memory, and stops at the first hit.

A cache miss is the moment the data is not there. The CPU stalls — its execution units sit idle while the line travels from the next level or from memory. A program that jumps through a linked list, following pointers to scattered addresses, misses on almost every node. Each pointer chase is a 200-cycle wait. A program that walks a contiguous array hits on almost every element after the first. The same number of bytes, the same arithmetic, and one runs fifty times faster because the access pattern keeps the cache full.

The cache also saves writes. A store goes to the L1 cache and the CPU moves on. The cache holds the modified line and writes it back to memory later, when the line is evicted or when another core asks for it. The write to memory, which is slow, happens outside the critical path of the instruction.

Hardware prefetchers watch the access pattern and pull lines into the cache before the CPU asks. A stride-1 access through an array triggers the prefetcher to grab the next few lines, so by the time the loop reaches them they are already in L1. The prefetcher is a bet on locality, and it wins often enough that a tight loop over contiguous memory can run at nearly one iteration per cycle, limited by the execution units rather than by memory.

The cache speeds up a program by turning 240-cycle waits into four-cycle waits, and by turning most of those four-cycle waits into one-cycle hits. The speedup is not a constant factor applied to every instruction. It is a ratio between the accesses the cache predicted and the ones it did not. A program written to respect the cache — contiguous data, sequential access, small working sets — gets the ratio. A program written against it pays the full latency on every load.

Okay — explain idempotency as it applies to an HTTP API, in the plain register already established.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as if it received it once. The second call does not duplicate the first. It does not charge the card twice, create two rows, or append a second record. It arrives, the server recognizes the operation, and the result is unchanged.

`GET` is idempotent by nature. It reads a resource and writes nothing. A thousand `GET` requests to `/users/42` return the same user, and the database is untouched. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. `PUT /users/42` with a body of `{"name":"Alice"}` sets the resource to that exact state. Send it ten times and the resource is still Alice. The tenth call overwrites the ninth, which overwrote the eighth, and the final state is the one the last request carried. `DELETE` is idempotent in the sense that matters: `DELETE /users/42` removes the user. A second `DELETE` to the same URL finds no user, returns 404, and changes nothing. The resource is gone after the first call and stays gone.

`POST` is the one that breaks the pattern. `POST /orders` with `{"item":"book"}` creates a new order. Send it twice and the server creates two orders, each with its own ID. The state after two calls is not the state after one. `POST` is not idempotent because each call appends rather than sets.

The distinction matters when the network lies. A client sends `POST /payments` to charge $50. The server processes the charge, sends a 200 response, and the response drops on the floor — a network failure, a timeout, a proxy that closed the connection. The client never received the 200. It does not know whether the charge happened. It retries. The server processes the second request and charges $50 again. The customer pays $100 for one order.

The fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique identifier — a UUID — and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key alongside the first request's result. When the second request arrives with the same key, the server looks it up, finds the stored result, and returns it without reprocessing. The charge runs once. The retry returns the original response. Stripe's API uses this pattern: every `POST` to `/v1/charges` accepts an `Idempotency-Key`, and a duplicate key returns the cached charge, not a new one.

Idempotency is a property of the operation, not the verb. `POST /users/42/deactivate` can be idempotent if deactivation is a state transition that holds once reached — a second call finds the user already inactive and returns success. `POST /users` that creates a new user each time is not. The HTTP method hints at the contract, but the server's behavior is what determines whether a repeated call is safe.

The guarantee is about state, not about the response. A second `DELETE` may return 404 where the first returned 204. The responses differ. The server state — user absent — is the same. An idempotent operation promises that the system's state after N calls matches its state after one, not that every call returns an identical payload.

Okay — explain how DNS resolves a name to an address, in the plain register already established.

A browser asks for `example.com`. The operating system hands that name to a resolver, and the resolver's job is to come back with an IP address. The address is what the browser needs to open a connection. The name is what a human can remember. DNS is the bridge, and it works as a chain of lookups, each one handing the next server a smaller piece of the question.

The resolver first checks its own cache. If it answered this query recently, it returns the address and stops. Most lookups end here. The rest travel a four-step path.

The resolver does not know where `example.com` lives, but it always knows where the root servers are. There are thirteen root server addresses, published in a file every operating system ships with. The resolver picks one and sends the query. The root server does not know the address of `example.com` either. What it knows is which servers are authoritative for the `.com` top-level domain. It returns a list of those servers' addresses.

The resolver takes that list, picks a `.com` server, and asks the same question. The `.com` server does not know the address of `example.com`. What it knows is which name servers are authoritative for `example.com` — the servers operated by whoever registered the domain. It returns those servers' names and addresses.

The resolver asks one of those authoritative servers for `example.com`. That server holds the actual record. It reads the zone file, finds the A record for `example.com`, and returns `93.184.216.34`. The resolver writes that address into its cache with a time-to-live — the number of seconds the record is valid — and hands it to the operating system, which hands it to the browser.

The time-to-live is what lets the system scale. The root servers answer every unresolved query on the planet. If every resolver asked them for every lookup, they would collapse. Instead, each answer carries a TTL, and the resolver caches it. A resolver that just fetched `example.com` at 11:00 will return the cached address at 11:01 without asking anyone. At 11:05, if the TTL was 300 seconds, the cache entry expires and the next query runs the full chain again.

The chain works because authority is delegated downward. The root servers own the top-level domains. The top-level servers own their registered subdomains. The authoritative servers for `example.com` own every record beneath it — `www.example.com`, `mail.example.com`, `api.example.com`. Each layer answers only for the slice it controls and points the resolver at the next layer. No single server holds the whole map. The map is distributed, and the delegation is what stitches it together.

A query for `www.example.com` follows the same path but stops one layer deeper. The resolver reaches the authoritative server for `example.com` and asks for `www.example.com`. That server holds the record or a CNAME pointing elsewhere. If the answer is a CNAME — `www.example.com` is an alias for `example.com` — the resolver starts a new lookup for the target name, running the same chain from the top or from the nearest cached delegation point.

The whole process turns a human-readable name into a 32-bit or 128-bit address in a few round trips, and caches the result so the next lookup costs nothing. The name is the question. The delegation is the path. The TTL is the expiration that keeps the answers fresh without flooding the root.

Okay — explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in the plain register already established.

A deadlock is two threads frozen, each holding a lock the other needs. Thread A locks mutex X, then tries to lock mutex Y. Thread B locks mutex Y, then tries to lock mutex X. A waits for B to release Y. B waits for A to release X. Neither releases. Both sleep. The program hangs.

Four conditions must hold at once. The threads hold locks and wait for more — that is *hold and wait*. A thread cannot take a lock another thread holds — that is *no preemption*. Each thread waits in a cycle — that is *circular wait*. Each lock belongs to exactly one thread at a time — that is *mutual exclusion*. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest fix breaks circular wait. Every thread in the program acquires mutexes in the same order. Thread A locks X, then Y. Thread B locks X, then Y. If A gets X first, B blocks on X before it touches Y. B never holds Y while waiting for X. The cycle never closes. The rule is one sentence: pick a global order for every mutex, and never lock a lower-numbered mutex while holding a higher-numbered one.

The rule is simple to state and hard to keep. A function that locks mutex 3 and calls a helper that locks mutex 7 is fine. A function that locks 7 and calls a helper that locks 3 breaks the order without any visible sign. The call graph hides the violation. Lock ordering works when the order is documented, enforced by tooling, and checked on every code change. Without that discipline, the deadlock moves from a runtime crash to a review-time argument, which is progress but not a guarantee.

A hash map stores values at array slots chosen by a key's hash. Two keys that hash to the same slot collide, and the map needs a rule for keeping both.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each slot. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list, and either updates an existing pair or appends a new node. On lookup, it walks the same list and compares keys. The cost grows with list length: a slot with eight entries takes eight comparisons in the worst case. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain. The lists carry a real cost — a pointer per entry, and a cache miss on every hop — but the structure never runs out of room, and deleting a node is unlinking it.

**Open addressing** stores every pair inside the array itself. On collision, the map probes a sequence of nearby slots until it finds an empty one. Linear probing checks slot *i+1, i+2, i+3…*: fast on modern hardware because the slots sit in the same cache line, but collisions cluster, and a cluster grows faster than the entries that feed it. Quadratic probing jumps by squares — 1, 4, 9 — which scatters probes and breaks clusters, but can skip every slot in a table whose size shares a factor with the step. Double hashing uses a second hash function as the step size, which gives the most uniform spread at the cost of two hash computations per probe. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Rust's `HashMap` all use open addressing.

Deletion in an open-addressed table cannot just clear a slot. A later key may have probed past that slot on insert; clearing it would break the probe chain and make that key vanish on lookup. The fix is a tombstone: the slot is marked deleted, probes skip past it, and inserts can reclaim it.

Every open-addressed map watches its load factor — the ratio of entries to slots. Past about 70%, probe lengths climb fast enough to erase the constant-time promise. The map allocates a larger array, re-hashes every entry into it, and discards the old one. Chained maps resize too, for the same reason: long lists turn lookups into linear scans.

The choice between the two is a trade between memory and locality. Chaining wastes a pointer per entry but stays stable under high load. Open addressing keeps the data compact and cache-friendly but degrades sharply once the table fills, which is why it resizes early.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table, built from one or more columns, that lets the database find rows without scanning them all. The common form is a B-tree: a sorted tree whose leaves hold the indexed column's values paired with pointers back to the full rows. A query filtering on that column descends the tree in O(log n) steps, reads the matching leaves, and fetches only those rows. An unindexed query reads every row in the table and discards the ones that do not match.

Indexes cost storage. A B-tree index on a million-row table occupies roughly the same disk space as the column data itself, and a composite index on several columns occupies more. Every index also costs writes. An `INSERT` that adds one row to a table with three indexes performs four writes: one to the table, three to the trees. `UPDATE` and `DELETE` touch every index built on the changed column. A table that takes 2 ms to insert into with no indexes takes 8 ms with three, because each index tree must be rebalanced and each leaf updated.

An index hurts when the query cannot use it. A B-tree is sorted left to right, so a filter on `last_name` serves a query for `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` but not `WHERE lower(last_name) = 'smith'`: the function breaks the sort order, and the planner falls back to a full scan. The same applies to `WHERE date_col >= '2024-01-01'` (usable) versus `WHERE extract(year FROM date_col) = 2024` (not usable). A query that wraps the indexed column in a function or casts its type reads every row anyway, while paying the write cost on every insert.

An index hurts when it is never queried. A column indexed "in case we need it" adds write latency to every insert and update and returns nothing, because the planner only uses an index when a query's filter, join, or sort matches its columns. Indexes that appear in no query plan are dead weight, and most databases expose a view — `pg_stat_user_indexes` in PostgreSQL, `sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats` in SQL Server — that shows the last time each index was read. An index with zero scans since the last statistics reset is a candidate for removal.

A composite index hurts when its column order is wrong. A B-tree sorts by the first column, then the second within ties, then the third within those. An index on `(last_name, first_name, city)` serves `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` and `WHERE last_name = 'Smith' AND first_name = 'Jane'`, but not `WHERE first_name = 'Jane'` alone, because the tree is not sorted by `first_name` at the top level. The leftmost prefix rule means a composite index is only usable for queries that filter on its leading columns in order.

The trade is read speed against write speed and storage. A table read often and written rarely benefits from every index its queries touch. A table written constantly and read by many different column combinations pays a high write cost for indexes that help only a few of those reads. The planner's `EXPLAIN` output shows whether a query uses an index or scans the table, which is the direct evidence for keeping or dropping one.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a series of messages. Each byte gets a sequence number, and the first byte of every segment carries that number in the TCP header. The receiver reads the sequence number, checks it against what it expected next, and either places the bytes in the right position in its receive buffer or holds them aside until the gap fills.

A segment arriving with sequence number 1001 tells the receiver these bytes occupy positions 1001 through 1008 in the stream. If the receiver already has bytes 1001 through 1020, it knows this segment is a duplicate and discards it. If it has 1001 through 1004, it keeps 1005 through 1008 and discards the overlap. If it has 1001 through 1000 — a gap — it stores the segment in the buffer and waits for 1001.

The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous byte it has. An acknowledgment of 1021 means "I have every byte through 1020; send 1021 next." This is a cumulative acknowledgment. If bytes 1021 through 1040 arrived but 1021 did not, the receiver still acknowledges 1021, because the chain has not advanced. The sender sees the same acknowledgment repeated and infers loss.

Out-of-order segments sit in the receiver's buffer until the missing piece arrives. The buffer is a fixed window whose size the receiver advertises in the TCP header — the window field. When the missing segment fills the gap, the receiver delivers the whole contiguous run to the application in order and sends a single acknowledgment for the new high-water mark. The application never sees bytes out of sequence; the buffer absorbs the disorder.

The sender keeps a copy of every unacknowledged segment in its own buffer. When an acknowledgment arrives, the sender discards the acknowledged copies and slides its send window forward. If an acknowledgment does not arrive within a timeout — the retransmission timeout, calculated from measured round-trip times — the sender retransmits the oldest unacknowledged segment. The timeout adapts: a connection over a 200 ms round trip sets a longer timeout than one over 2 ms, because the sender measures the time between sending a segment and receiving its acknowledgment and smooths it into an estimate.

The sequence number is a 32-bit field, so it wraps after 4,294,967,295 bytes. TCP handles this by treating sequence numbers as modular arithmetic: a receiver compares numbers using signed subtraction, so 10 is "before" 4,294,967,290 even though 10 is the smaller integer. The initial sequence number is chosen randomly, not zero, which prevents a delayed segment from an old connection landing in a new one with a sequence number that happens to match.

The ordering guarantee rests on three mechanisms working together: sequence numbers that name every byte, a receive buffer that reassembles out-of-order arrivals, and cumulative acknowledgments that tell the sender which bytes the receiver has made contiguous. Strip any one and the stream breaks.

A mutex protects against one thing: two threads executing the same code path at the same time and corrupting shared state. The name is mutual exclusion — one thread holds the lock, the other waits.

A mutex protects against a lost update. Thread A reads a counter at 7, thread B reads the same counter at 7, both add 1, both write 8. The counter should be 9. Wrapping the read-modify-write in a mutex makes thread B wait until thread A finishes, so B reads 8 and writes 9. Without the lock, the increment is not atomic: the CPU loads the value, adds to a register, and stores it back, and a context switch between those instructions is where the update vanishes.

A mutex protects against torn writes. Thread A writes a 64-bit value to a field while thread B reads it on a 32-bit machine where that write takes two memory cycles. B can see the upper four bytes from the new value and the lower four from the old. The lock forces B to wait until A's write is complete.

A mutex protects against structural corruption. Two threads inserting into a linked list at the same time can each update a next-pointer, and one update overwrites the other, leaving a node unreachable or the list circular. The lock makes the pointer swaps sequential.

A mutex does not protect against reordering by the compiler or the CPU. A store to a flag variable can appear to another thread before a store to the data that flag guards, because the compiler reorders for register efficiency or the CPU reorders for cache and pipeline. The fix is a memory barrier, and a mutex acquire and release insert barriers: code before the release cannot move after it, and code after the acquire cannot move before it. The barrier is what makes the lock correct on weakly-ordered architectures like ARM, where the CPU is free to reorder stores that have no dependency between them.

A mutex does not protect against deadlock. Two threads each holding one lock and waiting for the other's lock block forever. A single lock acquired twice by the same thread without release blocks forever unless the mutex is recursive, which tracks the owner and a count and unlocks only when the count reaches zero.

A mutex does not protect against priority inversion. A low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority thread preempts the low-priority thread, so the high-priority thread waits for a thread that is not even running. The priority inheritance protocol raises the low-priority thread's priority to match the waiter's until it releases the lock.

The scope a mutex guards is the code between acquire and release, not the data itself. A shared variable protected by mutex M in one function is unprotected if another function touches it without acquiring M. The lock is a convention the code follows, not a property the data carries. Languages that bundle the lock with the data — a synchronized method in Java, a monitor in Hoare's model — make the convention harder to miss but do not change the mechanism: the thread takes a lock, does its work, and releases it, and the release is what lets the next thread in.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. The question is always the same: which objects can still be touched, and which cannot?

**Tracing** starts from the roots. A root is a pointer the runtime always has: stack variables in every active thread, static and global fields, handles pinned for native calls. The collector walks from those roots through every reference they hold, then through references those objects hold, marking each object it reaches. Anything unmarked at the end is unreachable. The collector frees it. This is how the JVM, .NET, V8, and Go all work — they trace, they do not count.

**Reachability** is transitive. If a root points to a `Customer` object, and that object points to an `Address`, the `Address` is reachable even though no root names it directly. The collector follows the chain. If the `Customer` becomes unreachable, the `Address` becomes unreachable too, on the next trace. The collector does not free the `Address` when the `Customer` dies; it frees it when nothing left alive can get to it.

**Reference counting** is the other approach, and it does not trace. Every object carries a count of incoming references. Assigning a pointer increments the count; overwriting or destroying one decrements it. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and the collector frees it immediately. CPython uses this for most objects. The cost is per-assignment overhead, and the fatal flaw is cycles: two objects pointing at each other keep both counts at one forever, even if nothing else reaches either. CPython runs a separate cycle detector periodically to break those. Swift uses reference counting and shifts the cycle problem to the programmer via `weak` and `unowned` references.

A tracing collector runs in phases. **Mark** walks the object graph from the roots and sets a bit on every reachable object. **Sweep** scans the heap and frees every object without the bit. The bit is then cleared for the next cycle. The whole heap is traversable, but the pause is proportional to the number of live objects, not the total heap — dead objects cost nothing to mark, and sweep touches them only to free them.

**Generational** collection exploits one observation: most objects die young. A local list, a temporary string, a parsed token — allocated and discarded within a function call. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. New allocations go in young. The young generation is collected frequently and cheaply, because it is small and most of its contents are already dead. Objects that survive several young-gen collections are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely. The JVM's G1 and ZGC, .NET's server GC, and V8's Orinoco pipeline all use generations. The win is simple: collecting a 2 MB young space takes milliseconds; collecting a 4 GB old space does not, so the collector avoids it.

**Concurrent** collection traces the heap while the program runs, not while it pauses. The hard part is mutation: the program changes a pointer the collector already visited, and the collector's picture of the live set goes stale. The fix is a write barrier — a small piece of code the runtime inserts on every pointer store. When the program writes a reference from an old object to a new one, the barrier records that the new object is now reachable from old space, and the collector revisits it. Go's GC, ZGC, and Shenandoah use barriers to keep the trace correct without stopping the program for more than a millisecond. The barrier is the tax; the near-zero pause is the return.

The collector does not know which objects are unused. It knows which objects are unreachable, and it infers unused from that. An object held in a long-lived cache that is never queried again is reachable and will not be collected, even though the program never touches it. The collector's promise is not "free what is unused" but "free what cannot be reached," and those two sets diverge in every long-running program.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled. The program works under one ordering and fails under another, and nothing in the code decides which ordering happens.

A bank account holds a balance of 100. Two threads each withdraw 40. The correct final balance is 20. The withdrawal code reads the balance, subtracts 40, and writes the result back. Three instructions: load, subtract, store.

Thread A loads the balance and sees 100. Thread B loads the balance before A stores, and B also sees 100. A subtracts 40 and stores 60. B subtracts 40 and stores 60. The final balance is 60. Forty dollars vanished. Both threads read the same starting value, and the store from whichever thread runs last wins, overwriting the other. The lost update is the visible damage.

The word *race* is apt. The threads are racing for the same memory, and the outcome turns on which one reaches the load and store instructions first. A single-threaded program cannot race against itself. The bug needs concurrency and shared state — the balance variable that both threads touch — and at least one operation that is not atomic, where a thread can be interrupted between reading the value and writing it back.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write indivisible. A mutex around the withdrawal forces thread B to wait until A has stored its result, so B loads 60 and stores 20. An atomic compare-and-swap does the same without a lock: the instruction writes the new balance only if the old balance still matches what the thread loaded, and retries if it does not. Either way the two operations no longer interleave.

Races are not limited to memory. A program that creates a file if it does not exist, then writes to it, races when two instances run at once: both check, both see no file, both create, and one overwrites the other's contents. A program that reads a shared flag, decides to stop, and exits while another thread writes the flag, races on the flag's value. The shape is the same in every case: check-then-act, where the check and the act are separate steps and the condition can change between them. The program acted on a picture of the world that was already stale by the time the action ran.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by holding copies of the data and instructions the processor is likely to need next, so the processor does not wait on the slow trip to RAM.

Main memory is far away. A load from DRAM takes roughly 100 nanoseconds on a modern desktop machine. A load from the L1 cache takes about one nanosecond. The cache is built from SRAM, which is faster than the DRAM that fills main memory but costs more per bit and draws more power, which is why a cache is small: a few kilobytes for L1, a few hundred for L2, a few megabytes for L3. The processor checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, then main memory. Each level is larger and slower than the one before it.

The cache exploits a property called locality. Temporal locality is the observation that a program that reads a memory location tends to read it again soon — a loop counter, a stack variable, a field on an object in a tight loop. Spatial locality is the observation that a program that reads one address tends to read nearby addresses soon — the next element in an array, the next instruction in a straight-line code sequence. The cache is built for both. When the processor requests a byte, the cache does not fetch just that byte. It fetches a block — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors — and stores the whole block in a cache line. The next read from the same 64-byte region hits the cache.

A cache hit is a load the cache served. A cache miss is a load the cache could not serve, which forces a fetch from the next level. The hit rate is the fraction of loads served from cache, and it dominates performance. A loop that sums an array of integers with a 4 KB stride — one int per cache line, touching a fresh line on every access — runs at the speed of main memory. The same loop summing the array sequentially runs at the speed of the cache, because each fetched line serves 16 consecutive loads before the next miss. The arithmetic is the same. The memory access pattern is not, and the memory access pattern decides the running time.

The cache helps because most programs touch the same data repeatedly and walk through memory in order. A linked list defeats both forms of locality: each node sits at a heap address unrelated to the last, so following the `next` pointer fetches a new cache line on every hop. An array of the same data, stored contiguously, lets one cache line serve several entries. Walking the array is faster by the ratio of cache hits to misses, which on a 100 ns DRAM and a 1 ns L1 is the difference between a program that waits and one that does not.

The cache also hides the cost of instruction fetch. A tight loop small enough to fit in the L1 instruction cache runs from cache on every iteration, and the fetch cost drops to zero. A loop whose body spills across multiple cache lines pays a miss each time a line falls out and must be refetched.

Hardware prefetchers sit beside the cache and guess what comes next. When they detect a program reading memory at a fixed stride, they fetch the next lines into the cache before the processor asks for them. The miss still happens, but it happens earlier, and by the time the processor needs the data the line has arrived. The prefetcher handles sequential and strided patterns well. It handles pointer-chasing badly, because the next address is data the prefetcher cannot read in time.

The speedup is not from doing the arithmetic faster. The ALU runs at the same clock rate either way. The speedup is from not waiting. A processor that hits L1 on every load retires instructions at its peak rate. A processor that misses to DRAM on every load stalls for hundreds of cycles per load, and the arithmetic units sit idle. The cache turns slow memory into fast memory by keeping the working set close, and the size of that working set relative to the cache is what decides whether a program runs fast.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server's state ends up where a single send would have left it. The second request does not duplicate the first. It does not charge the card twice, create two rows, or append a second record. It either repeats the original effect or recognizes that the effect already happened and does nothing.

`GET` is idempotent by nature. It reads state and changes nothing, so ten identical `GET` requests return the same data and leave the server untouched. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A `PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada. Send it once, send it a hundred times: user 42 is still named Ada. The request replaces the target resource's state, and replacing the same state with the same value is a no-op after the first. `DELETE` is idempotent by the same logic. `DELETE /articles/7` removes article 7. A second call finds no article 7 and returns 404, or returns 204 if the implementation treats "already gone" as success. Either way, the server state — article 7 absent — is the same after both calls.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST /orders` with the body `{"item": "book"}` creates a new order. Send it twice and the server creates two orders, charges the card twice, ships two books. The request names a collection, not a specific resource, and each call appends to that collection. This is why payment APIs wrap `POST` in an idempotency layer: the client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header, the server stores the key with the first response, and a second request carrying the same key returns the stored response instead of running the handler again. Stripe's API does this. The key is a server-side deduplication contract, not a property of HTTP itself.

The distinction matters because networks retry. A client sends a `POST`, the server processes it, the response drops on the floor, and the client times out and sends again. Without an idempotency key, the server runs the handler twice. With one, the server looks up the key, finds the stored result from the first call, and returns it. The client sees one order, not two.

Idempotency is about server state, not the response body. A `DELETE /articles/7` returns 200 the first time and 404 the second. The bodies differ. The state — article 7 gone — does not. An API is idempotent when repeated calls converge on the same state, not when they return the same bytes.

The HTTP spec defines idempotency as a property of the method, but real APIs break the spec. A `PUT /counters/1` that increments a counter instead of replacing it is not idempotent, because each call changes the value. The method says "replace," the handler says "increment," and the second call wins. The contract is only as good as the handler behind it.

Okay: explain how DNS resolves a hostname to an IP address, in the plain register already established.

A browser asks for `example.com`. The operating system hands the question to a resolver, and the resolver asks a chain of servers until one of them answers with an address.

The call starts in the stub resolver — a small piece of code inside the operating system or the C library. The stub does not know any addresses. It reads `/etc/resolv.conf` on Linux or the system network settings on Windows, finds the IP address of a recursive resolver — often the home router's address, or an ISP's server, or `1.1.1.1` — and sends the query there. The stub's only job is forwarding.

The recursive resolver receives the query and begins the walk. It does not know `example.com` either, but it knows where to start. Every recursive resolver carries a built-in list of the thirteen root server addresses, published as a file called the root hints. The resolver picks one root server and sends the query for `example.com` to it.

The root server does not answer with an address. It answers with a referral: a list of name servers for the `.com` top-level domain. The root server knows who runs `.com` but not what lives inside it. The referral is a set of NS records — names like `a.gtld-servers.net` — and the resolver must resolve those names to addresses before it can go further. This is glue: A records bundled with the referral so the resolver can reach the next server without a second round trip.

The resolver now queries a `.com` server, asking for `example.com`. The `.com` server also does not answer with an address. It returns a referral to the authoritative name servers for `example.com` — the servers run by the organization that registered the domain, or by a registrar like Namecheap or Cloudflare. Again, the resolver gets NS records and glue addresses.

The resolver queries the authoritative server for `example.com`. This server holds the actual records for the domain. It reads its zone file, finds an A record for `example.com` that says `93.184.216.34`, and returns that address. The resolver caches the answer — storing it for the time-to-live named in the record, often 300 or 3600 seconds — and hands the address back to the operating system, which hands it to the browser.

The whole walk — root, TLD, authoritative — typically takes three round trips on a cold cache. A warm cache shortens it to zero. The recursive resolver caches every referral and every answer it receives, so a second request for `example.com` within the TTL returns from memory without a single network call. A request for `shop.example.com` after `example.com` has been resolved skips the root and TLD steps, because the resolver already knows where the `example.com` servers live.

The system is hierarchical. The root delegates to `.com`, `.com` delegates to `example.com`, and each layer answers only for the slice of the namespace it owns. No single server holds the full map. The map is distributed across millions of authoritative servers, and the resolver assembles the path one delegation at a time.

DNS runs over UDP port 53 for queries and responses that fit in 512 bytes. A response larger than that — a DNSSEC-signed answer, a long TXT record — triggers a fallback to TCP, where the resolver reconnects on port 53 and reissues the query. The protocol switched to TCP because DNSSEC signatures inflated responses past the UDP limit, and dropping them would have broken signed domains.

The lookup is fast because it is cached at every layer. The browser caches. The operating system caches. The recursive resolver caches. The authoritative servers do not cache, but they answer from files they control. A request that misses every cache pays three round trips, maybe 30 milliseconds over a good connection. A request that hits the resolver's cache pays one round trip to the resolver, maybe a millisecond. The difference is two orders of magnitude, and the cache is what makes the system usable.

Okay: explain what a deadlock is and one concrete way to avoid it, in the plain register already established.

A deadlock is two threads frozen forever, each holding a lock the other needs. Thread A takes lock 1, thread B takes lock 2, A waits for lock 2, B waits for lock 1. Neither releases. Neither advances. The program stops.

Four conditions must hold at once. Mutual exclusion: the locks can be held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: each thread holds a lock while asking for the next. No preemption: a thread cannot be forced to give up a lock it holds. Circular wait: the waiting threads form a ring, A waiting on B, B waiting on A. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The classic trigger is lock ordering. A function that transfers money from account X to account Y locks X, then locks Y. A concurrent function transferring from Y to X locks Y, then locks X. The first holds X and wants Y; the second holds Y and wants X. The transfers interleave at exactly the wrong moment and both stall.

The fix is to impose a global order on the locks and acquire them in that order every time. If every thread locks the lower-numbered account before the higher-numbered account, the circular wait cannot close. The transfer from account 3 to account 7 locks 3, then 7. The transfer from account 7 to account 3 also locks 3, then 7. One thread gets 3 first, the other waits for 3, and the one holding 3 proceeds to 7, finishes, and releases both. The second thread then takes 3 and 7 in turn. No ring.

The order can be any total order the program applies consistently. Account ID, memory address of the object, a name sorted alphabetically. What matters is that every thread acquires the same set of locks in the same sequence, so the last thread to request the first lock in the sequence waits, and the thread holding it runs to completion. The constraint is global: one function that grabs locks out of order breaks the guarantee for every other function that touches those locks.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array. It computes an integer from the key, then maps that integer to an array index. Two keys can land on the same index. The map needs a strategy for that case.

**Chaining** keeps a linked list at each array slot. When two keys collide, both entries live in the same list. A lookup walks the list and compares keys one by one. The list stays short under a good hash function, so the walk is fast. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` use this approach. The cost is extra memory for list-node pointers.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the array itself. On collision, the map probes other slots by a fixed rule. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the index: slot 1, then 4, then 9. Double hashing computes a second hash to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than fixed steps. Python's `dict` and Ruby's `Hash` use open addressing.

Deletion adds a complication. Removing an entry and leaving a bare hole breaks probe sequences, because a later search stops at the first empty slot. Open-addressing maps mark deleted slots with a tombstone flag. The slot reads as empty for insertion but as occupied for lookup, so probe chains stay intact.

Load factor governs performance. It is the ratio of stored entries to array size. As it rises, collisions multiply. Chaining's lists grow longer; open addressing's probe runs stretch. Most maps resize the array when the load factor crosses a threshold — 0.75 in Java's `HashMap`, 0.66 in Python's `dict` — and rehash every entry into the new array. Resizing is O(n) but amortizes to O(1) per insertion over a sequence of writes.

A bad hash function defeats both strategies. If every key hashes to the same value, chaining collapses into one long list and open addressing degrades to a linear scan. The function must distribute keys uniformly across the array. Cryptographic hashes are unnecessary for this; a fast, well-mixed non-cryptographic hash like SipHash — which Python uses for strings — suffices and resists collision-flooding attacks where an adversary crafts keys that share a bucket.

A database index is a separate structure that stores a subset of a table's data in a form optimized for fast lookup. It trades write speed and storage for read speed.

The most common form is the B-tree index. A B-tree keeps sorted keys in a balanced tree, so a point query — `WHERE user_id = 42` — descends a few levels of nodes instead of scanning every row. A table with ten million rows might satisfy that query in four or five disk reads instead of ten million. PostgreSQL, MySQL's InnoDB, and SQL Server all use B-tree variants as their default.

Indexes also serve range queries. Because the keys are sorted, `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'` walks a contiguous slice of the tree. A hash index, by contrast, supports only equality lookups — it cannot serve ranges at all.

An index hurts in three situations.

First, writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update the index as well as the table. A table with six indexes pays seven write costs for one row insertion. A high-throughput insert workload — log ingestion, event capture — slows down under indexing in direct proportion to the count of indexes.

Second, selectivity. An index on a column with few distinct values — a boolean `is_active` flag, a `status` column with three states — returns large fractions of the table per lookup. The database's query planner abandons the index and scans the table directly when it calculates that the index will touch more than roughly five to ten percent of the rows. The index then consumes storage and write capacity while serving no reads. PostgreSQL exposes this decision in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output as a switch from an Index Scan to a Sequential Scan.

Third, redundancy. Two indexes on `(last_name, first_name)` and `(last_name)` overlap; the first covers any query the second serves. The second index adds write overhead with no read benefit. Index audits catch these by listing all indexes on a table and comparing their column prefixes.

A composite index serves queries that filter on multiple columns, but column order matters. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` and `WHERE last_name = 'Smith' AND first_name = 'Jane'`. It does not serve `WHERE first_name = 'Jane'`, because the B-tree sorts by `last_name` first, and `first_name` is only sorted within each `last_name` group. This is the leftmost-prefix rule, and it is the most common reason an index sits unused while a query runs slow.

The planner's cost estimate is the final arbiter. A query that should use an index but does not usually has a stale statistics table — the planner's row-count estimates drift from reality after bulk loads or deletions. Running `ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL or `UPDATE STATISTICS` in SQL Server refreshes those estimates and often fixes the plan without touching the indexes themselves.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as discrete messages. Each byte gets a sequence number. The first byte's number is not zero; it is a random 32-bit value the sender picks at connection setup, called the initial sequence number. The randomness blocks an attacker from predicting sequence numbers and injecting forged segments into the stream.

A TCP segment carries two fields: the sequence number of its first byte, and an acknowledgment number. The acknowledgment number tells the other side which byte it expects next. If a receiver gets bytes 1 through 1000, it sends back an ACK of 1001. That single number confirms receipt of everything before it. TCP does not acknowledge individual segments; it acknowledges the highest contiguous byte received.

The sender transmits segments, starts a timer for each, and waits for the ACK. If the timer fires, the sender retransmits. This is how TCP recovers from loss: the receiver notices a gap, the sender's timer expires, and the missing bytes arrive again.

Gaps are common. Segments take different network paths and arrive out of order. Segment 3 might reach the receiver before segment 2. TCP handles this with a receive buffer. The receiver stores segment 3, notes that bytes 2001 through 3000 are present, and sends a duplicate ACK of 2001 — the first missing byte. When segment 2 arrives, the buffer fills the gap, and the ACK jumps forward to 3001.

The application never sees the gap. TCP holds out-of-order bytes in the buffer and delivers them to the application only in sequence order. The socket read returns bytes 2001 through 3000 as a contiguous block, regardless of how they arrived on the wire.

Duplicate ACKs also drive fast retransmit. A receiver sends a duplicate ACK for every out-of-order segment that arrives, because each one triggers the same "I am still missing byte 2001" response. When the sender sees three duplicate ACKs in a row, it infers loss without waiting for the timer and retransmits the missing segment immediately. Three is the threshold in RFC 5681 because a single duplicate ACK can come from packet reordering, not loss; three in a row makes loss the likely cause.

Flow control keeps the receiver from drowning. The TCP header carries a window size — the number of bytes the receiver has room to buffer. A receiver reading slowly advertises a small window; the sender stops transmitting when the window fills. A zero window tells the sender to wait entirely. The receiver updates this value in every ACK.

Congestion control governs the sender's rate against the network, not the receiver. The sender maintains a congestion window separate from the receive window and sends at whichever is smaller. It starts small — one segment, in the original specification — and doubles the window each round trip until it detects loss. This is slow start. On loss, it cuts the window, in older TCP variants by half, and switches to additive increase: one segment per round trip instead of doubling. The cycle probes for bandwidth, backs off under pressure, and probes again.
