The sequence number space is finite: 32 bits, about 4.3 billion values. A high-throughput connection on a fast link can wrap the counter in seconds. TCP handles wraparound with modular arithmetic — sequence numbers compare by circular distance, not raw magnitude — and with the timestamp option defined in RFC 7323, which disambiguates wrapped numbers by pairing them with a clock value. Without timestamps, a retransmitted segment could land in the wrong position after a wrap, corrupting the stream.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes against shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can touch the same memory at the same instant. Thread A reads `balance`, adds 100, writes it back. Thread B reads `balance` in the gap between A's read and A's write, adds 50, writes its own result. A's update vanishes. This is a data race, and the result is wrong regardless of language or hardware. The C11 and C++11 memory models call it undefined behavior. Go's race detector aborts on it. Rust refuses to compile it.

A mutex — mutual exclusion lock — fixes this by serializing access. Before touching the shared variable, a thread acquires the lock. After, it releases. Only one thread holds the lock at a time, so the read-add-write sequence runs as an indivisible block. Thread B waits at the acquire call until A releases.

The lock protects whatever the holding thread touches between acquire and release. That region is the critical section. A mutex on a bank account's `balance` field protects `balance` and nothing else. A mutex on a whole linked list protects every node if the critical section spans the whole traversal, or just the head pointer if the section only updates the head. The scope of protection is the scope of the lock, not the scope of the data structure.

What a mutex does not protect against is as important.

It does not protect against deadlock. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Both block forever. The fix is lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same sequence across all threads — or a single lock that covers both resources. POSIX offers `pthread_mutex_timedlock` to detect this at runtime; Go's `sync.Mutex` offers no timeout, so the deadlock is permanent.

It does not protect against priority inversion. A low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs. The high-priority thread blocks, and a medium-priority thread that needs no lock keeps the low-priority thread from running, so the high-priority thread stays blocked. The Mars Pathfinder rover hit this in 1997: a low-priority meteorological thread held a lock the high-priority bus-management thread needed, and the watchdog timer reset the system. The fix is priority inheritance, which temporarily raises the lock holder's priority to match the waiter's. POSIX supports this via the `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` protocol; Linux's `rt_mutex` implements it for the kernel's own locks.

It does not make operations atomic across multiple locks. A thread that acquires lock 1, updates `balance`, releases, then acquires lock 2, updates `fee`, releases has two critical sections, not one. Another thread can observe the state after the first release and before the second acquire — `balance` changed, `fee` not yet. A transaction or a single lock covering both fields is the fix.

It does not protect memory on a different machine. A mutex is a process-local construct. Two processes on separate nodes sharing a database row need a database lock, a distributed lock service, or optimistic concurrency control — not a mutex. Redis's `SET NX`, PostgreSQL's `SELECT FOR UPDATE`, and etcd's lease-based locks serve that case. A mutex in one process cannot see the other process at all.

The cost is contention. Every acquire is a kernel transition if the lock is contended — a context switch costing roughly 1 to 10 microseconds on modern x86 hardware, depending on whether the waiter spins first. Uncontended locks use atomic instructions in user space and cost tens of nanoseconds. Linux's `futex` and Go's `sync.Mutex` both follow this pattern: spin briefly in user space, then call into the kernel. A lock held for a nanosecond of real work but contended by eight threads spends most of its wall time in the kernel.

The discipline is: lock the smallest region that preserves correctness, hold the lock for the shortest time that does so, and never call code that can block — network I/O, disk I/O, another lock — while holding it unless the lock ordering is provably safe.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that no live object can reach. "Live" means reachable: starting from a set of roots, the collector traces every pointer to every object, and every object reachable through that trace is live. Everything else is garbage.

The roots are the entry points — global variables, stack frames, CPU registers, anything the running program can touch directly. The collector walks from roots through references the way a program would, marking each object it finds. This is the mark phase of a tracing collector. After marking, the sweep phase walks the heap and frees every unmarked object. McCarthy described this scheme in 1960 for Lisp, and it is still the backbone of most collectors in Java, Go, .NET, and V8.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object carries a counter; every assignment of a pointer to it increments the counter, every drop of a pointer decrements it, and the collector frees the object when the counter hits zero. Objective-C, Swift under ARC, and C++'s `shared_ptr` work this way. It fails on cycles. Object A points to B, B points to A, both counters sit at 1, and neither drops to zero even though nothing outside the cycle references either. A tracing collector finds the cycle unreachable because no root reaches it. A pure reference counter does not, so cycle detection must be bolted on — Swift's runtime does this with a periodic tracing pass for weak references.

Tracing collectors split by how they move objects. A mark-sweep collector leaves survivors in place and frees the gaps. The heap fragments over time, and allocation slows as the allocator searches for a fit. A copying collector moves every survivor into a new region during the mark, leaving the old region free for the next round. This compacts the heap and makes allocation a pointer bump. The cost is moving objects and fixing up every pointer that references them. Semispace copying, described by Cheney in 1970, divides the heap into two halves and copies survivors from one to the other, so only half the heap is usable at any time.

Generational collection exploits the observation that most objects die young. A 1995 study by Ungar and Jackson measured allocation lifetimes across Smalltalk programs and found that 80 to 98 percent of objects never survive a collection. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. New allocations go in the young region, which the collector scans frequently. Objects that survive several young-generation collections get promoted to the old region, which the collector scans rarely. This cuts the work per collection because the young region is small and most of its contents are already dead. HotSpot, V8, and .NET all use generational layouts.

The hard problem is the pause. A stop-the-world collector halts every application thread while it traces and sweeps. For a large heap, the pause can run hundreds of milliseconds. Go's collector, designed for low latency, runs most of its mark work concurrently with application threads and targets a pause under one millisecond. The tradeoff is throughput: concurrent collectors spend more total CPU on collection than stop-the-world collectors because they must handle the application mutating the heap while they trace. Go solves the mutation problem with a write barrier — a small piece of code the compiler inserts at every pointer write, which tells the collector when the application creates a new reference during the mark. The barrier adds overhead to every pointer store, which is why Go programs with heavy pointer churn run slower than equivalent programs using value types.

The collector does not know which fields are pointers and which are raw integers. A conservative collector treats every word that looks like a pointer as one, never freeing an object whose address happens to match a stored integer. Boehm's C and C++ collector works this way, because C's type system does not carry the runtime type information a precise collector needs. A precise collector knows the layout of every object — either from type metadata, as in Java and Go, or from compiler-generated stack maps — and traces only real pointers. Precise collectors reclaim more memory and can move objects, because they can fix up every reference. Conservative collectors cannot move objects safely, since a stored integer that looks like a pointer cannot be rewritten.

Finalizers run before reclamation but after the object is unreachable. The collector queues the finalizer, and the runtime executes it, usually on a separate thread. Finalizers resurrect the object: it is reachable again while the finalizer runs, because the finalizer receives a reference to it. This breaks the invariant that unreachable means collectable, so collectors with finalizers need at least two collection cycles to reclaim a finalized object — one to queue the finalizer, one to collect the object after the finalizer drops its reference. Java deprecated `Object.finalize` in 2018 for this reason and replaced it with `Cleaner`, which keeps the same two-cycle cost but confines the resurrection to a phantom reference that the application cannot reach directly. Go's `runtime.SetFinalizer` carries the same cost; the Go team recommends explicit `Close` calls instead.

A race condition is a bug where a program's output depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads it, adds 50, writes 150. Thread B reads it at the same instant, adds 30, writes 130. The balance is 130. Fifty dollars vanished. The hardware ran both reads before either write, and the later write overwrote the earlier one.

The word "race" fits. Both threads race to read before the other has written. The winner's update survives. The loser's disappears. Swap the timing and the result changes — 180 instead of 130, or 150 instead of 180. The code is correct in isolation and wrong under concurrency.

The balance example is a data race, the most common form. The C11 and C++11 standards call it undefined behavior. Go's race detector catches it at runtime. Rust's borrow checker refuses to compile it. The fix is a mutex: one thread acquires the lock, reads, adds, writes, releases. The other thread waits at the acquire call and sees the updated balance.

Race conditions do not require threads. A program checks whether a file exists, then opens it. Between the check and the open, another process deletes the file. The open fails. This is TOCTOU — time-of-check to time-of-use — and it is a race against the filesystem. The fix is to open the file directly and handle the error if it is missing, collapsing the check and the use into one operation.

Distributed systems carry the same shape at a larger scale. Two orders arrive for the last item in stock. Server A reads the inventory, sees one unit, ships it. Server B on a different node reads the inventory at the same moment, sees one unit, ships it. One unit went to two customers. The fix is a transaction or a conditional write — PostgreSQL's `SELECT FOR UPDATE` locks the row; Redis's `WATCH` aborts the transaction if the value changed. The principle is the same: make the read and the write one indivisible step.

The defining trait is not speed or threads. It is the gap between operations that should be atomic but are not. Close the gap and the race disappears.

Okay, explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

A CPU cache is a small block of SRAM sitting between the processor core and main memory. Main memory is DRAM, and a read from DRAM costs roughly 200 cycles on a modern desktop chip. A read from the L1 cache costs 4 cycles. The cache holds copies of the memory locations the processor touched recently, so most reads hit the cache instead of paying the 200-cycle round trip to RAM.

The speedup comes from two properties of real programs, not from the cache hardware itself. The first is temporal locality: a program that reads address X tends to read X again soon. A loop counter, a stack variable, an array element in a tight loop — all get touched many times in a short span. The cache keeps them close. The second is spatial locality: a program that reads address X tends to read X+4 and X+8 soon. An array walk, an instruction stream, a struct field access all move through memory in order. The cache exploits this by fetching in blocks, not single addresses. A cache line is 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. One miss pulls all 64 bytes from RAM into the cache, and the next seven 8-byte reads hit the cache for free.

Caches sit in a hierarchy. The L1 is smallest and closest — 32 kilobytes per core on Intel's Golden Cove, split into 32 KB for instructions and 32 KB for data, with a 4-cycle latency. The L2 is larger and farther out — 2 megabytes per core on the same chip, 14-cycle latency. The L3 is shared across all cores — 30 megabytes on a 12-core die, 50-cycle latency. Beyond L3 sits DRAM at 200 cycles. Each level catches the misses of the level above it. A program whose working set fits in L1 runs at full speed. The same program with a working set that spills L1 but fits in L2 pays the 14-cycle penalty on the overflow. Spill L2 and the penalty jumps to 50. Spill L3 and the program stalls for 200 cycles per access, which is why a memory-bound loop can run fifty times slower than the same loop over data that fits in cache.

The cache does not read individual addresses on a miss. It reads a whole 64-byte line, and it places that line by a hash of the memory address. Most caches are set-associative: an address maps to one of several slots in a set, and the cache checks all slots in the set in parallel. Intel's L1 data cache is 8-way associative, meaning each set holds eight lines. If nine active memory addresses all hash to the same set, the cache evicts one to make room, and the next read of the evicted address misses again. This is a conflict miss — the data was in the cache, but the mapping forced it out. A direct-mapped cache, with one slot per set, is cheaper to build but suffers more conflict misses. A fully associative cache, where any address can go in any slot, avoids conflicts entirely but costs more power and silicon to search.

Cache misses come in three kinds, and the distinction matters for tuning. Compulsory misses happen on the first read of a block, because the data was never in the cache. Capacity misses happen because the working set exceeds the cache size, so old lines get evicted before they are reused. Conflict misses happen because the set-associative mapping forces evictions even when the cache has free slots elsewhere. A program that strides through a 100-megabyte array with a 64-byte step touches one cache line per access, pays a compulsory miss every time, and gets no benefit from the cache at all. The same array walked with a 4-byte step reuses each line sixteen times and runs near cache speed. This is why column-major versus row-major traversal order changes performance by an order of magnitude on large matrices in C, where rows are contiguous.

The hardware prefetcher watches access patterns and pulls lines into the cache before the processor asks for them. A sequential array walk triggers the prefetcher after two or three misses, and subsequent lines arrive while the core is still computing on earlier ones, hiding most of the RAM latency. A pointer-chasing walk — following a linked list through random heap addresses — defeats the prefetcher, because each address depends on the data at the previous address and there is no pattern to predict. This is why a linked list traversal can be slower than an array traversal by a factor of ten or more, even when both hold the same number of elements.

Writing to memory adds a second path. A write-through cache copies every store to both the cache and RAM, which is simple but spends a full 200-cycle write on every store. A write-back cache marks the cache line as dirty and writes it to RAM only when the line is evicted, so most stores complete at L1 speed. The dirty bit on the line tracks this. When another core or a DMA device reads an address whose cached copy is dirty, the cache must write the line back before supplying the data. Multi-core chips enforce this with a cache coherence protocol — MESI on x86 and ARM — which tags each line as modified, exclusive, shared, or invalid and coordinates transfers between cores so no core reads a stale value. A store from core A to a line cached on core B invalidates B's copy, forcing B to miss on its next read of that address. False sharing happens when two cores write to different variables that happen to share one 64-byte line: each write invalidates the other core's copy, and both cores stall on coherence traffic even though they never touch the same variable. Padding the variables to separate lines fixes it.

The cache speeds up a program by turning 200-cycle memory reads into 4-cycle cache reads, and it does that by betting that the program will touch the same data and the neighboring data again soon. Real programs do, overwhelmingly. The programs that do not — pointer-chasing, strided, or working-set-spilling workloads — run at RAM speed regardless of the cache, and the cache hierarchy's job is to make that case rare.

Okay, explain what idempotency means for an HTTP API, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once. RFC 9110 defines it for HTTP methods. `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent. `POST` and `PATCH` are not.

`GET` is idempotent because it reads state without changing it. A thousand reads leave the database untouched. `DELETE` is idempotent because deleting resource 42 once removes it, and deleting it again leaves the same end state: resource 42 is gone. The second response differs — `200 OK` the first time, `404 Not Found` the second — but the server state is identical. Idempotency governs state, not response bodies.

`PUT` is idempotent because it replaces a resource wholesale. A `PUT /users/42` with body `{"name": "Alice"}` sets user 42 to Alice. Sending it a hundred times sets user 42 to Alice a hundred times. The result is Alice. `POST /users` with the same body creates a new user each time. A hundred sends produce a hundred users. That is the distinction: `PUT` targets a specific resource and overwrites it; `POST` asks the server to invent a new resource, and each request invents another.

`PATCH` is not idempotent because it describes a change, not a target state. A `PATCH /users/42` with `{"balance": +50}` adds 50 to the balance on every send. Two sends add 100. The end state depends on the request count. A `PATCH` that sets `{"name": "Alice"}` happens to be idempotent, but the method does not guarantee it. `PUT`'s full-replacement semantics do.

Networks drop requests. A client sends `PUT /users/42`, the server applies it, the response vanishes in transit. The client does not know whether the server received the request. It retries. Because `PUT` is idempotent, the retry is safe: the server applies the same overwrite, the state is correct, no duplicate user exists. A dropped `POST /users` is worse. The client retries, the server creates a second user, and the database now holds two Alice records from one intended action. This is why payment systems assign an idempotency key — a client-generated UUID sent in a header — so the server can recognize the retry and return the first response instead of charging the card twice.

The retry argument is the practical reason the method contract matters. Proxies retry idempotent requests on failure; they do not retry non-idempotent ones. HTTP/2's `GOAWAY` frame tells a client which requests the server processed before a connection closed, and the client resubmits only the ones past that boundary. If the method were `POST`, the client would have to guess, and a wrong guess duplicates the work.

Idempotency is a property of the method's contract, not of a particular implementation. A server that increments a counter on `GET` violates the contract. The method is still idempotent by specification; the implementation is broken. The contract is what proxies, clients, and frameworks rely on, and a server that breaks it silently corrupts the assumptions that make retries safe.

Okay, explain how DNS turns a name into an address, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

A browser asks for `www.example.com`. The operating system hands that name to a resolver, which is usually a library routine called `getaddrinfo`. The resolver's job is to return an IP address. It does this by walking a hierarchy of servers, each one knowing a little more than the last.

The resolver first checks its own cache. If it asked for `www.example.com` recently, the address is still there, and the lookup ends in microseconds. If not, it checks the `hosts` file — `/etc/hosts` on Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows — which holds manual overrides. If the name is absent from both, the resolver goes to the network.

It starts with a root server. There are thirteen root server addresses, published in a file called the root hints zone, which ships with every operating system. The resolver picks one and sends a query for `www.example.com`. The root server does not know the address. It knows which servers hold `.com`, and it returns that list.

The resolver picks a `.com` server from the list and sends the same query. The `.com` server does not know `www.example.com` either. It knows which servers hold `example.com`, because the registrar that sold `example.com` recorded those servers with the `.com` registry. It returns that list.

The resolver picks an `example.com` server and asks again. This server holds the zone file for `example.com`, which is the authoritative list of every name in that domain. The zone file contains an A record for `www` — a line that maps the name to an IPv4 address, say `93.184.216.34`. The server returns that record. The resolver hands the address to the browser, caches the record for the number of seconds the record's time-to-live field specifies, and the lookup is done.

Three round trips: root, top-level domain, authoritative. Each one is a UDP packet out and a UDP packet back, costing a network round trip. A cold lookup from a home connection in New York to a server in London pays roughly 70 milliseconds per round trip, so the full walk costs 210 milliseconds. A warm lookup, where the resolver has cached the `.com` server list from a previous query, skips the root step and costs two round trips. A hot lookup, where the final record is cached, costs zero.

Most users never touch this chain directly. Their operating system forwards the query to a recursive resolver run by their ISP or by a public provider like Cloudflare at `1.1.1.1` or Google at `8.8.8.8`. The recursive resolver performs the entire walk on the client's behalf and caches every step. The first user in a neighborhood to look up `www.example.com` pays the full 210 milliseconds. Every subsequent user whose query hits the same recursive resolver gets the cached answer in a single round trip — five to ten milliseconds.

The chain works because authority delegates downward and never upward. The root servers are operated by twelve organizations under ICANN oversight. The `.com` registry is run by Verisign under contract. The `example.com` servers are run by whoever bought the domain. Each layer answers only for the slice below it, and the resolver climbs until it reaches the layer that holds the answer.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither proceeds. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Both sleep forever. The program hangs without crashing, which makes the bug hard to find in production logs.

The four conditions were named by Coffman in 1971. Mutual exclusion: a lock is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread keeps its lock while asking for the next. No preemption: locks release only when the holder chooses. Circular wait: the dependency graph forms a loop. Break any one and the deadlock cannot occur.

Lock ordering breaks circular wait. Every thread acquires locks in the same sequence. If the rule is "lock 1 before lock 2," thread A takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B waits at lock 1 while A holds it, but once A finishes and releases both, B acquires lock 1 and then lock 2. The loop never forms.

The discipline fails when the order is not global. A third thread that takes lock 2 before lock 1 reintroduces the cycle. A function that acquires a lock internally hides the order from the caller, who cannot know the sequence. The fix is a single documented order, enforced by lint rules or by wrapping the lock primitives so a violation throws at runtime. Go's `go vet` checks lock order in the standard `sync` package; Clang's ThreadSanitizer reports lock-order inversions on detection.

A hash map turns a key into an array index, then stores the value at that index. Two different keys can produce the same index. The map has to keep both.

The common fix is chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list. When a second key lands on an occupied bucket, the map appends it to that list. A lookup walks the list and compares keys one by one until it finds the match. The cost grows with list length.

The other fix is open addressing. No lists; every entry lives in the array itself. A new key probes neighboring slots — linear, quadratic, or via a second hash — until it finds an empty one. Lookups follow the same probe sequence. Deletion is harder: removing an entry would break the chain, so the map writes a tombstone marker that probes skip past but later insertions can overwrite.

Load factor is occupied slots divided by total slots. As it rises, collisions rise and lookups slow. Most maps resize — allocate a larger array, rehash every entry into it — when the factor crosses a threshold, often 0.7. Chaining tolerates higher factors because lists absorb overflow; open addressing needs the threshold lower, since a full array has nowhere to probe.

A poor hash function clusters keys into a few buckets and turns the map into a slow linked list. A good one spreads keys evenly, which is the entire premise the structure rests on.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each paired with a pointer back to the full row. The database walks this structure instead of scanning the table.

Without an index, a query for `users WHERE email = 'x'` reads every row in the table and compares the email field. With a B-tree index on `email`, the database descends a balanced tree of comparisons and finds the matching entry in roughly log₂(n) steps. A million-row table takes about twenty comparisons instead of a million.

A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on both columns, or on `last_name` alone. It does not serve a query that filters on `first_name` alone, because the tree is sorted by `last_name` first and the `first_name` values are scattered across its branches.

Indexes cost storage and write speed. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on an indexed column must update the index structure as well as the table. A table with five indexes takes roughly six times as long to write a row as an unindexed table, because the database maintains six structures instead of one.

An index hurts when its query pattern does not match it. A query like `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x'` cannot use a plain index on `email`, because the `LOWER` function transforms the stored value into something the tree never sorted. The database falls back to a full scan, and the index sits unused, collecting write overhead for nothing.

A partial index narrows the cost. `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) WHERE status = 'open'` indexes only the rows that match the condition, which shrinks the structure and skips maintenance on every closed order. This pays off when the filtered set is the one queries actually search.

The tradeoff is mechanical. An index trades write work and disk space for read speed on a specific query shape. Adding one without knowing the queries that run against the table adds cost without benefit.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as discrete messages. Each byte gets a sequence number. The first byte the connection sends might be number 1, the next 2, and so on, though in practice the starting number is random to guard against confusion with an old connection's packets.

When a sender writes 500 bytes, it labels the first byte with its sequence number and transmits that number in the TCP header. The receiver reads the header, checks the sequence number against what it expected, and places the bytes in the right slot in its receive buffer. If bytes 1 through 100 arrive, then 201 through 300, the receiver holds the second batch and waits for 101 through 200.

The receiver acknowledges received data. Its acknowledgment number tells the sender the next byte it expects, not the last byte it got. If the receiver got bytes 1 through 100, it sends ACK 101. If it then got 201 through 300 but is still missing 101, it sends ACK 101 again. A repeated acknowledgment tells the sender which gap to fill.

The sender retransmits the missing segment. TCP does not number packets; it numbers bytes, so a retransmission can even carry different byte boundaries than the original if the protocol stack chooses. The receiver fits the retransmitted bytes into the gap, advances its acknowledgment once the hole closes, and releases the now-contiguous data to the application above it.

The application never sees gaps. TCP buffers out-of-order segments and hands data upstream only in sequence-number order. A byte at position 201 waits in the buffer until 101 through 200 arrive, then all 200 bytes pass up together. What the application reads is a continuous, ordered stream, regardless of the order the wires delivered it.

A mutex protects a shared resource from concurrent access that would corrupt it.

Two threads running at the same time can both reach the same variable. Thread A reads the value 5, adds 1, and writes 6. Thread B reads the value 5, adds 1, and writes 6. Two increments happened. The variable went up by one. This is a race condition, and the result is wrong.

A mutex — mutual exclusion lock — draws a boundary around the code that touches the shared variable. A thread must acquire the lock before entering that section and release it on the way out. While thread A holds the lock, thread B cannot enter. It blocks, waiting, until A releases. Only then does B acquire, enter, and proceed.

The protected region is the critical section. Whatever happens inside it — reading, writing, checking a condition, updating a structure — happens for one thread at a time. The mutex serializes access. Concurrent becomes sequential within that boundary.

A mutex is not free. A thread that blocks on a lock does no useful work while it waits. If two threads contend heavily for one lock, the program loses the parallelism it was written to gain. A lock held too long turns many threads into one.

A mutex also does not compose without care. Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y. Thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. Neither moves. This is deadlock — two threads, two locks, circular waiting. The program hangs. Ordering locks consistently across the codebase prevents it: always acquire X before Y, never the reverse.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread by default. If a function acquires a lock and calls another function that tries to acquire the same lock, the thread blocks on a lock it already holds. A recursive mutex permits this — the same thread can acquire the same lock multiple times, releasing it only when the last acquisition unwinds. The standard mutex does not, and the self-deadlock is a common bug.

The mutex solves one problem: it makes a sequence of operations on shared state atomic with respect to other threads. Everything outside that guarantee — which lock protects which data, how long it is held, what order locks are taken — is the work the programmer still has to do.

A program allocates memory for objects it creates. It cannot free that memory while any part of the program can still reach it. Garbage collection is the process of finding which objects are no longer reachable and returning their memory to the heap.

The collector starts from roots. Roots are the things the program can touch directly: local variables on every thread's stack, static and global fields, and the CPU registers that hold references. Every object a root points to is live. Every object those objects point to is also live. The collector walks this graph, marking each object it reaches. Anything unmarked at the end is garbage.

That is the mark phase. The sweep phase follows. The collector scans the heap, finds every unmarked object, and adds its memory back to the free list. It also clears the marks on the live objects so the next cycle starts clean.

Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps. Live objects end up scattered across the heap with holes of freed memory between them. A program that allocates many small objects fragments the heap this way. Compaction fixes it: the collector slides every live object toward one end of the heap, closing the gaps, and updates every pointer to reflect the new address. The heap becomes contiguous again, and allocation is a simple bump of a pointer.

Compaction costs time. Moving objects means updating every reference to them, which requires knowing where those references are. A collector that moves objects is a moving collector, and it must pause the program threads while it works — a stop-the-world pause — because the pointers are in flux and the program cannot safely read them mid-move.

Generational collection cuts the cost. Most objects die young: a function creates a temporary list, returns, and the list is garbage. A generational collector divides the heap into a young region and an old region. It collects the young region frequently and the old region rarely. Since the young region is small, its collection is fast, and it catches most of the garbage without scanning the whole heap.

Objects that survive several young-region collections get promoted to the old region. The old region fills slowly, and when it does, the collector runs a full collection: mark the entire heap, sweep, compact. This is the expensive pass, and the generational design exists to postpone it.

The core idea is reachability. An object is alive if a path exists from a root to it. The collector traces those paths, and anything off the path is memory the program has already forgotten.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing between operations, and that timing is wrong.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads the balance, sees 100, and prepares to add 50. Thread B reads the balance at the same instant, sees the same 100, and prepares to add 30. Thread A writes 150. Thread B writes 130. Two deposits happened. The balance went up by 30. Fifty dollars vanished.

The operations were not atomic. "Read, add, write" is three steps, and the threads interleaved between the read and the write. Thread B acted on a value it read before thread A finished writing, so A's write overwrote B's, and B's deposit never landed.

A mutex fixes this. Thread A acquires the lock, reads 100, adds 50, writes 150, releases the lock. Thread B blocks at the acquire until A finishes, then reads 150, adds 30, writes 180. The balance is correct. The lock made the three steps indivisible, so no thread can read a value the other is mid-way through changing.

Race conditions hide in code that looks correct in isolation. Each thread's logic is sound. The bug lives in the gap between the steps, where another thread slips in and acts on stale state. The fix is always the same shape: collapse the gap so the read and the write cannot be separated.

Okay, explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain register.

A CPU runs at billions of cycles per second. Main memory runs far slower. A processor that fetched every instruction and every piece of data from RAM would spend most of its time waiting. A cache is a small block of fast memory built into the chip that sits between the processor and RAM, holding copies of the data the processor is most likely to need next.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element 4 right after element 3. A function that executes one instruction fetches the next instruction a byte or two ahead. This property is called locality. Spatial locality means nearby memory gets touched soon. Temporal locality means the same memory gets touched again. The cache exploits both.

When the processor reads a byte, the cache does not fetch just that byte. It fetches a block — typically 64 bytes — from RAM and stores it. The next read from that block hits the cache and returns in one or two cycles instead of the two to three hundred cycles a RAM fetch costs. A miss sends the request to RAM and stalls the processor until the data arrives.

Modern chips have three cache levels. L1 sits closest to the core, splits into separate banks for instructions and data, and runs at full speed — a hit takes about four cycles. L2 is larger and slower, around ten cycles. L3 is shared across all cores on the chip and takes roughly forty cycles. All three are still far faster than the trip to RAM.

The cache replaces old data to make room for new data. When a block needs to load and the cache set is full, the hardware evicts the least recently used block on the assumption that data untouched for a while will not be needed soon. A program that streams through a large array once fills the cache and immediately overwrites it, gaining nothing. A program that reuses the same small set of values hits the cache repeatedly and runs at the speed of the cache, not the speed of RAM.

The speedup is mechanical. The cache turns slow memory accesses into fast ones by keeping the right data close. A program written to fit its working set inside the cache can run an order of magnitude faster than one that thrashes it.

Okay, explain idempotency in the context of an HTTP API, in plain register.

An HTTP request is idempotent when sending it once has the same effect as sending it ten times. The server's state after the tenth request matches its state after the first. The response bodies may differ — the second `DELETE` returns 404 because the resource is already gone — but the resulting state of the system does not.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. It reads data and changes nothing, so repeating it changes nothing. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A `PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada. Sending it again sets the name to Ada again. The result is one user named Ada, not two.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST /orders` with `{"item": "book"}` creates one order. Sending it twice creates two orders. The server treats each request as a new command, not a statement of desired state. This is why payment endpoints that use `POST` need a separate guard against duplicate submissions: an idempotency key, sent in a header, that the server recognizes and short-circuits on the second attempt.

`DELETE` is idempotent in intent. The first call removes the resource. The second call finds nothing to remove and returns an error, but the resource is still gone. The end state — resource absent — is the same either way.

The distinction matters under network failure. A client sends a `PUT`, the server applies it, but the response drops. The client does not know whether the request landed. With an idempotent method, the client retries the same `PUT` and risks nothing. With a non-idempotent `POST`, a blind retry doubles the order. The safe move is to query first or use a deduplication key, because the protocol method alone will not protect the state.

Idempotency is a property of the method's contract, not a guarantee the server always honors. A badly written `PUT` handler that appends to a list instead of replacing it breaks the contract. The HTTP specification declares the property; the server implementation must uphold it.

Okay, explain how DNS resolves a domain name to an IP address, in plain register.

A browser types `example.com` into its address bar. The browser hands that name to a resolver, which is usually a server run by the ISP or a public resolver like Google's 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1. The resolver's job is to return an IP address, and it does this by walking a tree of servers from the top down.

The resolver starts at a root server. There are thirteen root server addresses, published in a file every operating system ships with, and the resolver picks one. It asks that root server for `example.com`. The root server does not know the answer. It knows only the top-level domains. It answers with a referral: the list of servers authoritative for the `.com` top-level domain.

The resolver takes that referral and asks a `.com` server the same question. The `.com` server also does not know the IP address. It knows which name servers hold the records for `example.com` specifically. It returns those name servers' addresses.

The resolver asks `example.com`'s authoritative name server for the address. This server holds the actual zone file for the domain. It finds the A record for `example.com`, which contains the IPv4 address `93.184.216.34`, and returns it. The resolver caches that answer for the time-to-live the record specifies, then hands the address back to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

Caching shortens this walk. The browser, the operating system, and the resolver each keep their own cache. A repeat lookup for `example.com` within the TTL window returns from the resolver's cache without contacting any server upstream. The root and `.com` referrals get cached too, so a resolver that recently looked up any `.com` domain skips the root query and goes straight to the `.com` servers for the next one.

The system is a hierarchy of delegations. The root delegates to `.com`, `.com` delegates to `example.com`, and the authoritative server at the bottom holds the answer. Each layer points to the next, and the resolver chases those pointers until one of them stops referring and starts answering.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it.

A deadlock is a state where two threads stop forever, each waiting for a lock the other holds.

Thread A acquires lock X. Thread B acquires lock Y. Thread A then tries to acquire lock Y, which B holds, so A blocks. Thread B tries to acquire lock X, which A holds, so B blocks. Neither thread releases its lock, because each needs the other's lock to proceed. Neither ever will. The program hangs.

Four conditions produce this: locks are held exclusively, a thread holding one lock waits for another, locks are not preempted by force, and a cycle exists in the wait graph. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The reliable fix is lock ordering. Pick a global order for every lock in the program — X before Y, always — and require every thread to acquire locks in that order. Thread A takes X then Y. Thread B also takes X then Y. B blocks at X until A releases it. Once A holds both locks and finishes its work, it releases them, and B proceeds. The cycle never closes.

The rule is simple to state and hard to enforce. A codebase with a hundred locks and a dozen engineers sees violations: a function deep in a call path takes Y then calls into code that takes X, reversing the order without anyone noticing. Static analysis tools that flag inconsistent lock acquisition order catch this. Without them, the deadlock surfaces only under specific thread timing, which means it appears in production and not in tests.

A hash map turns a key into an array index, then stores the value at that index. Two keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has a policy for it.

The common policy is chaining. Each slot in the array holds a pointer to a linked list rather than a single entry. When a key hashes to an occupied slot, the new entry joins the list. A lookup walks that list, comparing keys one by one until it finds the match or reaches the end. The cost grows with list length.

Open addressing takes the other road. There is no list; the entry lives in the array itself. A collision sends the map probing other slots according to a fixed sequence. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by growing intervals — one, four, nine — to spread entries out. Double hashing computes a second probe step from a second hash function, which avoids the clustering that linear probing suffers when many keys land near the same slot.

Deletion under open addressing has a cost. Removing an entry and leaving an empty slot breaks the probe chain for any key that was inserted past it. The map marks the slot as a tombstone — not empty, not occupied — so a probe sequence continues past it. Tombstones accumulate and slow lookups until the map rehashes.

Load factor is the ratio of stored entries to array slots. As it rises, collisions rise with it. Chaining degrades gracefully: lists get longer, lookups get slower, but nothing breaks. Open addressing degrades sharply: the array fills, probe sequences lengthen, and once the array is full no new entry can be placed without growing. Most open-addressed maps resize and rehash every entry when the load factor crosses a threshold, often around 0.7.

The choice between the two is a trade over memory and cache. Chaining spends a pointer per entry and scatters list nodes across the heap. Open addressing packs entries into one contiguous array, which a CPU cache prefetches well, but it pays for that locality with sensitivity to load factor and a harder deletion path.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row. It holds a copy of one or more columns, sorted, each entry pointing back to the row it came from. A query against an indexed column reads the index, finds the matching keys in sorted order, and fetches only those rows. Without the index, the database reads the whole table to find them.

The index earns its keep on queries that run often and return few rows. A ten-million-row table with an index on `user_id` finds a single user in a handful of disk reads. Without it, the database scans all ten million. The same index accelerates joins: if the join column is indexed on both sides, the database matches rows by walking two sorted structures instead of comparing every pair.

Indexes cost. Every index is a file on disk and a structure in memory. A table with six indexes uses seven times the storage of the table alone for the index set, and each index must stay in the buffer pool to be useful, competing with the table and with every other index for that RAM.

Writes pay at every index. An `INSERT` adds a row to the table and then inserts an entry into each index in its sorted position. A `DELETE` removes from each. An `UPDATE` to an indexed column deletes the old entry and inserts a new one, because the sort position changed. A table with five indexes takes six writes per inserted row. On a system doing ten thousand inserts per second, that is sixty thousand index maintenance operations per second, and the database serializes them in the same transaction as the table write.

An index hurts when it serves a query that no longer runs, or when it duplicates another index's leading columns. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` also serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone; a separate single-column index on `last_name` is dead weight. The database still maintains it on every write. Indexes on columns with low cardinality — a `status` column holding three values across a hundred million rows — rarely help a query, because the database still fetches a large fraction of the table, and the index adds a lookup step the scan did not need.

The index that helps one query can slow the whole system. A reporting query that runs once a night benefits from an index, but if that index slows ten thousand writes per minute during the day, the trade is wrong. Dropping the index and accepting the nightly scan costs less overall. The decision is not whether indexes are good, but whether the read time saved exceeds the write time spent, across the real workload, not the expected one.

Okay, explain how TCP keeps data in order, written in plain White/Orwell register.

TCP sends data as a stream of bytes, not as a sequence of messages. The sender breaks that stream into segments, and the network can deliver those segments out of order, duplicate them, or drop them. TCP's job is to reconstruct the original byte stream at the receiver regardless of what the network did in between.

Every byte in the stream has a position number, starting from an arbitrary value TCP calls the initial sequence number. Each segment carries in its header the sequence number of its first byte, and the receiver knows the length of the segment, so it knows the position of every byte inside. A segment arriving third can be placed correctly beside one that arrived first, because both carry absolute positions in the same stream.

The receiver tracks the next byte it expects. That number is the sequence number of the earliest byte it has not yet received. When a segment arrives, the receiver checks its sequence number against that expected value. If the segment's first byte matches the expected number, the bytes are in order. The receiver passes them to the application and advances the expected number by the segment's length.

If a segment arrives with a sequence number higher than expected, there is a gap. The bytes before that gap have not arrived. The receiver stores the out-of-order segment in a buffer and sends an acknowledgement back carrying the expected sequence number — the low end of the gap, not the high end of what arrived. That acknowledgement tells the sender: everything before this number is received, send it again from here. The sender retransmits the missing segment. When it arrives, the gap closes, the buffered out-of-order segments fall into place, and the receiver advances the expected number across all of them.

The acknowledgement is cumulative. An ACK for sequence number 5000 means every byte before 5000 is received, whether those bytes arrived in one segment or twenty, in order or out of order. A later ACK for 6000 supersedes the earlier one. This is what makes the scheme robust against lost ACKs: a duplicate or delayed acknowledgement carries no danger, because each one confirms a position, not a single delivery.

The receive buffer is bounded. TCP advertises its current window size in every segment it sends, telling the sender how many bytes it can accept beyond the last acknowledged position. If the application reads slowly, the window shrinks. If it shrinks to zero, the sender stops. This keeps the receiver from being forced to hold more out-of-order data than it has room for.

What holds the stream together is that every byte has one number, every acknowledgement names a position, and the receiver hands bytes to the application only in ascending order. Segments can arrive in any sequence the network produces. The numbers put them back.

Okay, explain what a mutex protects against, in plain White/Orwell register.

A mutex protects against concurrent access to shared state. Two threads running at the same time can both read and write the same variable. Without coordination, one thread's write overwrites the other's, or a thread reads a value mid-update and sees a corrupted mix of old and new bytes. The mutex prevents this by allowing only one thread into the guarded section at a time.

The mechanism is ownership. A thread acquires the mutex before entering the critical section and releases it on exit. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that tries to acquire it blocks — it stops running and waits. The operating system or runtime suspends the waiting thread and wakes it when the holder releases. Only one thread holds the mutex at any moment, so only one thread touches the shared data inside the section.

A mutex protects against data races. A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location, at least one of them writes, and no synchronization orders the accesses. The result is undefined behavior in languages like C and C++: torn reads, lost updates, crashes. The mutex makes the accesses ordered and atomic as a group. Thread A acquires, writes the balance, releases. Thread B acquires, reads the balance, releases. Neither sees the other's partial work.

A mutex does not protect against the things it is often blamed for. It does not prevent deadlock. If thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2, while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1, both block forever. The mutex created the deadlock; it did not prevent it. It also does not make individual operations atomic across the whole program — it protects only the state inside the section between acquire and release. A thread that reads a value under one mutex and writes it back under another has no protection, because the value can change between the two sections.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy in its basic form. If a thread holding a non-recursive mutex tries to acquire it again, it deadlocks against itself. A recursive mutex permits re-entry by the same thread and increments a counter, releasing only when the counter returns to zero. This solves the self-deadlock but signals a design where the critical section's boundaries are unclear.

The cost is contention. Every acquire and release is a pair of atomic operations, and a contended mutex adds a context switch when a thread blocks. A critical section reached by a thousand threads per second becomes a serial bottleneck: all thousand pass through one at a time. The mutex makes the section correct and slow under load. Narrowing the section — holding the mutex for the fewest instructions possible — is the discipline that keeps correctness from costing throughput.

Okay, explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, in plain White/Orwell register.

Garbage collection reclaims memory the program can no longer reach. A running program holds references to objects through variables, fields, and the call stack. An object is live if a path of references connects it from one of those roots. An object is garbage if no such path exists. The collector's job is to find the garbage and free the bytes.

The marking collector starts from the roots and walks every reference it can follow. Each object it reaches, it marks. Each object it cannot reach, it leaves unmarked. When the walk finishes, the unmarked objects are garbage — no root, no path, no way for the program to touch them again. The collector sweeps the heap, frees every unmarked object, and clears the marks on the survivors for the next cycle.

This is reachability, not liveness in the strict sense. An object that the program will never use again but still holds a reference to is not garbage by this definition. The collector frees what is unreachable, not what is unwanted. A program that retains references to dead objects in a long-lived list will leak memory under any tracing collector, because the reference path keeps the object marked.

The mark-and-sweep walk pauses the program. The collector cannot trace a heap that is changing under it, so it stops the mutator threads, walks the object graph, sweeps, and resumes. On a heap of millions of objects that pause can run hundreds of milliseconds. The concurrent collectors in modern runtimes — Go's, the JVM's G1, .NET's — do most of the marking work while the program runs, shortening the stop-the-world phase to the barriers at the start and end of a cycle.

Sweeping leaves the heap fragmented. Free objects are scattered among live ones, so allocating a large object may fail even when enough total free bytes exist. The compacting collector fixes this by moving every live object to one end of the heap, leaving a single contiguous free range behind. Moving objects means every reference to them must be updated to the new address. The collector does this during the pause, rewriting pointers as it copies.

The copying collector splits the heap into two halves and allocates only from one. When that half fills, it copies every live object to the empty half, packing them end to end, then the halves swap roles. The old half becomes the free space. This makes allocation trivial — a pointer bumps forward by the object's size — and compaction is free, because the copy already packs. The cost is that the program uses only half the heap at any time.

Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. They partition the heap into a young region and an old region. New allocations go to the young region, which is small and collected often. A young-region collection is fast because the region is small and most objects in it are already garbage. Objects that survive several young collections are promoted to the old region, which is collected rarely. This trades a frequent cheap collection for a rare expensive one, and it works because the allocation pattern is real: short-lived temporals dominate most workloads.

Reference counting takes a different road. Every object carries a count of references pointing to it. A reference is created, the count goes up. A reference is dropped, the count goes down. The count hits zero, the object is garbage, and it is freed immediately, no trace needed. The cost is that every assignment to a pointer pays a pair of atomic updates, and a cycle of objects each referencing the other never reaches zero even when the cycle as a whole is unreachable. A reference-counted system either leaks cycles or needs a separate tracing collector to find them.

What unifies the tracing approaches is the graph walk. The collector does not ask whether an object is useful. It asks whether the program can still get to it. The answer comes from following references from the roots through the live object graph, and whatever the walk cannot touch is memory the program has already abandoned.

Okay, explain what a race condition is with a concrete example, in plain White/Orwell register.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome of a program depends on the order in which two or more concurrent operations execute, and that order is not controlled. The operations race for access to shared state. Whichever finishes first changes what the others see, and the result depends on the winner.

Consider a bank account with a balance of 100. Two threads each withdraw 40. The correct final balance is 20. The withdrawal code reads the current balance, subtracts 40, and writes the result back. Thread A reads 100. Thread B reads 100 before A writes. Both compute 60. Both write 60. The final balance is 60. Forty dollars vanished.

The interleaving that caused it is legal under the hardware. The CPU ran both reads before either write, because nothing told it not to. The two threads had no synchronization between the read and the write, so the scheduler could place their instructions in any order it chose. The program's correctness depended on an ordering it never enforced.

The bug is not that a thread read a stale value. Each thread read a value that was current at the moment of the read. The bug is that the value changed between the read and the write, and neither thread knew. The read-modify-write sequence looked atomic to the programmer but was three separate instructions to the machine, and another thread slipped between them.

A mutex fixes this specific race. A thread acquires the mutex before reading the balance and releases it after writing. While A holds the mutex, B blocks on the acquire and does not read until A has written 60 and released. B then reads 60, writes 20. The final balance is correct. The mutex serialized the two withdrawals, turning a race into a sequence.

Not every race is a data race. A data race is the specific case where two threads access the same memory location, at least one writes, and no synchronization orders the accesses. A race condition is broader: it includes cases where all accesses are synchronized but the higher-level logic still depends on ordering. A thread checks whether a file exists, then opens it. Between the check and the open, another thread deletes the file. The open fails. No shared variable was corrupted, but the program's behavior depended on uncontrolled timing. That is a race condition without a data race.

The defining property is the gap between check and use. A program inspects some state, decides what to do, and acts on that decision. Between the inspection and the action, the state changes. The decision was based on a world that no longer exists. The fix is always the same shape: close the gap. Hold a lock across the check and the action, or use an atomic primitive that combines them into one indivisible step, so that no other thread can change the state the decision rests on.

Okay, explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain White/Orwell register.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. Main memory is slow. A modern CPU can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but reading a value from DRAM takes roughly 100 nanoseconds. The cache delivers the same value in one to three. That gap is the reason the cache exists.

The cache works because of locality. Programs do not read memory at random. They read an instruction, then the next instruction. They walk an array element by element. They call a function, then execute the statements inside it. The cache exploits this by fetching data in blocks, not single bytes. When the CPU requests a byte at address 1000, the cache loads a 64-byte line covering addresses 1000 through 1063. The next seven reads land in that line and cost nothing from main memory.

A cache miss is the moment the requested data is not in the cache. The CPU stalls, waits for the line to arrive from DRAM, and then resumes. A cache hit is the opposite: the data is present, and the read completes in one cycle. The ratio of hits to misses determines how close the program runs to the CPU's peak speed. A loop scanning an array sequentially hits on nearly every access. A loop chasing pointers through a linked list misses on nearly every node, because each node can live anywhere in memory and the prefetcher cannot predict where the next one is.

Modern CPUs have three levels of cache. L1 is smallest and fastest, 32 to 48 kilobytes, delivering in one cycle. L2 is larger, around 1 megabyte, taking roughly 10 cycles. L3 is largest, 8 to 32 megabytes, taking 30 to 50 cycles. Each level catches what the one above missed. A request that misses all three goes to DRAM and pays the full 100-nanosecond cost.

The cache also saves writes. A store goes to the L1 cache, and the cache line is marked dirty. The CPU continues executing. The cache writes the dirty line back to main memory later, in bulk, when the line is evicted or the core explicitly flushes it. This batches slow memory writes the same way the line fetch batches reads.

What makes the cache speed up a program is the ratio. A program whose accesses are predictable and packed hits the cache on most accesses and runs near the CPU's clock speed. A program whose accesses scatter misses on most of them and runs at DRAM speed, which is roughly a hundredth of the CPU's peak. The same CPU, the same instructions, can run a hundred times faster or slower depending on whether the memory pattern gives the cache something to work with.

Okay, explain what idempotency means for an HTTP API, in plain White/Orwell register.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as if it had been sent once. The second request does not duplicate the first. It does not create a second record, charge a card a second time, or append a second row. The server either performs the operation again and the result is unchanged, or it recognizes the repeat and does nothing.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. A `GET` request reads a resource and changes nothing, so issuing it ten times leaves the server in the same state as issuing it once. `PUT` is idempotent by design. A `PUT` sends a full representation of a resource, and the server stores it at the named URL. Sending the same `PUT` twice stores the same representation twice, and the stored resource is identical either way. The second request overwrites the first with the same data.

`DELETE` is idempotent in its contract. The first `DELETE` on `/users/42` removes the user. The second `DELETE` on `/users/42` finds no user at that URL and returns 404, or returns 204 with no content. The server state after the second request is the same as after the first: user 42 is gone. The response body may differ, but idempotency is about server state, not about the bytes returned.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST` submits data to a handler, and the handler decides what to do. A `POST` to `/orders` with a cart of three items creates an order. Sending that same `POST` twice creates two orders. The server has no way to know the second request is a repeat unless the client provides something extra. This is why payment endpoints are the classic non-idempotent hazard: a network timeout after the server has charged the card but before the response reaches the client leads the client to retry, and the card is charged twice.

The fix for non-idempotent `POST` is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique identifier — a UUID — and sends it in a header such as `Idempotency-Key`. The server stores that key alongside the first request's result. When a second request arrives with the same key, the server looks it up, returns the stored result, and does not re-execute the operation. The key turns a non-idempotent endpoint into an idempotent one by making the server remember what it already did.

The distinction matters because HTTP clients retry. A browser, a mobile app, or an intermediate proxy that loses the response to a request cannot tell whether the server received it. The safe action is to retry. If the endpoint is idempotent, the retry is harmless. If it is not, the retry is a duplicate. The HTTP specification marks `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent so that clients and proxies know which requests they can retransmit without asking the server whether the first attempt landed. `POST` carries no such guarantee, and the cost of treating it as if it did is a second order, a second charge, a second row in the database.

Okay, explain how DNS turns a name into an address, in plain White/Orwell register.

A browser asked for `www.example.com` needs its IP address before it can open a connection. DNS is the system that returns that address. It works by walking a tree of nameservers, each one responsible for a different level of the name, until one of them holds the answer.

The walk starts at the recursive resolver. This is the server the operating system contacts when an application calls `getaddrinfo`. Its address is configured in the OS or handed out by the network via DHCP. The resolver's job is to chase the name across the DNS hierarchy and hand the final address back to the operating system. It does not know the answer itself; it finds it.

The resolver begins at the root nameservers. There are thirteen root addresses, published in a file called the root hints, which every recursive resolver ships with. The resolver picks one and sends it a query for `www.example.com`. The root server does not know the address. It knows only which servers are authoritative for the top-level domains. It returns a referral: a list of nameservers for the `.com` zone.

The resolver sends the same query to one of those `.com` nameservers. This server also does not know the address of `www.example.com`. It knows which servers are authoritative for the `example.com` zone. It returns a referral to those servers.

The resolver sends the query to the `example.com` nameserver. This server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds a record for `www` — an A record containing an IPv4 address, or a CNAME record pointing to another name that the resolver must then resolve. For an A record, the nameserver returns the address. The resolver caches it for the time-to-live specified in the record, then returns it to the operating system, which hands it to the application.

Each step in that walk is a separate UDP packet on port 53. The resolver sends a question, waits for a response, and sends a new question to the next server. A full recursive resolution for a name not in cache takes four round trips: one to the root, one to the top-level domain, one to the authoritative server, and the final response back to the client. Each round trip costs the network latency between the resolver and that server.

Caching collapses those round trips. The operating system caches the result. The browser caches it. The recursive resolver caches every referral it receives along the way, not just the final answer. On the next request for any name under `.com`, the resolver skips the root and goes straight to the `.com` nameservers, because it already knows their addresses from the previous walk. On the next request for `www.example.com`, it skips the root and the top-level domain and asks the `example.com` nameserver directly. A name that has been recently resolved returns from cache in zero round trips.

The time-to-live on each record controls how long the cache holds it. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver serves the cached address for one hour, then discards it and asks the authoritative server again. A short TTL of 60 lets a domain change its address and see the change propagate in a minute, but it forces the resolver to repeat the full walk every minute. A long TTL of 86400 means one walk per day, but a change takes up to a day to reach everyone.

The system works because the name is hierarchical and each level delegates downward. The root delegates to `.com`. The `.com` servers delegate to `example.com`. The `example.com` server holds the record for `www`. No single server knows every name on the internet. Each one knows its piece and knows who holds the next piece, and the resolver follows that chain until the last server gives it a number.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in plain White/Orwell register.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads are stuck, each waiting for a resource another holds, and none will give up what it has. The system stops. No thread progresses. No error fires. The deadlock is silent, and it lasts until the process is killed.

The mechanism is a cycle of waits. Thread A holds lock 1 and tries to acquire lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and tries to acquire lock 1. A waits for B to release lock 2. B waits for A to release lock 1. Neither releases, because each is blocked mid-acquire and cannot run the code that would release its own lock. The wait is permanent. The cycle has no exit.

The four conditions that produce this were named by Coffman in 1971. Mutual exclusion: the locks are held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one lock requests another. No preemption: a thread cannot be forced to release a lock it holds. Circular wait: a chain of threads exists where each holds a lock the next one needs, and the last thread in the chain holds a lock the first one needs. Break any one of the four and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest condition to break is circular wait. Impose a global order on every lock in the program and require every thread to acquire locks in ascending order. Thread A wants lock 1 and lock 2. It acquires lock 1 first, then lock 2. Thread B wants the same two locks. Under the ordering rule, B must also acquire lock 1 first, then lock 2. B cannot hold lock 2 and wait for lock 1, because the rule forbids acquiring lock 2 before lock 1. The cycle cannot close. If A holds lock 1, B blocks on lock 1 before it ever touches lock 2, and A runs to completion, releases both, and B proceeds.

The discipline is total. A single thread that acquires locks out of order breaks the guarantee for the whole program. A function that acquires a lock internally must document which lock it takes, so callers who already hold a lock know whether calling that function violates the order. A lock acquired inside a callback or a virtual method call is the common place the order breaks, because the caller does not know which lock the callee will reach for. The ordering rule works only when every lock in the program has a position in the order and every code path respects it.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in a fixed array. It computes an integer from the key — the hash — and maps that integer onto an array index, typically by taking the remainder modulo the array length. Two keys that land on the same index collide.

There are two ways to handle that.

**Chaining** keeps a linked list at each array slot. On insert, the map appends the new entry to that slot's list. On lookup, it walks the list and compares keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The cost grows with the list length. If the table holds *n* entries across *m* slots, the average list length is *n/m* — the load factor. A load factor of 0.75 means three quarters of the slots hold one entry on average; a load factor of 4 means each list averages four entries, and every lookup pays for that walk. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain.

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the array, no lists. When a slot is taken, the map probes the next slot by some rule and keeps going until it finds an empty one. Linear probing checks index, index+1, index+2. Quadratic probing jumps by squares: index+1, index+4, index+9. Double hashing computes a second hash to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed stride. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Go's `map` all use open addressing.

The tradeoff is locality against deletion. Chaining scatters entries across heap-allocated list nodes but deletes in O(1) — unlink the node. Open addressing keeps entries contiguous in the array, which is cache-friendly, but deletion leaves a tombstone marker in the slot so later probes don't stop short and miss entries that were inserted past it. Too many tombstones slow lookups, which is why open-addressed maps rehash to compact themselves.

Both schemes degrade as the load factor rises. The standard fix is to allocate a larger array — usually double the current size — recompute every key's index, and copy entries over. That rehash is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert, the same way `std::vector`'s growth copies are amortized across appends.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It holds a copy of one or more columns plus a pointer back to each row, kept in sorted order so a lookup can binary-search instead of scanning every row.

Without an index, finding the rows where `status = 'shipped'` means reading the whole table and checking each row. With an index on `status`, the database finds the matching entries in the index in O(log n) time, then fetches only those rows. On a ten-million-row table where three thousand match, that is the difference between reading ten million rows and reading three thousand.

A B-tree index, the common kind, is a balanced tree of sorted keys. Each internal node narrows the range; each leaf holds a key and a row pointer. PostgreSQL, MySQL with InnoDB, and SQL Server all default to B-trees. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` sorts by last name first, then first name within each last name, so it serves queries that filter on last name alone but not queries that filter on first name alone — the leftmost column sets the sort order.

Indexes hurt in three ways.

They cost storage. An index is a copy of part of the table. Indexing five columns on a million-row table can double the disk footprint.

They slow writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update the index too, keeping the tree balanced and sorted. A table with six indexes takes roughly seven times longer to insert a row than a table with none — one write for the row, six for the indexes. A high-write, low-read table like a transient event log pays that cost on every row and rarely gets the benefit.

They miss when the query does not match the index shape. A query like `WHERE lower(email) = 'x@y.com'` cannot use a plain index on `email` because the function transforms the value; the sorted keys no longer correspond to the transformed output. PostgreSQL solves this with an expression index — `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` — but the plain index sits unused. Similarly, `WHERE status <> 'shipped'` often skips the index because the inequality matches most of the table, and the planner decides a sequential scan is cheaper than thousands of random index lookups followed by row fetches.

The planner makes that call using table statistics, not the index's existence. It estimates how many rows a predicate matches and chooses between an index scan and a sequential scan based on that count. If it expects ten rows and the predicate actually matches nine hundred thousand, it picks the wrong path. Stale statistics cause this; `ANALYZE` refreshes them.

A covering index avoids the row fetch entirely. If a query selects only `status` and `order_id`, and an index on `(status, order_id)` exists, the database reads both values from the index leaf and never touches the table. That removes the random I/O that makes index lookups expensive on spinning disks — each row fetch is a seek to a different disk block. On SSDs the seek cost is lower, but the extra reads still consume bandwidth and cache.

The rule is not "index columns you query." The rule is index columns where the query narrows the result set sharply and the write rate tolerates the maintenance cost. A column with three values across ten million rows does not narrow anything; an index on it helps no query and slows every insert. A column that identifies one row out of ten million narrows everything; an index on it turns a full scan into a handful of reads.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a series of messages. Every byte gets a sequence number.
