The first byte's number is not zero; it is a random 32-bit value the sender picks during the handshake, and each subsequent byte counts up from there. A 1000-byte segment carrying sequence number 7000 covers bytes 7000 through 7999.

The receiver acknowledges what it has. An ACK carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects — the lowest byte it has not yet received. ACK 8000 means "I have everything up to 7999; send 8000 next." This is cumulative: if bytes 7000–7999 and 9000–9999 arrived but 8000–8999 did not, the receiver sends ACK 8000 twice, once for each segment it got. The gap stays unacknowledged.

The sender keeps every sent segment in a retransmission buffer until it sees the ACK that covers those bytes. A timer runs per segment. If the ACK does not arrive before the timer fires — the segment was lost, or the ACK was lost — the sender retransmits. The timer is not fixed. TCP measures the round-trip time on each connection and sets the retransmission timeout from a smoothed average plus a variance margin. A one-millisecond link to a host in the next rack gets a timeout near one millisecond; a 200-millisecond link across an ocean gets a timeout near 400.

Out-of-order arrival is the core problem. Segments travel through routers that reorder them, and retransmitted segments arrive after segments sent later. The receiver handles this with a sliding window. It tracks which byte ranges it has received inside the window it advertised to the sender. When a gap fills — the missing 8000–8999 segment finally arrives — the receiver sends a single ACK for the new contiguous high-water mark. If 7000–9999 is now complete, that ACK is 10000, regardless of how many segments arrived in the meantime.

The receiver does not hand bytes to the application one segment at a time. It buffers what it has and delivers a contiguous run to the application only up to the first gap. Bytes 9000–9999 sitting in the buffer while 8000–8999 is missing stay in the kernel's receive buffer, unseen by the application, until the gap closes. The application sees a byte stream in order, with no holes, because the receiver held back the out-of-order tail.

The sender's window is the mirror. The receiver advertises a window size in every ACK — how many bytes of free buffer space it has. A window of 65535 means the sender may transmit up to 65535 bytes past the acknowledged point before waiting. As the application reads from the receive buffer, the window opens and the receiver advertises a larger value in its next ACK. If the application stops reading, the window shrinks to zero. A zero-window ACK tells the sender to stop; it then sends periodic one-byte probes to test whether the window has reopened, which keeps the connection alive without flooding a full receiver.

Sequence numbers are 32 bits and wrap. A 10 Gbps link sends 1.25 billion bytes per second, so the counter rolls over in roughly 3.4 seconds. TCP handles this with PAWS — Protection Against Wrapped Sequence numbers — which stamps every segment with a 32-bit timestamp from the sender's clock. A segment with an older timestamp is treated as a stale duplicate even if its sequence number falls inside the current window, because the timestamp disambiguates the two passes through the number space.

The result is a byte stream that arrives in order at both ends, despite loss, reordering, and duplication on the wire underneath. The sequence number names each byte. The cumulative ACK reports the contiguous frontier. The retransmission buffer fills gaps. The sliding window bounds how far ahead the sender can run. Everything else in TCP — congestion control, slow start, fast retransmit — sits on top of that ordering machinery and reacts to the same ACK stream.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state across threads.

Two threads running on two cores can both touch the same variable at once. Thread A reads `count`, gets 5, adds 1, writes 6. Thread B reads `count` in the nanosecond between A's read and A's write, also gets 5, adds 1, also writes 6. Two increments produced one. The lost update is a race condition, and the mutex exists to prevent it.

A mutex — mutual exclusion lock — has two states, locked and unlocked. A thread calls `lock()` before touching the shared data and `unlock()` when done. If thread A holds the lock, thread B's `lock()` blocks until A releases it. Only one thread enters the critical section at a time. The operating system or language runtime implements the block: on Linux, `futex` spins briefly in user space, then falls back to a kernel sleep if the lock does not come free quickly. POSIX calls it `pthread_mutex_t`, C++ `std::mutex`, Go `sync.Mutex`, Java `synchronized`.

What the mutex does not do is protect against reordering by the compiler or the CPU. The compiler can move a write above the `lock()` call if nothing visible stops it. A CPU with out-of-order execution can do the same. The fix is a memory barrier, and `lock()` and `unlock()` insert one implicitly on architectures that need it — x86, ARM, RISC-V all differ in how weak their memory model is. Acquire semantics on `lock()` prevent reads and writes below it from moving up. Release semantics on `unlock()` prevent reads and writes above it from moving down. Without those barriers, thread B could see the lock as free but read stale data from inside the critical section.

A mutex protects against one thread seeing a half-written value. A 64-bit integer write is atomic on x86-64 but not on a 32-bit ARMv5, where the write happens as two 32-bit stores. Thread B reading between the two stores gets a value that was never written — high 32 bits from the new value, low 32 bits from the old. The mutex makes the write appear instantaneous to other threads because no other thread can read until `unlock()`.

A reentrant mutex allows the same thread to call `lock()` twice without deadlocking. POSIX calls this `PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE`. A plain mutex does not: the second `lock()` on the same thread blocks forever waiting for the first to release, and the first will not release because it is blocked inside the same call stack. Go's `sync.Mutex` is non-reentrant by design; the Go authors consider reentrancy a sign that the lock scope is wrong.

Deadlock is the cost. Thread A locks mutex 1 then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then tries to lock mutex 1. Both wait forever. The fix is a lock ordering discipline — every thread acquires the two mutexes in the same order — or a single lock that covers both resources. A lock-free data structure avoids the problem entirely by using atomic compare-and-swap operations instead of a mutex, trading simpler deadlock reasoning for harder correctness proofs about the algorithm itself.

The mutex is the blunt instrument. It serializes access, which means the protected section runs on one thread at a time no matter how many cores the machine has. A critical section that holds the lock for ten milliseconds on a four-core machine under four-thread contention spends thirty milliseconds waiting for every ten milliseconds of work. Narrow the scope: lock, touch the data, unlock. Hold the lock across the minimum number of statements, never across I/O.

A program allocates memory it no longer needs. Garbage collection reclaims that memory automatically, on the basis that the runtime can tell which objects are still reachable and treat the rest as free.

The collector starts from roots. Roots are the things the program can reach without following any pointer: global variables, local variables on every thread's call stack, CPU registers holding object references. Every object reachable from a root, directly or through a chain of pointers, is live. Everything else is garbage.

**Tracing** walks that graph. The collector marks every object reachable from the roots, then sweeps the heap and frees anything unmarked. Lisp's original collector, described by John McCarthy in 1960, worked this way. The .NET CLR, the Java HotSpot JVM, Go, and V8 all trace.

Mark-sweep leaves fragmentation. Free blocks scatter between live objects, and a large allocation may fail even when the total free space is enough, because no single gap is big enough. Mark-compact fixes this by sliding live objects to one end of the heap after marking, leaving a single contiguous free region. The cost is copying every live object on every collection. The JVM's throughput collector uses mark-sweep-compact.

**Copying** collection splits the heap into two halves. The program allocates in one half, called from-space. When it fills, the collector copies every live object from from-space into the empty half, to-space, packing them contiguously. From-space is then wiped and reused. This costs time proportional to the number of live objects, not the total heap size — a heap full of garbage collects cheaply, because most objects are never copied. Lisp machines and Smalltalk used copying collectors. HotSpot's young generation uses it.

**Reference counting** takes a different approach. Every object carries a count of how many pointers reference it. Assignment increments the target's count and decrements the old target's. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and can be freed immediately — no tracing pass. CPython uses reference counting for every object. The cost is two counter updates on every pointer write, and the failure mode is cycles: two objects pointing at each other keep both counts at one forever, even when nothing else references either. CPython runs a tracing collector periodically to break those cycles. Swift uses ARC — automatic reference counting — and requires the programmer to break cycles manually with `weak` references, because Swift has no tracing collector as a backstop.

The hard problem is pause time. A tracing collector that stops every thread while it walks the heap can freeze a program for tens or hundreds of milliseconds on a large heap. Three answers exist.

**Generational** collection exploits the observation that most objects die young. The heap is split into a young generation and an old generation. New objects allocate in the young generation, which is small and collected frequently. Objects that survive several young-gen collections promote to the old generation, which is large and collected rarely. A ten-megabyte young generation collects in a millisecond; a ten-gigabyte old generation collects in a second. HotSpot, .NET, V8, and Go all use generational collection or a variant.

**Concurrent** collection runs the tracer on a separate thread while the program keeps mutating the heap. The collector must handle the case where the program changes a pointer the collector has already visited, which would cause the collector to miss the now-reachable object. Read or write barriers — small fragments of code the compiler inserts around every pointer access —record those changes so the collector can revisit. Go's collector is concurrent and uses a write barrier during the mark phase. HotSpot's G1 and ZGC are concurrent. The tradeoff is throughput: the barriers add overhead to every pointer write, and the collector thread competes with the program for CPU.

**Incremental** collection breaks the trace into small slices and interleaves them with program execution, bounding each pause. The same barrier machinery tracks mutations between slices. This trades many short pauses for a few long ones. V8's Orinoco collector is incremental and concurrent.

The collector that fits depends on the workload. A short-lived batch job tolerates a full stop-the-world collection at exit. A web server handling ten thousand requests per second needs sub-millisecond pauses and pays the barrier cost to get them. A real-time controller needs hard bounds and uses collectors like Metronome, the IBM JVM's real-time collector, which fragments the pause into slices small enough to meet a deadline.

A race condition is what happens when two threads reach shared data at the same time and the result depends on which one gets there first. The program's output stops being a property of the code and becomes a property of the scheduler's timing.

A bank account holds 500 dollars. Two threads each withdraw 100. The correct final balance is 300. The code reads the balance, subtracts 100, writes it back. Thread A reads 500. Thread B reads 500 — before A has written its result. A subtracts 100, writes 400. B subtracts 100, writes 400. Two withdrawals produced one. The account holder lost 100 dollars and the program reported nothing wrong.

The failure is silent. No exception fires. No assertion trips. The code runs to completion and returns a number that was never the correct state of the account. Run the same program a thousand times and the bug appears on some runs and not others, because the operating system scheduler interleaves the threads differently each time. A test that passes once does not prove the code is correct; it proves the scheduler happened to interleave that run safely.

The cause is the gap between read and write. The balance is read at one instruction and written at another, and between those two instructions the value is stale — it lives in a CPU register, not in memory, and no other thread can see that the thread is about to act on it. The two threads operate on the same snapshot, each blind to the other.

The fix is to make the read and the write atomic with respect to each other. A mutex around the balance update forces thread B to wait until thread A has both read and written. A compare-and-swap instruction does it without a lock: the CPU writes the new value only if the memory location still holds the value the thread read, and if it does not, the thread retries. Either way the two operations become one, and the interleaving that caused the loss cannot occur.

The deeper point is that "two operations that look sequential in the source" are not sequential in execution. The compiler, the CPU cache, and the scheduler all reorder and interleave work. A race condition is the name for the bug that appears when the code assumes they do not.

Okay, explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

A CPU runs at four gigahertz. Main memory runs at roughly three hundred megahertz. The processor executes an instruction in a quarter of a nanosecond, but fetching an operand from DRAM takes eighty nanoseconds — the speed of light across copper and silicon, plus the time to drive a memory bus. That gap is two hundred cycles of stall. The cache exists to close it.

A cache is a small block of SRAM built into the processor die. SRAM uses six transistors per bit and responds in one or two cycles, where DRAM uses one transistor and one capacitor per bit and must refresh its charge constantly. The trade is speed against density: SRAM is fast but large and expensive, so the cache holds a fraction of what main memory holds.

Modern processors stack three levels. The L1 cache is thirty-two kilobytes, split into separate banks for instructions and data, and the core reaches it in four cycles. The L2 cache is a quarter megabyte and costs twelve cycles. The L3 cache is eight to thirty-two megabytes, shared across all cores on the die, and costs forty cycles. Main memory costs two hundred. Each level is larger and slower than the one above it.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns. A loop that sums an array reads element zero, then element one, then element two — consecutive addresses, one after another. This is spatial locality: data near a recently accessed address is likely to be accessed soon. The cache exploits it by fetching in blocks, not single bytes. A cache line is sixty-four bytes on x86 and ARM. One miss pulls sixteen adjacent integers from memory into the cache, and the next fifteen reads hit the cache at four cycles instead of paying eighty nanoseconds each.

A function that calls `sqrt`, then calls `sqrt` again on the next loop iteration, executes the same instructions repeatedly. This is temporal locality: data accessed once is likely to be accessed again soon. The cache holds recently used lines at the top of the hierarchy, so the second call finds the instructions already in L1.

When the core requests a byte, the hardware checks L1, then L2, then L3. A hit returns the data at that level's latency. A miss at L3 goes to DRAM and pays the full two hundred cycles. The hit rate determines performance. A loop that walks a sixty-four-byte struct array sequentially hits L1 on every access after the first. A loop that follows a linked list through random heap addresses misses on nearly every node, because each node's address is unpredictable and the prefetcher cannot stay ahead.

The prefetcher is a separate piece of hardware that watches the stream of memory addresses and fetches cache lines before the core asks for them. A stride pattern — every thirty-two bytes, or every forty9six — lets it pull the next line into L1 while the core is still computing on the current one. Random access defeats it. A binary search through a sorted array touches one element, then one halfway across the array, then one a quarter of the way from that — each access is a cache miss because the address is unpredictable, and the prefetcher cannot guess the branch direction. This is why a binary search on a large array can be slower than a linear scan of a small one: the linear scan hits cache, the binary search misses.

Writes go through the cache too. A store writes to L1 and marks the line dirty. The dirty line writes back to memory later — when the cache evicts it to make room for a new line, or when another core requests that address. The replacement policy is pseudo-LRU: when a set is full, the hardware evicts the line least recently used, approximated to keep the logic fast. A four-megabyte L2 with sixty-four-byte lines holds sixty-five thousand lines; the policy decides which one leaves when the set fills.

Cache coherence keeps the cores consistent. Core A writes to address 0x1000, updating its L1. Core B holds the same line in its L1, now stale. The coherence protocol — MESI on x86 and ARM — invalidates core B's copy before core A's write completes. Core B's next read misses, fetches the updated line from core A or from L3, and gets the new value. The cost is a round trip across the interconnect, tens of cycles, but the alternative is two cores computing on different values for the same address.

The cache turns the eighty-nanosecond memory wall into a four-nanosecond common case. The program runs at the speed of its cache hits, not its memory latency. A program that fits its working set in L2 runs ten times faster than the same program whose working set spills to DRAM, on the same hardware, with the same algorithm. The cache is why data layout — struct size, array stride, allocation locality — often matters more than the operation count.

Okay, explain idempotency for an HTTP API, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once. The second call does not duplicate the first. It either repeats the same effect, which is harmless, or reports the effect already happened.

`GET /articles/42` is idempotent by nature. It reads a row and returns it. Ten identical requests return the same body, and no row changes. `PUT /articles/42` with the same body is idempotent by contract. The first call sets the title to "Pumps"; the second sets it to "Pumps" again. The stored value is identical either way.

`POST /articles` is not. The first call creates article 100 and returns its ID. The second call creates article 101. Two requests, two rows, two IDs. The client cannot safely retry, because retry means a second article.

The problem arrives on the network. A client sends `POST /orders`, the server creates the order, the server sends the response, and the connection drops before the client reads it. The client does not know the order was created. It retries. The server creates a second order. The customer is charged twice for one purchase.

HTTP solves this for the methods that are already idempotent. RFC 9110 defines `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent, so a client or proxy can retry them safely after a timeout. `POST` and `PATCH` are not. A proxy that retries a timed-out `POST` without an agreement from the application is broken by spec.

The application solves it for `POST` with an idempotency key. The client generates a unique string — a UUID — and sends it in the `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores that key alongside the order it creates. On the retry, the server finds the key, recognizes the request as a repeat, and returns the stored response from the first call instead of creating a second order. Stripe's API documents this pattern in its idempotent requests guide. The key makes a non-idempotent method behave idempotently for the duration the server keeps the record.

`DELETE` carries a subtlety. The first `DELETE /orders/100` removes the order and returns 200. The second returns 404, because the order is gone. The response differs, but the state is the same: the order does not exist after either call. Idempotency is about the resulting state, not the response body. A method that returns 200 on the first call and 404 on the second is still idempotent, because no second deletion occurred.

`PUT` carries the opposite subtlety. A `PUT` that sets a counter to 5 is idempotent. A `PUT` that appends to a list is not — it is a `POST` wearing a `PUT` verb, and two calls produce a list with the item twice. The method label does not grant idempotency. The handler's effect on the resource does.

Okay, explain how DNS resolves a hostname to an IP address, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

A browser asks for `example.com`. The operating system hands that question to a resolver, and the resolver returns an address like `93.184.216.34`. Between those two events sit a tree of servers, a chain of queries, and a cache at every level.

The process starts in the stub resolver, a small library inside the operating system. It does not answer the question itself. It sends a UDP packet to port 53 of a recursive resolver — the address configured in `/etc/resolv.conf` or handed out by DHCP, often a server run by the ISP, by Google at `8.8.8.8`, or by Cloudflare at `1.1.1.1`. The stub resolver's job ends there. The recursive resolver does the rest.

The recursive resolver checks its cache first. If it asked for `example.com` ten minutes ago and the record's time-to-live has not expired, it returns the cached address without contacting anyone. The TTL is a number the domain owner sets in the zone file; a high-traffic site might set 3600 seconds, a site preparing to change addresses might set 60. The cache is why DNS is fast in practice: the first lookup traverses the tree, and every lookup after that reads memory.

On a cache miss the resolver begins at the root. The root servers are thirteen named clusters, `a.root-servers.net` through `m.root-servers.net`, operated by ICANN, Verisign, and ten other organizations. Their addresses are published in a file called the root hints, which ships with every recursive resolver. The resolver picks one and sends it a query for `example.com`.

The root server does not know the address. It knows which servers hold the top-level domains. It returns a list of the nameservers for `.com` — the generic top-level domain servers run by Verisign under `a.gtld-servers.net` through `m.gtld-servers.net`. The resolver caches those NS records too, with a TTL of roughly two days, so it never asks the root again for any `.com` name until that cache expires.

The resolver sends the same query to a `.com` server. That server also does not know the address, but it knows which nameservers hold `example.com` — the authoritative servers the domain owner registered with their registrar, something like `a.iana-servers.net`. It returns those names and their addresses as glue records.

The resolver sends the query to the authoritative server for `example.com`. That server holds the zone file, the master list of records for the domain. It reads the A record for `example.com`, finds `93.184.216.34`, and returns it. The resolver caches that answer for the TTL in the record, then hands it back to the stub resolver, which hands it to the browser.

Four queries, four answers: root to `.com`, `.com` to `example.com`'s nameservers, those nameservers to the address. Each step narrows the question. The root delegates to the TLD, the TLD delegates to the authoritative server, the authoritative server answers. The resolver is the one thing that walks the whole path; every other server points to the next one and stops.

The protocol carries more than addresses. A query for `www.example.com` might return a CNAME record pointing to `example.com`, which means the resolver starts a second lookup for `example.com` and follows it to its A record. A mail server lookup sends a query for the MX record type and gets back a hostname plus a priority number, which the mail client resolves to an address in a second round. The record type is a field in the query, and the server returns only records that match it.

UDP carries most queries because the answers are small and a single round trip suffices. A response that exceeds 512 bytes, or a zone transfer between primary and secondary nameservers, switches to TCP. DNSSEC adds signature records that push responses past the UDP limit, which is why signed domains often answer over TCP without the client asking for it.

The system's weakness is the unauthenticated query. A resolver that asks the root for `.com` nameservers trusts whatever addresses come back, because the original DNS protocol has no way to verify that the answer came from the real server. DNSSEC fixes this by signing each record with a key the parent zone publishes, letting the resolver verify the chain from root to leaf. Adoption is partial: `.gov` and `.net` are signed, `.com` is signed, but many individual domains under them are not, and a resolver that demands DNSSEC on an unsigned domain gets no answer at all.

The system's strength is the cache at every layer. The browser caches. The operating system caches. The recursive resolver caches. The root is queried once per TTL per TLD, not once per user. A billion lookups for `google.com` in an hour produce a handful of queries to Google's authoritative servers and a billion cache hits in between. The tree is deep, but the walk is rare.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

Two threads, each holding a lock the other needs, wait forever. That is a deadlock.

Thread A locks the database connection, then tries to lock the print spool. Thread B locks the print spool, then tries to lock the database connection. A holds what B wants. B holds what A wants. Neither lets go. Both sleep. The program hangs.

Four conditions produce this, identified by Edsger Dijkstra in 1965. Mutual exclusion: only one thread holds a lock at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one lock requests another. No preemption: locks release only when the holder chooses, not by force. Circular wait: a ring of threads each wait for the next one's lock. Break any one and deadlock cannot occur.

The cleanest to break is circular wait. Impose a global order on every lock in the program. Number the database connection 1 and the print spool 2. Every thread that needs both acquires them in ascending order: connection first, spool second. Thread A locks 1 then 2. Thread B locks 1 then 2. Thread B blocks at the first lock while A holds it, so B never reaches the spool. When A finishes and releases both, B proceeds. The ring never closes.

The discipline is total or it is nothing. A single thread that locks out of order — grabbing the spool before the connection — breaks the guarantee for every other thread, even those that followed the rule. This is why lock ordering belongs in a project's conventions, not in individual functions. The Linux kernel documents lock order in `Documentation/locking/lockdep-design.rst` and enforces it at runtime with `lockdep`, a validator that flags any acquisition out of order before it ships.

The cost is a loss of flexibility. A thread that enters a function holding lock 3 cannot acquire lock 1, even briefly, without releasing 3 first and reacquiring it after. The order is global, so it constrains code that never deadlocks today to prevent code that might tomorrow.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array of buckets. The hash function does the conversion; the array holds the values. When two distinct keys hash to the same index, a collision occurs, and the map needs a strategy to keep both pairs retrievable.

The two strategies in production use are separate chaining and open addressing.

**Separate chaining** gives each bucket its own list. The array slot holds a pointer to the head of a linked list (or, in some implementations, a small array or a tree). On insert, the map hashes the key, walks to the corresponding bucket, and appends the new key-value pair to that bucket's list. On lookup, it hashes the key, finds the bucket, then walks the list comparing keys with `equals` until it finds a match or reaches the end. Collisions lengthen the list, so a bucket with eight colliding pairs requires up to eight comparisons on lookup. Java's `HashMap` works this way; since Java 8, it converts a bucket's linked list to a red-black tree once the list exceeds eight entries, turning an O(n) walk into an O(log n) one when a bucket gets heavy.

**Open addressing** stores all entries directly in the array itself. On collision, the map probes for the next open slot according to a fixed rule. Linear probing checks `index + 1`, then `index + 2`, and so on, wrapping around at the array's end. Quadratic probing jumps by squares: `index + 1`, `index + 4`, `index + 9`. Double hashing uses a second hash function to compute the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than a fixed stride. On lookup, the map probes the same sequence until it finds the key, hits an empty slot (meaning the key is absent), or has checked every position. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence derived from the hash; `dict` keeps at most two-thirds of its slots full and resizes when that threshold is crossed.

Both strategies degrade as the load factor — the ratio of stored entries to array slots — climbs. A load factor of 0.75 means three quarters of the slots are occupied. Past that, collisions multiply, probe sequences lengthen, and lookups slow. The map responds by allocating a larger array (typically twice the size) and rehashing every entry into its new position. Rehashing is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert, because it happens rarely relative to the number of operations between resizes.

The tradeoff between the two is memory locality versus collision tolerance. Open addressing keeps everything in one contiguous array, so a probe sequence touches adjacent cache lines, which modern CPUs fetch efficiently. But it degrades badly once the table fills past about 70 percent, because long probe chains form. Separate chaining tolerates higher load factors without catastrophic slowdown, because each bucket's list absorbs collisions independently, but it spends a pointer per entry on list overhead and scatters list nodes across the heap, which is cache-unfriendly.

A map that never resizes, never rehashes, and uses a weak hash function will collide on a large fraction of its keys. A map that resizes at the right threshold, uses a hash function that distributes bits uniformly, and picks a probing strategy that avoids clustering will keep average lookup time close to O(1) even with millions of entries.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It holds a copy of one or more columns plus a pointer back to the full row, kept in an order that makes lookup fast. The point is to avoid scanning every row.

Without an index, finding all employees in department 42 means reading the entire `employees` table, row by row, and discarding the ones that do not match. A million-row table means a million reads. With a B-tree index on `department_id`, the database walks a balanced tree to the first row where `department_id = 42`, then reads consecutive entries until the value changes. That is three or four tree levels plus the matching rows — perhaps a dozen reads instead of a million.

The index trades write speed and storage for read speed. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on an indexed column must also update the index tree, which may split or merge nodes. An index on a table that takes heavy writes costs real time on every transaction. It also costs disk space: the index is a second copy of the data, and a table with five indexes can spend more bytes on indexes than on the rows themselves.

An index hurts when the database cannot use it, or when it serves a query that does not need it. Five cases cover most of the damage.

A query wrapped in `WHERE LOWER(last_name) = 'smith'` cannot use a plain index on `last_name`, because the `LOWER` function transforms the value and the index holds the original. The database falls back to a full scan, and the index sits unused, still collecting write overhead. The fix is a functional index on `LOWER(last_name)`, or dropping the function from the query.

A multi-column index on `(last_name, first_name)` cannot serve a query that filters on `first_name` alone. The B-tree is sorted by `last_name` first, so `first_name` values are scattered across the whole index. The database does a full scan. Column order in a composite index is the order the tree sorts by; a query must constrain the leading columns to use it.

An index on a column with few distinct values — a `status` column holding `open`, `closed`, or `pending` — rarely helps. The index partitions a million rows into three piles of 333,000. The database still reads a third of the table, and the index adds a lookup per row. Low cardinality columns are usually better left unindexed, or indexed with a bitmap index if the database supports it.

A table that serves mostly writes and few reads pays the index cost on every insert and gets little back. A logging table that absorbs 10,000 rows per second and gets queried once a week does not need indexes on the log columns. The reads are rare enough that a full scan is cheaper than the write overhead of maintaining trees.

A covering index — one that includes every column the query selects — can turn a lookup plus a row fetch into a single index read. But it widens the index, which multiplies storage cost and slows writes further. It pays off when the query runs often and the extra columns are narrow.

The rule is mechanical. An index earns its place when it serves a query that runs often, on columns with many distinct values, that the query filters or joins on directly, without wrapping functions. It costs write time and disk space every moment it exists, whether the query runs or not. Dropping an unused index is the cheapest performance win available, because it removes overhead from every write and reclaims storage immediately.

TCP gives each byte a number. The sender attaches a sequence number to the first byte in every segment, and every subsequent byte counts up from there. A 500-byte segment with sequence number 1000 covers bytes 1000 through 1499; the next segment starts at 1500.

The receiver collects these segments and may get them out of order. Segment 1500 can arrive before segment 1000 if the network reorders them. The receiver holds the early segment in a buffer, notes the gap, and waits. When segment 1000 arrives, the receiver places both in the buffer by sequence number, delivers bytes 1000 through 1999 to the application in order, and discards the buffer copy.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. The acknowledgment number in the receiver's reply is the next byte it expects. An ACK of 2000 means bytes 1 through 1999 arrived intact and the receiver wants byte 2000 next. If bytes 1000 through 1499 arrived but 1500 through 1999 did not, the receiver sends ACK 1500, because that is the first missing byte. The sender retransmits from 1500.

A gap means the receiver holds everything after it but cannot deliver any of those bytes to the application, because the application must see a contiguous stream. A 10,000-byte gap at position 5000 blocks delivery of bytes 5001 onward until 5000 fills in. The buffer has a finite size — the receive window — and the sender must stop transmitting once the receiver advertises a window of zero, or the excess data will be dropped.

The three-way handshake establishes the starting number. The sender picks an initial sequence number that is not zero and not predictable, because a predictable start lets an attacker inject segments with the right numbers. The receiver replies with its own initial sequence number. Both sides then count bytes from those starting points for the life of the connection.

Sequence numbers are 32 bits, so they wrap after 4,294,967,295 bytes. TCP handles this by comparing sequence numbers as unsigned integers on a circular range, not as linear counts. A segment with sequence number 100 can arrive after one with sequence number 4,294,967,250 and still be the next byte, because 100 is the next position after 4,294,967,295 on the circle.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can both reach the same variable at the same instant. Thread A reads `balance`, adds 100, writes it back. Thread B reads `balance` in the gap between A's read and A's write, adds 50, writes it back. A's write is lost. The balance gained 50, not 150. This is a data race, and the mutex exists to prevent it.

A mutex is a lock with one owner. A thread calls `lock` before touching the shared data and `unlock` after. While one thread holds the lock, every other thread that calls `lock` blocks — it stops running and waits until the holder calls `unlock`. The operating system or runtime puts the waiting thread to sleep and wakes it when the lock frees. Only one thread is ever inside the critical section at a time, so the reads and writes cannot interleave.

The mutex protects the *invariant*, not just the memory cell. A bank transfer withdraws from one account and deposits into another. Between the two updates, the books do not balance. A mutex held across both operations keeps any other thread from observing the half-finished transfer. Without it, a concurrent audit thread can read the total mid-transfer and see a sum that is wrong by the transfer amount.

A mutex does not protect against everything. It does not protect against deadlocks, which it causes: if thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both stop forever. It does not make individual operations atomic across multiple locks; it is one lock, guarding one scope. It does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread unless it is a recursive mutex, which counts nested locks and requires the same number of unlocks. A plain mutex locked twice by the same thread deadlocks against itself.

It also does not protect memory it does not cover. A mutex on `balance` does nothing for `account_name` if both are shared and both are touched by the same threads. The scope of the lock must match the scope of the data. A lock too narrow leaves races; a lock too wide serializes threads that could have run in parallel, turning a concurrent system into a sequential one and wasting the extra cores.

The cost is contention. Every `lock` call is a potential stall. If ten threads contend on one mutex, nine wait while one works. The lock holder should do as little as possible — compute the result, update the field, release. Reading a shared counter under a lock to increment it by one is correct but slow if a thousand threads do it per second; an atomic integer does the same work without the lock and without the stall.

A mutex is the right tool when the critical section touches multiple variables that must change together, or when the operation is too complex for an atomic primitive. It is the wrong tool when a single atomic read-modify-write would suffice, or when the shared state is read-only after initialization and needs no lock at all.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. The question is always the same: which objects are still live, and which are dead?

**Tracing** starts from the roots. The roots are the things the program can touch directly: stack variables, static fields, registers, JNI handles in the JVM. The collector walks from each root along every reference it holds, marking each object it reaches. Anything reached is live. Anything not reached is dead. The sweep phase then walks the heap and reclaims every unmarked object. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme Java and .NET use.

The walk is a graph traversal. Object A holds a reference to B, B holds one to C, and the collector follows each edge. A cycle does not fool it. If A points to B and B points back to A, but nothing reachable points to A, the collector never starts from either one. Both die. This is the advantage over reference counting, which cannot break cycles on its own.

**Reference counting** takes the other approach: it counts, at each object, how many references point to it. Every assignment increments a count; every drop decrements one. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and can be freed immediately. CPython uses this for most objects. The cost is two counter updates on every pointer write, and the cycle problem: two objects pointing only to each other keep each other's count at one forever. CPython runs a separate cycle detector to break those.

Tracing collectors split the heap to shorten the pause. **Generational** collection rests on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. A newly allocated object goes into the young generation. The collector scans the young generation frequently and cheaply, because it is small and most of its contents are already garbage. Objects that survive several young-gen collections get promoted to the old generation, which the collector scans rarely. The JVM's G1 divides the heap into regions and collects the ones with the most garbage first, trading some throughput for bounded pause times.

**Concurrent** collectors do the marking work while the application threads run, to avoid stopping the program. The cost is harder bookkeeping. A thread can mutate the graph mid-trace — change a reference the collector already passed — so the collector uses write barriers: a small piece of code that runs on every pointer update and records the change so the collector can correct itself. Shenandoah and ZGC do most of their work concurrently and aim for sub-millisecond pauses on heaps of hundreds of gigabytes.

The pause is the visible cost. A stop-the-world collector halts every application thread for the duration of the mark or the sweep. A young-gen collection on a 100 MB nursery might pause for five milliseconds. A full heap collection on a 32 GB heap without generational splitting can pause for seconds. The collector's job is to reclaim memory without stopping the program long enough for the program to notice.

A race condition is what happens when two threads reach shared data at the same time, and the outcome depends on which one gets there first. The program is correct if thread A runs before thread B, and wrong if they overlap. The scheduler decides, and the scheduler does not promise anything.

Consider a bank balance stored as a plain integer, shared by two threads. Thread A deposits 100. Thread B deposits 50. The deposit is three instructions: read the balance, add the amount, write it back. Thread A reads 500 and computes 600. Thread B reads 500 before A writes, computes 550, and writes 550. Thread A then writes 600. The balance is 600. It should be 650. Fifty dollars vanished.

The lost update is the race. Both threads read the old value, both write a new value, and one write clobbers the other. The thread that loses was not wrong about its arithmetic. It was wrong about its assumption that the value it read was still current when it wrote.

The failure is nondeterministic. Run the program a thousand times and the balance might be correct 990 of them, because the scheduler happened to serialize the threads. The ten wrong runs happen under load, on a different core count, or on a faster machine where the gap between read and write shrinks. A test that passes on the developer's laptop fails on the build server, or fails in production at 3 a.m. on the day traffic spikes.

The fix is to make the three instructions atomic with respect to each other. A mutex around the read-add-write block forces the threads to take turns: one finishes the whole deposit before the other starts. An atomic fetch-and-add does the same work in one hardware instruction, which is cheaper when the operation is this simple. Either way, the second thread reads the value the first thread wrote, and the balance lands at 650 every time.

The race exists because the code let two threads touch the same memory without coordination. The hardware will execute both threads simultaneously across cores, and nothing in the deposit logic asked it not to. The bug is not in the scheduler or the hardware. It is in the code that assumed sequential execution in a concurrent system.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It stores the data and instructions the processor is most likely to need next, so the processor does not have to wait for main memory.

Main memory is slow. A 3 GHz processor executes an instruction every 0.33 nanoseconds, but fetching a value from DRAM takes roughly 100 nanoseconds. That is 300 cycles the processor spends idle, waiting for a single number. The cache closes that gap. A value fetched from the L1 cache arrives in about 1 nanoseconds — three cycles. The L2 cache takes roughly 4 nanoseconds, and the L3 cache takes 12 to 30. Each level is larger and slower than the one above it.

The cache works because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns, and the two strongest patterns are temporal locality and spatial locality. Temporal locality says a value the processor just read will probably be read again soon. A loop variable `i` is touched on every iteration. Spatial locality says a value near one the processor just read will probably be read soon. Walking through an array element by element touches consecutive addresses. The cache exploits both.

When the processor requests a byte, the cache does not fetch one byte. It fetches a cache line — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors — and stores the whole line. If the next instruction reads the adjacent byte, it is already in the cache. An array of 4-byte integers means one cache miss pulls in 16 integers. The first costs 100 nanoseconds; the next 15 are free.

A cache miss is the moment the cache does not have what the processor asked for. The processor stalls, the hardware fetches the line from the next level down, and the wait begins. A cache hit is the opposite: the data is present, and the read completes in one cycle. The hit rate is the fraction of accesses that find their data in the cache. A program with a 99 percent L1 hit rate spends little time waiting. Drop that to 90 percent and the misses alone can double the running time, because each miss costs a hundred cycles.

The cache is finite. An L1 cache is 32 to 64 kilobytes; the L2 is 256 kilobytes to 1 megabyte; the L3 is 8 to 32 megabytes, shared among all cores. When the cache fills, the hardware evicts the least recently used line to make room. A program that strides through memory with a pattern larger than the cache size will thrash: every access evicts a line the program still needs, and the hit rate collapses. Reading a 100-megabyte array sequentially in a loop that revisits it will thrash the L1 and L2 entirely, because the array is three times the L3.

The practical consequence is that two algorithms with the same big-O complexity can run at very different speeds. A linked list and an array both let a program iterate through N elements in O(N) time. But the array stores its elements contiguously, so sequential access hits the cache on every element after the first. The linked list scatters its nodes across the heap, so each node is a pointer chase to a new address, and each chase is likely a cache miss. On a million elements, the array walk might take 2 milliseconds and the list walk 40, because the list spends most of its time waiting on DRAM.

The cache turns memory access from a fixed cost into a variable one. Two reads of the same size take 1 nanosecond or 100, depending on whether the data was already close to the processor. A program that respects locality — packing related data together, accessing it in order, keeping working sets small — runs fast because it hits the cache. A program that ignores locality runs at the speed of main memory, which is to say it runs slow.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server treats the second as if it were the first. The result is the same, and no extra side effect occurs.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. Two identical `GET /users/42` calls return the same user record, and neither call changes anything on the server. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. `PUT /users/42` with a body of `{"name": "Ada"}` sets the name to Ada; sending it again still sets the name to Ada, not "AdaAda." `DELETE` is idempotent in the sense that matters. `DELETE /users/42` removes user 42; a second call finds no user 42 and removes nothing, leaving the server in the same state as after the first call.

`POST` is not idempotent. `POST /orders` with `{"item": "book"}` creates one order; sending it again creates a second order. The server does something new each time, and the state diverges with each repeat.

The distinction is about side effects, not responses. A `DELETE` that returns 200 the first time and 404 the second is still idempotent, because the resource state after both calls is identical: the resource is gone. The HTTP specification defines idempotency in terms of the server's state, not the response body or status code.

The practical value is retry safety. Network connections drop. A client sends `PUT /users/42`, the server updates the record, the response is lost in transit, and the client does not know whether the request landed. An idempotent method lets the client resend the same `PUT` without risk of duplicating the update or corrupting the state. A non-idempotent `POST` cannot be retried this way — the second call creates a second order, and the client is charged twice.

The contract is the server's to honor. The HTTP method declares the intent, but the server's handler must implement it. A `DELETE` handler that appends to an audit log on every call is still idempotent with respect to the resource, because the resource state is the same after repeats. A `PUT` handler that increments a counter instead of replacing the value breaks the contract, because the counter differs on each call. The method name is a promise; the handler is what keeps it.

Okay, explain DNS resolution, plain register, every sentence carrying a fact.

DNS turns a hostname like `www.example.com` into an IP address like `93.184.216.34`. The process is a chain of lookups across servers that each hold a piece of the answer.

The browser asks the operating system's resolver, usually a library called `getaddrinfo`. The resolver checks its local cache first. If it has the address from a recent lookup, it returns it and the process stops. If not, it sends a UDP query to port 53 of the configured recursive resolver — the one in `/etc/resolv.conf` or the one DHCP handed the machine.

The recursive resolver does the walking. It starts at the root nameservers, whose 13 logical addresses are compiled into every resolver as a fixed list. The query asks for `www.example.com`, and the root server answers with a referral: it does not know the address, but it knows which servers hold `.com`. The referral is a list of authoritative nameservers for the `.com` top-level domain.

The resolver sends the same query to a `.com` nameserver. That server answers with a referral to the authoritative nameservers for `example.com` — the servers operated by whoever registered the domain. The resolver sends the query one more time, to one of those servers. The `example.com` nameserver holds the actual record for `www`, and it returns the A record: `93.184.216.34`. The resolver caches that answer for the record's time-to-live, hands it to the browser, and the browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

Each step narrows the question. The root answers "who handles `.com`?" The TLD server answers "who handles `example.com`?" The authoritative server answers "what is the address of `www.example.com`?" Three round trips, three answers, each one closer to the address.

The caching is what keeps the system alive. The root nameservers serve billions of queries per second. If every browser lookup went to the root, the root would collapse. The time-to-live field on each record tells resolvers how long to hold the answer before asking again. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver keeps the address for an hour; the next lookup in that window returns from cache in microseconds, and the root never sees it.

The protocol carries more than addresses. A mail server lookup asks for MX records, which list the hosts that accept mail for a domain and their priority. A reverse lookup asks for a PTR record, which maps an address back to a name. A name lookup for an IPv6 address asks for an AAAA record, which holds a 128-bit address. The query format is the same in each case; the record type changes.

The whole system is a distributed database with no single server holding the full map. The root knows the TLDs, the TLDs know the registrants, the registrants know their own hosts. A lookup walks that tree from the top down, caches what it finds, and returns the address in a few milliseconds on a warm cache or a few hundred on a cold one.

A deadlock is what happens when two threads each hold a lock the other needs, and both wait forever. Thread A takes lock 1, then asks for lock 2. Thread B takes lock 2, then asks for lock 1. Neither gives up what it holds. Neither gets what it wants. Both stop.

The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Mutual exclusion means only one thread owns a lock at a time. Hold-and-wait means a thread holding one lock can request another. No preemption means the system will not force a lock away from its holder. Circular wait means the waiting threads form a loop: A waits on B, B waits on A. Break any one of the four and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest break is lock ordering. Every thread acquires locks in the same global order. If the rule is "lock 1 before lock 2," thread A takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B also takes lock 1, then lock 2. Thread B blocks at lock 1 while A holds it, so B never reaches lock 2. Thread A finishes its work, releases both, and B proceeds. The circle never closes.

The cost is discipline. A new thread that grabs locks in the wrong order breaks the invariant and reintroduces the deadlock. A codebase with fifty locks needs a documented order, and every path through the code must follow it. The rule is simple to state and hard to keep: pick an order, write it down, never deviate.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer to pick a slot in an array. Two different keys can produce the same integer. The map has to store both. That situation is a collision, and every hash map handles it.

## Why collisions are guaranteed

The hash function maps a key space larger than the slot count onto the slot indices. Pigeonhole principle: if there are more possible keys than slots, at least two keys share a slot. A good hash function spreads keys evenly, so collisions are rare, but it cannot eliminate them. The map's design assumes they happen on every insert, not as an edge case.

## Two strategies

Every implementation picks one of two answers: store the colliding keys in a small list at that slot, or find them another slot elsewhere in the same array.

### Chaining

Each slot holds a pointer to a linked list (or a dynamic array) of entries. An insert computes the slot, walks the list, replaces the value if the key exists, and appends a new node if it does not. A lookup walks the same list and compares keys with `equals`.

The cost is the list length. If the hash function distributes keys uniformly and the load factor (entries divided by slots) stays under 1, the average list holds one or two entries and a lookup does constant work. As the load factor rises, lists grow and lookups degrade toward linear time. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain; Java converts a long chain to a red-black tree at threshold 8 so a worst-case lookup stays O(log n) instead of O(n).

### Open addressing

There is no per-slot list. The entry goes in the array itself. On a collision, the map probes another slot according to a fixed sequence and places the entry in the first empty one. A lookup follows the same probe sequence from the home slot, comparing keys until it finds the key, finds an empty slot, or has checked every slot.

Three common probe sequences:

- **Linear probing** — check slot `h`, then `h+1`, `h+2`, and so on, wrapping at the array end. Cache-friendly: the CPU prefetcher walks contiguous memory. The drawback is clustering. A run of occupied slots grows faster than chance, because any collision inside the run extends it, and long runs make every insert and lookup inside them slower.
- **Quadratic probing** — check `h`, `h+1²`, `h+2²`, `h+3²`. This breaks up the tight clusters linear probing creates, but it can still form secondary clusters along the probe path, and it is not guaranteed to visit every slot unless the table size is prime.
- **Double hashing** — use a second hash function to set the probe step: `h + i·h₂(key)`. The step varies by key, so keys that collide at the home slot follow different paths. This avoids both primary and secondary clustering. It costs a second hash computation per probe and makes the cache behavior worse, because consecutive probes can land far apart.

Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Rust's `std::collections::HashMap` all use open addressing. Python uses a variant called **open addressing with perturbation**, combining the hash with a per-probe perturbation sequence so the probe path scatters rather than stepping by a fixed increment.

## Deletion

Chaining deletes a node from the list. Open addressing cannot simply clear a slot, because a probe sequence might have skipped past that slot and stored a colliding key further on; clearing the slot would break the chain and make that key unreachable. The fix is a tombstone: the slot is marked deleted, probes treat it as occupied for traversal but empty for insertion, and the map rebuilds itself once tombstones accumulate.

## Resizing

Both strategies resize when the load factor crosses a threshold. The map allocates a larger array (usually double the capacity), rehashes every entry into its new slot, and frees the old array. Resizing is O(n) for that single operation but amortized O(1) per insert across the map's lifetime, because it happens after every n inserts, not before each one. Chaining tolerates higher load factors than open addressing before resizing, because chained lists keep working at load factor 5 while an open-addressed table at load factor 0.9 spends most of its time probing.

## The trade

Chaining wastes a pointer per entry and allocates a node per insert, which fragments memory and costs cache misses on list traversal. Open addressing keeps entries in one contiguous array, so a probe touches memory the prefetcher has already pulled in, but it degrades fast as the table fills and it makes deletion awkward. The choice is extra memory and allocator pressure against cache locality and resize sensitivity.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. The table holds rows in the order they were written. The index holds pointers to those rows, ordered by a chosen column.

A query for `users WHERE email = 'x@y.com'` without an index reads every row in the table and compares the email field. That is a full table scan. With an index on `email`, the database finds the matching entry in the index in logarithmic time, then reads the single row it points to. On a million-row table, the difference is reading one block instead of reading the whole file.

## What an index stores

Most indexes are B-trees. A B-tree keeps sorted keys in a balanced tree, so a lookup descends a few levels and stops. The leaf nodes hold the indexed column's value and a pointer back to the row. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` sorts by last name first, then first name within each last name. It serves queries that filter on last name alone, but not queries that filter on first name alone, because the sort order groups by the leftmost column.

PostgreSQL also offers hash indexes, which serve only exact-match lookups, and GiST and GIN indexes, which serve full-text search and array containment. The B-tree remains the default because it serves equality, range, and ordering queries in one structure.

## When an index helps

An index pays off when a query reads a small fraction of the table. A lookup by primary key touches one row. A query returning 50 rows from a million-row table, filtered on an indexed column, reads the 50 index entries and the 50 rows. The index turns a million-row scan into fifty random reads.

The database's query planner makes this decision. It estimates how many rows a predicate will match. If the estimate says the predicate matches a large fraction of the table, the planner skips the index and scans, because sequential reads of the whole table are faster than thousands of random index-then-table lookups. A query that matches 30% of a table is usually faster with a full scan.

## When an index hurts

Every index adds cost to writes. An `INSERT` that adds one row to the table also adds one entry to every index on that table. A table with five indexes pays six writes for one inserted row. A `DELETE` or `UPDATE` that changes an indexed column removes and reinserts the index entry, which can split a B-tree node and force rebalancing. A table that takes heavy writes and few reads will slow down as indexes accumulate.

Indexes also consume disk and memory. A B-tree index on a large text column can approach the size of the table itself. The database caches frequently used index pages in RAM, so a large index on a rarely queried column displaces pages that the working set needs. An index that the query planner never chooses is pure overhead: it costs writes, costs storage, and serves no query.

A common failure is indexing a column with low cardinality. An index on a `boolean active` column has two values. A query for `WHERE active = true` matches roughly half the table, so the planner ignores the index and scans. The index sits unused, still collecting its tax on every insert and update.

## The trade

An index trades write speed and storage for read speed. The right index makes a query a thousand times faster. The wrong index makes every write slower and serves nothing. The decision is per-query: index the columns that appear in predicates on queries that return few rows, and leave the rest unindexed.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a bag of independent packets. Each byte gets a sequence number. The first byte of a connection carries an initial sequence number chosen at random during the handshake, and every byte after it counts up from there.

A sender writes 1000 bytes. It labels the first byte with its sequence number, say 7000, and the last with 7999. The receiver reads the sequence number on the incoming segment and places the bytes in the correct position in the stream buffer. If segment 7000 arrives after segment 8000, the receiver holds 8000 in a buffer and waits. When 7000 lands, the receiver writes both runs to the stream in order and delivers them to the application.

The acknowledgment closes the loop. The receiver sends back an ACK carrying the sequence number of the next byte it expects. An ACK of 8000 means bytes 7000 through 7999 arrived intact and in order. A gap means the receiver is still holding later bytes out of order. The sender's retransmission timer fires for the missing segment, the sender resends it, and the gap fills.

The sequence number is a byte offset, not a packet count. A segment carrying 500 bytes advances the sequence by 500. A retransmitted segment carrying a different size still fits the same offset window. This is why a receiver can reassemble a stream from segments that arrived duplicated, fragmented, or reordered by the network underneath.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state across two or more threads.

A thread is a sequence of instructions that the scheduler can pause anywhere. A thread reads `balance`, adds 100, writes `balance` back. If a second thread reads `balance` between the first thread's read and its write, it reads the old value, adds its own 100, and writes back. The first thread's 100 is gone. The lost update is the race condition.

The mutex fixes this by making the read-modify-write block indivisible. A thread locks the mutex before touching `balance` and unlocks it after. While the mutex is held, every other thread that calls `lock` blocks — the operating system parks it until the holder calls `unlock`. One thread in, the rest out. The section of code between `lock` and `unlock` is the critical section, and the mutex serializes access to it.

What a mutex does not do is enforce order. Two threads that each lock the same mutex run in whatever order the scheduler picks. The mutex guarantees that they do not overlap; it does not guarantee which goes first. If thread A must complete before thread B starts, a mutex alone is the wrong tool — a condition variable or a barrier sequences that.

A mutex also does not protect against deadlock. Thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2. Thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Both sleep forever. The lock exists; the discipline of lock ordering is what makes it safe.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. A program allocates objects as it runs. Some it holds onto — in variables, in fields, in the call stack. Some it drops. The collector's job is to tell the living from the dead and reclaim the dead.

## The root set

Every collector starts from a fixed set of roots: the registers, the local variables on every thread's stack, and the global references the runtime keeps. These are the things the program can touch right now. An object reachable from a root is alive. An object reachable only through another alive object is also alive. Everything else is garbage.

## Tracing

The collector walks the graph. It marks every root, then follows every pointer out of each marked object and marks what it finds, and so on until it has touched every reachable object. This is the mark phase. When the walk finishes, the heap splits in two: marked objects the program still uses, and unmarked objects the program has forgotten.

The sweep phase frees the unmarked ones. The collector scans the heap, returns each unmarked block to the free list, and clears the mark on the survivors so the next cycle starts clean. Mark-and-sweep is what Java, .NET, and Go's original collector all do in their core.

## The pause

Tracing takes time proportional to the live objects. While the collector walks the graph, the program cannot move pointers, or the collector would follow a stale reference into freed memory. So the runtime stops every thread. This is the stop-the-world pause. A heap with ten gigabytes of live objects means a pause long enough to notice — tens or hundreds of milliseconds, enough to drop a frame, miss a deadline, or trip a health check.

Generational collection cuts that down. Most objects die young: a loop allocates a temporary string, the function returns, the string is garbage. A generational collector splits the heap into a young region and an old region. It collects the young region often and cheaply, because it is small and most of it is already dead. Objects that survive several young collections get promoted to the old region, which the collector scans rarely. The HotSpot JVM's young generation pause is typically a few milliseconds on a modest heap.

## Copying and compaction

Mark-and-sweep leaves holes. Dead objects scatter through the heap, and the free list becomes a patchwork of small gaps. A program that allocates a large object may not find a contiguous gap even when enough total memory is free. This is fragmentation.

A copying collector solves it. It divides the heap into two halves and allocates only in one. At collection time it copies every live object from the active half into the empty half, packing them contiguously, and leaves the old half entirely free. No holes. The cost is that the program can only use half the heap at a time, and copying long-lived objects every cycle wastes work — which is why copying pairs with generational design, copying only the young region where most objects are about to die anyway.

A compacting collector does the same packing in place, sliding live objects toward one end of a single heap region and freeing the tail. The .NET GC compacts the small-object heap on each collection; the large-object heap is mark-and-sweep only, because moving a multi-megabyte array is too expensive.

## Reference counting

Reference counting is the other path. Each object carries a counter. Assign a pointer, the counter goes up. Drop a pointer, the counter goes down. Hit zero, free the object immediately. No tracing, no pause, no separate collector thread.

The failure mode is cycles. Object A points to B, B points to A, nothing else points to either. Both counters read 1. Both are garbage. Neither drops to zero. A reference-counting collector needs a separate cycle collector to find these, which means running a trace anyway — Python's `gc` module exists for exactly this reason, on top of CPython's per-object refcounts. Swift's ARC puts the same burden on the programmer, who must break cycles manually with `weak` references.

## The trade

Tracing collectors pause the program but handle any graph, cycles included. Reference counting never pauses but leaks cycles without help and spends a counter update on every pointer assignment. The collectors that feel fast — Go's concurrent GC, Java's G1, .NET's server GC — are tracing collectors that do most of the mark work while the program runs, accepting some bookkeeping overhead to keep the pauses short. The pause is the thing every design is trying to shrink.

A race condition is what happens when two threads reach shared data at the same time, and the result depends on which one gets there first. The program is correct if thread A goes before thread B, and wrong if B goes before A. Neither thread is broken on its own. The bug lives in the gap between them.

A bank account holds a balance of 100. Two threads each read the balance, add 50, and write it back. The correct final balance is 200. Thread A reads 100. Thread B reads 100. Thread A adds 50 and writes 150. Thread B adds 50 and writes 150. The account gained 50 instead of 100. One update is gone.

The lost update is the signature failure. Thread A's write sits in memory for a fraction of a microsecond before thread B overwrites it. B never saw A's work, because B read the balance before A wrote it. The scheduler paused A between its read and its write, and B slipped through the gap. The same code run a thousand times might produce 200 on 999 runs and 150 on one. The bug is nondeterministic, which is what makes it hard to reproduce and hard to fix by trial.

The fix is to make the read, the add, and the write one indivisible operation. A mutex around the balance block serializes the two threads: A locks, reads, adds, writes, unlocks, and only then does B enter. The gap closes. The balance reaches 200 every time. The cost is that the threads no longer run in parallel on that piece of state — one waits while the other works. That is the trade the mutex buys correctness with.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. Main memory takes roughly 100 nanoseconds to answer a read. The cache answers in one or two. The speedup comes from the gap between those two numbers.

The cache works because of a pattern called locality. A program that reads the byte at address 1000 almost always reads 1001 next. It also tends to read 1000 again later. The first pattern is spatial locality: nearby addresses get touched together. The second is temporal locality: the same address gets touched more than once. The cache exploits both.

The hardware does not fetch single bytes. It fetches a cache line — a contiguous block, 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM processors. When the CPU reads address 1000, the memory controller pulls all 64 bytes starting at the aligned boundary and copies them into the cache. The next read at 1001 hits the cache instead of main memory. A loop that walks an array sequentially fills the cache once per 64 bytes and serves the other 63 reads from it.

A cache hit is a read the cache satisfies. A cache miss is a read the cache cannot satisfy, which forces a trip to main memory. The hit rate is the fraction of reads the cache answers. A loop over a contiguous array hits at 63 out of 64 reads, a rate of 98 percent. A loop that jumps through memory by strides larger than a cache line misses on every read and gets no benefit at all.

Modern CPUs carry three cache levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, 32 kilobytes per core, answering in four clock cycles. L2 is larger and slower, 256 kilobytes to one megabyte, answering in roughly 14 cycles. L3 is shared across all cores, several megabytes, answering in roughly 40 cycles. Main memory is the fallback at 300 cycles. A read checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. The first hit stops the search.

The cache is finite, so it evicts. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, the controller discards an old line to make room. The replacement policy is usually least-recently-used: the line that has gone longest without a read gets thrown out. A program that streams through a large array larger than the cache evicts the first lines before it finishes the loop, so a second pass over the same array misses again. A program that reuses a small working set keeps it hot in L1 and hits on every access.

The practical consequence is that two algorithms with the same operation count can run at different speeds. A row-major traversal of a C array reads contiguous memory and hits the cache. A column-major traversal of the same array jumps by one row width each read, misses on every line, and runs an order of magnitude slower. The cache turns memory layout into a performance variable, not just a correctness one.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state it would after one. The second request does not duplicate the first's effect. The network makes this matter: connections drop, timeouts fire, clients retry. An API that doubles a charge on retry is broken. An API that returns the same result on retry is safe to call again.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. It reads state and changes nothing, so ten identical `GET` requests produce ten identical responses and leave the server untouched. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A `PUT /users/42` with a body sets user 42 to that body. The first call creates the user. The second call overwrites the user with the same body. The state after the second call equals the state after the first. `DELETE` is idempotent the same way: `DELETE /users/42` removes user 42, and a second call finds no user 42 and removes nothing. The end state is identical.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST /orders` with a body creates a new order each time. Ten retries produce ten orders. The server has no way to tell the tenth request from the first, because each carries the same body to the same URL, and the URL names a collection, not a specific order. This is why payment endpoints that take `POST` are dangerous under retry: a dropped response after the server has processed the charge leaves the client unsure whether the charge happened, and a retry risks a second charge.

The fix for non-idempotent `POST` is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique identifier — a UUID — and sends it in a header, conventionally `Idempotency-Key`. The server records the key on first receipt, processes the request, and stores the response. A second request with the same key arrives. The server checks its store, finds the key, and returns the stored response without reprocessing. The duplicate is caught before it touches state. Stripe's API uses this pattern on its charge and transfer endpoints; the key persists for 24 hours, after which the server treats a reused key as a new request.

The key makes the server's behavior match the client's intent. The client is not asking to create a second order. It is asking whether the first order was created. Without the key, the server cannot distinguish the two. With the key, the server recognizes the retry and answers from its record. The charge happens once. The client gets its confirmation. The retry is free.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a tree of servers from the top down. The tree is the Domain Name System, and it maps human-readable names to the 32-bit or 128-bit numbers that network software routes packets by.

A browser asks for `www.example.com`. The resolver, usually a library inside the operating system, starts with the root. The root is the top of the tree, served by thirteen clusters of servers identified by the letters A through M. The root does not know `www.example.com`. It knows only which servers hold the top-level domains — `com`, `org`, `net`, the country codes. The resolver picks a root server, sends the query, and receives a referral: a list of name servers authoritative for `com`.

The resolver sends the same query to a `com` server. That server does not know `www.example.com` either. It knows which servers hold `example.com`. It returns a referral to the name servers authoritative for that domain.

The resolver sends the query to an `example.com` name server. This server holds the actual records. It finds `www.example.com` in its zone file, reads the address record, and returns the address — say, `93.184.216.34`. The resolver hands that address to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to it.

Each answer carries a time-to-live, a number of seconds the resolver may cache it. The root and TLD referrals carry TTLs measured in days. The leaf record's TTL is whatever the domain owner set — minutes for a service that moves between machines, hours for a stable host.
