Postgres calls this a bitmap heap scan, and on a low-selectivity column it loses to the sequential scan it tried to avoid.

The planner decides. It estimates how many rows the predicate matches, weighs the cost of random index reads against a sequential scan, and picks the cheaper path. A good index is one the planner picks often. A bad index is one it never picks, or picks and regrets, while the writes pay for it on every transaction.

TCP sends data as a stream of bytes, not as discrete messages. The sender numbers every byte with a 32-bit sequence number, starting from a random value chosen during the three-way handshake. The first data byte the sender transmits carries the sequence number agreed in that handshake, and each subsequent byte increments it by one.

The sender writes segments to the network, each carrying a range of sequence numbers. IP can deliver these segments out of order. A segment sent fourth might arrive before a segment sent second, because it took a different route or hit a shorter queue. The sequence numbers let the receiver reconstruct the original order regardless of arrival sequence.

The receiver buffers what arrives. It tracks the sequence number of the next byte it expects, the left edge of the receive window. If bytes 1 through 1000 have arrived and byte 1001 has not, the receiver holds bytes 1002 through 5000 in a buffer and waits. It delivers bytes to the application only in contiguous order from that left edge. Bytes that arrived early sit in the buffer until the gap fills.

The receiver acknowledges received data. Its ACK field carries the sequence number of the next byte it wants, which is also the first byte of the gap. An ACK of 1001 tells the sender that bytes 1 through 1000 arrived intact. An ACK of 5001 tells it bytes 1 through 5000 are contiguous and delivered. The receiver does not ACK bytes past a hole individually; it repeats the ACK for the left edge until the missing byte fills the gap. TCP is cumulative: every acknowledgment confirms everything up to that number, not just the latest segment.

The sender keeps a send buffer of unacknowledged bytes and a timer for the oldest one. If the timer fires before an ACK arrives, the sender retransmits. The sender also infers loss from duplicate ACKs. If the receiver gets byte 1002 but not 1001, it sends ACK 1001, holds 1002, and waits. If 1003 and 1004 then arrive, it sends ACK 1001 twice more. Three duplicate ACKs for the same number tell the sender that bytes past 1001 are arriving, so 1001 itself was lost, not delayed. The sender retransmits 1001 without waiting for the timer. This is fast retransmit.

The sequence number space is finite: 32 bits, about 4.3 billion values. On a ten-gigabit link the sender exhausts that space in 3.4 seconds. The random start position, the ISN, prevents an old segment from a previous connection carrying a sequence number that falls inside the current window and corrupting the stream. The ISN changes on every connection, so a stale segment from an earlier incarnation lands outside the current sequence range and the receiver discards it.

The window size governs how much unacknowledged data the sender can push. The receiver advertises a window in every ACK, telling the sender how much buffer space remains. If the application reads slowly, the window shrinks. If it shrinks to zero, the sender stops. This keeps the sender from overflowing the receiver's buffer and dropping bytes it cannot hold, which would force retransmission.

Order, then, is not a property of the network. The network delivers segments in whatever order it manages. Order is a property TCP constructs on top, by numbering bytes, buffering gaps, acknowledging the left edge, and retransmitting what the acknowledgments say is missing. The application sees a byte stream in the order the sender wrote it, because the receiver holds the pieces and releases them only when they form an unbroken run.

A mutex protects one thing: the invariant a thread can violate by running at the wrong time.

A program with two threads shares memory. Thread A reads a balance of 100, adds 50, and writes 150. Thread B reads the same balance of 100 before A writes, subtracts 30, and writes 70. The final value is 70 or 150, not the correct 120. The balance is shared state, and the read-modify-write sequence is the critical section. A mutex makes that section atomic — one thread enters, the other waits.

The mutex is a flag with a queue. A thread calls lock before the critical section and unlock after. The first thread to lock proceeds. The second thread blocks on the lock call and sits in the kernel's wait queue for that mutex. When the first thread unlocks, the kernel wakes one waiter. The flag is the ownership bit; the queue is the list of threads sleeping until ownership transfers.

Ownership is the part that matters. The thread that locked the mutex is the only thread that may unlock it. The kernel tracks the owner. If thread B tries to unlock a mutex thread A holds, the call fails. This stops a thread from releasing a lock it never acquired and letting a third thread walk into a critical section mid-operation.

A mutex protects against data races, where two threads read and write the same memory cell with at least one write, and no ordering between them. The C++ and Rust memory models call this undefined behavior. The hardware cause is real: on an x86 or ARM core, a read and a write to the same address from two cores can interleave at the cache-line level, and without synchronization the compiler and CPU can reorder the instructions themselves. The mutex emits memory barriers that force the other cores to see writes in the order the critical section issued them. Without the barrier, thread A's write to the balance might sit in its store buffer while thread B reads the stale cache line, even after A unlocked.

A mutex does not protect against deadlock. Thread A locks mutex X then mutex Y. Thread B locks Y then X. Both block forever. The lock order, not the mutex, prevents this — every thread acquires the same set of mutexes in the same order, and the deadlock cannot form.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy. A thread locks a mutex, then calls a function that locks the same mutex again. On a plain mutex the second lock blocks and the thread deadlocks against itself, because it is waiting for a lock it already holds and cannot release. A recursive mutex permits the reentrant lock by counting acquisitions and requiring the same count of unlocks. The trade is that the critical section is now larger and harder to reason about, because the inner function assumed it had exclusive access and the outer function already had it.

The cost is contention. When two threads hit the same mutex, one sleeps. Sleep is a context switch — the kernel saves registers, schedules another thread, and later restores them, a few microseconds on modern hardware. A mutex under heavy contention serializes the work: ten threads on one mutex run no faster than one. The fix is not a faster mutex but less shared state, or a finer-grained lock that protects a smaller region so the threads spend less time waiting and more time running.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. The program allocates objects on a heap. It holds some objects through references — variables, fields, array slots — rooted in the stack, the processor registers, and the global variables. An object is live if a path of references leads from a root to it. An object is dead if no path does. The collector's job is to find the dead ones and reclaim their space.

The tracing collector starts from the roots and walks every reference it can follow. It marks each object it reaches. When the walk finishes, the unmarked objects are unreachable. The collector sweeps the heap, frees every unmarked object, and clears the marks on the rest. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme McCarthy described in 1960 for Lisp.

Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps. Dead objects scatter through the heap, and the free space fragments into pieces too small for the next allocation. A moving collector fixes this. After marking, it copies the live objects into a fresh region of memory, packing them end to end. Every reference that pointed to an old location now points to the new one. The old region is free in one piece. This is copying collection, the basis of Lisp machines and most generational collectors. It trades copy work for compactness: dead objects cost nothing to free, because they are simply overwritten.

Most objects die young. A benchmark or a web request allocates temporary strings, scratch lists, and intermediate results that vanish when the function returns. The generational hypothesis observes this pattern and splits the heap by age. New objects go into a young region. The collector scans the young region often, because most of its contents are dead and the scan is cheap. Objects that survive several young collections promote to an old region. The collector scans the old region rarely, because its objects tend to stay live. The JVM, .NET, and V8 all use generational collection.

The hard part is the roots. A collector must find every reference in every stack frame and every register, or it will free an object the program still uses. A compiler that knows about the collector emits a stack map: a table that records, for every safe point in the code, which registers and stack slots hold references. The collector reads the map, pulls the roots, and traces. A compiler that does not know about the collector requires the runtime to keep references in a separate structure the collector can walk. C and C++ fall in this gap, which is why precise garbage collection for them is rare and conservative scanning — treating any word that looks like a pointer as a pointer — is the fallback. A conservative scanner holds onto dead objects by mistake, because a word that coincidentally matches a heap address looks like a live reference.

The collector must also stop the program. While the collector traces, the program cannot change the references, or the collector might mark an object as live, watch the program drop the last reference to it, and miss the death. The pause is the stop-the-world gap. The program halts at a safe point, the collector traces and frees, and the program resumes. The pause length grows with the number of live objects, not the heap size, because dead objects cost no work to find in a copying scheme — they are the space the collector does not copy.

Concurrent collectors cut the pause. They trace while the program runs, which requires a barrier: a write barrier intercepts every reference write and records it, so the collector can re-examine objects the program touched mid-trace. The JVM's G1 divides the heap into regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first, pausing only to evacuate the live objects in a chosen region. Shenandoah and ZGC run most of the tracing and copying concurrently with the program, aiming for sub-millisecond pauses on multi-gigabyte heaps. The trade is throughput: the barriers and the coordination work cost cycles the program could spend on its own computation.

Reference counting takes a different road. Every object carries a count of the references pointing to it. A new reference increments the count; a dropped reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, the object is dead and the collector frees it at that moment, no tracing required. Python, Objective-C, and Swift use reference counting. Its weakness is cycles: two objects that reference each other keep each other's count above zero, even if nothing else references either. A cycle collector — Python's `gc` module, Swift's occasional cycle scan — must run a tracing pass to find and break these. Reference counting also pays on every assignment, not in batches, which makes it slower than tracing for short-lived objects in tight loops.

The choice between tracing and reference counting is a choice about where the cost lands. Tracing collects work into bursts, pauses the program, and handles cycles for free. Reference counting spreads the cost across every operation, frees memory at the moment of death, and needs a separate mechanism for cycles. Neither finds garbage by magic. Both walk the reference graph from the roots and treat the unreachable as free.

A race condition is a bug where a program's output depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not fixed.

Two threads share a counter. Both read 7. Both add 1. Both write 8. The counter should be 9. It is 8. One increment is lost. The read and the write are separate instructions, and the scheduler can pause one thread between them and run the other. The name comes from the two threads racing for the same memory cell, each assuming it is the only one touching it.

The fix is a lock or an atomic instruction. A lock makes the read-add-write sequence indivisible: one thread finishes before the other starts. An atomic instruction like `fetch-and-add` does the same work in hardware, without a separate lock. Either way the counter reaches 9.

The bug is not that the answer is sometimes wrong. It is that the answer is unpredictable, and the failure is silent. A program with a race can run a thousand times and pass every test, then fail in production because the scheduler picked a different order on a busier machine.

A CPU cache is a small block of fast memory sitting between the processor core and main memory. It speeds up a program by holding copies of the bytes the program is most likely to read next.

The speed gap it bridges is physical. A modern core runs at three or four gigahertz. A memory access from DRAM takes around one hundred nanoseconds, which is two or three hundred clock cycles the core spends idle. A cache hit returns the same data in one to four cycles. The cache turns a three-hundred-cycle wait into a one-cycle fetch.

The cache works because programs do not read memory at random. They read the next instruction, the next array element, the next field in a struct. This is locality of reference, and it has two forms. Temporal locality says a byte the program just touched it will touch again soon — a loop counter, a stack variable. Spatial locality says a byte near one the program touched will be touched soon — the next element in an array, the next field in a struct. The cache exploits both.

The hardware cache is built from cache lines. A line is the unit of transfer between cache and memory, typically sixty-four bytes. When the core requests a byte from an address not in the cache, the memory controller does not fetch just that byte. It fetches the entire sixty-four-byte line containing it and writes it into the cache. The next seven bytes of that array, or the next few fields of that struct, are now in the cache. If the program reads them next, the access is a hit. The line fetch is the mechanism that turns spatial locality into speed.

Modern CPUs stack three levels of cache. The L1 is smallest and closest, thirty-two kilobytes on a typical x86 core, split into a thirty-two-kilobyte instruction cache and a thirty-two-kilobyte data cache. It hits in four cycles. The L2 is larger, around one megabyte, and hits in ten to fifteen cycles. The L3 is shared across all cores on the die, thirty to sixty megabytes, and hits in forty to fifty cycles. A miss past the L3 goes to DRAM and costs the full hundred. The hierarchy catches what each level above missed.

The cache replaces lines when it fills. A set-associative cache maps each memory address to a specific set of cache lines, usually eight or twelve, and evicts the least recently used line in that set when a new line arrives. The mapping is a hash of the address bits, and it means a program that strides through memory at a power-of-two interval can force every access to the same set, evicting lines before the program reads them again. This is a cache conflict miss. The data was in the cache, but the access pattern pushed it out.

A program that walks a contiguous array hits the cache on every element after the first, because each sixty-four-byte line brings in the next eight doubles. A program that follows a linked list through heap memory misses on every node, because each node sits at an address the cache has no reason to hold. The first runs at memory bandwidth. The second runs at memory latency. The difference between bandwidth and latency is the difference between a program that uses the cache and one that fights it.

The cache also makes writes faster. A store to a cached line writes to the cache and marks the line dirty. The core moves on. The memory controller writes the dirty line back to DRAM later, when the cache needs the slot for a new fetch or when the core explicitly flushes it. This lets the core issue writes at cache speed instead of waiting for DRAM on every store.

The cache does not speed up a program by doing the work faster. It speeds it up by doing less work — by keeping the bytes the program needs next already inside the core, so the core never asks DRAM for them at all.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once.

`GET` is idempotent by nature. It reads a resource and changes nothing, so the tenth call returns the same body as the first. `PUT` is idempotent by contract. A `PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets the resource at that path to that exact representation. The first call creates or overwrites the user. The second call overwrites it with the same values. The stored state is identical. A client that loses the response and retries the request does not corrupt the resource.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST /orders` with the body `{"item": "book"}` creates a new order each time. Ten retries produce ten orders. The server treats each request as a new event, not a statement of desired state. This is why payment endpoints and order-creation endpoints break under retry: the network drops the response, the client resends, and the server charges twice.

`DELETE` is idempotent in outcome if not in response. The first call removes the resource and returns `200`. The second call finds nothing at that path and returns `404`. The server state is the same after both: the resource is gone. The status codes differ, but idempotency is about state, not response equality.

The practical problem is the gap between the method's contract and a real server's behavior. A `PUT /users/42` that also appends to an audit log is not idempotent in the strict sense, because the log grows on each call. The resource state is stable, but a side effect is not. RFC 9110 defines idempotency as the property that "the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests is the same as the effect of a single request," and it notes that this does not mean the server must return the same response. The audit log is the kind of side effect the RFC leaves to the implementer.

The fix for non-idempotent operations under retry is an idempotency key. The client sends a unique token in a header — `Idempotency-Key: 7a3f9b2c` — with the first request. The server stores the key and the response. On a retry with the same key, the server returns the stored response instead of running the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern on its charge endpoints. The key turns a non-idempotent `POST` into an idempotent operation by making the server remember the first result and replay it.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a tree.

The tree has a root at the top, top-level domains below it, and individual domains below those. The name `www.example.com` has four labels. The root is the empty label after the final dot. The top-level domain is `com`. The domain is `example`. The host is `www`. Resolution starts at the root and descends one label at a time.

A resolver does the walking. The resolver is the program a machine runs to answer DNS queries — `systemd-resolved` on a Linux box, the stub resolver inside a home router, or a recursive server like Unbound or BIND. When an application calls `getaddrinfo("www.example.com")`, the operating system hands the name to the resolver. The resolver's job is to return an IP address or report that none exists.

The resolver does not know the address. It learns it by asking. Its first question goes to a root server. The Internet has thirteen root server addresses, labeled A through M, operated by twelve organizations. The resolver knows these thirteen addresses by hardcoding; they ship with the operating system. A query to a root server asks for `www.example.com`. The root server does not know the address, but it knows which servers hold the `com` zone. It returns a referral: a list of authoritative servers for `com`.

The resolver caches that referral. It picks a `com` server and sends the same query. The `com` server does not know `www.example.com` either, but it knows the authoritative servers for `example.com`. It returns a referral to those. The resolver caches this one too.

The resolver picks an `example.com` server and asks for `www.example.com`. This server holds the zone file for `example.com`, and the zone file contains the record for `www`. The server returns the address — `93.184.216.34`, for instance — in an A record. The resolver caches the answer, hands it to the operating system, and the operating system hands it to the application. The whole walk took three round trips: root to `com` to `example.com`.

Caching shortens the walk. The first resolver to ask for `www.example.com` pays the full three-trip cost. Every resolver that shares its cache — and every downstream client that uses that resolver — gets the answer from memory. The answer carries a time-to-live, a number of seconds the resolver may hold it before discarding. A TTL of 3600 means the cached answer is good for an hour. After it expires, the next query repeats the walk. The TTL is the knob a domain owner uses to balance freshness against load: a short TTL pushes changes out fast but sends more queries to the authoritative servers; a long TTL cuts traffic but leaves stale answers in caches after a change.

The root and the top-level domains see the most traffic because every uncached query starts there. The root servers answer hundreds of thousands of referrals per second. Anycast routes their single IP addresses to dozens of physical machines spread across the world, so a query from Tokyo hits a root server in Tokyo, not one in Virginia. The thirteen addresses are thirteen service points, not thirteen machines.

The system works because each server knows only its piece and points the resolver to the next piece. The root knows `com`. The `com` servers know `example.com`. The `example.com` servers know `www`. No single server holds the whole map. The resolver assembles the answer by following the chain, and the cache keeps the chain from being walked more often than the TTL demands.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither can proceed.

Thread A locks file X, then tries to lock file Y. Thread B locks file Y, then tries to lock file X. A waits for B to release Y. B waits for A to release X. Both wait forever. The program hangs. No crash, no error message, no recovery. The threads sit in the kernel's wait queue, each sleeping until a lock that will never come free comes free.

The condition is circular wait. A holds what B needs. B holds what A needs. The cycle has no exit. Coffman named this condition in 1971, along with the three others that must hold for a deadlock to exist: mutual exclusion, meaning a resource belongs to one thread at a time; hold and wait, meaning a thread keeps its resources while requesting more; and no preemption, meaning a thread's resources cannot be taken from it by force. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The fix is to break circular wait. Every thread acquires locks in the same order. If A locks X before Y, and B locks X before Y, the cycle cannot close. Thread B tries to lock X, finds A holding it, and waits. A finishes, releases both, and B proceeds. The order is a convention the code follows at every lock site. A lock hierarchy published in a project's conventions document gives every thread the same map.

The cost is discipline. A function that locks Y and calls a function that locks X breaks the hierarchy without the caller knowing. The deadlock hides inside the call graph, and the convention that prevented it in the visible code fails inside the invisible code. The hierarchy works when every lock acquisition follows it, and fails when one does not.

A hash map stores values in an array of buckets. The hash function turns a key into an integer, which the map reduces modulo the array length to pick a bucket. Two different keys can land in the same bucket — a collision.

Three strategies handle it. Separate chaining hangs a linked list off each bucket; on collision, the new entry joins the list, and a lookup walks the list comparing keys. Open addressing stores every entry in the bucket array itself; on collision, the map probes neighboring slots by a fixed rule — linear probing checks the next slot, quadratic probing checks slots at growing intervals, double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step. Robin Hood hashing, a variant of open addressing, moves earlier-inserted entries aside when a new key would sit farther from its home bucket, keeping the worst-case probe distance low.

Load factor — entries divided by buckets — governs performance. As it rises, chains lengthen and probe sequences stretch. Most maps resize when the factor crosses a threshold (0.75 in Java's `HashMap`, 0.66 in Python's `dict`), allocating a larger array and rehashing every entry into its new bucket. A good hash function spreads keys uniformly, making collisions rare; a poor one clusters them, and a lookup degrades from constant time to linear.

A database index is a separate structure that stores one column's values in sorted order alongside pointers to their rows. The database walks this structure instead of scanning the table, which turns a million-row search into a handful of comparisons.

A B-tree index keeps values in a balanced tree, so a lookup for `users.email = 'x@y.com'` touches log₂(n) pages — roughly 20 for a million rows — instead of all million. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` sorts by last name first, then first name within each last name, so it serves queries that filter on both columns or on last name alone, but not on first name alone. A unique index enforces no duplicates while it speeds lookups.

Indexes hurt in three ways. They cost storage: an index on a 50-column table can nearly double the disk footprint. They slow writes: every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on an indexed column must update the index too, so a table with five indexes takes six writes per row change. They mislead the planner: an index on a column with two values, like `orders.is_active`, where 95% of rows are true, makes the planner choose an index scan that reads almost every row in fragmented order — slower than a straight table scan.

The last case is the common trap. An index helps when it narrows the result to a small fraction of the table, typically under 10%. Past that, the index adds a random read per matching row, and random I/O costs more than the sequential scan it replaced.

TCP gives each byte a position number. The sender labels every segment with a 32-bit sequence number — not a per-message counter, but the byte offset within the connection's stream — and the receiver answers with an acknowledgment number naming the next byte it expects. If segments arrive out of order, the receiver holds them in a reorder buffer and delivers bytes to the application only in sequence, so a gap at position 1000 blocks delivery even as 1001 through 5000 sit waiting.

The acknowledgment is cumulative: `ACK 5000` means every byte up to 4999 has arrived, not just the one at 4999. This keeps the protocol durable under packet loss — a lost ACK does not force retransmission, because a later ACK covers the same ground. The sender keeps each segment in an unacknowledged window until the matching ACK arrives, then discards it. If a retransmission timer fires first, the sender sends the segment again.

Flow control and congestion control bound the window differently. The receiver advertises a window size in every ACK — the free space in its buffer — and the sender never pushes more unacknowledged bytes than that. Congestion control, a sender-side addition from 1988, probes for bandwidth by growing the window until packets drop, then halving it. Both limits apply; the tighter one wins.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes against shared memory.

Two threads run at once on two cores. Thread A reads `balance` into a register, adds 100, writes it back. Thread B does the same with a withdrawal. If A reads while B has the value in a register but has not written yet, one update vanishes. The lost write is the race condition — the outcome depends on which core finished first, and neither is correct.

The mutex fixes this by making the read-modify-write sequence atomic. A thread locks the mutex before touching `balance` and unlocks after. While one thread holds the lock, the other blocks on the lock call and does not proceed until the first releases. The critical section — the code between lock and unlock — runs uninterrupted with respect to other critical sections guarded by the same mutex.

What a mutex does not do: it does not make individual operations atomic, it makes sections of code mutually exclusive. It does not prevent deadlocks on its own — if thread A holds mutex M1 and waits for M2 while thread B holds M2 and waits for M1, both stall forever. It does not protect against memory reordering without a memory barrier; the lock operation includes one implicitly on most architectures, but a mutex around `balance` does nothing for a second variable accessed without it.

The cost is contention. If ten threads contend on one mutex, nine wait while one works, and the program runs at single-thread speed for that section. The lock itself is cheap when uncontended — a single atomic compare-and-swap on x86 — but the waiting is not.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that a program can no longer reach. The collector's job is to distinguish garbage from live objects, and the criterion is reachability: an object is live if a chain of references connects it to a root, and garbage if no such chain exists.

Roots are the starting points. They live in CPU registers, on the call stack as local variables, and in global or static fields. The collector treats every root as alive by definition and traces outward from there.

**Mark-and-sweep**, the oldest design, works in two passes. The mark pass walks the object graph from every root, setting a flag on each object it touches. The sweep pass scans the whole heap and frees any object whose flag is unset, then clears the flags for the next cycle. It leaves memory fragmented — free blocks scattered between live ones — and allocation slows as the heap fragments.

**Copying collection** solves fragmentation by splitting the heap into two halves. The program allocates in one half until it fills. The collector then copies every reachable object from the full half into the empty half, packing them contiguously, and the program resumes allocating in the now-filled other half. Free memory is always one contiguous block. The cost is that the program uses only half its heap; the benefit is that allocation is pointer bumping — increment a pointer by the object size, done.

**Generational collection** rests on an empirical observation: most objects die young. The heap is split into a young generation and an old generation. New objects allocate in the young space, which the collector scans frequently and cheaply. Objects that survive several young-gen collections promote to the old space, which the collector scans rarely. This cuts the cost of a cycle because the collector skips the old generation most of the time. The trap is cross-generational pointers — an old object holding a reference to a young one — which the collector tracks with remembered sets, small tables that record which old objects point into the young generation, so it does not have to scan the entire old space to find them.

**Concurrent collection** runs the collector alongside the program's own work rather than stopping the world. The trade is complexity: the program can modify the object graph mid-trace, so the collector needs read or write barriers — small code snippets inserted at every pointer read or write — to notice changes and re-examine objects the program touched during the scan. Stop-the-world pauses are simpler and longer; concurrent pauses are shorter and harder to build.

The criterion never changes. An object is garbage when no root can reach it, and the collector's work is to prove that fact by walking the graph. Every design above is a different strategy for doing that walk cheaply.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads the balance, adds 50, and writes 150. Thread B reads the balance, subtracts 30, and writes 70. If A reads before B writes, B's write overwrites A's, and the balance becomes 70 instead of 120. Fifty dollars vanished. The hardware did exactly what it was told. The code never told it the two operations had to happen in sequence.

The balance example is a data race: two threads touch the same memory, at least one writes, and nothing forces them to take turns. A mutex fixes it. Thread A locks before reading and unlocks after writing; thread B does the same. While one holds the lock, the other waits, so the read-modify-write sequence runs uninterrupted.

Race conditions do not require shared memory. Two processes write to the same file. Process A reads the file, appends a line, and writes it back. Process B does the same. If A's write lands between B's read and B's write, A's line is gone. The file is shared state; the lock is a file lock or a write that appends atomically.

The defining trait is not speed. It is the absence of a guarantee. A program that runs a thousand times without the race firing has the same bug as one that fails every time. The thousand clean runs prove nothing, because the order was never fixed.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping the data the processor is most likely to need next.

The cache works because of locality. A program that reads `array[0]` almost always reads `array[1]` next — that is spatial locality, the tendency of accesses to cluster in address ranges. A program that reads the same variable in a tight loop shows temporal locality, the tendency to touch the same address repeatedly. The cache exploits both. When the processor requests an address, the cache grabs a whole block of neighboring bytes — a cache line, 64 bytes on x86 — and stores it, betting that the next request falls inside that line.

The bet pays off. A register access takes one cycle. An L1 cache hit takes three or four cycles. Main memory takes two hundred. If the data sits in L1, the processor does not wait. If it sits in L2, the wait is ten or twelve cycles. L3 adds another forty. Each miss pushes the request one level farther out, and each level costs an order of magnitude more.

A cache miss stalls the pipeline. The processor issues a load instruction, checks L1, finds nothing, and waits for the data to arrive from the next level. During that wait it cannot do useful work on that thread. A program that misses the cache on every access runs at memory speed, not processor speed — and memory is fifty times slower than the chip.

The program that walks an array front to back hits the cache on every element after the first, because each 64-byte line covers eight 8-byte values. The program that jumps through the same array by strides of 64 bytes misses on every access, fetching a full line each time to use one value from it. Same data, same operation, different order — one runs fast, the other runs at memory bandwidth.

Cache size sets the limit. An L1 cache holds 32 kilobytes on a typical x86 core. A program that touches 32 KB of data in a loop fits in L1 and runs at full speed. Double the working set and it spills into L2, adding eight cycles per access. The transition is sharp, not gradual — the cost jumps when the data stops fitting.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends up in the same state as if it were sent once.

`GET /users/42` is idempotent by nature. It reads data and changes nothing, so a hundred repeats leave the database untouched. `PUT /users/42` with body `{"name":"Ada"}` is idempotent by contract. The first call sets the name to Ada. The second call sets the name to Ada again. The final state is identical to the state after one call, even though the server executed the write twice.

`POST /users` with body `{"name":"Ada"}` is not idempotent. The first call creates user 1. The second call creates user 2. Two requests produce two resources where one request produced one. The operation accumulates.

`DELETE /users/42` is idempotent in the state it leaves behind. The first call removes the user. The second call finds no user and returns 404. The responses differ, but the server state — user 42 absent — matches the state after the first call. Idempotency is about the resulting state, not the response body.

The property matters because networks duplicate requests. A client sends `POST /payments`, the server processes it, the response drops on the floor, and the client retries. Without a guard, the customer is charged twice. The standard fix is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique token in an `Idempotency-Key` header, the server stores the token with the first response, and a retry with the same token returns the stored response instead of running the operation again. Stripe's `Idempotency-Key` header works this way. The server treats the key as the deduplication boundary — same key, same outcome, no second charge.

The HTTP spec labels `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` idempotent, and `POST` and `PATCH` not. The label describes the method's intent, not a guarantee. A `PUT` handler that appends to a list instead of replacing it breaks idempotency. The contract is in the handler, not the verb.

DNS resolves a hostname through a hierarchy of servers, each answering only the part it knows.

The resolver is the first stop. It runs at the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1. The browser hands it `www.example.com`, and the resolver checks its cache. If it has the address, it returns it. If not, it begins the walk.

The resolver asks a root server for `www.example.com`. There are 13 root server addresses, operated by organizations like Verisign and ISC, but hundreds of physical instances behind those addresses via anycast. The root server does not know the address. It knows who does: the top-level domain servers for `.com`. It returns a list of those.

The resolver asks a `.com` TLD server for `www.example.com`. The TLD server does not know the address either. It knows the authoritative servers for `example.com`, the ones operated by whoever bought that domain. It returns their addresses.

The resolver asks `example.com`'s authoritative server for `www.example.com`. This server holds the actual record. It returns an A record with an IPv4 address like `93.184.216.34`, or an AAAA record with an IPv6 address. The resolver caches that answer for the record's time-to-live — a number of seconds set by the domain owner — and hands it to the browser.

The whole walk is four queries: root, TLD, authoritative, done. Each layer delegates downward, and only the last holds the answer. Caching shortens the walk. A second lookup for `www.example.com` in the same minute returns from the resolver's cache without a single upstream query, and a lookup for `mail.example.com` skips the root and TLD because the resolver already cached their addresses from the first walk.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and both wait forever. Neither releases what it holds until it gets what it wants, and neither gets what it wants until the other releases. The program freezes at that point.

Thread A locks file 1, then asks for file 2. Thread B locks file 2, then asks for file 1. A holds file 1 and waits for file 2. B holds file 2 and waits for file 1. The cycle closes. A cannot proceed without file 2, B cannot proceed without file 1, and no force exists to break the symmetry. This is the classic deadlock: a circular wait between two actors, each holding one lock and blocked on another.

Four conditions must hold at once for a deadlock to exist. Mutual exclusion: the resource belongs to one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread keeps its lock while asking for the next. No preemption: the lock cannot be taken by force; only the holder releases it. Circular wait: a ring of threads exists where each holds a resource the next one needs. Break any one and deadlock becomes impossible.

The cheapest fix breaks circular wait by imposing a global order on locks. Assign every lock a number. Rule: a thread may acquire lock N only if it holds no lock with a number higher than N. Under that rule, a cycle cannot form, because a cycle would require a thread to hold a high-numbered lock and wait for a lower-numbered one, which the rule forbids. In the file example, if file 1 is lock 1 and file 2 is lock 2, thread B — which would lock file 2 first — must instead lock file 1 first, then file 2. Both threads now grab file 1 before file 2. One of them gets file 1, the other waits, and the one that waits holds nothing the first one needs. The cycle never opens.

The cost of lock ordering is discipline. Every lock in the program needs a place in the order, and every code path that takes two or more locks must respect that order. A single violation — one function that grabs lock 7 while holding lock 3 — reintroduces the deadlock the scheme was built to prevent. The benefit is that the proof is structural: the order itself is the argument that no cycle exists, and the argument holds as long as the order holds.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. The hash function spreads keys across the array's slots, called buckets. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision, and the map needs a rule for storing both.

The oldest rule is chaining. Each bucket holds a pointer to a linked list. A key that hashes to an occupied bucket appends to that list. Lookup walks the list, comparing each stored key against the target. The cost grows with the list's length. If all keys collide into one bucket, the map degrades to a linear search.

Open addressing takes a different shape. Every entry lives in the array itself, not in a side list. A collision sends the map probing other slots by a fixed rule. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next, until it finds an empty one. Quadratic probing jumps by squares of the index: one slot, then four, then nine. Double hashing computes a second hash from the key and uses that as the step size, which spreads probes more evenly than a fixed stride.

Probing has a failure mode chaining avoids. Deleting an entry from a probed table leaves a gap, and a later probe sequence that passed through that slot would stop early and miss keys stored beyond it. The fix is a tombstone: the deleted slot is marked as occupied-for-probing but empty-for-insertion. Tombstones accumulate, though, and a table with many of them slows lookups until it is rehashed.

Both schemes depend on the load factor: the ratio of stored entries to array slots. Chaining tolerates a factor above one, because lists can grow without bound. Open addressing hard-caps at one, because a full array has nowhere to probe. Most implementations resize when the factor hits a threshold — 0.75 in Java's `HashMap`, 0.5 to 0.66 in many open-addressed tables — and rehash every entry into a larger array. Resize is the most expensive operation a map performs, which is why capacity is often set at construction.

The hash function itself determines how often collisions happen in the first place. A function that clusters keys into a narrow range of buckets makes every collision strategy work harder. A good function distributes keys uniformly across the full bucket range and minimizes collisions in practice, so the lists stay short or the probe sequences stay close to home.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It holds a sorted copy of one or more columns, each entry paired with a pointer back to the full row. The database queries the index instead of scanning the table when a filter or join touches an indexed column.

Without an index, a query like `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 417` reads every row in `orders` and discards the ones that do not match. A table with ten million rows does ten million comparisons. With a B-tree index on `customer_id`, the database walks a balanced tree of height four or five, lands on the leaf nodes holding `417`, and reads only those pages from disk. The work drops from millions of reads to a handful.

The index pays for that speed in three ways.

Storage. Every index is a separate file or segment. An index on a wide column in a large table can approach the table's own size. Three indexes on one table can triple the storage footprint.

Write cost. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update the index too. A table with five indexes does six writes for one row insertion: one to the table's heap, five to the index trees. Bulk loads into an empty table run faster if the indexes are dropped first and rebuilt after.

Planner misfires. The query optimizer picks an index when it estimates the index read is cheaper than a full scan. That estimate depends on table statistics, which drift as rows change. A stale statistic can send the optimizer to an index that matches few rows, forcing a random read for each one. A sequential scan of a million-row table can beat an index lookup that returns two hundred thousand rows, because random I/O is an order of magnitude slower than sequential. The planner also ignores indexes wrapped in functions: `WHERE lower(email) = 'x'` uses no index on `email` unless a matching function-based index exists.

Multi-column indexes carry their own constraint. An index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on `last_name` or both columns. A query filtering only on `first_name` cannot use it, because the index is sorted by `last_name` first and `first_name` only within each `last_name` group. The column order fixes which queries the index serves.

The practical rule follows from the cost. An index earns its place when it serves a query run often enough that the read savings outweigh the write overhead and storage cost across every write the table absorbs. A query run once a day on a table written to a thousand times an hour does not justify the index. A query run a thousand times a second on a table written once an hour does.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. Each byte gets a position in that stream, and every segment the sender transmits carries the position of its first byte in its header. The receiver reads that number and uses it to place the segment's bytes in their correct order before delivering them to the application.

The sender breaks the stream into segments. Segment one carries bytes 1 through 1000, segment two carries 1001 through 2000, segment three carries 2001 through 3000. The network does not guarantee these arrive in order. Segment two might cross a faster route than segment one and reach the receiver first.

The receiver handles this with a buffer. Segment two arrives, the receiver sees its sequence number is 1001, and holds it in the buffer because byte 1001 cannot be delivered until byte 1 arrives. Segment one arrives next, goes into the buffer, and the receiver now has a contiguous run from byte 1 through 2000. It delivers that run to the application and frees the buffer space.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment segment the receiver sends back carries the sequence number of the next byte it expects — the first byte after the longest contiguous run it has received. If the receiver has bytes 1 through 2000 in order, its acknowledgment says 2001. The sender reads that number and knows everything below it arrived intact.

A gap means loss. If the receiver has bytes 1 through 1000 and 2001 through 3000, its acknowledgment still says 1001, because byte 1001 is the first missing byte. The sender sees 1001 come back three times and treats the repetition as a signal that segment two was lost in transit. It retransmits segment two. This is called a duplicate acknowledgment, and TCP uses it to detect loss without waiting for a timer.

The timer is the other loss detector. The sender starts a retransmission timer when it sends a segment. If the timer expires before an acknowledgment arrives for those bytes, the sender retransmits. The timer's duration adapts to the measured round-trip time between sender and receiver, because a timeout on a fast local link means something different from a timeout on a satellite link with a 600-millisecond round trip.

Order and reliability are the same mechanism. The sequence number gives every byte a position, the buffer holds bytes that arrived out of that position, and the acknowledgment tells the sender where the contiguous run ends. The receiver never delivers a byte to the application until every byte before it has arrived and been delivered. The application sees a stream in the order the sender wrote it, regardless of what the network did to the segments in between.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes against shared state.

Two threads running on separate cores can both touch the same memory in the same instant. Thread A reads `balance` at the start of a deposit, adds 100, and writes the result back. Thread B reads `balance` in the gap between A's read and A's write, gets the old value, adds 50, and writes back. A's 100 is gone. The final balance is 50 higher, not 150. The mutex exists to close that gap.

A mutex is a lock with one owner. A thread acquires the mutex before touching the shared data and releases it after. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that tries to acquire it blocks — it stops running and waits. The operating system or the runtime puts the waiting thread to sleep and wakes it when the mutex is free. Only one thread at a time is inside the critical section.

The protection is narrower than it looks. A mutex guards the data that every holder of that mutex agrees to touch only while holding it. A thread that writes to `balance` without acquiring the mutex is not stopped by the mutex. The lock is a convention, enforced by cooperation, not by the hardware. A second mutex does not protect data covered by the first. The discipline is: one mutex per shared resource, every access through that mutex.

Mutexes do not protect against deadlocks on their own. Thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2. Thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Both sleep forever. The fix is an ordering rule: if every thread acquires mutexes in the same global order, no cycle can form. A thread that needs both acquires 1, then 2, never the reverse.

The cost is contention. Ten threads contending for one mutex serialize on it — only one runs the critical section at a time, and the other nine wait. A mutex held for ten microseconds across a thousand calls per second costs ten seconds of blocked time per second. The remedy is to hold the lock for the shortest interval that keeps the data consistent: acquire it, update the shared state, release it, and do every computation that does not touch shared data outside the lock.

A mutex is not the only synchronization primitive, and choosing it matters. A spinlock busy-waits instead of sleeping, which wastes CPU but avoids the context-switch cost of putting a thread to bed — the right trade on a short critical section under low contention, the wrong one on a long section. A read-write lock allows many concurrent readers but one writer, which helps when reads dominate and writes are rare. An atomic operation updates a single word without any lock at all, which removes the critical section entirely for simple counters and flags. The mutex remains the general case: the primitive that protects a region, not a single word, and that composes with other mutexes under ordering rules to cover multi-part state.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches, then frees it. The core question is reachability: can any running code still get to this object?

The roots are the starting points. Every root is a pointer the runtime can find without following other pointers — global variables, static fields, local variables on every thread's call stack, CPU registers holding object references. An object is reachable if a path of pointers leads from some root to it. Unreachable objects are garbage.

Mark-and-sweep traces that path. The collector starts at the roots and walks every pointer it finds, marking each object it reaches. When the walk stops, every marked object is live and every unmarked object is not. The collector then sweeps the heap: it scans every object, frees the unmarked ones, and clears the marks on the rest. The heap is not compacted, so allocation carves free space from a free list of gaps left by freed objects. Fragmentation follows — the heap becomes a patchwork of live objects and holes.

Copying collection avoids the holes. It divides the heap into two halves. The program allocates in one half until it fills. The collector then copies every reachable object from the full half into the empty half, packing them contiguously. The old half becomes the next free space. Freeing takes no work: unreachable objects are simply never copied, and the old half is overwritten wholesale. The cost is that the program runs with half its heap, because only one half holds live data at a time.

Mark-and-compact keeps one heap and fixes fragmentation another way. The marking phase works like mark-and-sweep. Instead of sweeping, the collector computes where each live object would land if slid toward the start of the heap, then moves them all in one pass and rewrites every pointer to the new address. The heap is contiguous after collection. The cost is the move and the pointer rewrite, which touches every live object.

Generational collection rests on an observation: most objects die young. A function that builds a temporary list and returns one element leaves the list nodes unreachable the moment the function returns. The collector splits the heap into a young region and an old region. New objects allocate in the young region. A collection of just the young region runs often and cheaply, because the young region is small and most of its objects are already dead. Objects that survive several young collections promote to the old region, which the collector scans far less often.

The hard part in a generational collector is the roots of the old region. A young collection needs to know which old objects point at young ones, or it cannot trace from those into the young region. Scanning the entire old region to find them defeats the purpose. The collector instead keeps a remembered set: a write barrier records a note every time the program stores a pointer from an old object into a young one. The young collection traces the roots plus the remembered set, and skips the rest of the old heap.

Concurrent collection addresses a different cost. A collector that stops the program while it works produces pauses — intervals where no application code runs. A pause on a 200-millisecond collection is invisible in a batch job and unacceptable in a user-facing system. A concurrent collector does most of its tracing and moving while the program runs, trading raw throughput for shorter pauses. The trade is real work: the program can change the heap while the collector examines it, so the collector must use barriers or snapshot the pointer graph to avoid freeing an object the program just made reachable.

Reference counting takes a fourth shape. Every object carries a count of pointers to it. A new pointer increments the count, a dropped pointer decrements it. The count hitting zero means no path reaches the object, and it is freed at that moment. The failure mode is cycles: two objects pointing at each other keep both counts above zero forever, even if nothing else reaches either. A cycle collector must run periodically to find and break those loops. Reference counting also pays on every pointer write, not just at collection time, which makes it expensive for pointer-heavy programs.

The choice among these is a trade over three axes: pause time, throughput, and memory overhead. Copying halves the heap. Mark-and-sweep fragments. Mark-and-compact moves everything. Generational bets that most garbage is young. Concurrent trades CPU for shorter pauses. No collector wins on all three. The runtime picks the one whose cost profile matches what the program does.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance of 100. Thread A reads the balance, adds 50, and writes 150 back. Thread B reads the balance before A writes, gets 100, adds 30, and writes 130. The final balance is 130. The 50 is gone. The program ran both deposits, but one overwrote the other because neither waited for the other to finish.

The word "race" names the problem. Both threads race to read and write the same memory. The winner's write survives. The loser's write lands on top of it and erases it. The outcome depends on which thread reached the read instruction first, and nothing in the program controls that.

The balance example is a read-modify-write race. The danger zone is the gap between reading the value and writing it back. Thread A enters that gap when it reads 100. Thread B enters the same gap, reads the same 100, and both compute against a stale value. A mutex closes the gap by allowing only one thread inside the read-modify-write sequence at a time. The second thread waits until the first finishes and releases the lock, then reads the updated balance.

A second shape is a check-then-act race. A function checks whether a file exists, and if not, creates it. Two threads call the function at the same time. Both check, both see no file, both create it. The second creation overwrites the first, or fails, or corrupts the file. The check and the act were two separate operations, and another thread slipped between them.

A third shape is a stale read without a write race. Thread A reads a flag set by Thread B. The compiler optimizes the read into a register and never checks memory again. Thread B sets the flag, but Thread A never sees the new value. There is no conflicting write, but the two threads disagree on the state of the same variable. The fix is a memory barrier or an atomic read that forces the thread to check memory.

Race conditions resist testing. A program with a race runs correctly a thousand times and fails on the thousandth, because the scheduler interleaved the threads differently that one run. The bug is nondeterministic: it depends on timing, and timing changes every run. A test that passes once proves nothing about the next run. This is why synchronization is designed into the program rather than tested in after the fact.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It holds copies of the data and instructions the processor is most likely to need next. When the processor requests a byte, the cache answers in one or two nanoseconds. Main memory takes a hundred.

The speed comes from physics. A cache is static RAM built into the same chip as the processor core. The wires are short and the silicon is close. Main memory is dynamic RAM on separate chips across a bus, and a signal crosses that bus at a fraction of the speed of light. Distance is latency. A cache hit avoids the trip.

Caches work because programs do not access memory at random. They access it in patterns, and those patterns are predictable. A loop that sums an array reads element 417 right after element 416. A function that calls `parse_token` will likely call `skip_whitespace` next, because `parse_token` calls it. The cache exploits two patterns. Spatial locality: if the processor touches address 416, it will soon touch 417, 418, 419. Temporal locality: if it touches an address once, it will touch it again soon.

Spatial locality drives the cache line. Memory is not fetched one byte at a time. The cache pulls data in blocks called lines, usually 64 bytes. A single read of address 416 loads the whole line — 416 through 479 — into the cache. The next seven reads of the adjacent bytes hit the cache and never reach main memory. An array traversal that reads ten thousand consecutive integers loads roughly fifteen hundred lines, not forty thousand individual words.

Temporal locality drives the replacement policy. A cache is small — a typical level-1 cache holds 32 to 48 kilobytes — and it fills up. When a new line arrives and the cache has no room, something must leave. The policy most caches use is least-recently-used: the line that has gone longest without being read is evicted. A loop body that fits in the level-1 cache stays there for every iteration, because it was just used and will be used again in nanoseconds.

Modern processors layer caches. The level-1 cache is smallest and closest, private to each core, answering in four cycles. The level-2 cache is larger, around 256 kilobytes, answering in twelve to fourteen cycles, also private. The level-3 cache is shared across all cores on the die, holds 8 to 32 megabytes, and answers in 30 to 50 cycles. Main memory answers in 200 to 300. A miss at level 1 that hits at level 2 costs ten extra cycles. A miss that goes all the way to main memory costs two hundred.

The cost of a miss dominates program speed. A processor that issues four instructions per cycle stalls when it requests data that is not in the cache. The core sits idle for the two hundred cycles it takes to fetch from main memory. A program that runs entirely from the level-1 cache executes at the processor's full rate. A program that misses the cache on half its memory accesses runs at a fraction of that rate, regardless of how fast the processor is clocked.

This is why data layout matters as much as algorithm. A linked list scatters its nodes across the heap. Each node sits at a different address, so following a pointer loads a new cache line for every node. Walking a million-node linked list triggers a million cache misses. An array of the same million elements packs them contiguously. Walking the array loads one cache line per sixteen elements, and the processor prefetches the next line before the code asks for it. Same algorithm, same operation count, different memory layout — the array runs ten to fifty times faster because it feeds the cache.

The cache turns memory access from a random-cost operation into a structured one. Access patterns that match the cache's assumptions run at the speed of the processor. Access patterns that fight those assumptions run at the speed of the bus. The gap between those two speeds is the single largest performance variable in a modern program.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once.

`GET` is the trivial case. A read does not change state, so a thousand reads leave the server where one read left it. The property holds by definition.

`PUT` is the instructive case. A `PUT /users/417` with body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 417's name to Ada. The first request sets it. The second request sets it again to the same value. The stored state after the second is identical to the state after the first. The operation is idempotent because it names a target resource and supplies a complete replacement value, not a delta.

`POST` is the counterexample. A `POST /orders` with body `{"item": "book"}` creates a new order. The first request creates order 1001. The second request creates order 1002. Two requests produced two resources. The state diverges with each call. `POST` is not idempotent because it appends rather than replaces, and the server assigns a new identifier each time.

`DELETE` is idempotent with a caveat. `DELETE /orders/1001` removes order 1001. The first request deletes it. The second request finds no order 1001 and does nothing. The end state — order 1001 absent — is the same after both. The response differs: the first returns 200, the second returns 404. Idempotency governs server state, not response equality. The two calls produce different bodies and status codes but leave the server in the same condition.

The property matters because networks duplicate. A client sends `PUT /users/417`, the server applies it, and the response vanishes in transit. The client does not know whether the request reached the server or the response died on the way back. It retries. An idempotent method makes that retry safe: applying the same write twice leaves the server where applying it once did. A non-idempotent method makes the retry a gamble. The client cannot tell whether it created one order or two, and the server cannot tell the duplicate from the original.

The HTTP specification names `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` idempotent and `POST` and `PATCH` not. `PATCH` earns its exclusion because a patch carries a delta, not a full replacement. A patch saying "add 50 to the balance" applied twice adds 100. A patch saying "set the name to Ada" applied twice is idempotent in effect, but the method does not guarantee it, because the semantics depend on the body's content rather than the method's contract.

A practical consequence follows. APIs that need creation to survive retries build idempotency on top of `POST` with a client-supplied key. The request includes an idempotency key — a UUID the client generates once and sends with every attempt at the same operation. The server records the key on the first request. A second request with the same key returns the stored response instead of creating a second resource. Stripe's idempotency keys work this way. The method stays `POST`, but the key gives it the retry safety that `PUT` provides by its own contract.

DNS resolves a hostname like `mail.example.com` to an address like `93.184.216.34` through a chain of queries, each handled by a different server.

The resolver starts the chain. That resolver usually belongs to the ISP or a public provider like Cloudflare at `1.1.1.1` or Google at `8.8.8.8`. When an application asks for a name, the operating system sends a UDP packet to port 53 on the resolver's address.

The resolver checks its cache first. If it asked for `mail.example.com` recently and stored the answer, it returns the address without contacting anyone else. The cache entry carries a time-to-live value, set by the name's owner, that tells the resolver how many seconds the answer stays valid. A common TTL is 300 seconds. When the TTL expires, the resolver discards the entry and asks again.

A cache miss sends the resolver to the root servers. The root servers are thirteen named clusters, `a.root-servers.net` through `m.root-servers.net`, operated by organizations like Verisign and the University of Maryland. The resolver picks one by address, often the one with the lowest measured round-trip time, and sends it a query for `mail.example.com`.

The root server does not know the address. It knows which servers handle the top-level domain, which is `com`. It returns a list of the `com` name servers: `a.gtld-servers.net` through `m.gtld-servers.net`. The root server's answer is a referral, not a resolution.

The resolver sends the same query to one of the `com` servers. That server also does not know the address of `mail.example.com`. It knows which servers are authoritative for `example.com`, because the registrant of `example.com` registered those servers with the `com` registry. It returns that list. A typical entry is `a.iana-servers.net`.

The resolver sends the query to the authoritative server for `example.com`. That server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds a record for `mail` — an A record containing `93.184.216.34` — and returns it. The resolver caches that answer for the TTL the record specifies, then hands the address to the operating system, which hands it to the application.

The full path is three round trips: root, top-level domain, authoritative server. Each adds latency proportional to the network distance between the resolver and the server queried. A resolver in London asking a root server in London, a `com` server in Amsterdam, and an authoritative server in Tokyo pays roughly one millisecond, ten milliseconds, and 280 milliseconds for the three hops. The first lookup for a cold cache is slow for this reason. Subsequent lookups hit the resolver's cache and return in under a millisecond.

The chain handles subdomains by adding hops. `api.staging.example.com` adds one more delegation: the `example.com` authoritative server refers the resolver to the servers authoritative for `staging.example.com`, which refer to the servers for `api.staging.example.com`. Each label separated by a dot can add a delegation, and each delegation is another round trip.

The protocol runs over UDP by default. A DNS response that exceeds 512 bytes, which happens when a domain returns many records, triggers a fallback to TCP. The resolver reopens the query over TCP port 53 to receive the full payload. DNSSEC, which signs records to prevent tampering in transit, adds signature records that push many responses past the UDP limit, making TCP a common path rather than an edge case.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads stop forever because each holds a resource the other needs.

Thread A acquires mutex 1. Thread B acquires mutex 2. Thread A then tries to acquire mutex 2 and blocks, because B holds it. Thread B tries to acquire mutex 1 and blocks, because A holds it. Neither releases what it has. Neither gets what it wants. Both sleep. The program hangs.

Four conditions must hold at once for this to happen. The threads hold resources exclusively — one mutex, one owner. They hold while waiting — a thread does not release mutex 1 before asking for mutex 2. The resources are not preempted — the operating system does not force a thread to give up a held lock. And a cycle exists — A waits for B, B waits for A, and the chain closes back on itself. Break any one of the four and the deadlock cannot form.

The avoidance is a lock ordering rule. Every mutex in the program gets a fixed rank, and every thread acquires mutexes in ascending rank order. If mutex 1 ranks below mutex 2, a thread that needs both acquires 1 first, then 2. No thread ever acquires them in the reverse order.

The rule breaks the cycle. A cycle requires one thread to acquire 1 then 2 while another acquires 2 then 1. Lock ordering makes the second acquisition impossible — the thread that needs both takes 1 first, same as the first thread. The two threads serialize on mutex 1. One wins, acquires 2, does its work, releases both. The other waits at mutex 1, then proceeds. The cycle cannot close because every thread enters the resource graph from the same node.

The cost is discipline. A new mutex added to the system needs a rank, and every code path that touches it alongside existing mutexes must follow the order. A thread that holds a high-ranked mutex and reaches for a low-ranked one violates the rule and reintroduces the deadlock. The ordering is a global invariant, not a local one, and the compiler cannot enforce it. The invariant lives in the code's conventions and in review.

A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array. A hash function turns each key into an integer, which the map uses as an array index. Two keys can hash to the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has a strategy for it.

**Separate chaining** keeps a linked list at each array slot. When two keys land on slot 4, both entries live in the list hanging off index 4. A lookup hashes the key, walks that slot's list, and compares keys with `equals` until it finds the match or reaches the end. The cost grows with list length. Java's `HashMap`, Go's `map`, and C++'s `unordered_map` all use this approach, though Java and Go store entries in array-backed structures rather than pointer-linked nodes, which improves cache locality.

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the array, no list. If the target slot is occupied, the map probes other slots by a fixed rule until it finds an empty one. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next: slot 4, 5, 6. Quadratic probing jumps by squares: slot 4, 5, 8, 13. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size, which spreads entries more evenly than either. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbed probe sequence. Robin Hood probing, a variant of open addressing, moves entries so that the entry farthest from its home slot wins a collision; this shortens worst-case lookups. Rust's `HashMap` used Robin Hood hashing before version 1.36, then switched to SwissTable, a compact open-addressing design from Google's Abseil library.

Both strategies degrade as the array fills. A map with 90% occupancy and chaining has long lists; a map with 90% occupancy and open addressing runs out of empty slots to probe. The map watches its load factor — the ratio of entries to array length. When the ratio crosses a threshold, the map allocates a larger array and reinserts every entry, which rehashes each key against the new array size. Java's `HashMap` resizes at 0.75. Python's `dict` resizes at roughly two-thirds. Rehashing is O(n) for that operation, but amortized O(1) per insertion across the map's lifetime, because resizing happens rarely relative to the number of insertions between resizes.

Deletion adds a wrinkle to open addressing. Removing an entry and leaving an empty slot breaks probe chains — a later key that probed past that slot would no longer be found. Open-addressing maps mark deleted slots with a tombstone flag. Lookups treat tombstones as occupied and keep probing; insertions treat them as empty and reuse them. Tombstones accumulate, though, and eventually the map rehashes to clear them even if the entry count has not grown.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It trades write speed and disk space for read speed.

The structure is usually a B-tree. The B-tree keeps the table's column values in sorted order, with a tree on top so a query can find a given value in O(log n) steps instead of scanning every row. A query for `WHERE user_id = 8143` reads a few tree nodes — perhaps three or four disk pages — and gets the matching row's location. Without the index, the database reads the entire table to check each row. On a ten-million-row table, that is the difference between reading a handful of pages and reading all of them.

A table can have many indexes. Each one answers a different question: an index on `email` speeds login lookups, an index on `created_at` speeds date-range reports. A composite index on `(last_name, first_name)` serves queries that filter on both columns, and also serves queries that filter on `last_name` alone, because the tree sorts by `last_name` first. It does not serve a query that filters on `first_name` alone, because `first_name` is only sorted within each `last_name` group.

Indexes hurt writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that changes an indexed column must update the index tree as well as the table. A table with five indexes pays six writes for one logical insert — one to the table's heap, five to the trees. On a high-throughput insert workload, a single unnecessary index can halve the write rate. PostgreSQL's documentation is explicit about this: each index adds overhead to every data modification.

Indexes hurt disk space. The index is a separate structure on disk. An index on a large text column can approach the size of the table itself. A table with six indexes can consume seven times its raw storage footprint. This cost also lives in memory: the database caches frequently used index pages in its buffer pool, and a large index evicts other useful pages.

Indexes hurt when the query does not use them. A query like `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x@y.com'` cannot use a plain index on `email`, because the `LOWER` function transforms the value after the index was built. The database scans the table anyway, and the index sits there consuming space and write capacity for nothing. The fix is a functional index on `LOWER(email)`, or rewriting the query to compare against the raw column.

Indexes hurt when selectivity is low. An index on a column with two values — `active` versus `inactive` — where 95% of rows are `active` helps little. The database reads the index, gets a list of row locations, then fetches each row from disk. If the index returns nine million rows out of ten million, the index has added a step without narrowing the search. The query planner sees this and skips the index, doing a sequential scan instead. The index still costs writes and space while providing nothing.

Indexes hurt when two of them fight. A query that filters on `status` and sorts by `created_at` can use an index on `status` to find matching rows, then sort them in memory. Or it can use an index on `created_at` to read rows in order, then discard those with the wrong `status`. The planner picks one. A composite index on `(status, created_at)` serves both needs in one pass. Without it, the database does redundant work, and the two single-column indexes each help a different query while wasting space on this one.

The cost is permanent. Every index on a table adds overhead to every write, for the lifetime of the table, whether or not any query uses it. An index that served a one-time report and was never dropped still slows inserts years later. The discipline is to add an index when a measured query is too slow, and to drop an index whose queries no longer run.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a series of messages. Each byte gets a sequence number. The first byte's number is not zero; it is a random 32-bit value the sender picks during the connection handshake, and every subsequent byte counts up from there. The randomness blocks an attacker who wants to predict sequence numbers and inject data into the stream.

A TCP segment carries a range of those bytes. Its header records the sequence number of the first byte in the segment and the length of the payload. A segment carrying bytes 1001 through 2000 has sequence number 1001. The receiver reads that header and knows exactly where the bytes belong in the stream.
