IP, the protocol that actually moves packets between machines, delivers them in any order. A packet routed through a slow path can arrive after a packet sent later through a fast one. A packet can also arrive twice. TCP's job is to hide that disorder from the application.

The receiver keeps a buffer and a variable called the expected sequence number. When a segment arrives, the receiver checks its sequence number against what it expects. If the segment carries exactly the expected bytes, the receiver writes them to the buffer, advances the expected number by the segment's length, and checks whether the next segment in the buffer also fits. A later segment that arrived early sits in the buffer until the gap before it fills.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment segment carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects — the number just past the last in-order byte it received. An ack of 5001 means the receiver has every byte up to 5000. This is a cumulative ack: it confirms everything before that point, even if some of those segments arrived out of order.

A gap means something was lost. If the sender transmits segments 1001, 2001, and 3001, and the receiver gets 2001 and 3001 but not 1001, the receiver buffers both and acks 1001. It keeps acking 1001 on every segment it sends back, because 1001 is still the next byte it needs. The sender sees repeated acks for the same number and infers a loss. TCP's fast retransmit rule fires after three duplicate acks: the sender resends the missing segment without waiting for its retransmission timer to expire.

The retransmission timer is the backstop. The sender starts a timer when it sends a segment. If the ack does not return before the timer expires, the sender resends. The timer's duration adapts to the measured round-trip time, using a weighted moving average and a variance estimate so that it is long enough to avoid resending data that is merely delayed but short enough to recover from real loss quickly.

Order emerges from this. The receiver reassembles the byte stream in sequence-number order, pulling early arrivals from its buffer as gaps fill. The application reading from the connection sees one continuous, in-order stream, regardless of the order the packets arrived in. The sequence numbers, the buffer, the cumulative acks, and the retransmission of gaps together turn IP's unreliable delivery into a reliable, ordered pipe.

A mutex protects against one thing: two threads inside the same critical section at the same time.

A critical section is a span of code that touches shared state. The shared state might be a counter, a linked list, a file, a hardware register. The defining property is that the operation must complete before another thread touches the same state. A thread incrementing a shared counter reads the current value, adds one, and writes it back. If a second thread reads the same current value before the first writes, both write the same result. The counter goes up by one instead of two. The mutex prevents this.

The mechanism is ownership. A thread calls `lock` before the critical section and `unlock` after. While one thread holds the lock, every other thread that calls `lock` blocks — it stops running and waits. The operating system or the language runtime parks the waiting thread and wakes it when the lock is free. Only one thread holds the lock at a time, so only one thread is inside the critical section at a time.

The mutex protects against data races. A data race is the specific condition where two threads access the same memory location, at least one of them writes, and nothing synchronizes the access. The result is undefined behavior in languages like C and C++: torn reads, corrupted structures, crashes that reproduce inconsistently. The mutex makes the accesses happen one after another, which removes the race.

The mutex does not protect against everything related to concurrency. It does not make a thread-safe API by existing on one method. A class with a locked `push` and a locked `pop` is safe for each call in isolation, but a caller that checks `size`, then calls `pop` based on the result, has a gap between the two calls where another thread can empty the container. The lock on each method does not cover that gap. Protecting the compound operation requires holding the lock across both calls, or using a higher-level abstraction.

A mutex can deadlock. Thread A locks mutex 1 then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then tries to lock mutex 1. Both wait forever. The fix is a lock-ordering rule: every thread acquires the mutexes in the same sequence. If all threads lock mutex 1 before mutex 2, the deadlock cannot occur.

A mutex has cost. The lock call enters the kernel if the lock is contended, which is a context switch measured in microseconds. An uncontended lock may stay in userspace — pthreads, Java's synchronized, and C++'s `std::mutex` all use fast paths that compare-and-swap in user memory before falling back to the kernel. The cost matters in tight loops. A counter incremented ten million times under a contended mutex spends most of its time in the kernel scheduler, not in the addition.

The mutex is the primitive that makes shared-memory concurrency safe. It enforces mutual exclusion on a span of code, and that exclusion is what turns a data race into a correct, sequential access.

A garbage collector finds memory the program no longer reaches. "No longer reaches" has a precise meaning, and the collector's method turns that meaning into a mechanical procedure.

The program holds references to objects through variables. A local variable in a running method points to a `Customer` object. That object holds a field pointing to an `Address` object. The collector calls the first kind — references held directly by the running program — **roots**. Roots are the entry points. They include local variables on thread stacks, static fields, and active method-argument slots. Everything else is reachable only if a path of references leads back to a root.

The collector traces those paths. Starting from every root, it walks references from object to object, marking each object it visits. A root points to a `Customer`; the collector marks the `Customer`, follows its `Address` field, marks the `Address`, follows that object's fields, and so on. When the walk finishes, every marked object is reachable. Every unmarked object is garbage. This is **marking**, and it is the core of tracing collection — the strategy used by the JVM, .NET's CLR, V8, and Go.

After marking comes sweeping. The collector scans the heap and frees every unmarked object. The memory returns to the free list for future allocation. Objects that survived the trace stay put. This is mark-and-sweep, the simplest form.

Mark-and-sweep leaves gaps. The heap fragments into small free regions scattered between live objects. A later allocation that needs one contiguous block fails even when enough total free memory exists. **Compacting** collectors solve this by sliding live objects together after the sweep, leaving one contiguous free region at the end. The collector must update every reference it moves, which adds work but eliminates fragmentation. The JVM's serial and parallel collectors compact.

Moving objects while the program runs breaks references. A `Customer` field still points to address 0x5000, but the `Address` object now lives at 0x4800. The collector fixes this, but the program cannot safely run while the collector reads and writes those pointers. Most collectors **stop the world**: they pause every application thread at a safe point, run the collection, then resume. The pause is the cost of correctness. A ten-gigabyte heap with a long reference chain can mean a pause of hundreds of milliseconds.

Generational collection cuts that cost. The empirical observation behind it is the **weak generational hypothesis**: most objects die young. A loop that builds a string per iteration allocates thousands of objects that become garbage before the loop ends. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. It collects the young generation frequently — it is small, so the pause is short — and promotes objects that survive several young-gen collections to the old generation. The old generation is collected rarely. Because most garbage is in the young generation, most collections are fast. The JVM, .NET, and V8 all use generational collection.

A different strategy avoids tracing entirely. **Reference counting** stores, with each object, a count of references pointing to it. Assignment increments the count; dropping a reference decrements it. When the count hits zero, the object is unreachable and the collector frees it immediately. CPython uses reference counting for its primary collection strategy. The cost is paid on every assignment rather than in batch pauses.

Reference counting breaks on cycles. Object A points to object B, object B points back to A, and nothing else points to either. Both counts sit at one. Both are garbage, and neither count reaches zero. CPython patches this with a tracing collector that runs periodically to find and break cycles. The tracing pass is the backstop; reference counting is the front line.

Concurrent collectors try to avoid stopping the world. The JVM's G1 and ZGC, and .NET's server GC, do most of their marking and relocation while application threads run. They still need short pauses at certain barriers — to update a root set, to flip a relocation pointer — but the pauses measure in milliseconds or sub-milliseconds rather than hundreds. The trade is complexity: the collector must handle the program mutating the object graph while the trace is in flight, which requires **write barriers** — hooks the runtime inserts around reference writes to tell the collector about changes it might have missed.

The collector's job is to compute reachability and reclaim the complement. Every strategy — mark-sweep, compacting, generational, reference counting, concurrent — is a different trade between pause time, throughput, and memory overhead on that one computation.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more threads. The program's output changes depending on which thread runs first, and neither thread is wrong on its own.

A bank account holds a balance of 100. Two threads each withdraw 60. The code reads the balance, checks whether it covers the withdrawal, subtracts, and writes the new balance back. Thread A reads 100. Thread B reads 100 before A writes. Both see enough money. A subtracts 60 and writes 40. B subtracts 60 and writes 40. The account lost 120 and holds 40. Sixty dollars vanished. The bank is short.

The race lives in the gap between reading and writing. The check-then-act sequence is not atomic. The balance can change between the moment a thread reads it and the moment a thread writes it, because another thread can slip in during that gap. The two operations race, and the loser overwrites the winner's result.

A mutex fixes this specific race. A thread locks the account before reading and unlocks after writing. The second thread blocks on the lock until the first finishes, so it reads the balance the first thread wrote, sees 40, and refuses the withdrawal. The operations serialize. The answer is correct.

Not every race is a data race. A data race is the narrower condition where two threads access the same memory location, at least one writes, and nothing synchronizes the access. The bank example is both: the threads race on the logic, and they race on the memory. A program can have a race without a data race if both threads use locks but the locks guard the wrong scope — each method is safe, the compound operation is not. A `size` check under one lock and a `pop` under another leaves a gap where a second thread empties the container between the two calls.

Races are hard to reproduce. Running the same test a thousand times may pass every time, because the scheduler interleaved the threads harmlessly each time. The failing interleaving occurs once in a million runs, in production, at 3 a.m. A test that passes proves nothing about a race. Proving absence requires either a synchronization primitive that makes the interleaving impossible, or a formal proof that the unsynchronized access is safe — a lock-free structure built on atomic operations with documented memory-ordering guarantees.

The defining trait is that the program's correctness depends on timing it does not control. The fix is to remove the timing dependence: make the operation atomic, lock the right scope, or use a structure whose concurrent behavior is specified.

A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that sits between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping the data the processor is most likely to need next.

Main memory is slow. A modern processor can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but fetching a value from DRAM takes 80 to 100 nanoseconds. That ratio means a cache miss costs roughly 200 to 400 instructions the processor could have run while it waited. The cache closes that gap. It is built from SRAM, the same kind of memory used for CPU registers, and it runs at a fraction of the processor's clock cycle. A hit returns data in one to four nanoseconds.

The cache works because of locality. Programs do not access memory at random. They access the same locations repeatedly — a loop variable, a running sum, a struct field read inside a loop. That is **temporal locality**: if a location was used recently, it will likely be used again. They also access nearby locations — walking an array element by element, reading the fields of a struct one after another. That is **spatial locality**: if a location was used, nearby locations will likely follow. The cache exploits both.

The unit of transfer between cache and main memory is the **cache line**, usually 64 bytes. When the processor requests a byte from memory, the memory controller does not send just that byte. It sends the entire 64-byte line containing it. The cache stores the whole line. If the program then reads the next byte in the same line, the request hits the cache. This is why sequential array access is fast: the first read misses, but the next 63 bytes are already in the cache. The same mechanism makes random access to a large array slow: each access lands on a different cache line, and every one misses.

Modern processors use three levels of cache. L1 is smallest and fastest, typically 32 kilobytes, split into a separate 32 KB cache for data and a 32 KB cache for instructions. L2 is larger, 256 KB to 1 MB, and unified. L3 is largest, 8 to 64 MB, shared across all cores on the die. Each level is a fallback. A request checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. The further it goes, the longer it takes. A miss in L1 that hits in L3 costs about 40 cycles. A miss that goes all the way to DRAM costs 300.

The cache is finite, so it must evict. When a new line arrives and the cache is full, the controller discards an old line to make room. The policy is usually least-recently-used: the line that has gone the longest without being read or written is the one thrown out. LRU assumes that the recent past predicts the near future, which is the same assumption behind temporal locality. It works well until the working set — the set of data the program is actively using — exceeds the cache size. Then every new access evicts a line the program still needs, and the next access to that line misses again. The cache thrashes. Performance collapses to near the speed of main memory.

Program layout determines cache behavior. An array of structs stores each record's fields contiguously, so reading one field pulls the others into the same cache line. If a loop touches only one field per record, the other fields waste cache space. A struct of arrays stores each field in its own contiguous array. The same loop reads one array end to end, and every byte in every cache line is useful. The struct-of-arrays layout can run several times faster for that loop, because it doubles or triples the effective cache density. This is why high-performance numerical code — game engines, signal processing, machine learning kernels — stores data in flat arrays rather than object graphs.

The cache also explains why linked lists are slow for traversal. Each node is allocated separately, and the next node's address bears no relation to the current one. Every hop lands on a new cache line, and every hop misses. A contiguous array walks through memory in order, and the hardware prefetcher — a circuit that watches access patterns and loads cache lines before the processor asks for them — pulls the next lines in ahead of time. The linked list defeats the prefetcher, because the pattern is a chain of pointers with no stride the hardware can predict.

The cache turns the gap between processor speed and memory speed into a bet. The bet is that the data the program needs is nearby in both time and space. When the program's access pattern honors that bet, it runs at the speed of the cache. When it does not, it runs at the speed of DRAM, and the processor spends its time idle, waiting for a wire.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends up in the same state as if it had been sent once.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. Two identical `GET /users/42` calls return the same user. The server's state does not change on either call, because `GET` is read-only. The second call is pure waste — bandwidth, a database read, a parse — but it does no harm.

`PUT` is idempotent by construction. `PUT /users/42` with body `{"name": "Alice"}` sets user 42's name to Alice. Sending it ten times leaves user 42 named Alice. The first call creates or overwrites the resource. Every subsequent call overwrites it with the same value. The final state is identical to the state after one call.

`DELETE` is idempotent by exhaustion. `DELETE /users/42` removes user 42. The first call deletes the user. The second call finds no user 42 and does nothing, or returns 404, or returns 204 — the choice varies by API. The server's state after the second call is the same as after the first: user 42 is gone. The response may differ, but idempotency is about state, not response.

`POST` is not idempotent. `POST /orders` with body `{"item": "book"}` creates a new order. Sending it twice creates two orders. The server's state after two calls holds two orders where one call would have produced one. This is why payment endpoints use `POST`: each call is a distinct, billable action.

The distinction matters when a network fails mid-request. A client sends `POST /orders`, the server creates the order, the server's response is lost to a dropped connection, and the client never receives confirmation. The client does not know whether the order was created. Retrying the `POST` creates a second order. The standard fix is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique token in a header, the server records the token with the first request's result, and a second request with the same token returns the stored result instead of creating a new order. Stripe's `Idempotency-Key` header works this way. The key turns a non-idempotent `POST` into an idempotent operation by making the server remember the first outcome.

Idempotency is a property of the operation, not the method. A `PUT` that increments a counter is not idempotent: ten calls produce ten increments. A `POST` that checks whether a resource exists and creates it only if absent is idempotent: the second call finds the resource and does nothing. The method name suggests the behavior, but the server's implementation determines it.

The HTTP specification declares `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` idempotent and `POST` and `PATCH` not. That declaration is a contract the server is expected to honor. A `DELETE` that toggles a flag instead of removing the resource breaks the contract, and a client that retries on network failure will get the wrong state. The method tells the client what it can expect; the server's code makes that expectation true or false.

DNS turns a human-readable name into a 32-bit or 128-bit network address. A browser given `www.example.com` needs that address to open a connection, and DNS is the lookup that produces it.

The resolver starts the work. On a laptop the resolver is a library inside the operating system, often backed by a local cache. On a home network it is a service on the router, or a stub resolver that forwards to an upstream server. The resolver's job is to return an answer or report failure, and it does this by walking a hierarchy of servers.

The name itself is that hierarchy, read right to left. The trailing dot is the root, usually invisible. `com` is a top-level domain. `example` is a domain registered under `com`. `www` is a host or service inside `example`. Each label hands the resolver a smaller piece of the namespace, and each piece is served by a different set of authority.

The walk begins at the root servers. Thirteen logical root server addresses, identified by the letters A through M and backed by over a thousand physical instances using anycast routing, serve the root zone. The resolver already knows their addresses; they are compiled into the system as a root hints file. The resolver picks one and sends a query for `www.example.com`.

The root server does not know the answer. It knows which servers are authoritative for `com`. It returns a referral: a list of the `com` top-level domain servers and their addresses. The root server's authority ends at `com`; it will not answer for anything inside `com` itself.

The resolver sends the same query to a `com` server. That server is authoritative for every second-level domain under `com`. It does not know `www.example.com` either, but it knows which name servers are authoritative for `example.com` — the ones the registrant listed when registering the domain. It returns those as another referral.

The resolver now asks the `example.com` name server. This server holds the actual records for the domain. It reads the query, finds a record for `www`, and returns the address. If the record is a name rather than an address — a CNAME pointing `www` to `example.com` — the resolver restarts the walk for that new name, or follows it inline depending on configuration.

The answer carries a time-to-live. The TTL is a number of seconds the resolver may cache the address before asking again. A TTL of 3600 means the resolver can reuse the answer for an hour. The TTL is what makes DNS fast under load: the first lookup for a popular site walks the full hierarchy, and every lookup after that returns from cache. It is also what makes DNS slow to propagate changes, because every cache between the authoritative server and the client honors its own TTL before checking for an update.

The protocol runs over UDP port 53 by default. A query and its response each fit in a single UDP packet, up to 512 bytes without extension mechanisms. If the response is larger — a DNSSEC signature chain, a long record set — the server sets a truncation flag in the response header, and the resolver retries over TCP on the same port to receive the full payload. DNSSEC itself adds cryptographic signatures to each record, letting the resolver verify that the answer came from the authoritative server and was not modified in flight.

The full walk is the worst case. A resolver with a warm cache holds the `com` server addresses from a previous lookup, so it skips the root. It may hold the `example.com` server addresses too, so it skips `com`. It may hold the final answer, so it asks no one. The cache is the reason a DNS lookup usually completes in a few milliseconds rather than the several round trips the hierarchy implies. The hierarchy provides correctness — every answer traces back to an authoritative source. The cache provides speed, and the TTL is the compromise between speed and freshness.

A deadlock is a state where two or more threads wait for each other, and none can move.

Thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1. A waits for B to release lock 2. B waits for A to release lock 1. Both sleep. Neither wakes. The program hangs.

Four conditions must hold at once. Mutual exclusion: each lock is held by one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one lock blocks waiting for another. No preemption: a thread cannot be forced to release a lock. Circular wait: a cycle of threads exists where each holds a lock the next one needs. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

Lock ordering breaks the cycle. The rule is that every thread acquires locks in the same global sequence. If all threads lock 1 before 2, the cycle is impossible. Thread A locks 1, then 2. Thread B wants 2, but 2 is not its first acquisition — it must get 1 first. B blocks on 1, which A holds. A proceeds to 2, finishes its work, and releases both. B wakes, gets 1, then gets 2. The wait is linear, not circular.

The fix works when the lock order is known and fixed. It breaks down when a thread must lock a resource whose identity it discovers at runtime — a graph traversal that locks nodes as it walks them, where the path determines the order. Two traversals entering the graph from opposite ends can still deadlock under a naive ordering rule. In that case the code needs a coarser lock that covers the whole structure, or a try-lock with backoff that detects the would-be cycle and retreats.

Deadlock is the cost of holding more than one lock at a time. A program that never does so cannot deadlock. A program that does must pick an order and hold to it.

A hash map turns a key into an array index, then stores the value at that index. Two keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has a policy for it.

**Chaining** keeps a linked list at each bucket. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list, and either updates an existing entry or appends a new node. On lookup, it walks the same list. The list is short when the hash function spreads keys evenly, so the common case stays near O(1). When it does not — adversarial input or a poor hash — one bucket collects many keys and a lookup degrades to O(n). Some implementations replace the linked list with a balanced tree past a threshold, capping the worst case at O(log n); Java's `HashMap` does this at eight entries per bucket.

**Open addressing** stores entries in the array itself. On collision, the map probes another slot by a rule: linear probing checks the next slot, quadratic probing jumps by growing squares, double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step. Lookup follows the same probe sequence until it finds the key or an empty slot. Deletion is the awkward operation — removing an entry outright would break the probe chain, so the map marks the slot as a tombstone and skips it during probes but treats it as occupied during inserts. Tombstones accumulate and slow lookups, so the map rehashes to clear them.

Both methods depend on the **load factor**: occupied slots divided by total slots. Chaining tolerates a factor above 1.0 because lists grow without bound. Open addressing must stay below 1.0 — there must be a free slot to probe into — and most implementations rehash when the factor hits 0.7 or 0.75, doubling the array and reinserting every entry at its new index. That rehash is O(n) but amortized across inserts, so any single insert is still O(1) on average.

The hash function is the load-bearing component. A function that clusters keys into a few buckets defeats either strategy. Modern maps combine a fast integer hash with a per-instance seed — Python's `dict`, Go's `map`, Rust's `HashMap` — so an attacker cannot predict which keys collide and force the worst case.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside the table. It trades disk space and write speed for read speed.

The common form is a B-tree. The tree holds the indexed column's values in sorted order, each leaf pointing to the row's location on disk. A query filtering on that column walks the tree — O(log n) comparisons — instead of scanning every row. A table of ten million rows might read four or five tree pages to find a match, where a full scan touches all ten million.

Indexes hurt on writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that changes an indexed column must update the tree as well as the table. One index doubles the write cost. Five indexes multiply it sixfold. A table that takes 2 ms to insert a row unindexed takes 12 ms with five indexes, because each insert maintains five sorted structures.

Indexes hurt when unused. A B-tree on a column no query filters on consumes disk and write bandwidth for nothing. The database maintains it on every write and never reads it. Production databases accumulate these — an index added for a one-time report, a duplicate index created by an ORM — and they sit there slowing inserts until someone finds and drops them.

Indexes hurt when they mislead the planner. A query on `last_name = 'Smith' AND city = 'Boston'` with separate single-column indexes on each picks one, filters, then re-checks the other condition against the results. If 'Smith' matches 50,000 rows and 'Boston' matches 5,000, the planner may choose the name index and read 50,000 rows to discard 45,000. A composite index on `(city, last_name)` reads the 5,000 and filters to the few Smiths there. The wrong index is slower than no index when it returns a large fraction of the table — the planner falls back to a scan when it estimates an index will touch more than roughly 5–20% of rows, but that estimate depends on statistics the database maintains, and stale statistics make the planner choose badly.

The rule is mechanical. An index pays for itself when it turns a scan into a seek on a query that runs often. It costs disk space, write latency, and maintenance on every write to the table. Adding one is a bet that the read savings exceed the write cost over the index's lifetime.

TCP sends data as numbered bytes, not as messages. Each byte gets a sequence number, and the sender writes that number on every segment it transmits.

The receiver collects segments in whatever order the network delivers them. Segment 2 may arrive before segment 1. A router dropped segment 3, but segment 4 came through. The receiver looks at the sequence number on each arriving segment and places the bytes in a buffer at their correct offset. Segment 4's bytes sit at position 3 in the buffer, waiting.

The receiver tells the sender what it has. Every acknowledgment segment carries the sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects — the first gap in the buffer. If the receiver has bytes 1 through 100 and 201 through 300, its acknowledgment says 101. That single number tells the sender everything: bytes 1–100 arrived, and 101 has not.

The sender keeps a copy of every unacknowledged segment. It starts a timer when it sends one. When the timer expires without an acknowledgment covering those bytes, the sender retransmits. Segment 3's timer fires, and the sender sends it again.

When segment 3 arrives on the second try, the receiver fills the gap. The buffer now holds 1 through 300 in order. The acknowledgment jumps from 101 to 301. The sender discards its copies of segments 1 through 3.

The application reading from the connection never sees the disorder. TCP hands bytes to the application in sequence-number order, pulling them from the buffer from the lowest unfilled position upward. Gaps block delivery — bytes 201 through 300 sit in the buffer until 101 through 200 arrive, because the application must receive byte 101 before byte 201.

The sequence number is a 32-bit counter that wraps after 4,294,967,295 bytes. A connection picks its starting number at random during the handshake, not at zero, so an old segment from a previous connection cannot land at the right offset in a new one and inject stale data. The random start, the per-segment number, the receiver's buffer, and the cumulative acknowledgment together rebuild the byte stream in order regardless of what the network did to the segments in transit.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of reads and writes on shared state.

Two threads run at once. Thread A reads a balance of 100, adds 50, and writes 150. Thread B reads the same balance of 100 before A writes, subtracts 30, and writes 70. The final balance is 70 or 150 depending on who wrote last. Neither result is correct. The 50 was lost or the 30 was. A mutex makes the read-modify-write sequence atomic — one thread completes it before the other starts.

The mutex is a lock with one owner. A thread acquires it before touching the shared data and releases it after. While thread A holds the mutex, thread B's call to acquire blocks — it stops running and waits. When A releases, the operating system wakes B. The shared data is never touched by two threads at once.

A mutex does not protect against deadlocks. Thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2. Thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Neither releases. The lock that prevented the race has frozen both threads. The fix is ordering — always acquire mutexes in the same sequence across all threads — and that fix is a discipline the programmer imposes, not something the mutex enforces.

A mutex does not protect memory it was not told to protect. A third thread that touches the balance without acquiring the mutex races against the two that do. The mutex is an agreement, not a barrier in hardware. Nothing prevents a thread from ignoring it except the code being correct.

A mutex does not protect against reentrancy from the same thread in most implementations. A thread that holds a mutex and calls a function that tries to acquire it again will deadlock on a non-recursive mutex, because the lock is already owned and the owner blocks on itself. Recursive mutexes permit this by tracking acquisition count, but they cost more and mask designs where a function's locking contract is unclear.

The mutex is the simplest correct tool for mutual exclusion. It costs a context switch when a thread blocks — microseconds on Linux, longer under contention. It does not compose: two mutexes acquired in different orders across two threads deadlock, and the compiler cannot catch it. It does not scale: a single mutex serializes every thread that touches the protected data, and the protected data becomes the bottleneck under heavy parallelism. The protection is real and the cost is real, and the cost is the point — the mutex buys correctness by making concurrent access sequential.

Garbage collection finds memory the program no longer reaches. The program allocates objects on a heap. Some objects hold references to others — a field, an array element, a local variable on a thread's stack. The collector treats these references as edges in a graph and the objects as nodes. Anything unreachable from the roots is garbage.

The roots are the starting points: the global variables, the static fields, the local variables on every thread's call stack, the CPU registers holding pointers. The collector traces from the roots, walking references edge by edge, marking every object it lands on as live. When the trace stops, every unmarked object is unreachable. The collector frees it.

That is the mark-and-sweep algorithm, and it is the skeleton underneath most collectors. The marking phase pauses the program's threads, because a graph that changes mid-trace produces wrong answers. The sweep phase walks the heap and reclaims unmarked memory. The pause length scales with the number of live objects and the heap size, not with the allocation rate. A program with ten gigabytes of live data pauses longer than one with ten megabytes.

The pause is the problem. A collector that stops the world for two hundred milliseconds breaks a real-time audio buffer, drops a network timeout, and stalls a web request past its deadline. Collectors evolved to shrink the pause, and the evolution produced two branches.

**Generational collection** rests on an empirical fact: most objects die young. A function allocates a temporary list, builds a string, returns, and the list is garbage. The collector splits the heap into a young generation and an old generation. It collects the young generation frequently — it is small, so the pause is short — and promotes objects that survive a collection or two to the old generation. The old generation is collected rarely. The young collection touches few objects and finishes in milliseconds. Java's G1, Go's garbage collector, and .NET's collector are generational.

**Concurrent collection** does the marking work while the program runs, not while it is paused. The collector starts a marking phase, lets the program's threads continue allocating and mutating, and handles the inconsistency by re-checking objects that changed during the trace. The pause shrinks to the time needed to install barriers at the start and end of marking, not the time to walk the whole graph. Go's collector targets a pause under one millisecond this way. The trade is CPU overhead — the marking threads compete with the program for processor cycles — and throughput drops during collection.

Sweeping can also run concurrently, and the freed memory can be returned through free lists rather than compaction. A free list is a linked list of free blocks; allocation pops a block of the right size. Fragmentation is the cost — the heap develops holes between live objects that no single allocation can fill. A compaction phase moves live objects together and rewrites their references, leaving a contiguous free region. Compaction eliminates fragmentation but requires a pause long enough to move objects and fix every pointer to them.

The collector does not call finalizers or destructors in a predictable order, and it may never call them at all if the heap does not fill before the program exits. A program that relies on finalization to close file handles or release database connections leaks those resources. The fix is explicit cleanup — a `close` call, a `defer`, a `using` block — and the collector handles only memory, because memory is the one resource the collector can reclaim safely by walking the graph.

The trace is correct because it is conservative in the right direction. An object that is reachable stays marked and survives. An object that is unreachable gets freed. The collector cannot free a live object, and the one risk on the other side — treating a non-pointer as a pointer and keeping dead memory — only wastes space, never corrupts the heap. The graph walk is the whole mechanism: start at the roots, follow the edges, keep what is connected, drop what is not.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

A bank account holds 100. Two threads each withdraw 60. Thread A reads the balance: 100. Thread B reads the balance: 100. Thread A subtracts 60, writes 40. Thread B subtracts 60, writes 40. The account lost 120 and holds 40. One withdrawal vanished. The bank is out 60.

The read and the write are separate instructions. The CPU executes them in that order — read, compute, write — but nothing forces one thread's three instructions to finish before the other's begin. The scheduler can pause thread A after its read and resume it after thread B's write, or interleave the two threads at any point. Each thread acts on a value it read before the other thread's write landed. That stale value is the race.

The fix is to make the read-compute-write atomic. A mutex around the balance ensures thread B cannot read until thread A has written. Thread B now reads 40, finds it cannot withdraw 60, and the transaction fails. The order is forced: A completes, then B starts. The result is the same every run.

Races are hard to find because they are nondeterministic. The scheduler decides the interleaving, and the interleaving changes between runs. A test that runs a million times and passes every time can fail on the million-and-first because the OS scheduled the threads differently, or because a different machine had a different number of cores. The bug exists in every run, but it only manifests when the interleaving hits the window between the read and the write.

The window is the whole problem. Every race has one — a gap between reading shared state and writing it back, during which another thread can change that state. Narrowing the window with finer-grained locks reduces the probability but does not eliminate the bug. Only making the operation atomic eliminates it, because atomicity removes the window entirely.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by storing copies of the data the processor is likely to read next.

Main memory is slow. A modern processor can execute several instructions per nanosecond, but fetching a value from DRAM takes 80 to 100 nanoseconds. That gap is a hundred cycles the processor spends idle, waiting on a wire. The cache closes it.

The cache is built from SRAM, which is faster than DRAM and more expensive. A typical x86 chip has three levels. L1 is 32 kilobytes per core and returns data in 1 to 2 nanoseconds. L2 is 256 kilobytes per core and takes 3 to 10 nanoseconds. L3 is shared across all cores, holds 8 to 32 megabytes, and takes 30 to 45 nanoseconds. Main memory sits behind all three at 80 to 100 nanoseconds. The processor checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, then RAM. A hit at any level avoids the slower levels below it.

The cache works because of locality. Programs do not read memory at random. They read an array element, then the next element. They execute an instruction, then the next instruction. The first is spatial locality — adjacent data gets used together. The second is temporal locality — a value used once is likely to be used again soon. The cache exploits both. When the processor requests a byte, the hardware fetches a whole block — 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM chips — into the cache line. If the program reads the next byte a cycle later, it is already there.

A loop summing an array of one million integers reads four million bytes. Without a cache, each read costs 100 nanoseconds, and the loop spends 400 milliseconds on memory. With a 64-byte cache line, each fetch pulls 16 integers. The first integer in a line costs 100 nanoseconds, and the next 15 cost one nanosecond each. The loop spends 25 milliseconds on memory. The cache cut the time by sixteenfold, because the access pattern matched the hardware's assumption.

The cache hurts when that pattern breaks. A program that jumps through an array in strides larger than a cache line — reading element 0, then element 4096, then element 8192 — fetches a 64-byte line for each access and uses 4 bytes of it. The other 60 bytes are wasted bandwidth. The cache provides no speedup, and the program runs at main-memory speed. This is why linked lists are slower than arrays for traversal: each node sits at a heap address unrelated to the last, so each pointer chase misses the cache. An array's elements are contiguous, so one line serves many reads.

Cache misses stall the processor. An L1 miss costs 3 nanoseconds to fetch from L2. An L2 miss costs 30 to fetch from L3. An L3 miss costs 100 to fetch from RAM. A program that misses on every access does not run at the processor's clock speed. It runs at memory speed, and memory is a hundred times slower. The cache is the reason a 4 GHz chip is not a lie — without it, the chip would spend 99 of every 100 cycles waiting, and the clock rate would measure nothing.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as sending it once.

`PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` is idempotent. The first request sets the name to Ada. The second request sets the name to Ada again. The stored value is Ada either way. A network failure after the server wrote the value but before the client received the response leaves the client unsure whether the write landed. It retransmits. The server applies the same write a second time, and nothing changes, because the second write produces the same result as the first.

`POST /users` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` is not idempotent. The first request creates user 42. The second request creates user 43. Two requests, two users. A retransmission after a network failure duplicates the record. The server cannot tell the second request from a new, legitimate request, because `POST` has no key the client supplies and the server can compare against.

The distinction is the key. `PUT` carries its identity in the URL — `/users/42` names the exact resource the request modifies. A repeat targets the same resource and overwrites it. `POST` sends data to a collection — `/users` — and lets the server assign the identity. A repeat creates a new identity each time, because the server has no way to know it saw this body before.

`DELETE /users/42` is idempotent. The first request removes the user. The second request finds no user at 42 and does nothing. The end state — no user 42 — is the same after one request or ten. `DELETE /users/42` followed by `DELETE /users/42` is not an error on the second call. A 404 response is correct, because the resource is gone, and gone is the target state.

`PATCH /users/42` with `{"name": "Ada"}` is idempotent when it sets a field. The same patch applied twice leaves the field at Ada. `PATCH /users/42` with `{"$inc": {"login_count": 1}}` is not idempotent. The first request increments the counter to 1. The second increments it to 2. The operation is relative, not absolute, and a repeat changes the result.

The HTTP specification marks `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` as idempotent. It marks `POST` and `PATCH` as not. The specification describes what a method means, not what a particular server does. A server that implements `PUT` by appending to a list instead of overwriting breaks the contract. A client that retries a `PUT` on that server gets a growing list, not a stable state. The idempotency is a promise the server keeps, not a property the method grants.

Retries are the reason the property matters. A client sends a request. A load balancer forwards it. The server processes it and writes the result. The network drops the response. The client times out and sends the request again. If the operation is idempotent, the retry is safe — the second write matches the first, and the client gets the response it missed. If the operation is not idempotent, the retry doubles the work: two charges, two records, two messages sent. The client cannot avoid the retry, because it cannot distinguish a dropped request from a dropped response. It can only rely on the server to make the retry harmless.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a tree of servers, each answering with the address of the next one down, until one server knows the answer outright.

A browser asks for `www.example.com`. The operating system hands the query to a resolver — usually the recursive DNS server run by the ISP or a public resolver like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8. The resolver does not know the address. Its job is to find the server that does.

The resolver starts at the root. The root servers are thirteen named clusters, designated A through M, operated by twelve organizations under ICANN oversight. Their addresses are built into the resolver's configuration. The resolver picks one and asks, "Where is `www.example.com`?"

The root server does not know `www.example.com`. It knows the top-level domain. It answers with a referral: a list of the servers authoritative for `.com`. There are roughly fifteen hundred of these, run by Verisign under contract with ICANN. The resolver picks one and asks the same question.

The `.com` server does not know `www`. It knows which name servers hold the records for `example.com`. It answers with a referral to those servers — say, `a.iana-servers.net` and `b.iana-servers.net`. The resolver picks one and asks again.

The `example.com` name server holds the actual record. It reads the zone file, finds the A record for `www`, and returns the address: `93.184.216.34`. The resolver caches that answer for the time-to-live the record specifies — often 300 seconds, sometimes 86,400 — and hands the address to the operating system, which hands it to the browser. The browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

The whole walk is three round trips: root, top-level domain, authoritative server. Each round trip is tens of milliseconds, so a cold lookup takes 50 to 150 ms. The cache is what makes DNS fast in practice. The resolver caches every referral and every answer. A second request for `www.example.com` returns from the resolver's cache in under a millisecond. A request for `mail.example.com` skips the root and `.com` legs, because those are cached, and goes straight to the authoritative server. A request for `www.example.org` skips only the root. The cache expires entries on their TTL, so a change to the address propagates after the TTL lapses, not before.

The record types matter. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address. An AAAA record maps to an IPv6 address. A CNAME record maps one name to another — `www.example.com` to `example.com` — and the resolver restarts the walk at the new name, following the chain until it finds an A or AAAA. An MX record lists the mail servers for a domain, each with a priority. A TXT record holds arbitrary text, used for domain verification and SPF policies. The query specifies which type it wants, and the authoritative server returns only that type.

The system is hierarchical because the namespace is. The root delegates `.com` to Verisign. Verisign delegates `example.com` to whoever registered the domain. That registrant delegates `www` or points it at an address. No server holds the whole map. Each holds its slice and points downward. The resolver assembles the path by asking, following the pointer, and asking again, and the cache shortens the path on every repeat.

Okay, explain what a deadlock is and one way to avoid it.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and both wait forever for the other to release it.

Thread A acquires mutex 1. Thread B acquires mutex 2. Thread A needs mutex 2 to continue, so it blocks. Thread B needs mutex 1 to continue, so it blocks. Neither releases what it holds. Neither wakes. The program hangs.

Four conditions produce this. The threads hold resources exclusively — one mutex, one owner. They hold while waiting — A keeps mutex 1 while asking for mutex 2. The resources are not preempted — nothing forces a thread to give up a held mutex. And there is a circular wait — A waits on B, B waits on A, the chain closes into a loop. Break any one and the deadlock cannot form.

The reliable fix is lock ordering. Pick a global order for every mutex in the program. Require every thread to acquire its mutexes in that order. Thread A acquires mutex 1, then mutex 2. Thread B must also acquire mutex 1 first, then mutex 2. If B needs mutex 2, it acquires mutex 1 first — and blocks there, because A holds it. B never gets mutex 2. A finishes its work, releases both, and B proceeds. The circular wait never closes, because both threads line up at the same mutex in the same sequence.

The discipline is global. One thread that acquires mutex 2 before mutex 1 breaks the order and reintroduces the deadlock. The compiler does not check it. The runtime does not enforce it. The ordering is a contract every piece of locking code must honor, and a violation anywhere in the program defeats the guarantee everywhere.

A hash map stores values at array slots chosen by a key's hash. Two keys that hash to the same slot collide, and the map needs a rule for keeping both.

**Chaining** hangs a linked list off each slot. On insert, the map hashes the key, walks the list, and either updates an existing pair or appends a new node. On lookup, it walks the same list and compares keys. The cost grows with list length: a slot with eight entries takes eight comparisons in the worst case. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `unordered_map` both chain. Java switches each list to a balanced tree past eight entries, turning the worst case from O(n) to O(log n) when keys are hostile or pathological.

**Open addressing** stores every pair in the slot array itself. A collision sends the probe to another slot by a fixed rule: linear probing checks the next slot, quadratic probing checks slots at growing intervals, double hashing uses a second hash function as the step. Robin Hood probing tracks how far each pair has traveled from its home slot and evicts a nearer pair for a farther one, cutting the longest probe chain. Lookup follows the same probe sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot. Deletion is the hard part: removing a pair and leaving an empty slot breaks the probe chain for anything inserted after it, so the map marks the slot with a tombstone that probes skip on insert but pass through on lookup. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Rust's `HashMap` all use open addressing.

The choice turns on memory and cache behavior. Chaining allocates a node per entry, which fragments memory and chases pointers on every lookup. Open addressing keeps pairs contiguous, so a probe sequence walks a cache line, not a pointer graph. But open addressing degrades fast as the array fills: at 90% capacity, the average probe length climbs sharply, so maps resize at a load factor around 0.7. Chaining tolerates load factors above 1.0 because the lists simply grow.

Resizing fixes the load problem, not the collision problem. When the array crosses its threshold, the map allocates a larger array — usually double — and rehashes every pair into it. Each pair lands at a new slot because the array size changed. This rehash is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert across the lifetime of the map.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row.

The common form is a B-tree. The tree sorts rows by a chosen column — say `last_name` — and stores them in order. A query for `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` walks the tree from root to leaf, touching four or five pages instead of reading the whole table. A table with ten million rows and no index answers that query by reading all ten million. With a B-tree on `last_name`, it reads a handful.

PostgreSQL, MySQL's InnoDB, and SQL Server all build B-tree indexes by default. PostgreSQL also offers GIN for array and JSONB containment, GiST for geometric and range types, and HASH for simple equality. The choice of structure matters, but the cost dynamics are the same.

Indexes hurt in three ways.

First, they cost storage. An index is a copy of part of the table, sorted and stored separately. Six indexes on a hundred-gigabyte table can add another sixty gigabytes. Disk and memory that hold indexes are disk and memory that do not hold table data.

Second, they slow writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update every index on that column. A table with five indexes takes roughly five times the write work of a table with none. On a high-throughput insert workload — a log table, an event stream — that overhead is the bottleneck.

Third, they can be useless or worse than useless. A B-tree on a column with two values, like a boolean `is_active` flag, splits ten million rows into two piles of five million. The planner reads half the table either way, so it ignores the index and does a sequential scan. The index sits on disk, consuming space and slowing writes, and serves no query. A query like `WHERE last_name LIKE '%son'` also defeats a B-tree, because the tree sorts by the start of the string and the pattern matches the end. The planner scans the table.

The planner decides whether to use an index, not the query author. PostgreSQL's `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows the chosen plan and its actual cost. If `Seq Scan` appears where an index exists, the planner judged the index more expensive than scanning the table. That judgment is usually right. Forcing an index with a hint, as MySQL's `USE INDEX` allows, often makes the query slower.

The rule is narrow. Index columns that appear in `WHERE` clauses joining or filtering on equality or range, and that have enough distinct values to cut the result set to a small fraction of the table. Do not index columns that return most of the rows, columns that change on every write, or columns no query filters on. Drop indexes that `EXPLAIN` never uses. A table with two well-chosen indexes outperforms a table with twenty guessed ones.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as a sequence of independent messages. Every byte gets a sequence number drawn from a 32-bit counter that starts at a random value agreed during the handshake. The receiver uses these numbers to put the bytes back in the order the sender wrote them.

The sender breaks the stream into segments. Each segment carries a contiguous range of bytes and is labeled with the sequence number of its first byte. Segment 1 might carry bytes 1000 through 1099, segment 2 bytes 1100 through 1199, segment 3 bytes 1200 through 1299. The network can deliver these in any order. Segment 2 can arrive before segment 1. A link between New York and Chicago can overtake a link through Denver if its queue is shorter.

The receiver holds a buffer and a counter called the expected sequence number. When a segment arrives, the receiver checks its sequence number against the counter. If the number matches, the bytes are in order: the receiver writes them to the buffer, advances the counter by the segment's length, and checks whether the next segment has already arrived. If segment 1200 through 1299 arrived early and is sitting in the buffer, the receiver writes it too and advances the counter again. This is how out-of-order arrival gets corrected.

If the number does not match, the segment is out of order or a gap exists. The receiver stores the segment in the buffer but does not advance the counter. It sends back an acknowledgment for the expected sequence number, which tells the sender: everything before this number arrived, send the rest. A duplicate acknowledgment — the same number repeated — signals a likely gap. After three duplicate acknowledgments, the sender retransmits the missing segment without waiting for its timer to expire. This is TCP's fast retransmit.

The acknowledgment itself carries the order. An ACK of 1300 means bytes 1000 through 1299 are contiguous in the receiver's buffer and ready for the application. The number is cumulative: it confirms everything up to that point, not just the last segment received. A receiver holding segments 1100 and 1200 but missing 1000 sends ACK 1000 repeatedly until the gap fills, even though later bytes are already in the buffer.

The application reading from the connection sees a single ordered stream. TCP hands bytes to the application in sequence-number order, never delivering byte 1100 before byte 1099. The reordering, the gap-filling, and the duplicate acknowledgments all happen below the application's read call. The stream the application sees is the stream the sender wrote.

A mutex protects one thing: shared memory touched by more than one thread at the same time.

Two threads running on separate cores can read and write the same variable. Thread A reads `balance` at 1000, adds 50, and writes 1050. Thread B reads `balance` at 1000 before A writes, adds 30, and writes 1030. The final value is 1030. Eighty dollars disappeared. The processor did exactly what it was told; the instructions just interleaved.

A mutex — mutual exclusion lock — serializes access. Before touching `balance`, a thread calls `lock`. If the mutex is free, the thread takes it and proceeds. If another thread already holds it, the calling thread blocks — the operating system parks it off the run queue — until the holder calls `unlock`. Only one thread holds the mutex at a time, so the read-modify-write sequence runs as an indivisible block. Thread A finishes its update before B begins, or vice versa. The answer is 1080 either way.

The mutex protects the *invariant*, not just the memory cell. A bank transfer debits one account and credits another. Without a lock, a thread can see the debit applied but the credit not yet applied, observing a state where money exists in neither account. A mutex held across both operations keeps the transfer atomic: other threads see the state before or the state after, never the state between.

What a mutex does not protect against is as important. It does not protect against deadlocks, which it creates. Thread A locks mutex 1 then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2 then tries to lock mutex 1. Both block forever. The fix is a lock ordering protocol — every thread acquires mutexes in the same global order — or a single lock that covers both resources. It does not protect against priority inversion, where a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority thread preempts the low-priority thread so the high-priority thread waits on a thread that cannot run. The classic fix is priority inheritance, which temporarily raises the low-priority thread's priority until it releases the lock.

A mutex is not a semaphore. A binary semaphore permits a thread to unlock a mutex it never locked, because the semaphore tracks a count, not an owner. A mutex tracks its owner and enforces that the same thread that called `lock` calls `unlock`. Releasing a mutex from the wrong thread is an error, caught at runtime on most implementations. This ownership is what distinguishes a mutex from a counting semaphore or a binary semaphore, and it is what makes a mutex the correct tool for protecting a critical section rather than for signaling between threads.

The cost is contention. Every `lock` call that finds the mutex held costs a context switch — the thread enters the kernel, gets descheduled, and wakes later when the holder releases. On a four-core machine, four threads hammering one mutex run no faster than one thread, because three are always waiting. The lock serializes the work. Reducing critical sections to the minimum necessary code, or using lock-free structures for simple counters, keeps threads on their own cores doing useful work instead of parked in a wait queue.

Okay, explain how garbage collection finds unused memory, in plain register with every sentence carrying a fact.

Garbage collection reclaims memory that the program can no longer reach. The collector must distinguish objects the program might still use from objects it has abandoned, and it must do this without the program's help.

The core idea is reachability. A set of roots anchors everything alive. The roots are the things the program can touch directly: stack-allocated variables in every running thread, global and static fields, and handles held by the runtime itself, such as JNI references in the JVM. An object is reachable if a path of pointers leads from a root to it. An object with no such path is garbage, because no thread can ever follow a pointer to it again.

**Tracing** is how most collectors walk that graph. Starting from the roots, the collector follows every pointer it finds, marking each object it reaches. When the traversal stops, every marked object is alive and every unmarked object is dead. The collector then sweeps the heap: it walks the allocation arena and frees any object whose mark bit is clear. This is mark-and-sweep, the algorithm McCarthy described in 1960 for Lisp.

The sweep phase touches the entire heap, which is slow on a large allocation. **Mark-and-compact** avoids that cost. After marking, it slides live objects together into one contiguous block, leaving the rest of the heap as a single free region. The dead objects vanish not by being freed one at a time but by being overwritten. Compaction also fixes fragmentation — the pockets of free space scattered between live objects that make new allocations fail even when total free bytes are sufficient. The JVM's serial and parallel collectors compact.

**Copying** collection takes compaction further. The heap is split into two halves, often called from-space and to-space. The program allocates only in from-space. When it fills, the collector copies every reachable object from from-space into to-space, packing them contiguously. Then it flips: to-space becomes the new from-space, and the old from-space is wiped clean in one move. Dead objects never get touched — they are simply overwritten on the next cycle. The cost is that half the heap is always unused. Young-generation collectors in the JVM, .NET, and V8 use copying, because most young objects die fast and the copy set is small.

**Reference counting** takes a different approach. Every object carries a count of pointers pointing to it. Assignment increments the target's count; overwriting or destroying a pointer decrements it. When the count hits zero, no pointer can reach the object, so the collector frees it immediately. CPython uses reference counting for every object. The weakness is cycles: two objects pointing at each other keep each other's count above zero even when nothing else points to either. CPython runs a separate tracing collector periodically to break cycles. Swift uses ARC — automatic reference counting — and pushes the problem to the programmer, who must declare weak or unowned references to break cycles by hand.

**Generational** collection exploits the observation that most objects die young. A program that allocates a million temporary strings and ten long-lived configuration objects will see the strings die within milliseconds and the configuration objects survive for the program's lifetime. The collector splits the heap into a young region and an old region. New allocations go to the young region, which is collected frequently and cheaply, usually by copying. Objects that survive several young-region collections get promoted to the old region, which is collected rarely. The JVM, .NET, and V8 are all generational. The gain is that the collector spends its time where the garbage is densest.

**Concurrent** collection tries to do this work while the program runs, rather than stopping it. The hard problem is mutation: while the collector traces the pointer graph, the program is rewriting pointers, potentially creating a path from a root to an object the collector already marked and will not visit again. The collector can miss that object and free it, corrupting the heap. The solutions involve write barriers — instructions the compiler inserts at every pointer write that tell the collector something changed, so it revisits the affected region. The JVM's G1 and ZGC, .NET's server GC, and Go's collector all run concurrently. Go's collector, in particular, is designed to keep stop-the-world pauses under a millisecond, trading some throughput to do it.

The collector finds unused memory by proving no path to it exists. Tracing walks the graph from the roots and frees what it never reached. Reference counting watches the pointer count and frees what hit zero. Every collector is a variation on one of those two strategies, and the variations trade pause time, throughput, and memory overhead against each other.

Okay, explain what a race condition is, with a concrete example, in plain register.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a counter. Both read it at 7, both add 1, both write 8. The counter should be 9. One increment is lost. The processor ran both reads before either write, and nothing forced the second thread to wait for the first to finish.

The name comes from the threads racing to complete a sequence. Thread A reads the counter, thread B reads the counter, thread A writes, thread B writes. The interleaving is legal at the hardware level — each instruction executes correctly — but the combined effect corrupts the data. Swap the order of the two reads and the answer comes out right. The bug is nondeterministic. It appears under heavy load, on machines with more cores, or when a thread is preempted at exactly the wrong moment. It disappears under a debugger, which changes the timing.

The counter example is the simplest case: a read-modify-write sequence interrupted between the read and the write. The same shape breaks larger operations. A transfer between two bank accounts reads the source balance, subtracts 100, reads the destination balance, adds 100, writes both. A second transfer running concurrently can read the source balance after the first subtracts but before the first writes, and the bank loses 100. The invariant — that the sum of the two balances stays constant — holds in each thread alone and breaks when the threads interleave.

The fix is to make the sequence atomic. A mutex around the read-modify-write forces one thread to finish before the next begins. The second thread reads the value the first wrote, not the stale value the first overwrote. The cost is that the threads serialize on the lock, but the answer is correct.

A race condition is not a deadlock. A deadlock is two threads each holding a resource the other needs, both stuck. A race condition is two threads both running, both writing, and the final state depending on which one wrote last.

Okay, explain how a CPU cache speeds up a program, in plain register.

A CPU cache is a small memory chip sitting between the processor core and main memory. It speeds up a program by storing copies of the bytes the processor is most likely to read next, so the core does not wait for the slow trip to RAM.

The speed gap is the problem. A modern processor core runs at roughly four gigahertz. DDR4 memory answers a request in about 60 nanoseconds, which is 240 clock cycles from the core's perspective. If every load went to RAM, the core would sit idle 99 percent of the time. The cache turns that 240-cycle wait into a four-cycle fetch for the most common case.

The cache works because programs do not read memory at random. They read addresses close to ones they just read, and they read the same addresses repeatedly. A loop summing an array touches element 0, then 1, then 2, in order. A function's local variables get read and written dozens of times in a few microseconds. The hardware bets on these two patterns, and it wins often enough to make the cache pay for itself.

The first pattern is spatial locality. When the processor requests a byte from RAM, the memory controller does not send just that byte. It sends a block of 64 contiguous bytes, called a cache line, and the cache stores the whole block. The next array element sits 8 bytes away, inside the same cache line, so the next read hits the cache instead of RAM. One 240-cycle fetch covers eight 64-bit integers.

The second pattern is temporal locality. The cache keeps recently used lines in fast storage. A loop variable read a thousand times in a thousand iterations stays in the cache, and every read after the first takes four cycles. The cache is small — a few tens of kilobytes on the fastest level — so it keeps only the most recent lines and discards the rest.

The cache is not one store but three, stacked by speed and size. The L1 cache sits on the processor core itself, holds about 32 kilobytes, and answers in four cycles. The L2 cache sits nearby, holds around 256 kilobytes, and answers in 12 cycles. The L3 cache is shared across all the cores on the chip, holds 8 to 32 megabytes, and answers in about 40 cycles. Main memory answers in 240. A load checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, then RAM. Each miss costs a longer wait, so the program runs at the speed of its hit rate.

The hardware manages all of this without the program's knowledge. The cache fills on every miss, evicts the oldest or least-used line when it needs space, and writes modified lines back to RAM on eviction. The program sees only the effect: the same load instruction takes four cycles or 240, depending on whether the address was touched recently.

The program's own behavior decides which. An array processed in element order hits the cache on every element after the first. The same array processed in random order misses on almost every element, because each 64-byte line holds eight elements but the access pattern jumps across lines. The cache line is the unit of memory the hardware moves, and the program's access pattern either fits that unit or fights it. A program that walks memory in order runs fast because the cache turns 240-cycle RAM reads into four-cycle hits. A program that jumps runs slow because it pays the 240 cycles on every access.

Okay, explain what idempotency means for an HTTP API, in plain register.

Idempotency means a client can send the same request twice and the server ends in the same state as if it were sent once. The second call does not duplicate the first call's effect.

`GET` is idempotent by definition. It reads a resource and changes nothing, so ten identical `GET` requests return the same representation and leave the server untouched. `PUT` is idempotent because it replaces a resource wholesale. A `PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada. Sending it a hundred times sets the name to Ada a hundred times. The final state is identical to the state after the first call.

`POST` is not idempotent. A `POST /orders` with the body `{"item": "book"}` creates a new order each time. Ten requests create ten orders. The server cannot tell whether the client retried because of a network failure or genuinely wants ten orders, so it does the work ten times. This is why payment endpoints double-charge when a connection drops after the server processes the request but before the response reaches the client.

`DELETE` is idempotent in the sense that matters. `DELETE /orders/99` removes order 99. The first call removes it. The second call finds nothing to remove and returns 404. The server's state after the second call — order 99 absent — matches the state after the first. The response differs, but idempotency is about state, not about the response body or status code.

The HTTP specification declares `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `HEAD` idempotent. It declares `POST` and `PATCH` non-idempotent. The spec describes what a correct implementation of each method does. It does not guarantee that a specific API honors that contract. A `DELETE /messages/last` that pops the most recent message off a queue is not idempotent: each call removes a different message. The method is idempotent in the spec's abstract sense, but the endpoint's behavior breaks the contract because the operation depends on state that the operation itself changes.

Retries are where idempotency earns its cost. A mobile client on a flaky cellular connection sends a `PUT`, the server applies it, the response is lost in a dropped packet, the client's retry logic sends the same `PUT` again. If the endpoint is idempotent, the retry is harmless. If it is not, the client and the server disagree about what happened. The same scenario with `POST` is the source of duplicate orders, duplicate payments, and duplicate account creations across every API that does not guard against it.

The fix for non-idempotent operations is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique token — a UUID — and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. On the second request with the same key, the server returns the stored result instead of running the operation again. Stripe's API uses this pattern on its charge and transfer endpoints. The key turns a non-idempotent `POST` into an idempotent operation by making the server remember what it already did. The cost is a lookup and a store on every request, and the need to garbage-collect keys after their retention window expires.

Okay, explain how DNS turns a name into an address, in plain register.

A browser asks for `www.example.com`. The operating system hands that name to a resolver, and the resolver comes back with an IP address like `93.184.216.34`. The work between those two events is the Domain Name System.

The resolver is usually a process run by the internet service provider or a public service like Google's `8.8.8.8` or Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1`. It does not know the answer. It knows where to find it.

The resolver starts at the root. The internet has thirteen root name servers, identified by the letters A through M. Each root server holds a list of the top-level domains — `com`, `org`, `net`, `uk`, `jp` — and the name servers responsible for each. The resolver picks a root server and asks: where do I find `com`?

The root answers with a referral. It does not resolve `www.example.com`. It gives the resolver the names and addresses of the `.com` name servers, which are operated by Verisign. The resolver caches that referral so it does not have to ask the root again for other `.com` names.

The resolver now asks a `.com` name server: where do I find `example.com`? The `.com` server holds records for every registered domain under `.com`. It answers with another referral, pointing to the name servers that host `example.com`'s DNS records. These are the authoritative servers — the ones run by the domain owner or their DNS provider, such as AWS Route 53 or Cloudflare.

The resolver asks the authoritative server for `example.com`: what is the address of `www.example.com`? The authoritative server holds the zone file, which is a list of records mapping names to values. It finds an A record for `www` and returns `93.184.216.34`. The resolver hands that address to the operating system, which hands it to the browser, and the browser opens a TCP connection to that address.

The whole walk — root, top-level domain, authoritative — takes three round trips on a cold cache. A resolver in New York asking a root server in Los Angeles, a `.com` server in Virginia, and an authoritative server in Dublin spends roughly 120 milliseconds in transit. Caching collapses that. The resolver stores every answer and every referral for a time-to-live specified in the record. The next request for any `.com` name skips the root. The next request for `www.example.com` returns from the resolver's cache in under a millisecond. The TTL is what lets DNS scale to eight billion queries a day without melting the root servers.

The system is hierarchical by design. The root delegates to `.com`, `.com` delegates to `example.com`, and `example.com` delegates to subdomains as it sees fit. Each layer answers only for the names it owns and points downward. No single server holds the whole map. The map is distributed across millions of name servers, and the resolver walks the tree one branch at a time until it reaches the leaf that holds the address.

A deadlock is two threads frozen forever, each holding a lock the other needs.

Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A waits for B. B waits for A. Neither moves. The program hangs.

Four conditions produce this. The threads hold locks exclusively — one thread per lock. They hold one lock while asking for another. The system does not force a timeout. And the lock order forms a circle: A wants 1 then 2, B wants 2 then 1. Break any circle and the deadlock dies.
