The fix is a lock ordering protocol. Every thread acquires mutexes in the same global order. If the rule is "lock 1 before 2," thread A locks 1 then 2, and thread B also locks 1 then 2. Thread B blocks at mutex 1 until A releases both. No circle forms. The cost is a thread sometimes waiting for a lock it could have taken, trading some concurrency for the guarantee that the system never freezes.

A hash map turns a key into an integer, then uses that integer as an index into an array. The hash function spreads keys across the array's slots, but two different keys can produce the same index. That is a collision, and every hash map has to decide what happens next.

The oldest method is chaining. Each slot in the array holds the head of a linked list. When a key lands on a slot already occupied, the new entry joins the list. Lookup walks the list, comparing keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The cost grows with list length. If every key hashed to the same slot, the map degrades to a linear search through one list. Java's `HashMap` and C++'s `std::unordered_map` both chain.

Open addressing takes the other road. There is no list. The entry lives in the array itself. When a key's slot is taken, the map probes neighboring slots according to a fixed rule until it finds an empty one. Linear probing checks the next slot, then the next. Quadratic probing jumps by squares. Double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size. Lookup follows the same probe sequence; deletion is harder because removing an entry outright would break the chain, so the slot is marked with a tombstone that a later insert can reclaim. Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Rust's `HashMap` all use open addressing.

The choice turns on memory and cache behavior. Chaining allocates a node per entry, which costs a pointer and a heap allocation. Open addressing stores entries inline in the array, so a probe sequence stays in contiguous memory and the CPU's cache lines pull in several entries at once. That locality is why modern implementations lean toward open addressing. The tradeoff is fragility under high load: as the array fills, probe sequences lengthen fast, and performance collapses near full capacity.

Both methods rely on resizing to stay efficient. The map tracks a load factor — the ratio of entries to slots. When the ratio crosses a threshold, the map allocates a larger array and reinserts every entry, which gives each key a fresh chance to land in an empty slot. Java resizes at 0.75. Python resizes at two-thirds. The rehash is O(n), but it amortizes to O(1) per insert across the map's lifetime because it happens rarely relative to the number of operations.

A third method, perfect hashing, avoids collisions entirely but only when the full set of keys is known in advance. It builds a two-level hash structure that maps each key to a unique slot with no probing and no lists. The cost is construction time and the inability to add unknown keys later. It fits static dictionaries — keyword tables in a compiler, routing tables fixed at build time — not general-purpose maps.

A database index is a second data structure stored alongside a table to make lookups fast without scanning every row. The most common form is a B-tree, which keeps sorted keys paired with pointers to the rows they came from. A query against a million-row table for `users.email = 'x@y.com'` reads a handful of B-tree pages instead of all million rows, turning an O(n) scan into an O(log n) descent.

Indexes hurt in three specific ways.

They cost storage. Every index duplicates the key columns plus row pointers. An index on a wide text column can approach the size of the table itself. A table with five indexes can need three times the disk of the unindexed table.

They slow writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` that touches an indexed column must update every index on that column in the same transaction. A table with six indexes takes roughly six times longer to insert into than the heap alone. On a write-heavy workload — event logging, telemetry ingestion, order book updates — this is the dominant cost.

They can be ignored. A query planner skips an index when it estimates the index will return a large fraction of the table, because random I/O through the index plus the row fetch is slower than a sequential scan. An index on a column with two values across a million rows, where the query asks for the common value, gets bypassed. The index sits there consuming space and slowing writes while doing no read work at all. The same happens when the query wraps the column in a function — `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x'` cannot use a plain index on `email`; it needs a functional index on `LOWER(email)`, or in Postgres a `text_pattern_ops` index for prefix `LIKE`.

The rule is workload, not table. An index earns its place when it serves queries that run often and return few rows relative to the table. It is dead weight when it serves rare queries, when it sits on low-cardinality columns, or when the table takes far more writes than the queries the index accelerates. Dropping an unused index is pure gain: writes get faster, storage shrinks, and no read path changes.

TCP sends data as a stream of numbered bytes, not as discrete messages. Every byte gets a sequence number from the sender, and the receiver uses those numbers to put the bytes back in the order they were sent.

The handshake sets the starting point. The client picks an initial sequence number and sends it in the SYN packet. The server acknowledges that number and sends its own. When the handshake finishes, both sides know where the other's byte count begins.

Each data segment carries the sequence number of its first byte. A segment carrying bytes 1000 through 1099 arrives with sequence number 1000. The receiver hands the bytes to the application in sequence order, holding any that arrive early in a buffer until the gap fills.

Loss is where the numbering earns its cost. If bytes 1000 through 1099 are lost but 1100 through 1199 arrive, the receiver stores 1100 through 1199 and sends back an acknowledgment for 1000 — the next byte it expects. That duplicate ACK tells the sender that everything before 1000 arrived and 1000 did not. The sender retransmits the missing segment. When it lands, the receiver releases the held 1100 through 1199 along with it, and the application sees an unbroken stream.

The acknowledgment is cumulative. An ACK for 1200 means every byte up to 1199 has arrived in order, regardless of how many segments carried those bytes or what order they arrived in. The receiver never acknowledges a gap. This is why a single ACK can cover a burst of segments and why a lost ACK does not always force a retransmission — a later ACK for a higher number covers the same ground.

Out-of-order arrival is routine. Packets take different routes through the network, and a later segment can beat an earlier one to the destination. The sequence numbers let the receiver detect this, buffer the early arrival, and reassemble the stream without the sender doing anything. The sender only learns about disorder when it sees duplicate ACKs, and it acts on them only when the disorder signals a loss worth retransmitting.

The sequence space is finite — 32 bits for the number, wrapping after roughly 4.3 billion bytes — but the protocol treats it as a circle. Both sides track where they are in that circle, and the wraparound is handled by modular arithmetic and window sizing that keeps old and new sequence numbers from colliding. A connection sending data at high speed wraps the counter in seconds; the protocol is built for that.

A mutex protects one thing: the interleaving of operations on shared state.

Two threads running on two cores can both touch the same memory in the same instant. A counter incremented by two threads at once can lose one of the increments. The read-modify-write is not atomic on its own: thread A reads 5, thread B reads 5, both write 6, and one increment is gone. A list being traversed by one thread while another thread inserts a node can crash the traversal or corrupt the list's pointers. A buffer being filled by a producer and drained by a consumer can hand out garbage if the read and write cross.

The mutex fixes this by making a section of code run as if no other thread were running it at the same time. A thread acquires the mutex before entering the section and releases it on the way out. While one thread holds the mutex, every other thread that tries to acquire it blocks — it stops running and waits. The operating system or the runtime puts the blocked thread to sleep and wakes it when the mutex is released. The protected section, called the critical section, runs one thread at a time, and the shared state inside it stays consistent.

What a mutex does not protect is everything outside the section. If a thread reads a shared variable without holding the mutex, it can see a half-written value or a stale cache. If two threads lock different mutexes for the same variable, neither mutex excludes the other. If a thread holds the mutex while calling code that tries to acquire it again, the thread deadlocks against itself — this is why most mutexes are not reentrant by default, and why the non-reentrant variant is the safer choice.

A mutex also does not protect against the compiler and the CPU reordering memory accesses. A write to a flag that signals "data is ready" can become visible to another thread before the write to the data itself, because the compiler reordered the stores or the CPU wrote them out of program order. The mutex prevents this too, but only at its boundaries: acquiring a mutex issues a memory barrier that flushes prior writes and invalidates stale reads, and releasing it issues a barrier that pushes the section's writes out to memory. Code that shares state without a mutex — using a bare flag, a volatile variable, or a lock-free queue — must supply its own barriers or use atomic operations with the right ordering, or it will break on a weakly-ordered architecture like ARM.

The cost is contention. When two threads want the same mutex, one waits. The wait is not busy-spinning in most implementations; it is a context switch, which costs microseconds and hands the CPU to another thread. A mutex held for a millisecond under heavy contention can serialize a workload that would otherwise run in parallel, turning eight cores into one. The discipline is to hold the mutex for the shortest distance that covers the shared access and no longer — not across a disk read, not across a network call, not across a computation that does not touch shared state.

A mutex is the simplest lock. It excludes one thread at a time. A read-write lock relaxes this: it lets any number of readers through simultaneously and excludes them only for a writer. A semaphore is a counter that admits N threads at once. A condition variable lets a thread release the mutex and sleep until another thread signals that the waited-for state has arrived. Each of these solves a specific coordination problem that a plain mutex would handle correctly but slowly.

Garbage collection finds memory that a program can no longer reach and returns it to the allocator. The core insight is that an object is dead when nothing alive still points to it.

Tracing collectors start from the roots — the registers, the stack frames, and the global variables that the running code can touch directly. From those roots, the collector walks every pointer it can find, marking each object it reaches. Anything unmarked at the end of the walk is garbage. This is mark-and-sweep, the scheme McCarthy described in 1960. The mark phase traces the live graph; the sweep phase walks the heap and frees everything that carries no mark.

The walk must pause the program's threads, because the graph of live pointers changes while the program runs. A collector that stops every thread for the whole trace is a stop-the-world collector. The pause length grows with the number of live objects, which is why tracing collectors spent decades chasing shorter pauses.

Generational collection cuts the work by exploiting one observed fact: most objects die young. The heap is split into a young region and an old region. New allocations go to the young region. A collection of just the young region is cheap because it holds few survivors, and it runs often. Objects that survive several young collections graduate to the old region, which the collector scans rarely. The JVM's G1 and the .NET CLR both organize their heaps this way.

Concurrent collection moves the trace off the application's threads. The collector marks objects while the program runs, which means it must handle the case where the program changes a pointer the collector has already visited. Read and write barriers are the mechanism: a barrier is a small piece of code the runtime inserts around pointer reads or writes, and it records the change so the collector can fix its accounting. The trade is throughput for pause length — the barriers cost cycles on every pointer operation, but the pauses shrink from hundreds of milliseconds to single digits.

Reference counting takes a different road. Every object carries a count of how many pointers refer to it. A pointer is assigned, the count rises. A pointer is dropped, the count falls. At zero, the object is dead and can be freed at once, with no trace. The cost is paid on every assignment rather than in batches, and the scheme cannot see cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other's count above zero forever. A pure reference counter needs a separate cycle collector to find those loops. CPython uses reference counting plus a tracing collector that runs periodically to break cycles. Swift's ARC and C++'s `shared_ptr` use reference counting alone and push the cycle problem onto the programmer.

Copying collection turns the sweep into a compaction. The heap is split into two halves. The program allocates in one half. At collection time, the collector copies every live object from the active half into the empty half, packing them contiguously, and leaves the dead ones behind. The two halves swap roles. Allocation is then bumping a pointer into free space, which is as fast as allocation gets. The cost is that the program can use only half the heap at a time, and copying large live objects is expensive. Young generations in generational collectors are usually copying, because young regions have few survivors and the copy is cheap.

The collector's job is to approximate the question "will this object ever be used again?" with the answerable question "can this object be reached from the roots?" The second is conservative: an object that is reachable but never touched again stays alive and holds its memory. A program that caches aggressively or holds long-lived references in static fields will keep that memory pinned regardless of which collector is running. The collector cannot reclaim what the program's own structure keeps visible.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the order in which two operations run, and that order is not controlled.

Two threads share a bank balance. Both read 100. Thread A adds 50, writes 150. Thread B subtracts 30, writes 70. The balance should be 120. It is 70. One update overwrote the other because the read and the write were not one operation. The threads raced for the same memory, and the loser's write erased the winner's.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write indivisible. A mutex around the balance update forces the threads through one at a time. Thread A reads 100, adds 50, writes 150, releases. Thread B reads 150, subtracts 30, writes 120. The answer is correct because the operations no longer interleave.

Races do not require threads. A signal handler that increments a counter while the main program reads it races against that program. A JavaScript callback that mutates an array while a loop iterates it races against that loop. The shared element is concurrent access to the same state without ordering.

The symptom is nondeterminism. The program produces a different result each run, or fails under load but passes in a test harness, or corrupts data once in ten thousand operations. The bug is real every time, but it surfaces only when the scheduler interleaves the threads in the losing order. That rarity is what makes races hard to reproduce and hard to fix by trial. The code is wrong on every execution; the hardware just does not always show it.

A CPU cache is a small amount of fast memory sitting between the processor and main memory. It speeds up a program by keeping the data the processor is most likely to touch next close enough that the processor does not have to wait for main memory.

The speed gap is the reason the cache exists. A modern processor can execute several instructions per nanosecond. A request to main memory takes 60 to 100 nanoseconds to come back. That is a hundred-cycle gap the processor would spend idle. The cache closes it. A hit in the L1 cache returns in one or two cycles. L2 takes roughly 14. L3 takes 30 to 40. The hierarchy exists because faster memory is smaller and more expensive, so the design layers it: a tiny L1 close to each core, a larger L2 beside it, a shared L3 across the cores, and main memory at the bottom.

The cache exploits a property called locality. Temporal locality is the tendency of a program to touch the same address again soon — a loop counter, a stack variable, a field read in a tight loop. Spatial locality is the tendency to touch nearby addresses soon — walking an array, reading consecutive fields from a struct. The cache uses both. On a load, it pulls in not just the requested byte but a whole block, called a cache line, usually 64 bytes. If the next load hits the same line, the data is already there.

A cache line is the unit of transfer between cache and memory. When the processor requests an address, the cache checks whether the line holding that address is present. If it is, the data returns at cache speed. If it is not, the cache fetches the line from the next level down, which may fetch from the level below that. The line arrives, is stored in the cache, and the requested bytes are handed to the processor. The eviction policy decides which existing line leaves to make room. Most caches use least-recently-used, which bets that a line untouched for a long time will stay untouched.

The performance gain comes from the hit rate. A program whose working set fits in L1 and accesses memory sequentially can see hit rates above 95 percent, which means most loads return in one cycle. A program that jumps through memory at random addresses — chasing pointers through a linked list, probing a hash table with poor locality — misses often. Each miss costs the full latency of the level it has to reach. A workload that misses to main memory on half its loads spends more time waiting for memory than executing instructions. The cache does not speed up that program. The program's access pattern defeats it.

This is why array traversal is fast and linked-list traversal is slow on the same data. A contiguous array packs neighboring elements into the same cache lines, so walking it produces one miss per line and the rest are hits. A linked list allocates each node separately, so each `next` pointer jumps to a new address, and each jump is likely a miss. The algorithmic complexity is the same — O(n) — but the constant factor differs by an order of magnitude because one pattern feeds the cache and the other starves it.

The cache also makes writes faster. A store writes to the cache, not to main memory, and the cache writes the line back to memory later, when the line is evicted or when another processor asks for it. This batches writes and lets the processor continue without waiting for main memory to acknowledge each one. Multi-core systems add a coherence protocol — MESI is the common one — that tracks which cache holds the current version of each line and invalidates stale copies in other cores' caches before a write goes through. The protocol keeps the caches consistent, and its cost is why false sharing hurts: two cores writing to different variables that happen to share a cache line force each other to invalidate and reload, even though the variables are unrelated.

The cache is invisible to the program's logic but decisive for its speed. The same algorithm can run ten times faster or ten times slower depending on whether its memory pattern gives the cache lines it can hold or lines it has to fetch.

Idempotency in an HTTP API means a client can send the same request twice and the server's observable state ends up the same as if it were sent once.

`GET` is idempotent by nature: it reads data and changes nothing, so the tenth call leaves the database identical to the first. `PUT` is idempotent by contract: a `PUT /users/42` with the body `{"name": "Ada"}` sets user 42's name to Ada, and repeating the call a hundred times still produces one user named Ada. `DELETE` is idempotent in the sense that matters: `DELETE /users/42` removes user 42, and a second call finds no user 42 and removes nothing, leaving the state unchanged.

`POST` is the method that breaks this. A `POST /orders` with the body `{"item": "book"}` creates a new order each time it arrives. Ten calls produce ten orders. The method is defined as non-idempotent, and servers treat it that way: proxies do not retry a `POST` automatically the way they retry a failed `GET` or `PUT`.

The practical value is recovery from network failure. A client sends `PUT /users/42`, the server applies the update, the response is lost on the way back, and the client does not know whether the request landed. An idempotent method lets the client resend without risk. The second `PUT` overwrites the first, the state is correct, and no duplicate exists. A non-idempotent method forces the client to guess or to build a separate deduplication layer.

Idempotency is a property of the method's effect on state, not of the response body. A `GET /timestamp` returns a different value each call, but it is idempotent because it writes nothing. A `DELETE` on an already-deleted resource returns `404` on the second call, but the resource state — absent — is the same as after the first call. The HTTP specification defines idempotency in terms of the side effect, not the payload.

Real APIs sometimes need idempotency where the method does not provide it. A payments service that accepts `POST /charges` cannot afford to create a second charge if the first request timed out. The common fix is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique token in a header, the server records the token with the first request's result, and a second request bearing the same token returns the stored result instead of running the operation again. Stripe's `Idempotency-Key` header works this way. The method stays `POST`, but the key gives it the safety of `PUT`.

The distinction that matters for an API designer is whether a repeated request is safe. Safe means a duplicate does no harm. Idempotent methods are safe to retry. `POST` is not, and the burden of making it safe falls on the application, not the protocol.

DNS turns a name into an address by walking a tree of servers, each one answering a smaller piece of the question.

The browser asks the resolver. The resolver is the first stop, usually a machine run by the ISP or a public service like Google's 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1. The resolver does not know the answer, but it knows where to start.

The start is the root. The root servers hold the addresses of the top-level domain servers. A query for `www.example.com` sends the resolver to the root, and the root answers with the address of the server for `.com`.

The resolver asks the `.com` server. The `.com` server holds the addresses of the name servers for every domain under `.com`. It answers with the address of `example.com`'s name servers.

The resolver asks `example.com`'s name server. That server holds the actual records for the domain. It finds the A record for `www`, which carries the IPv4 address — say, `93.184.216.34` — and returns it. The resolver hands the address to the browser and caches the answer for the time the record's TTL allows.

The walk is four questions and four answers: resolver to root, root to `.com`, `.com` to `example.com`, `example.com` to the address. Each step narrows the question. The root never holds `www.example.com`; it holds the delegation for `.com`. The `.com` server never holds `www`; it holds the delegation for `example.com`. Only the authoritative server for the domain holds the record itself.

Caching shortens the walk. The resolver caches every answer it receives. A second request for `www.example.com` within the TTL returns from the resolver's cache without contacting any server upstream. The browser and the operating system also keep their own caches, so a repeated lookup may never reach the resolver at all. The cost of the full walk is paid once, then amortized across every request until the TTL expires.

The system is recursive from the client's view and iterative from the resolver's. The browser asks the resolver one question and waits. The resolver does the walking, asking one server at a time and following the chain. The client never sees the root or the `.com` server; it sees only the resolver, which returns the final address or an error.

The records carry more than addresses. An A record maps a name to IPv4. An AAAA record maps to IPv6. A CNAME record maps one name to another, which sends the resolver off to resolve the target from the start. An MX record names the mail server for a domain. The query type tells the resolver what to ask for, and the walk is the same.

The system's weakness is the unencrypted query. A traditional DNS request travels over UDP port 53 in plaintext. A network observer between the client and the resolver can read every name the client looks up. DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS wrap the query in an encrypted transport, closing that window. The resolver still walks the chain upstream in the clear unless it uses a protocol like DNS over TLS toward the authoritative servers, which most do not. The privacy ends at the resolver's front door.

A deadlock is a state where two threads each hold a resource the other needs, and neither will give up what it holds. Both wait forever. The program stops making progress on those threads, and no error fires.

The classic shape is the dining philosophers. Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks, one between each pair. Each needs two forks to eat. If every philosopher picks up the fork on their left at the same instant, every fork is held, and no philosopher can pick up a second. Each waits for a neighbor to put a fork down. No one does. They starve.

The same shape appears in code. Thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. A holds 1 and waits for 2. B holds 2 and waits for 1. Neither moves. The condition is circular wait: a cycle in the graph of threads holding and requesting locks.

Four conditions must hold at once for a deadlock to exist. Mutual exclusion: a resource belongs to one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread holding one resource can ask for another. No preemption: a held resource cannot be taken by force. Circular wait: a cycle of threads each waiting for the next one's resource. Break any one and deadlocks become impossible.

The simplest way to break the cycle is a lock ordering. Every thread acquires the mutexes in the same global order. If mutex 1 must be acquired before mutex 2, then thread A locks 1 then 2, and thread B locks 1 then 2. Thread B cannot hold 2 while waiting for 1, because it never acquires 2 until it has 1. The cycle cannot form. The wait graph stays a straight line.

The cost is discipline. Any code path that locks two mutexes must know the order, and a violation anywhere reintroduces the deadlock. A thread that locks mutex 5, then calls a function that locks mutex 3, has broken the order if 3 ranks below 5. The ordering must be documented, and the call graph must be audited against it. Lock hierarchies work when the set of locks is small and fixed. They break down when a library hands back a lock it acquired internally, or when a callback acquires a lock the caller did not expect.

A second approach is to acquire all locks atomically. Lock mutex 1 and mutex 2 together, or not at all. If a thread cannot get both, it releases the one it holds and tries again. This eliminates hold-and-wait, the second condition. The cost is livelock: two threads can each grab and release the same mutexes in lockstep, never making progress, never deadlocking either. The fix is a random backoff before retrying, which breaks the symmetry.

A third is to avoid waiting at all. `try_lock` returns immediately if the mutex is held. A thread that fails to acquire a second lock releases the first, does something else, or backs off. This trades blocking for retry logic, and it works when the contested window is short and the retry is cheap.

The dining philosophers have a specific fix under lock ordering: number the forks, and have each philosopher pick up the lower-numbered fork first. Four philosophers pick up fork 1, then fork 2, or fork 2 then fork 3, and so on. The fifth philosopher — sitting between fork 1 and fork 5 — picks up fork 1 first, then fork 5. That philosopher reaches across the table for the lowest-numbered fork, breaking the symmetry. The cycle cannot close. Everyone eats.
